title: Thomas Quarry hominins (~773 ka) basal to the Homo sapiens lineage
claim: Hominin fossils from Thomas Quarry I (Casablanca, Morocco), dated to approximately 773,000 years ago, are basal to the Homo sapiens lineage and push the African origin of the last common ancestor of humans and Neanderthals to the older end of the genetic split estimates — with northwest Africa now central to the deep-roots story, linked to other African regions by population movement across the Sahara during wetter phases.
place: Thomas Quarry I, Casablanca, Morocco

title: Tromerosaurus solumons — the mosaic tyrannosaur (Oldman Formation, 2026)
claim: A new tyrannosaurid genus and species, Tromerosaurus solumons, described October 2026 from a partial skeleton excavated in 2010–2011 from the Upper Cretaceous Oldman Formation of Alberta (~76 Ma, Campanian), mixes features of both major tyrannosaurid subfamilies — a mosaic of gracile albertosaurine and robust tyrannosaurine characters — and supports a younger divergence of the two lineages with rapid character acquisition during the Late Cretaceous (Santonian–Maastrichtian). The description also reassigns the 'largest adult Gorgosaurus' specimen to Tromerosaurus.
place: Oldman Formation, Alberta, Canada (exposures associated with the upper Oldman Formation; exact locality in the describing paper)

title: The first adult T. rex trackway — Hell Creek, North Dakota, described 2026
claim: A peer-reviewed study published in September 2026 in the Journal of Vertebrate Paleontology (DOI 10.1080/02724634.2026.2706201) (Falkingham, Hups, Tamez-Galvan, Bercovici & Lyson) formally describes 'a large tridactyl trackway from the Upper Cretaceous Hell Creek Formation of North Dakota, likely attributable to an adult Tyrannosaurus rex' — the first known multi-step adult tyrannosaur trackway: four consecutive three-toed prints (left-right-left-right) across ~7 m (23 ft), each print ~1 m long and 0.6–0.8 m wide, stride ~4 m (13 ft), yielding an estimated walking speed of ~3.5–4.5 mph (5.6–7.2 km/h). The prints were found in July 2025 by Colorado high-school science teacher Kent M. Hups (volunteer research associate, Denver Museum of Nature & Science) on Dakota Prairie Grasslands ~2.5 miles northwest of Marmarth, ND, ~33 m below the top of the Hell Creek Formation (~66.5 Ma). High-resolution 3D surface scans were analyzed by lead author Peter Falkingham in England via computer and VR; three exposed prints were scheduled for helicopter removal to the Denver Museum of Nature & Science in autumn 2026. Trackmaker attribution rests on size, narrow-elongate toe shape (theropod, not the broad-toed Edmontosaurus, the only other Hell Creek animal that big), location, and the local abundance of adult T. rex remains; the authors' own wording is 'likely attributable' and the measurements are presented as approximate because the impressions are strongly weathered.
place: Hell Creek Formation near Marmarth, southwestern North Dakota (Dakota Prairie Grasslands)

title: The K-Pg boundary's microfossil witness: the planktic foraminiferal turnover and the <2,000-year recovery
claim: The planktic foraminiferal turnover at the K-Pg boundary is the extinction's highest-resolution fossil witness. Cretaceous planktic foraminifera vanish at the boundary horizon worldwide, and the first new Paleocene species — Parvularugoglobigerina eugubina, the base of Biochron P0 — appear within thousands of years of the impact: Lowery et al. 2026's 3He recalibration at six boundary sites gives Biochron P0 a duration of 3.5–11.1 kyr (average 6.4 kyr) and puts the first new species under 2,000 years after the Chicxulub impact — replacing the long-accepted ~30 kyr estimate that assumed constant sedimentation across the boundary. The selectivity is real and mechanistic: Rui Ying et al. 2026's EcoGENIE model of the first 100 post-impact years reproduces the fossil pattern — large forams and zooplankton die, small phytoplankton and mixotrophs survive — with impact-driven darkness plus body-size-dependent extinction thresholds doing the work.
place: K-Pg boundary global — stratotype El Kef, Tunisia (plus the six 2026 3He sites spanning Europe, North Africa, the Gulf of Mexico)

title: The rock that fell: end-Cretaceous extinction
claim: 66.04 million years ago an asteroid 10–15 km wide struck Chicxulub (Yucatan, 21.40°N 89.52°W), ending the non-avian dinosaurs and ~75% of species. Ruthenium isotopes (Fischer-Gödde et al. 2024) identify a carbonaceous-type impactor from beyond Jupiter; nickel isotopes (Makhatadze et al. 2026) narrow it to a CO (Ornans-class) chondrite. The kill-mechanism evidence has shifted from sulfur aerosols toward fine silicate dust (Senel et al. 2023; Johnson et al. 2026). Deccan Traps volcanism is the main competing cause (Keller camp, 2025 book) — current peer-reviewed consensus holds the impact as the trigger and main driver, Deccan a contributing stressor.
place: Chicxulub, Yucatan Peninsula, Mexico

title: Infernogallus jamesi — the 'hell chicken' and its first complete skull (Hell Creek, 2026)
claim: A new caenagnathid species, Infernogallus jamesi ('hell chicken'), described in Nature Communications 2026 from the Hell Creek Formation (~66 Ma), preserves the first nearly complete skull ever found for the caenagnathid group of toothless, beaked, birdlike theropods — a 26-pound (12-kg) turkey-sized animal whose jaw mechanics point toward a fruit-eating diet, widening the documented dietary range of late-Cretaceous feathered dinosaurs at the K-Pg boundary.
place: Hell Creek Formation, Montana / South Dakota / North Dakota

title: The Cambrian explosion: the fossil record's rapid animal diversification, ~541–520 Ma
claim: The fossil record shows a geologically rapid diversification of animal body plans in the early Cambrian, ~541–520 million years ago: most animal phyla first appear in Cambrian strata, preserved in exceptional soft-bodied detail across multiple independent localities worldwide — the Burgess Shale (Canada, 1909, ~508 Ma), Chengjiang (China, 1984, ~518 Ma), Sirius Passet (North Greenland, ~518 Ma), Doushantuo/Weng'an (China), and now the Huayuan biota (China, 2026, ~512 Ma, post-Sinsk extinction). The Cambrian base is fixed at the Fortunian GSSP, Fortune Head, Newfoundland (541 Ma). The small shelly fossils mark the boundary interval. The 'explosion' is a fossil-record pattern; whether it was a biological radiation or a taphonomic unveiling is the live dispute.
place: Fortune Head, Newfoundland (Fortunian GSSP); the Lagerstätten span Canada, China, Greenland

title: Yujingia glutenotunica (2026): the tentacled ancestor that killed the burrowing-worm reading
claim: The 2026 Current Biology paper by Kaiyue He, Degan Shu, Graham Mussini and colleagues describes Yujingia glutenotunica, a ~518-million-year-old fossil from the Maotianshan Shales (Yunnan, China — the Chengjiang biota), interpreted as close to the last common ancestor of the ambulacrarians (modern starfish, sea urchins, and acorn worms). The 8–22 mm animal carried two sets of appendages: feather-like feeding tentacles that captured suspended particles, and a second set for temporary seabed anchoring — an active particle-feeding lifestyle. The paper's central argument: this contradicts the long-standing hypothesis that the ambulacrarian common ancestor was a burrowing worm that filtered food through its throat and gill openings. The authors (incl. Degan Shu, Northwest University) frame it as evidence that ecology — the chordate branch streamlining for movement, the ambulacrarian branch anchoring and specializing for particle feeding — drove the two deuterostome lineages onto divergent body plans.
place: Maotianshan Shales, Yunnan Province, China (Chengjiang biota)

title: Herugavialis cairensis (2026) — the crocodile in the Sphinx's stone
claim: A new genus of ancient crocodile, Herugavialis cairensis, was identified in 2026 from fossils in the Mokattam Formation — the same Middle Eocene (~45 million-year-old) limestone from which the Great Sphinx of Giza was carved. The reclassification (Burke et al., Royal Society Open Science, 7 Oct 2026) moves a 1920s skull (Müller 1927, 'Tomistoma cairense') into its own genus via CT re-analysis; the genus name honors Heru (Horus), after the coincidence that the skull — like the Sphinx — is missing the tip of its snout.
place: Gebel Mokattam, east of Cairo, Egypt (the formation the Sphinx was carved from)

title: The contested Nuvvuagittuq microfossils
claim: Hematite tubes, filaments, and knobs in jasper of the Nuvvuagittuq Supracrustal Belt (Quebec) are microfossils of iron-metabolizing bacteria that lived 3.77–4.28 billion years ago near seafloor hydrothermal vents.
place: Nuvvuagittuq Supracrustal Belt, northern Quebec (Hudson Bay east coast)

title: The oldest rocks on Earth — Nuvvuagittuq at 4.16 Ga (the clock, not the fossil)
claim: The Nuvvuagittuq Supracrustal Belt (northern Quebec) contains the oldest dated rocks on Earth: crosscutting intrusions dated to 4.16 billion years by two independent samarium–neodymium chronometers (O'Neil et al., Science, June 2025), making this the only known intact rock record of the Hadean eon.
place: Nuvvuagittuq Supracrustal Belt, Hudson Bay east coast near Inukjuak, Quebec

title: The contested 3.7 Ga Isua 'stromatolites'
claim: The cone-shaped structures in the 3.7-billion-year-old Isua Greenstone Belt (southwest Greenland) are fossilized microbial stromatolites — life on Earth by 3.7 Ga.
place: Isua supracrustal belt, southwestern Greenland

title: Homo sapiens emerged ~300,000 years ago in Africa
claim: The earliest fossils attributed to Homo sapiens are the Jebel Irhoud (Morocco) remains, dated 315 ± 34 thousand years ago by thermoluminescence — a mosaic of modern facial morphology with an archaic elongated braincase; the evidence now supports a pan-African, gradual emergence rather than a single ~200 ka East African origin.
place: Jebel Irhoud, Morocco (west of Marrakech)

title: The Bhitardari chert — the oldest directly dated rock with a confirmed biosignature (3.497 Ga)
claim: A carbonaceous chert at Bhitardari (Singhbhum Craton, eastern India) dated 3.497 ± 5 Ma by syn-depositional tuffaceous zircons contains laminated kerogen with biological carbon-isotope depletion (d13C -30.9 per mil) and Raman-confirmed indigenous organics — the tightest radiometric life–age link at ~3.5 Ga.
place: Bhitardari, Singhbhum Craton, eastern India

title: The Apex chert 'microfossils' are pseudofossils — the 2026 resolution
claim: The filamentous carbon-rich microstructures of the ~3.465 Ga Apex chert (Warrawoona Group, Pilbara, Western Australia), identified by Schopf (1993) as fossil cyanobacteria — until recently accepted as the oldest morphological evidence of life on Earth — are pseudofossils: reorganized carbonaceous matter in hydrothermal chert, not cells.
place: Apex chert, near Marble Bar, Pilbara, Western Australia

title: The most widely accepted fossil evidence of life
claim: The oldest widely accepted fossil evidence of life on Earth is the stromatolite reef of the Strelley Pool Chert, Pilbara, Western Australia — layered structures built by microbial communities ~3.43 billion years ago.
place: Strelley Pool Chert, East Pilbara, Western Australia

title: Musango matusadonaensis — Zimbabwe's fifth dinosaur, and the end of the homogeneous southern fauna
claim: A new early sauropodomorph dinosaur species, Musango matusadonaensis, described in 2026 from a partial associated skeleton found on the southern margin of Lake Kariba, Zimbabwe, shows that Late Triassic southern Africa held distinct regional dinosaur communities rather than one homogeneous fauna — a fifth dinosaur named from Zimbabwe, living ~210 million years ago while dinosaurs were diversifying toward Jurassic dominance.
place: Musango Archosaur Site, southern margin of Lake Kariba, Zimbabwe — Pebbly Arkose Formation (approximate regional pin, southern shore)

title: Drimolen Homo erectus DNH 127 (2026)
claim: In September 2026, a La Trobe-led team published 18 new hominin fossils from Drimolen Main Quarry, South Africa — including DNH 127, the first adult Homo erectus cranial fossil from the site — confirming the species' first appearance in southern Africa at 2.0 million years ago, ~200,000 years earlier than the Dmanisi adults; the same paper documents microevolutionary change in co-occurring Paranthropus robustus (larger teeth and chewing muscles between 2.0 and 1.8 Ma), supporting the subspecies P. robustus ukusa.
place: Drimolen Main Quarry, Cradle of Humankind, Gauteng, South Africa

title: Brontosaurus excelsus — the thunder lizard
claim: Brontosaurus excelsus — the 'thunder lizard' — was a real Late Jurassic sauropod. Othniel Charles Marsh named the species in 1879 from a partial skeleton (type specimen YPM 1980) found at Como Bluff, Wyoming, during the Bone Wars. In 1903 Elmer Riggs sank Brontosaurus into Apatosaurus on the principle of taxonomic priority (Marsh had named Apatosaurus ajax first, in 1877), so the name sat unused for 112 years. In 2015, a ~300-page peer-reviewed revision of Diplodocidae (Tschopp, Mateus & Benson, PeerJ 3:e857, 7 April 2015) — 477 morphological characters scored across 81 specimens — found Brontosaurus distinct enough to stand as its own genus again, with three species: B. excelsus, B. parvus, and B. yahnahpin.
place: Como Bluff, Wyoming — type locality (Morrison Formation)

title: Dragon Man identified as Denisovan (2025 molecular work)
claim: The Harbin ('Dragon Man') cranium — a Middle Pleistocene skull with thick brow ridges, a roomy braincase, and cheeks between Neanderthal ruggedness and modern delicacy — has been identified as a Denisovan individual: mitochondrial DNA recovered from its dental calculus (maternal line) matched Denisovans from Denisova Cave, and 95 ancient proteins from the petrous bone (19,299 peptides) placed it with Denisovans at 98–100% statistical support, with three Denisovan-associated amino-acid variants (one high-confidence). After 15 years as a genome without a face, the Denisovans have a skull.
place: Harbin, Heilongjiang, China (cranium found 1933, described 2021)

title: Birds are living theropod dinosaurs
claim: Birds are not merely descended from dinosaurs — they are theropod dinosaurs, the one dinosaur lineage to survive the K-Pg extinction. Feathered non-avian theropods (Sinosauropteryx 1996 onward, scores of Liaoning taxa, Norellraptor barsboldi 2026) plus skeletal synapomorphies (furcula, three-fingered manus, hollow thin-walled bones, semi-lunate carpal, brooding posture, air-sac pneumaticity) make the dinosaur–bird link a scientific consensus.
place: Liaoning Province, China (feathered theropod beds)

title: Yuezhuornis yangyuanensis (2026) — the runner-bird
claim: In October 2026, paleontologists described Yuezhuornis yangyuanensis, a crow-sized Jurassic bird (~150 Ma) from Fujian, China, with undersized wings suggesting it was more runner than flier — complicating the paradigm that the early avian body plan evolved almost exclusively under selection for flight (Wang et al., Nature, Oct 2026).
place: Fujian Province, southeastern China

title: Yuezhuornis yangyuanensis — the Jurassic flightless bird
claim: A crow-sized (~800 g) avialan from the Zhenghe Fauna of Fujian, China (~148-150 Ma, Late Jurassic), described October 2026 (Xu, Wang, Lin et al., Nature 658:690-697, DOI 10.1038/s41586-026-10972-z) as the earliest known bird to have lost (or diminished) the ability to fly. Forelimbs ~one-third shorter than hindlimbs; limb proportions match modern ground-dwelling birds (377 living species compared); retains dinosaurian traits — serrated teeth, hyperextensible deinonychosaur-style second toe. Placed just above Archaeopteryx within Avialae, closest relative Zhengheornis. The authors' reading: early bird evolution explored non-flight niches from the start, not a linear march toward better flight.
place: Zhenghe County, Fujian Province, China — Zhenghe Fauna (approximate county coordinates)

title: Adult Sinovenator — the troodontid grows up (Ningcheng Basin, 2026)
claim: A new adult postcranial skeleton of Sinovenator changii from the Jehol Biota of the Ningcheng Basin, Inner Mongolia, described October 2026, provides the first adult ontogenetic data for this early troodontid and expands its known geographic range beyond Liaoning's Yixian Formation — refining the dinosaur–bird transition record with growth data, not just feathers.
place: Ningcheng Basin, Inner Mongolia, China (Jehol Biota)

title: First-star imprints in a metal-poor galaxy overdensity (Li/Kakiichi et al. 2026)
claim: A metal absorber at redshift z=5.945 along the sightline to quasar SDSS J0100+2802 shows a carbon-and-silicon over-abundance pattern consistent with Population III supernova yields; the absorber sits inside a protocluster-like overdensity of 17 spectroscopically confirmed galaxies with a mean gas-phase metallicity of ~3% solar — the strongest environmental evidence yet that first-star formation and its chemical imprints lingered into the end of reionization.
place: Sightline to quasar SDSS J0100+2802 (RA ~01h00m, Dec +28°02') — the absorber at z=5.945

title: The Guantou small-theropod footprints — mid-Cretaceous Jialingpus trackways, Dongyang, Zhejiang, published 2026
claim: On 20 October 2026, a peer-reviewed paper in MDPI Fossils (2026, 4(4), 30) described newly discovered small theropod footprints from collapsed rock blocks of the Lower Cretaceous Guantou Formation at the Shangantian tracksite, Dongyang City, Zhejiang Province, eastern China: at least 18 natural molds on a single siltstone slab, minute tridactyl tracks 6.8–8.8 cm long, tentatively assigned to Jialingpus isp., with three single-step trackways indicating slow walking speeds of 0.4–0.8 m/s (1.4–2.9 km/h) — enriching mid-Cretaceous dinosaur track diversity in Zhejiang and informing Jialingpus morphometric variation across the Jurassic–Cretaceous boundary.
place: Shangantian tracksite, Dongyang City, Zhejiang Province, China

title: Invictibellatrix amberina — Europe's first megaraptoran
claim: A new megaraptoran theropod species, described October 2026 from a partial braincase collected on the Isle of Wight and held unstudied at the Natural History Museum, London since 1924, is the first confirmed European member of the Megaraptora — a group of large-armed, long-clawed theropods previously known from Asia and the southern continents — and its placement supports the Asia→Europe→Gondwana dispersal route over southern island-hopping.
place: Isle of Wight, UK — southwest coast, Wessex Formation (found at the foot of a cliff by R. W. Hooley)

title: The Udon Thani trackway — Thailand's first Udon Thani dinosaur footprints, announced 2026
claim: On 20 October 2026, Thailand's Department of Mineral Resources announced that six tridactyl impressions exposed in sandstone of the Phu Phan Formation inside Phu Hin Chom That–Phu Phrabat National Park, Udon Thani province, are genuine dinosaur footprints — a single trackway, each print ~29 cm long and ~26 cm wide, attributed by the agency to a carnivorous theropod (~120 Ma, Early Cretaceous), estimated ~1.42 m at the hip and ~6.3 m long, comparable in build to Siamotyrannus isanensis. The site was first noticed by a tourist's photograph posted to Facebook on 18 October 2026; park rangers measured the impressions on 19 October.
place: Phu Hin Chom That–Phu Phrabat National Park, Kut Chap District, Udon Thani Province, Thailand

title: The Paluxy 'man tracks'
claim: Fossil human footprints ('giant man tracks') occur alongside dinosaur tracks in the Cretaceous limestone of the Paluxy River near Glen Rose, Texas, proving humans and dinosaurs walked the same riverbed at the same time.
place: Paluxy River, Glen Rose, Texas (Dinosaur Valley State Park area)

title: Denny — the first-generation Neanderthal/Denisovan hybrid (~90 ka)
claim: Denisova 11 ('Denny'), ~90,000 years old from Denisova Cave: nuclear genome ~38.6% Neanderthal / 42.3% Denisovan; maternally Neanderthal (mtDNA). A first-generation hybrid of a Neanderthal mother and a Denisovan father — the father himself carried Neanderthal ancestry 300-600 generations earlier, implying interbreeding was common, not rare.

title: The Youngest Toba Tuff (~74 ka) — the dated catastrophe
claim: The Youngest Toba Tuff — a super-eruption in northern Sumatra, Indonesia, dated 73.88 ± 0.32 ka (Storey et al. 2012, 40Ar/39Ar) — the largest explosive volcanic eruption of the Quaternary (VEI 8; thousands of cubic kilometres of magma). It left a caldera lake ~100 km long, laid a dated ash isochron from the Indian Ocean to the South China Sea and across South Asia, and left sulfate and cryptotephra fingerprints in both Greenland (GISP2) and Antarctic ice cores. It happened inside the Homo sapiens dispersal window — a catastrophe with a date, not a cause of one.
place: Lake Toba caldera, northern Sumatra, Indonesia

title: The main out-of-Africa dispersal, ~50-70 ka
claim: All living non-African human populations descend from a single main dispersal of Homo sapiens out of Africa ~50-70 thousand years ago; earlier exits (Misliya ~180 ka, Apidima ~210 ka, Zhirendong, Tam Pa Ling) left fossils and tools but no surviving genetic legacy. The Sahul landmass (Australia/New Guinea) was settled ~60-65 ka via two routes (a southern corridor through Indonesia and a northern corridor toward the Philippines/New Guinea), crossing open water by boat.
place: Bab al Mandab strait, Red Sea (the southern exit); exit routes also northern (Sinai/Levant)

title: Madjedbebe — Australia's 65,000-Year Story
claim: Humans occupied the Madjedbebe rock shelter in northern Australia (Kakadu) by about 65,000 years ago — the earliest known human presence in Australia — arriving by sea voyage from Sunda, alongside megafauna and within sight of Homo floresiensis on Flores.
place: Madjedbebe rock shelter, Kakadu, Northern Territory, Australia

title: Penghu 2 & 3: leg bones attributed to Denisovans by collagen proteomics (2026 preprints)
claim: Two dredged leg bones from the Penghu Channel (Penghu 2 femur, Penghu 3 tibia) belong to Denisovans, identified via collagen proteomics (COL1A2 R996K), with an estimated age of ~45-43 ka from co-dredged fauna and inferred statures of ~1.8-1.9 m.
place: Penghu Channel, Taiwan Strait (dredged — no secure provenance)

title: The September 2026 '40,000 BCE Great Pyramid' press telling
claim: The Great Pyramid of Giza was built c. 40,000 BCE — millennia before the pharaohs — as reported in a September 2026 press telling (dailygalaxy, 2026-09-10) based on an engineer's weathering measurements of the pyramid's stone.
place: Giza Plateau, Egypt

title: Peopling of the Americas: three lines converge on 14–20 ka, reviewed 2026-10-17 (VIII.c third pass)
claim: Three independent lines of evidence — ancient-DNA population-split timing, the archaeological site record, and environmental/ice-sheet data — converge on a 14,000–20,000-year-ago window for the arrival of the ancestors of today's Indigenous Americans, per Potter et al. 2026 (Current Opinion in Genetics & Development). The genetic data show a major branching event around 15 ka dividing Northern and Southern Native American lineages; post-14-ka arrival conflicts with the split timing; pre-25-ka arrival finds no genomic population-split support. This is the convergence argument's fifth demonstration case: genetics, archaeology, and paleoenvironment sharing no method, landing in the same window.
place: North America (continental)

title: Atlantis (Plato's account)
claim: That Atlantis — a vast maritime empire 'beyond the Pillars of Hercules' with a concentric-ringed capital city, founded by Poseidon's descendants and destroyed in a single day and night — was a real historical place, as Plato describes it in the Timaeus and Critias (c. 360 BCE).
place: Claimed: beyond the Pillars of Hercules (Strait of Gibraltar) — no physical site

title: Kuk Swamp — Independent Agriculture in the New Guinea Highlands
claim: People in the Wahgi Valley of the New Guinea highlands were practicing agriculture by about 10,000 years ago — planting taro and banana on the Kuk Swamp wetland margin — independently of any Near Eastern farming tradition.
place: Kuk Swamp, Wahgi Valley, Papua New Guinea Highlands

title: The Black Sea deluge hypothesis
claim: The Black Sea deluge hypothesis (Ryan & Pitman, 1997, Columbia University): as the last ice age waned, rising Mediterranean waters breached the Bosphorus Sill ~9,400 years ago, catastrophically flooding the then-freshwater Black Lake — drowning ~70,000 km² of Neolithic shoreline and possibly seeding the flood memories behind the Mesopotamian and Genesis stories. Giosan et al. (Quaternary Science Reviews, Jan 2009) counter that the rise was only 5-10 m, drowning ~2,000 km² — 'hardly of biblical proportions.' The hypothesis is unresolved: the reconnection happened; its catastrophic character and any link to flood traditions remain contested.
place: Black Sea basin / Bosphorus Sill

title: The 'Chinchorro mummy has the oldest tattoos' myth (DEBUNKED)
claim: The world's oldest tattoos belong to a Chinchorro mummy from South America, dated to around 6000 BCE — older than Ötzi the Iceman.
place: Coastal Chile/Peru (Chinchorro culture region)

title: The oldest mirrors: obsidian discs of Çatalhöyük
claim: The earliest identifiable mirrors are hand-sized polished obsidian discs from Çatalhöyük, Anatolia, dated ~6000–5900 BCE — highly polished volcanic glass found in burial contexts.
place: Çatalhöyük, Konya Plain, Turkey

title: The Persian Gulf's retreating head — Eridu and Ur on a coast that left
claim: In the early Holocene the head of the Persian Gulf stood far north of its present position: c. 5000 BP the shoreline lay near Eridu and Ur (Tell el-Muqayyar), on the evidence of Larsen & Evans 1978, Lambeck 1996, and Sanlaville 1989 as synthesized in the geoarchaeological literature. The Gulf then retreated south as the Tigris-Euphrates delta prograded, reaching its current configuration c. AD 1000 via the Shatt al-Arab delta's growth south of Basra (Al-Hamad et al. 2017; Aqrawi 2001; Bogemans et al. 2017). The exact position of the shoreline at 6000 BP is still debated — Jotheri et al. 2018's remote-sensing work in the Uruk region finds the marine transgression never reached the Uruk area (~300 km from the present shoreline).
place: Head of the Persian Gulf, southern Iraq — the migrating Holocene shoreline

title: The Chang'e-6 lunar cratering chronology
claim: The lunar cratering chronology function, revised with Chang'e-6 far-side samples (2.807 Ga basalts and 4.247 Ga South Pole–Aitken norite impact melts), shows near-side and far-side impact flux indistinguishable within uncertainty — a single unified global chronology in which impact activity declines smoothly and rapidly from planetary accretion, with no cataclysmic spike.
place: Chang'e-6 landing site, Apollo crater, South Pole–Aitken Basin, lunar far side

title: The moving substrate — the synthesis argument of master-list VIII.h
claim: The map's own ground moves: river avulsions, delta migrations, and shoreline shifts mean that ancient texts' geographic descriptions ("the port of X," "the mouth of the Y," "on the coast") cannot be pinned at their modern coordinates without a substrate baseline. Pins at excavated sites are stable (the site does not move); textual geography without a dated substrate reconstruction carries a precision grade no better than 'region' and risks tens-of-kilometers error. Demonstration exhibits: the Persian Gulf head (coastline at c. 5000 BCE near Eridu/Ur per Larsen & Evans 1978 / Lambeck 1996 / Sanlaville 1989, never reaching Uruk per Jotheri et al. 2018; Gulf reached its current configuration c. AD 1000 via Shatt al-Arab progradation), the Nile's defunct branches (Canopic branch — Naukratis's river — and Pelusiac branch silted; the Pelusiac's lower-reach death c. AD 25 per the 1973 Science survey; Pi-Ramesse/Qantir abandoned when its river dried), and the Yellow River's 1855 Tongwaxiang avulsion (Yellow Sea to Bohai).
place: Southern Mesopotamia / Nile Delta / North China Plain (three demonstration zones)

title: The White Temple on the Anu ziggurat, Uruk
claim: The Anu ziggurat at Uruk — the oldest known ziggurat, begun c. 4000 BCE and raised in at least ten rebuilds to ~12 m — carried the White Temple on its summit (Uruk III, c. 3500–3000 BCE): a 17.5 × 22.3 m tripartite temple, whitewashed inside and out, shining across the flat plain and visible over the city's walls.
place: Anu ziggurat, Uruk (Warka, Iraq)

title: The Late Heavy Bombardment telling
claim: The inner solar system suffered a cataclysmic spike in impacts at ~3.9 billion years ago — the 'Late Heavy Bombardment' — a solar-system-wide storm of asteroids that scarred the Moon, Earth, and the terrestrial planets long after their formation.
place: Chang'e-6 landing site, Apollo crater, South Pole–Aitken Basin, lunar far side

title: Uruk, one of the world's first great cities
claim: Uruk in southern Mesopotamia grew into one of the world's first true cities, reaching urban scale (tens of thousands of inhabitants, monumental precincts like the Eanna) during the Uruk period, c. 3800-3200 BCE.
place: Uruk (Warka)

title: Uruk, one of the world's first great cities
claim: Uruk in southern Mesopotamia grew into one of the world's first true cities, reaching urban scale (tens of thousands of inhabitants, monumental precincts like the Eanna) during the Uruk period, c. 3800-3200 BCE.
place: Uruk (Warka)

title: Hisarlık is Troy — and the Hittite Wilusa
claim: That the tell at Hisarlık in northwest Anatolia is the Troy of the epic tradition — and the Wilusa of 13th-century BCE Hittite diplomatic texts.
place: Hisarlik (Troy), Tevfikiye, Çanakkale Province, Turkey

title: The chewing sticks — humanity's first toothbrushes
claim: Chewed twigs with frayed, brush-like ends were used to clean teeth in Mesopotamia by ~3500 BCE and in Egypt by ~3000 BCE; the practice continues today as the miswak (Salvadora persica).
place: Southern Mesopotamia (Babylonian context)

title: The clay envelopes of Uruk, c. 3500-3100 BCE
claim: Hollow clay balls (bullae) enclosing accounting tokens, sealed and seal-impressed, were in use in Uruk-period Mesopotamia c. 3500-3100 BCE as tamper-proof containers of recorded information — the envelope's oldest known ancestor.
place: Uruk (Warka), southern Iraq — the type-site region; examples from multiple Mesopotamian sites

title: 'The envelope was invented in 1840' — DEBUNKED
claim: The telling that 'the envelope was invented in 1840' (by Edwin Hill and Warren de la Rue, or in the year of the Penny Post).
place: London — where the 1840s telling was born

title: The invention of cuneiform writing
claim: Cuneiform writing was invented in southern Mesopotamia (Uruk), with the earliest proto-cuneiform tablets dated c. 3400-3200 BCE — the earliest known true writing system.
place: Uruk

title: Ötzi's 61 tattoos — the world's oldest preserved (3370–3100 BCE)
claim: Ötzi the Tyrolean Iceman — the naturally mummified man found in the Ötztal Alps in 1991, dated 3370–3100 BCE — bears 61 tattoos (thin parallel black lines and crosses on the spine, left calf, right instep, ankle joints, left wrist, and torso), making him the oldest tattooed human remains discovered to date.
place: Ötztal Alps, Austrian-Italian border (discovery site); body at the South Tyrol Museum of Archaeology, Bolzano

title: Kani Shaie 2025 — the Uruk expansion reaches the Zagros foothills
claim: In 2025 the Kani Shaie Archaeological Project (KSAP, University of Coimbra CEAACP — co-directed by André Tomé, Steve Renette, Maria da Conceição Lopes, Michael Lewis) excavated a monumental public-or-ritual building of the Uruk period (c. 3300–3100 BCE) on the summit tell at Kani Shaie, in the Basian Basin at the western edge of the Zagros Mountains, Sulaimania province, Iraqi Kurdistan — with an associated fragment of a gold earring, an Uruk-period cylinder seal, and decorative wall cones of Uruk monumental-architecture type — the strongest newly excavated exhibit in a decade for the Uruk expansion's eastern reach.
place: Kani Shaie, Basian Basin, Sulaimania province, Iraqi Kurdistan (approximate — site coordinates not yet published)

title: Narmer and the unification of Egypt
claim: Narmer (c. 3100 BCE) unified Upper and Lower Egypt, founding the First Dynasty; the Narmer Palette depicts him wearing the crowns of both lands.
place: Hierakonpolis (find spot of the Palette)

title: The Narmer Palette as a documentary record of the unification
claim: The Narmer Palette (siltstone, c. 3100 BCE, found 1897-98 by Quibell and Green in the Main Deposit of the temple of Horus at Hierakonpolis) depicts an actual historical event — Narmer's defeat of a Lower-Egyptian foe and unification of the Two Lands — rather than being a purely symbolic composition.
place: Hierakonpolis (Kom el-Ahmar) — find spot of the Palette, Main Deposit

title: The Narmer Palette as 'the first historical document in the world'
claim: The Narmer Palette is the oldest Egyptian — or the first-ever — historical record (Brier & Hobbs: 'The oldest Egyptian historical record'; the Egyptian Museum's own page: it 'has been considered the first historical document in the world').
place: Hierakonpolis (Kom el-Ahmar) — Main Deposit

title: The Narmer Palette's making — the 2026 tool-mark study (preliminary)
claim: New 2026 imaging of the Narmer Palette shows tool marks, possible changes to the carved scenes, and evidence of damage and repair — meaning the object has a production history beyond its finished iconography. Dr. Kathryn Piquette (with stonecarver Mick Oakey, Essex Egyptology Group, March 2026 lecture): high-resolution computer-enhanced images of the palette compared against experimental stonecarving on a similar stone slab with replica tools, in an attempt to reverse-engineer the production process. Findings are preliminary, presented as a lecture, and not yet peer-reviewed.
place: Hierakonpolis (the palette's find spot, 1897–98)

title: Retainer sacrifice at Umm el-Qaab — the 2026 forensic re-reading
claim: The hundreds of subsidiary burials around the First-Dynasty royal tombs at Umm el-Qaab (Abydos) include victims of retainer sacrifice — people killed to accompany the king in death. The 2026 forensic re-examination (Roselyn Campbell, Purdue University, Frontiers in Environmental Archaeology): 46 skulls surviving from Flinders Petrie's early-20th-century excavations (Duckworth Collection, University of Cambridge) were re-examined with modern forensic methods; 18 of the 46 (39%) carry major fractures judged perimortem and probably fatal — mostly linear fractures (thin cracks without inward displacement, distinct from depressed fractures a mace would leave), plus sharp-force injuries including a chopping wound to one individual's eye. The study supports Petrie's century-old suspicion that the simultaneous burials around the king were killings, while acknowledging the 28 skulls without such injuries are unexplained, and that the skulls are a surviving sample, not the whole buried population.
place: Umm el-Qaab, Abydos, Upper Egypt

title: The measured ancient alignments (archaeoastronomy ledger)
claim: A subset of ancient monuments carry sky alignments that survive measurement and dating: Stonehenge's solstitial axis (the Avenue on the summer-solstice sunrise alignment, Neolithic-Bronze Age phases), the Great Pyramid's near-cardinal orientation (arcminute-level precision, 4th Dynasty), Chankillo's thirteen towers as a working solar calendar (4th c. BCE, Peru) — while other claimed alignments fail on measurement or stay contested (Nabta Playa's proposed solstice alignments remain disputed among specialists). The fringe 'impossible knowledge of the heavens' reading is not needed to explain any measured alignment.
place: Stonehenge (family anchor; Chankillo -9.56,-78.23; Giza 29.9792,31.1342; Nabta Playa 22.53,30.75)

title: The 'candles lit the premodern world' telling
claim: Before electric light, candles were the main source of artificial light for ordinary people in the premodern world.
place: British Isles (control sample)

title: The 'Jesus copied the dying-and-rising gods' claim
claim: Popular internet-level versions of Frazer's 'dying-and-rising god' category claim Jesus was modeled on pagan saviors (Osiris, Tammuz, Attis, Adonis). Scholarship killed this parallel: Jonathan Z. Smith (1987 Encyclopedia of Religion) dismissed the category as 'largely a misnomer based on imaginative reconstructions and exceedingly late or highly ambiguous texts', arguing gods who 'died' did not return and those who returned never truly 'died'. Tryggve Mettinger's 2001 monograph found pre-Christian death-and-return for Baal, Melqart, and Dumuzi — but none match the structure of the Christian claim, and he warned against hypostasizing a single type.
place: Eastern Mediterranean (scholarly debate, not a place)

title: Meretneith's serekhs — the 2026 digital re-reading (First Dynasty female king)
claim: Meretneith of Egypt's First Dynasty (c. 3000–2900 BCE) ruled as a king in her own right — not merely a queen consort — as evidenced by her name written in the royal serekh, the emblem that marked Egyptian rulers. The 2026 re-reading (Susan Kelly et al., Prague Egyptological Studies 2026) digitally enhanced a 1940s photograph of a lost mud stopper from an unknown Saqqara tomb (Walter B. Emery's archive, Egypt Exploration Society, London): the signs in the name portions of the second and third serekhs are consistent with the main sign used to write Meretneith's name, identifying her with the primary mark of rulers. The authors propose a staged political career: the serekh beside Djer's marks co-regency; tomb seals confirm a later regent/king's-mother role; studies estimate she ruled at least 30 years in one capacity or another. The claim is new and awaits scholarly reception.
place: Saqqara (unknown tomb excavated in the 1940s)

title: The Yamnaya steppe migration (~3000–2500 BCE)
claim: Around 3000–2500 BCE, a large-scale population movement carried people of the Yamnaya (Pit-Grave) culture out of the Pontic-Caspian steppe — the grass sea north of the Black Sea, in what is now Ukraine and Russia — into central and northern Europe. The migrants were cattle-and-sheep pastoralists who had adopted wheels and wagons around 3300 BCE. Ancient DNA shows the Corded Ware population of what is now Germany drew about three-quarters of its ancestry from the steppe newcomers — 'the largest migration into Europe in the last 5000 years' (Anthony). The migration is the leading explanation for the spread of Indo-European languages into Europe: the inference from genes to language rests on the migration's magnitude (if the people came in those numbers, their language came with them).
place: Pontic-Caspian steppe (Yamnaya homeland) → central/northern Europe (Corded Ware horizon)

title: Alulim, first king of Eridu
claim: The Sumerian King List opens with Alulim of Eridu as the first king, reigning a mythical 28,800 years 'before the flood'.
place: Eridu (traditional)

title: The Babylonian soap recipes (c. 2800/2200 BCE)
claim: The earliest recorded evidence of soap-like materials dates to around 2800 BCE in ancient Babylon: clay tablets carry written soap recipes — the ~2200 BCE formula of water, alkali, and cassia oil, and a Nabonidus-reign (556-539 BCE) recipe of uhulu (ashes), cypress oil, and sesame seed oil.
place: Babylon, Mesopotamia

title: Gilgamesh, king of Uruk
claim: The Sumerian King List names Gilgamesh as king of Uruk with a 126-year reign; he may be the historical kernel behind the Epic of Gilgamesh.
place: Uruk

title: The Step Pyramid of Djoser
claim: Pharaoh Djoser (c. 2670 BCE, Third Dynasty) built the Step Pyramid at Saqqara, designed by his vizier Imhotep — the first monumental stone building in Egypt and a prototype for later pyramids.
place: Saqqara

title: Enmebaragesi of Kish
claim: Enmebaragesi, king of Kish (c. 2600 BCE), is the earliest Sumerian king attested outside the King List itself, named in a contemporary alabaster vase inscription.
place: Kish

title: The Harappan (Indus Valley) Civilization
claim: A planned urban civilization covering the Indus river system and beyond — with Harappa, Mohenjo-daro, Dholavira, Ganweriwala, and Rakhigarhi among its great cities — at its mature height from c. 2600 to 1900 BCE, spread over a larger area than contemporary Mesopotamia or Egypt.
place: Mohenjo-daro, Sindh (representative pin; the civilization spans the Indus-Ghaggar system)

title: The Indus Script Is Undeciphered
claim: The Indus civilization's sign system — ~4,000 inscriptions, ~400 signs, mostly 5–6 symbols long, longest 34 — has never been convincingly deciphered. In January 2025 the Tamil Nadu government offered a $1,000,000 prize for a decipherment accepted by archaeological experts; as of this record it stands unclaimed.
place: Mohenjo-daro seals (corpus spans the Indus system)

title: The tomb of Sekhentiu-Ptah, 'keeper of the king's secrets' — 2026 Saqqara discovery
claim: Excavations at Saqqara's Bubasteum necropolis uncovered an Old Kingdom tomb of the senior official Sekhentiu-Ptah (keeper of the king's secrets, royal chamberlain, priest of Maat, supervisor of the royal library) with three sealed stone sarcophagi found intact in their original positions, an intact false door, painted funerary cartonnage, alabaster ritual tools, a wooden falcon statue, and over 100 ushabti figurines; parts of the complex were looted in antiquity.
place: Bubasteum necropolis, Saqqara, Egypt

title: The Great Pyramid of Khufu at Giza
claim: The Great Pyramid at Giza was built for Pharaoh Khufu (c. 2560 BCE), the largest of the three Giza pyramids; workers' graffiti inside names Khufu's crews.
place: Giza

title: The Lagash omitted archive — the royal inscription control on the King List's Early Dynastic sequence
claim: The Lagash royal inscription archive — contemporary Early Dynastic royal records that the Sumerian King List never names — is an independent control on the King List's dynastic scheme: the Treaty of Mesilim (c. 2500 BCE, the king of Kish arbitrating Lagash and Umma's Gu'edena border, the oldest known boundary treaty), the Vulture Stele of Eannatum (c. 2450 BCE, the earliest identified victory monument, with its oath-bound border settlement), the Cone of Enmetena, and the reform cones of Urukagina (c. 2350 BCE). Lagash's inscribed royal line (Ur-Nanshe through Urukagina, ED III) runs parallel in time to the King List's named dynasties of Kish I, Uruk I, Ur I and Kish III — the archive's existence and sequence are established from contemporary inscriptions, not from any later copy.
place: Telloh (Girsu) and Tell al-Hiba (Lagash), Dhi Qar, Iraq

title: Karnak on a river island — the temple the substrate chose
claim: The temple of Amun-Ra at Karnak (Luxor, Egypt) was built on a fluvial terrace island formed between Nile channels — the only known such high-ground-in-water configuration in the area, recalling the primeval-mound of Egyptian creation myth — with permanent occupation becoming possible only after 2520 BCE +/-420 (Old Kingdom), and subsequent occupants engineering the channels themselves (desert-sand dumping to make land).
place: Karnak, Luxor, Egypt

title: The Kingdom of Kush
claim: The Kingdom of Kush — the Nubian kingdom along the Nile from the First Cataract south, with capitals successively at Kerma, Napata (near Jebel Barkal), and Meroë — was a major independent civilization of the ancient Nile Valley, with state-level organization, temple building, iron working, and its own writing, spanning roughly two thousand years.
place: Napata / Jebel Barkal (representative capital; Kerma and Meroë also pinned in media)

title: Ku-Baba, the tavern-keeper who became king
claim: The Sumerian King List's 3rd dynasty of Kish names Ku-Baba — 'the woman tavern-keeper' (munus-kas-de-a), the only female ruler in the entire list — as reigning 100 years and 'establishing the foundation of Kish'; she is also named in the Weidner Chronicle's literary history of kingship.
place: Kish (Tell al-Uhaymir, traditional)

title: Sixteen tablets against the evil demons
claim: The Utukkū Lemnūtu ('evil demons') is a canonical sixteen-tablet series of bilingual (Sumerian-Akkadian) exorcistic incantations directed against evil demons, ghosts, and other malefactors; some incantations derive from 3rd-millennium BCE compositions, and the series was transmitted for over two millennia as the professional lore of the āšipu (exorcist). The Metropolitan Museum holds tablets 3, 12, and 16; tablet 12 (Seleucid) treats demonic disruption of nature and agriculture with a scapegoat ritual.
place: Nineveh / Assur, Assyria

title: The Yunmin and Iti mastaba — 2026 Saqqara discovery
claim: A joint Egyptian-Spanish mission excavated a late Fifth Dynasty mastaba at the Mariette Cemetery north of Saqqara (reign of Djedkare Isesi, c. 24th century BCE) with two decorated funerary chapels — the main chapel of the senior official Yunmin (judge, court director, chief of the petition-handling scribes) and the southern chapel of his father Iti (scribal official of agricultural lands and offerings) — with reliefs retaining vivid original color.
place: Mariette Cemetery, north Saqqara, Egypt

title: Osiris: the murdered, reassembled, enthroned god of the dead
claim: The Egyptian tradition attests Osiris as a god who was murdered (by his brother Seth), dismembered, reassembled by Isis, and enthroned as judge and king of the dead — a death-and-return attested from the Old Kingdom onward, forming the theological core of Egyptian funerary religion.
place: Abydos (Osiris cult center; Osireion)

title: The destruction argument: deletion and destruction, read properly, are evidence
claim: Deletion and destruction, read properly, are historical evidence: what a regime erases proves the hand that feared it (the chisel's mark grades the belief that commissioned the hammer — evt-attestation-rule-001); what catastrophe preserves proves the archive that was there (fire bakes clay to permanence — evt-fire-baked-archives-001; Vesuvius carbonized the only intact ancient library — evt-herculaneum-pherc1667-2026-001); and the measured pattern of what is missing, checked against what should have survived, is itself a record. Destruction is deposition.
place: Multi-site method claim (Ebla, Herculaneum, Alexandria, Baghdad)

title: Dumuzi becomes Tammuz: a documented cross-cultural transmission
claim: The Sumerian Dumuzi is the same figure as the Akkadian and Hebrew Tammuz — one god transmitted across languages and empires, his lament cult reaching the Jerusalem Temple court (Ezekiel 8:14).
place: Sumer to Babylonia to Jerusalem (the Dumuzi-Tammuz route)

title: The preservation paradox: palace fire bakes Ebla's archives to permanence
claim: The cuneiform archives of Palace G at Ebla (Syria) survived for ~4,300 years because the palace burned: sun-dried clay tablets stored on wooden shelves were fire-baked by the palace's destruction (c. 2300 BCE) and collapsed in place, preserving the archive's original shelving order — destruction as the mechanism of preservation.
place: Tell Mardikh (Ebla), Syria — Palace G

title: The exposed-infant-on-the-river topos: Sargon's basket as the older witness
claim: The birth narrative of Sargon of Akkad — exposed as an infant in a reed basket caulked with bitumen, set on the river, recovered and raised by a water-drawer — is attested in cuneiform copies (Neo-Assyrian, preserving older tradition; Brian Lewis, The Sargon Legend, ASOR 1978). The exposed-infant-on-the-river topos therefore predates the Moses birth narrative (Exodus 2) by roughly a millennium in its attested form. Whether the Exodus writer knew Sargon's legend directly, or both drew on a shared older topos, is a literary judgment, not a provable borrowing.
place: Akkad / Mesopotamia (legend's setting; copies from Nineveh)

title: The King List as political charter (the legitimation thesis)
claim: The Sumerian King List was composed and redacted to legitimize contemporary rulers' claims to power over Babylonia — the 'Chronicle of the One Monarchy' in which kingship, a single institution, passes from city to city — rather than to record political history; the Weld-Blundell recension's ending with the Isin dynasty marks it as Isin's turn as rightful inheritor of the Ur III legacy.
place: Isin (whose dynasty the WB 444 recension ends with)

title: The King List's dynasties overlapped — the sequential 'one monarchy' is editorial
claim: The Sumerian King List's dynasties did not all rule sequentially: several city-state dynasties were contemporary with each other, so the list's 'kingship was taken to [city]' sequence — the one-monarchy formula — is an editorial arrangement, not a political record of Mesopotamia.
place: Southern Mesopotamia (Kish, Uruk, Ur, Lagash, Mari, Akkad)

title: Udug: the word that didn't pick a side
claim: The Sumerian udug (Akkadian utukku) was originally a neutral class-term for spirits — the word itself did not connote good or evil. Gudea of Lagash (c. 2144–2124 BCE) asked a goddess to send him a 'good udug' for protection; exorcism texts invoke the good udug against the evil udug (udug-hul / utukkū lemnūtu), the evil ones blamed as vectors of physical and mental illness. The belief-phenomenon is multiply attested across two millennia of cuneiform texts; the entities are not graded.
place: Lagash (Telloh), southern Mesopotamia

title: The "House of Abraham" at Ur — Saddam-era tourist designation with no archaeological basis
claim: A specific excavated house at Tell el-Muqayyar (Ur) is presented to visitors as the house / birthplace of the biblical Abraham.

title: Dumuzi/Tammuz: the shepherd-god condemned, dragged down, and portioned between worlds
claim: The Sumerian tradition attests Dumuzi (Akkadian Tammuz) as a shepherd-god condemned to death by Inanna's 'look of death' (igi mu-un-ši-in-bar), seized by the galla-demons, and granted a divided fate — six months in the underworld, six months above (shared with his sister Geshtinanna) — with laments for him attested into the Hebrew Bible (Ezekiel 8:14).
place: Southern Mesopotamia (Nippur — tablet copies; Uruk — Dumuzi's city)

title: The Kish I reign spans are mathematically constructed, not chronology
claim: The post-flood First Dynasty of Kish reign lengths in the Sumerian King List (Gushur 1,200 through Aga 625 years, ~24,510 years total) are arithmetically designed numbers — most exact multiples of 60 (1,200 = 20×60, 960 = 16×60, 840 = 14×60, 720 = 12×60, 600 = 10×60, 420 = 7×60, 300 = 5×60), with perfect squares among them (900 = 30² for Zuqaqip, Melem-Kish, Ilku, and Enmebaragesi; 324 = 18² for Meshkiangasher of Uruk I) — a different numerical scheme from the antediluvian set (sars of 3,600, ners of 600, sosses of 60).
place: Kish (Tell al-Uhaymir), Iraq — the manuscripts' findspots vary (Nippur, Larsa, Susa, Sippar)

title: The King List's one-at-a-time dynastic sequence is false
claim: The Sumerian King List presents the dynasties of the Early Dynastic period as strictly sequential — kingship held by one city at a time, passed from city to city only when the previous city was 'smitten with weapons'. Contemporary evidence contradicts this: cities the list serializes (Kish, Uruk, Ur, Lagash) held power at the same moment; the list omits the Dynasty of Lagash entirely although its rulers are contemporary with listed kings (Ur-Nanshe(k) of Lagash was roughly contemporaneous with Mes-Anne-pada of Ur; the list's 45 pre-Sargonic rulers cannot have reigned sequentially in the period Lagash's 11 rulers cover); only seven pre-Sargonic SKL kings are attested in contemporary Early Dynastic inscriptions; the ESF-funded ARCANE project's final volume on third-millennium Mesopotamia lists no pre-Sargonic SKL ruler unless corroborated by contemporary inscriptions; recent handbooks warn the SKL should not be used as a historical source for the Early Dynastic period at all. The omission of important cities (Lagash, Larsa) is treated as deliberate.
place: Southern Mesopotamia (Kish, Uruk, Ur, Lagash, Adab, Mari, Akshak)

title: The Sumerian King List
claim: A cuneiform list of Sumerian kings, beginning with kings 'before the flood' whose reigns are given in tens of thousands of years, then continuing with historically plausible dynasties.
place: Southern Mesopotamia (copies found at Nippur, Larsa, Babylon)

title: The Sumerian King List
claim: A cuneiform list of Sumerian kings, beginning with kings 'before the flood' whose reigns are given in tens of thousands of years, then continuing with historically plausible dynasties — not a single text but a literary composition with a version history: at least 16 tablets/fragments, the oldest a Ur III-period copy (USKL, colophon: copied under Shulgi, 2084-2037 BCE) whose pre-Sargonic section is completely different, the rest Old Babylonian, differing by copying errors and deliberate editorial changes.
place: Southern Mesopotamia (copies found at Nippur, Larsa, Babylon, Susa, Tell Leilan)

title: The Code of Ur-Nammu — the earliest extant law code
claim: The Code of Ur-Nammu (c. 2100-2050 BCE), issued in the name of the Ur III king Ur-Nammu (2112-2095 BCE) — or possibly published by his son Shulgi — is the earliest extant written law code: 57 laws in casuistic if-then form, mostly compensation-based (fines rather than lex talionis), preserved on tablets now in the Schøyen Collection and the Istanbul Archaeological Museum.
place: Ur (Tell el-Muqayyar), Iraq

title: Abraham
claim: Patriarch of the Abrahamic traditions; said to have journeyed from Ur of the Chaldees to Canaan, and to be the ancestor through whom Judaism, Christianity, and Islam trace covenantal descent.
place: Ur (traditional: Tell el-Muqayyar, southern Iraq — consensus, contested)

title: The 'Apiru/'Habiru in the Bronze Age sources
claim: The 'Apiru (Akkadian ḫa-bi-ru / SA.GAZ) appear in Bronze Age texts from the early 2nd millennium through the 12th century BCE — the Amarna letters (c. 1350 BCE, ~60 occurrences), Egyptian New Kingdom administrative records, and the Mari, Nuzi, Alalakh, and Hittite archives — as a social category of displaced persons, mercenaries, laborers, and outsiders. In those texts the term is a status label, not an ethnic self-designation.
place: Tell el-Amarna, Egypt (densest attestation cluster; the term's range runs Mesopotamia–Levant–Egypt)

title: The Mesopotamian flood tradition
claim: Great-flood survivor narratives circulated in Mesopotamian literature centuries before the biblical account — Sumerian Ziusudra (Nippur tablet, pre-2000 BCE), the Old Babylonian Atrahasis epic (ca. 1630 BCE), and the Akkadian Gilgamesh Tablet XI — sharing the core structure: divine warning, boat, animals, mountain, birds, sacrifice. Direct literary borrowing of Genesis from Gilgamesh is NOT established; scholars argue shared tradition rather than word-for-word copying.
place: Shuruppak (Tell Fara), Ziusudra's city, southern Iraq

title: Isaac, son of Abraham
claim: Isaac, son of Abraham and Sarah, the heir of the covenant in the biblical tradition (Genesis 17–28); the binding of Isaac (Akedah) is the central event of his narrative.
place: Hebron / Beersheba (traditional)

title: Isaac, son of Abraham
claim: Isaac, son of Abraham and Sarah, heir of the covenant in the biblical tradition (Genesis 17-28); the binding of Isaac (Akedah) is the narrative center. Attested in Genesis, Hebrews 11:17-19 (Isaac as type, Abraham 'able even to raise him from the dead'), and Qur'an 37:112-113 (Ishaq 'a prophet from among the righteous', Saheeh International). All attestations belong to one textual family.
place: Hebron / Beersheba (traditional)

title: Ishmael, son of Abraham
claim: Ishmael, son of Abraham and Hagar, blessed in Genesis 17:20 to become a great nation of twelve rulers; Islamic tradition traces the Arabs' (and Muhammad's) lineage to him.
place: Paran / Sinai-Negev corridor (traditional)

title: Ishmael, son of Abraham
claim: Ishmael, son of Abraham and Hagar, blessed in Genesis 17:20 to become a great nation of twelve rulers; expelled with Hagar to the wilderness of Paran (Genesis 21); the Ishmaelite tribal genealogy in Genesis 25:12-18 dwells 'from Havilah unto Shur... before Egypt' (east of Egypt, not near Mecca). Paul's allegory (Galatians 4:21-31): Ishmael the child of the flesh, Isaac the child of promise. The Qur'anic Isma'il: prophet alongside Abraham, co-raiser of the House's foundations (Qur'an 2:125-129); the sacrifice narrative (37:102-107) names NO son. Islamic tradition links Arab genealogy (Quraysh via 'Adnan) to Ishmael.
place: Paran / Sinai-Negev corridor (traditional)

title: Ishmael, son of Abraham
claim: Ishmael, son of Abraham and Hagar, blessed in Genesis 17:20 to become a great nation of twelve rulers; expelled with Hagar to the wilderness of Paran (Genesis 21); the Ishmaelite tribal genealogy in Genesis 25:12-18 dwells 'from Havilah unto Shur... before Egypt' (east of Egypt, not near Mecca). Paul's allegory (Galatians 4:21-31): Ishmael the child of the flesh, Isaac the child of promise. The Qur'anic Isma'il: prophet alongside Abraham, co-raiser of the House's foundations (Qur'an 2:125-129); the sacrifice narrative (37:102-107) names NO son. Islamic tradition links Arab genealogy (Quraysh via 'Adnan) to Ishmael.
place: Paran / Sinai-Negev corridor (traditional)

title: The ancient parasols: shade-umbrellas before the rain umbrella
claim: Parasols — umbrellas used as sun-shades and emblems of rank — existed in the ancient Near East and China millennia before the modern rain umbrella: royal parasols in ancient Assyria and Egypt (conventionally ~4,000 years, carried by servants for kings), waterproof oil-paper and silk umbrellas in China (conventionally 11th c. BCE), early folding forms (conventionally c. 21 CE), and the Roman umbraculum as a sun-shade for women and priests.
place: Ancient Near East & China (iconographic record: Assyrian reliefs at Nimrud/Nineveh, Egyptian tomb paintings, Chinese texts)

title: The antediluvian reign lengths are schematic, not historical
claim: The Sumerian King List's eight antediluvian kings did not literally reign 28,800 to 43,200 years each (241,200 years total): every reign is expressible in the Sumerian sexagesimal units sars (3,600), ners (600), and sosses (60), none of the eight kings is verified as historical by any contemporary inscription or excavation, and the antediluvian section is absent from some recensions including the Nippur majority copies.
place: Southern Mesopotamia (Eridu, Bad-tibira, Larag, Sippar, Shuruppak — the five antediluvian cities)

title: Ur of the Chaldees = Tell el-Muqayyar (identification)
claim: The biblical 'Ur of the Chaldees' (Hebrew 'Ur Kasdim, Genesis 11:28, 31) is identified with the excavated Sumerian city of Ur at Tell el-Muqayyar in southern Iraq — the identification proposed by Henry Rawlinson (1862) and popularized by Leonard Woolley's excavations (1922 onward).
place: Tell el-Muqayyar (Ur), Dhi Qar Governorate, Iraq

title: Ur of the Chaldees = Tell el-Muqayyar (identification)
claim: The biblical 'Ur of the Chaldees' (Hebrew 'Ur Kasdim, Genesis 11:28, 31) is identified with the excavated Sumerian city of Ur at Tell el-Muqayyar in southern Iraq — the identification proposed by Henry Rawlinson (1862) and popularized by Leonard Woolley's excavations (1922 onward).
place: Tell el-Muqayyar (Ur), Dhi Qar Governorate, Iraq

title: Proto-Sinaitic — the first alphabet (c. 1800 BCE)
claim: The earliest alphabetic writing is the Proto-Sinaitic script, invented c. 19th-16th century BCE — roughly seven centuries before the Phoenician abjad — by Semitic-speaking workers in Egyptian service, working from hieroglyphic signs by the acrophonic principle (the 'Egyptian origin of the Semitic alphabet').
place: Serabit el-Khadim, Sinai Peninsula (turquoise-mining region; Wadi el-Hol on the Theban desert road is the second anchor)

title: The 'Pythagorean' triples of Old Babylon — Plimpton 322 & YBC 7289, c. 1800 BCE
claim: Old Babylonian scribes (c. 1822-1762 BCE, Larsa, the age of Hammurabi) knew and used the relationship between the sides of right triangles: the Plimpton 322 tablet lists 15 rows of Pythagorean triples (integer sets satisfying a² + b² = c²), and the YBC 7289 school tablet computes the diagonal of a square as 1;24,51,10 in sexagesimal (~1.41421296, i.e. √2 to six sexagesimal places) — the 'diagonal rule' in working use roughly twelve centuries before Pythagoras of Samos was born.
place: Larsa (Tell as-Senkereh), southern Mesopotamia — attributed provenance

title: The Weld-Blundell Prism (WB 444)
claim: The Weld-Blundell Prism is the only relatively undamaged, complete surviving witness of the Sumerian King List: a four-sided baked-clay prism (~20 x 9 cm), inscribed in Sumerian cuneiform in two columns per face, found at Larsa in 1922 and dated to year 11 of Sin-magir of Isin (c. 1800 BCE).
place: Larsa (findspot; prism now in the Ashmolean Museum, Oxford)

title: The ukkinu: the Babylonian assembly that voted Marduk king
claim: In Enūma Eliš (the Babylonian Epic of Creation, Tablet II–III), the divine assembly is the mechanism of cosmic government: the gods are summoned by ministerial herald (Gaga/Kakka), 'make ready for a feast, at a banquet let them sit, let them eat bread, let them mix wine, that for Marduk, their avenger they may decree the fate.' Drunk at the banquet, the assembled gods invest Marduk — 'they granted him the right to exercise kingship over the gods' (Tablet IV) — and in Tablet VI the same assembly presides as a court: 'Let the great gods be here in Assembly,' Kingu is tried and executed for the uprising, and the fifty great gods take their seats to divide the stations of heaven and netherworld. The council decrees fates (šīmatu), names, and destinies; it is where divine kingship is voted, not born.
place: Nineveh (copies); Babylon (composition)

title: Lamashtu: four thousand years of fear
claim: Mesopotamians believed in, performed rituals against, and made amulets warding off the demoness Lamashtu (Sumerian DIMME) — attested from Old Babylonian incantations through the Neo-Assyrian period, roughly 4,000 years of continuous fear.
place: Mesopotamia

title: The 'Moses inscription' telling (Serabit el-Khadim, 2025-2026)
claim: The press telling that Proto-Sinaitic inscriptions at the Serabit el-Khadim turquoise mines (c. 1800-1600 BCE) contain the name 'Mose' and may be the handwriting of the biblical Moses — from Michael S. Bar-Ron's draft thesis (Ariel University, 2025), reported by the Daily Mail and National Geographic in August 2025 and recirculated in 2026. The telling grades the press claim, not the inscriptions (which are real and long known).
place: Serabit el-Khadim, South Sinai (ancient turquoise mines; temple of Hathor)

title: The Bar-Ron Proto-Sinaitic 'Moses' reading (2026)
claim: In 2026, researcher Michael S. Bar-Ron (Ariel University) proposed that two Proto-Sinaitic inscriptions (Sinai 357 and 361) from the turquoise mines at Serabit el-Khadim, Egypt, c. 1800-1600 BCE, read 'zot m'Moshe' ('This is from Moses') and 'ne'um Moshe' ('A saying of Moses') — presented as a possible extra-biblical attestation of the name Moses centuries before the Exodus narratives. The inscriptions are real Middle Bronze Age carvings; the Moses reading is one researcher's proposal, contested by specialists and not peer-reviewed. It does not constitute a verified contemporary attestation of the figure and does not overturn evt-moses-figure-attestation-001.
place: Serabit el-Khadim, Sinai Peninsula, Egypt (turquoise mines)

title: Hammurabi of Babylon
claim: Hammurabi, sixth king of Babylon's First Dynasty, reigned c. 1792-1750 BCE (middle chronology), unifying southern Mesopotamia under Babylonian rule; his reign is documented by year names, royal inscriptions, and an extensive archive of letters.
place: Babylon

title: The middle chronology for Hammurabi and Old Babylon
claim: The middle chronology is the correct absolute chronology for the Old Babylonian period: Hammurabi of Babylon reigned 1792–1750 BCE, the fall of Babylon to Mursili I dates to 1595 BCE, and the fall of Ur to 2004 BCE — against the rival high (Hammurabi 1848–1806), low (1728–1685), and ultra-low/new (1696–1654) chronologies.
place: Babylon, Iraq

title: The Code of Hammurabi
claim: Hammurabi promulgated a law code of 282 laws, inscribed on a 2.25-meter dark-igneous stele (traditionally called 'diorite' since Scheil 1902; the Louvre identifies the material as basalt — the lithology is an unresolved scientific question per the peer-reviewed 2026 Comment, Liu & Xu, npj Heritage Science 14:141), covering commerce, family, labor, and criminal justice — one of the oldest and most complete legal codes known.
place: Susa (find spot; originally erected at Babylon or Sippar)

title: 'Hammurabi's Code was the first written law code' (the telling, killed)
claim: The popular telling that Hammurabi's Code (c. 1754 BCE) was the first written law code in human history.
place: Babylon (stele findspot: Susa, Iran — carried as 12th-century BCE war booty)

title: The Tell el-Koua Second Intermediate Period settlement (2026)
claim: In June 2026, Egypt's Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities announced the discovery of a Second Intermediate Period settlement at the Tell el-Koua site in the Wadi Tumilat region — the ancient corridor linking the eastern Nile Delta with Egypt's eastern frontier. The site includes 15th Dynasty (Hyksos-period) tombs and evidence of occupation continuing into the 18th Dynasty, spanning the transition from Hyksos rule to the New Kingdom — the era that has long figured in scholarly debates over the historical setting of the Exodus. This is context for the Hyksos-expulsion hypothesis, never evidence of the Exodus itself.
place: Tell el-Koua, Wadi Tumilat, eastern Delta, Egypt

title: The Theran (Santorini) eruption
claim: That the island of Thera in the Aegean erupted catastrophically in the Late Bronze Age — an eruption ~60x Mount St. Helens that buried the town of Akrotiri, collapsed the volcanic center into a caldera, and sent tsunamis toward Minoan Crete ~110 km south.
place: Santorini (Thera), Aegean Sea

title: The Venus Tablet of Ammisaduqa
claim: Twenty cuneiform copies in six groups (oldest copied at Babylon c. 720-704 BCE under Sargon II; main copy K.160 recovered from Ashurbanipal's library at Nineveh) preserve 21 years of Venus's heliacal risings and settings — first and last visibility before sunrise and after sunset — originally observed during the reign of the Babylonian king Ammisaduqa, fourth king after Hammurabi. It is the principal relative anchor for Old Babylonian absolute chronology.
place: Babylon (copies); principal copy recovered at Nineveh

title: The Venus Tablet of Ammisaduqa
claim: Twenty cuneiform copies in six groups (oldest copied at Babylon c. 720-704 BCE under Sargon II; main copy K.160 recovered from Ashurbanipal's library at Nineveh) preserve 21 years of Venus's heliacal risings and settings — first and last visibility before sunrise and after sunset — originally observed during the reign of the Babylonian king Ammisaduqa, fourth king after Hammurabi. It is the principal relative anchor for Old Babylonian absolute chronology.
place: Babylon (copies); principal copy recovered at Nineveh

title: The Fall of Babylon to Mursili I (1595 BCE, middle chronology)
claim: The First Dynasty of Babylon ended when the Hittite king Mursili I marched down the Euphrates, sacked Babylon, and carried off the cult statue of Marduk from the Esagila; the last Amorite king, Samsu-Ditana, fell. In the middle chronology the sack dates to 1595 BCE; the date is one of the absolute anchors of Old Babylonian chronology (1651 / 1595 / 1531 / 1499 BCE across the four schemes).
place: Babylon, Iraq

title: The Kassite Dynasty of Babylon (c. 1595–1155 BCE)
claim: The Kassite dynasty ruled Babylon from c. 1595 to 1155 BCE — roughly 440 years, the longest dynasty in Mesopotamian history: a stable, literate great-power era (the Amarna age: Kadashman-Enlil I and Burna-Buriaš II corresponding with Egypt's Amenhotep III), not a dark age. Kassite kings kept Akkadian as the language of administration and cuneiform as its script, copied Hammurabi's Code for six centuries, and left the kudurru boundary stones as their own documentary record.
place: Babylon, Iraq

title: The Temple menorah burned olive oil
claim: The seven-branched menorah of the Temple in Jerusalem burned pure beaten olive oil — seven oil lamps on a gold lampstand — not wax candles.
place: Jerusalem (the Temple)

title: The Crossing of the Yam Suf (Exodus 14)
claim: In Exodus 14, Moses stretches out his hand over the yam suf and the sea parts — the waters standing as walls on the right hand and on the left while Israel crosses on dry ground, and the returning water drowns Pharaoh's army.
place: Eastern Nile Delta candidate zone — Ballah Lakes / Lake Timsah / Lake of Tanis (disputed; no agreed pin)

title: The Exodus
claim: The biblical tradition holds that the Israelites, enslaved in Egypt, departed under Moses, crossed the sea, and wandered the wilderness before entering Canaan.
place: Sinai / Nile Delta (route traditionally placed here; unattested)

title: The Exodus narrative is literally accurate in every detail as written
claim: The Exodus narrative (Exodus 1-15) is literally accurate word-for-word as written: the ten plagues occurred as described, the census figure of 603,550 fighting men (Numbers 1:46) is a literal headcount, and a departure of roughly two million people from Egypt is historically accurate as stated.
place: Sinai / Nile Delta (route traditionally placed here; unattested)

title: Baal's return: death at Mot's hands, the rains coming back
claim: The Ugaritic Baal Cycle (KTU 1.1–1.6, c. 1400–1200 BCE) attests the storm-god Baal's death at the hands of Mot (Death) and his return — with Anat's slaughter of Mot and the restoration of the rains — a pre-Christian dying-and-rising narrative in which the god's death is the dry season and his return the weather.
place: Ugarit (Ras Shamra, Syria)

title: El's assembly at Ugarit: the council of the sons of El
claim: At Late Bronze Age Ugarit (14th–12th c. BCE), the divine assembly is a documented institution: El presides over the mphrt bn il ('the assembly of the sons of El') — the seventy sons of El (cf. Deut 32:8's 'seventy'), deliberating kingship, war, and fate. The Baal Cycle's council scenes (KTU 1.2 i, iii–iv) show the assembly in session: El presiding from his tent at the source of the cosmic rivers, Yam's messengers demanding Baal's surrender before the seated gods, Athirat interceding with El for Baal's palace, the vote-style deliberation by which divine authority moves. The assembly is not metaphor; it is the pantheon's government.
place: Ugarit (Ras Shamra), northern Levant coast

title: The name 'Moses' as Egyptian (contested)
claim: The personal name 'Moses' (Hebrew Mosheh) is of Egyptian origin — the standard scholarly reading deriving it from Egyptian msi/ms ('child, born of, son'), the common element of New Kingdom theophoric names (Thutmose, Ramose, Ahmose, Ptahmose, Ramesses). The Hebrew etymology given in Exodus 2:10 ('because I drew him out of the water', from mashah 'drew out') is a folk etymology — Hebrew wordplay on an Egyptian-sounding name, not the name's origin.
place: Egypt/Levant onomastics (the name, not the person)

title: The 2026 Samuha (Kayalıpınar) royal archive announcement
claim: Türkiye's Ministry of Culture and Tourism announced on 8 October 2026 that archaeologists recovered 131 cuneiform tablets and fragments at Kayalıpınar (ancient Samuha) in the 2026 season, bringing the reported royal archive total to 184 tablets and fragments with 53 found in 2025; the texts are attributed to King Tudhaliya II's reign and include Hittite and Hurrian, covering military, administrative, ritual, and royal-household affairs; excavators call it the most extensive Hittite royal archive found in the 21st century and one of the largest concentrations of Hittite documents outside Hattusa; translation and excavation are ongoing.
place: Kayalıpınar (ancient Samuha), Türkiye

title: The Shasu of Yhw in the Egyptian lists
claim: Two New Kingdom Egyptian temple topographical lists contain 't3 sh3sw yhw3' — 'the land of the Shasu of Yhw' — the oldest extra-biblical occurrence of the divine name YHWH in human records. The Soleb list (temple of Amenhotep III, Nubia, c. 1400 BCE) carries the name among the Shasu lists; the Amarah West list (Ramesses II, c. 1300 BCE) repeats the 'Shasu of Yhw' entry and separately names 'the land of the Shasu of Seir' (t3 sh3sw s3rr). Egypt knew a group called the Shasu attached to the name Yhw, located in the Seir/Edom/Midian region — the biblical tradition's own homeland of YHWH (cf. Deut 33:2, Judg 5:4, Hab 3:3, 1 Kgs 19). This grades the NAME's antiquity and geography, never the Exodus.
place: Soleb, Nubia (Sudan) — temple of Amenhotep III; also Amarah West, Nubia — temple of Ramesses II

title: Adonis: the mourned youth, the withering gardens, the witnessed return
claim: The tradition attests Adonis as a youth-god mourned in the annual Adonia festival (rooftop laments, the withering 'gardens of Adonis') and celebrated in return — with a pre-Hellenistic Phoenician pedigree: the Damu/Adon of Byblos, the male deity beside the Lady of Byblos in the Amarna letters, and early-Christian witnesses (Origen, Jerome) who describe the festival without claiming it as theirs.
place: Byblos (Gebal, Lebanon) — the Adonis river, the Lady of Byblos

title: The divine council: a shared West Semitic concept
claim: The idea of a heavenly council of gods is attested in Late Bronze Age Ugaritic texts (the assembly of El, KTU, 13th–12th c. BCE) and in the Hebrew Bible (Psalm 82's 'council of El', Job, 1 Kings 22, Daniel 7) — same cultural world, with Israelite writers reshaping the vocabulary around YHWH's sovereignty. Deuteronomy 32:8's Qumran/Septuagint reading ('sons of God' / 'angels of God') against the Masoretic 'sons of Israel' shows the concept was live and edited.
place: Ugarit (Ras Shamra), northern Levant coast

title: The Shiloh favissa: ritual repository of sacrificial remains
claim: The subterranean ritual repository (favissa) at Tel Shiloh contains roughly 10,000 animal bones interspersed with cultic chalices, votive bowls, and ceremonial vessels — systematically buried sacred paraphernalia from Late Bronze Age sacrificial activity, re-analyzed in an exhaustive September 2026 reassessment published via the Enoch Seminar & Biblical Archaeology surveys.
place: Tel Shiloh (Khirbet Seilun), West Bank

title: The denominator rule: where VIII.d's silence ends and VIII.f's destruction begins
claim: The timeline's two negative-evidence rules — VIII.d (silence is ambiguous: absence of evidence is not evidence of absence, and not evidence either) and VIII.f (deletion and destruction, read properly, are evidence) — are not rivals. They are one rule applied with and without a denominator. The baseline is the denominator: the expected survival rate for a given medium in a given climate under a given regime's archiving and destroying habits. Where the baseline is a GUESS, VIII.d retains jurisdiction — silence stays ambiguous (Herculaneum: ~1,800 scrolls found, library size unknown, so 'what else the villa held' is not evidence). Where the baseline is a MEASUREMENT, VIII.f operates — the pattern of what is missing, checked against what should have survived, is itself a record. The Kadesh case is the crossover exhibit: Egyptian royal inscriptions never record defeats (the regime baseline — Ramses II's battle reliefs claim victory), so the monuments' silence about the stalemate is VIII.d silence; but once the regime baseline is stated, that systematic silence becomes an VIII.f-pattern — the equal-terms treaty DOES survive on temple walls (Karnak, Ramesseum) in the Hittite and Egyptian versions alike, so the boasting is measurable policy, not news. The Oxyrhynchus case is the climate exhibit: ~500,000 papyrus fragments from the rubbish mounds vs almost none from Rome's damp soil — taphonomy, not literacy; Rome's papyrus 'silence' is evidence of groundwater, not of lesser bureaucracy. The honesty fence that keeps this from becoming a universal solvent: the baseline itself must be evidenced, not assumed. 'Of course nothing survived — it all burned' is unfalsifiable when the regime's archiving rate is unknown; the Alexandria single-fire telling died precisely on this (the expected survival was asserted, not measured — evt-library-alexandria-001 DEBUNKED). When the baseline is a guess, VIII.d governs; when it is a measurement, VIII.f governs; and the work of the historian is moving cases across that line by measuring denominators.
place: Oxyrhynchus (climate exhibit); Kadesh/Qadesh (regime exhibit); Herculaneum (denominator exhibit)

title: Marco Polo brought noodles to Italy from China
claim: Marco Polo, returning to Venice in 1295 from his years in Asia, brought noodles home from China, thereby introducing pasta to Italy.
place: Venice (the claimed homecoming, 1295)

title: Battle of Kadesh (c. 1274 BCE): the battle both kings claimed to win
claim: In year 5 of Ramesses II (c. 1274 BCE), Egyptian and Hittite armies fought at Kadesh on the Orontes (Tell Nebi Mend, south of Lake Homs, modern Syria) — one of the largest chariot battles of the Late Bronze Age. Both empires' records agree a battle happened; they do not agree on who won. The Egyptian version (the Poem and the Bulletin, inscribed at Karnak, Luxor, Abydos, Abu Simbel, the Ramesseum) tells it as a personal triumph of the pharaoh, who was deceived by Hittite spies, ambushed, and rallied his forces. The Hittite tradition tells it as a checked Egyptian invasion: Kadesh was never captured, and Ramesses withdrew south to Egypt. The modern scholarly reading is a stalemate: Ramesses survived near-disaster and drove the Hittites from the field on the second day, but failed to take the city — and Kadesh and Amurru, the disputed territory the battle was fought over, stayed Hittite. Egypt's 'victory' is a single-tradition claim.
place: Kadesh on the Orontes (Tell Nebi Mend) — pinned at Homs, Syria

title: The silence argument (VIII.d): absence of evidence is not evidence of absence — but it is not evidence either
claim: The synthesis-docket argument d ('Silence is ambiguous — Kadesh. Absence of evidence is not evidence of absence, but it is not evidence either'), stated as the timeline's method rule with its Kadesh exhibit and its honest refinement. The rule: (1) Silence is not evidence. Egyptian royal monuments never recorded defeats — Ramses II's Kadesh walls are proof of the mechanism — so the absence of an Egyptian record for an event (e.g., the Exodus, evt-exodus-001) is expected silence and moves no grade either way. (2) Silence IS informative where evidence would be expected: the expected-evidence refinement. The Babylonian chronicle series records Nebuchadnezzar's campaigns year by year through his 11th year (594 BCE); its silence on the 586/587 BCE destruction of Jerusalem is silence at the tablets' edge, not silence inside the coverage — an honest, narrow distinction the record carries. And the Kadesh correction: if we had only Ramesses's wall, 'Egypt won' would be the record. The Hittite account exists, and the 1258 BCE treaty between equals exposes the stalemate.
