The rule's discipline is the schema's falsifiability line: a claim cannot be rescued by 'absence of evidence' unless it states what evidence WOULD exist if it were true — the standard the timeline's contact-proof-bar record (evt-contact-proof-bar-001) states in advance. (3) The failure mode, named: 'absence of evidence' used as an apologetic blanket that excuses every failed prediction. That is the rule misused, and the misuse is itself a pattern the map can mark.
place: Kadesh on the Orontes (the exhibit's geography)

title: The silence argument (VIII.d): absence of evidence is not evidence of absence — but it is not evidence either
claim: The synthesis-docket argument d ('Silence is ambiguous — Kadesh. Absence of evidence is not evidence of absence, but it is not evidence either'), stated as the timeline's method rule with its Kadesh exhibit and its honest refinement, strengthened 2026-10-16 with an independent philosophical formulation and a public-domain literary form. The rule: (1) Silence is not evidence. Egyptian royal monuments never recorded defeats — Ramses II's Kadesh walls are proof of the mechanism — so the absence of an Egyptian record for an event (e.g., the Exodus, evt-exodus-001) is expected silence and moves no grade either way. (2) Silence IS informative where evidence would be expected: the expected-evidence refinement. The Babylonian chronicle series records Nebuchadnezzar's campaigns year by year through his 11th year (594 BCE); its silence on the 586/587 BCE destruction of Jerusalem is silence at the tablets' edge, not silence inside the coverage — an honest, narrow distinction the record carries. (3) The independent formulation: Timothy McGrew, 'The Argument from Silence' (Acta Analytica, 2013) — arguments from silence are distinctive precisely because 'there is typically a source (or set of sources) from which the evidence is (rightly or wrongly) expected'; it is the absence of evidence from THAT source that drives the argument. McGrew's treatment is a philosopher's version of the timeline's expected-evidence refinement, arrived at from logic rather than from the Kadesh walls — convergence on the rule from an independent discipline. (4) The literary form: Doyle's 'Silver Blaze' (1892, public domain) — the dog that did not bark in the night tells Holmes the intruder was no stranger. Silence is informative only where a bark was expected. (5) The Kadesh correction stands: if we had only Ramesses's wall, 'Egypt won' would be the record. The Hittite account exists, and the 1258 BCE treaty between equals exposes the stalemate — re-verified 2026-10-16 (Bryce: both sides claimed victory; modern reading a stalemate; treaty of Kadesh, year 21 of Ramesses II, 1258 BCE, earliest known international peace treaty). The rule's discipline is the schema's falsifiability line: a claim cannot be rescued by 'absence of evidence' unless it states what evidence WOULD exist if it were true — the standard the timeline's contact-proof-bar record (evt-contact-proof-bar-001) states in advance. (6) The failure mode, named: 'absence of evidence' used as an apologetic blanket that excuses every failed prediction. That is the rule misused, and the misuse is itself a pattern the map can mark.
place: Kadesh on the Orontes (the exhibit's geography)

title: Treaty of Kadesh (c. 1258 BCE): the earliest surviving international peace treaty
claim: In year 21 of Ramesses II (c. 1258 BCE), Egypt and Hatti signed the Treaty of Kadesh between Ramesses II and the Hittite king Hattusili III (Muwatalli II's brother and successor) — sixteen years after the Battle of Kadesh, and ending the borderland conflicts in Syria. The treaty was written on a silver tablet; a Hittite cuneiform clay copy was excavated at Hattusa (now in the Istanbul Archaeology Museum), and an Egyptian version survives on papyrus and temple walls (Karnak, Ramesseum). Its terms: mutual non-aggression, mutual defense against external enemies, and extradition of fugitives. It is widely described as the earliest known surviving international peace treaty; a replica hangs at the United Nations headquarters. The treaty's existence is evidence that the Kadesh-era stalemate held: it is a treaty between equals, not a victor imposing terms.
place: Treaty concerns Kadesh region on the Orontes (Homs, Syria); texts found at Hattusa (Turkey) and Karnak (Egypt)

title: The Admonitions of Ipuwer (Papyrus Leiden I 344 recto)
claim: The Admonitions of Ipuwer survive in a single damaged hieratic manuscript, Papyrus Leiden I 344 recto (Rijksmuseum van Oudheden, Leiden), a 19th-Dynasty copy (c. 1250 BCE) of a Middle Kingdom composition (late 12th Dynasty, c. 1850-1700 BCE) in the Egyptian 'national distress' lament genre; a sage named Ipuwer laments a world turned upside down ('the river is blood', rank reversals, Asiatics in the Delta).
place: Rijksmuseum van Oudheden, Leiden (findspot unknown, probably Memphis-Saqqara area)

title: The Merneptah Stele: earliest mention of 'Israel'
claim: Pharaoh Merneptah's victory stele (c. 1207 BCE) names 'Israel' as a people in Canaan — the earliest known extra-biblical attestation of the name.
place: Thebes (find spot)

title: The cowrie as currency
claim: The money cowrie (Monetaria moneta, syn. Cypraea moneta), harvested chiefly in the Maldives, circulated as a genuine currency across the Indian Ocean world and West Africa for centuries: a Bengal standard (3,840 shells to the rupee in the 19th century), a regular West African market currency from the 16th to the 19th century, and the 'sine qua non' of the European slave trade's purchasing price — before collapsing under 19th-century inflation when European traders flooded West Africa with cheaper Zanzibar cowries.
place: Maldives (harvest) → Bengal → Bight of Benin/West Africa (circulation)

title: The yazatas of the Avesta
claim: The Avesta — the Zoroastrian scripture — attests a developed angelology: named divine beings called yazatas ('worthy of worship'), who serve as the good powers under Ahura Mazda, each with a domain (Mithra of contract, Sraosha of conscience and the soul's journey, Rashnu of judgment, Anahita of waters, Tishtrya of rain, Verethragna of victory). The Yashts (hymns 5, 8, 10, 13–19) are dedicated to individual yazatas; the Yasna liturgy invokes them collectively.
place: Eastern Iran / southern Central Asia (Bactria–Margiana; the Avestan composition zone — disputed)

title: 'The face that launched a thousand ships' — Helen's abduction as the war's cause
claim: That the Trojan War was caused by Paris's abduction (or elopement) of Helen of Sparta — 'the face that launched a thousand ships' as a historical casus belli.
place: Hisarlik (Troy), Tevfikiye, Çanakkale Province, Turkey

title: The Trojan Horse — the Greeks took Troy in a giant wooden horse
claim: That the Greeks captured Troy by concealing soldiers inside a giant wooden horse, which the Trojans dragged through their own gates, after which the soldiers emerged at night and opened the gates — the horse mechanism as history, as literally described.
place: Hisarlik (Troy), Tevfikiye, Çanakkale Province, Turkey

title: Troy VIIa burned ~1180 BCE — a city destroyed, an attacker unnamed
claim: That Troy VIIa — the Late Bronze Age city at Hisarlık — suffered violent destruction by fire around 1180 BCE, with evidence of attack (arrowheads, unburied dead, emergency food stores, a packed lower town). The agent of destruction (Greek attackers, earthquake, or both) is contested.
place: Hisarlik (Troy), Tevfikiye, Çanakkale Province, Turkey

title: 'The Phoenicians invented the alphabet' — the schoolbook claim
claim: The Phoenicians invented the alphabet around 1050 BCE — the schoolbook version: the Phoenician abjad as the first true alphabet.
place: The Levantine coast (Byblos, Tyre, Sidon — the Phoenician cities that did the standardizing, not the inventing)

title: The monumental Iron I structure at Tel Shiloh
claim: The Associates for Biblical Research (ABR) excavations at Tel Shiloh (Khirbet Seilun), in their 2025 and 2026 seasons, exposed a monumental Iron I building; the June 2026 season located its southern wall, allowing the full footprint to be reconstructed — east-west orientation, proportions reported to match the biblical Tabernacle's dimensions (Exodus 26–27). The season also recovered a bent-axis city gate (1 Samuel 4's Eli's gate) and three Middle Bronze Age storage jars with charred grain beneath the later deposits.
place: Tel Shiloh (Khirbet Seilun), West Bank

title: The Shiloh structure as the biblical Tabernacle
claim: The monumental Iron I structure excavated at Tel Shiloh (2025–2026 ABR seasons) is the biblical Tabernacle — the portable sanctuary that housed the Ark of the Covenant at Shiloh.
place: Tel Shiloh (Khirbet Seilun), West Bank

title: The Yellow River's first prehistoric diversion (~3000–2600 BP): the Taihang-foothill course
claim: Around 3000–2600 years before present, the lower Yellow River underwent a dramatic channel displacement — its first prehistoric diversion documented in the sediment record — flowing northward into the Bohai Sea through the foreland depression along the eastern foothill of the Taihang Mountains. Frequent floods after ~3000 BP infilled the lower-reach depressions, accelerating the formation of the North China Plain and driving human migration from the Taihang piedmont into the central plain.
place: Eastern Taihang foothills foreland / North China Plain (diversion pathway into the Bohai Sea)

title: David, king of Israel
claim: David (traditional dates c. 1040-970 BCE) founded a dynasty centered on Jerusalem; the 9th-century Tel Dan stele's reference to the 'House of David' provides extra-biblical attestation of his dynasty.
place: Jerusalem

title: David, king of Israel
claim: David (traditional dates c. 1040-970 BCE) founded a dynasty centered on Jerusalem; the 9th-century Tel Dan stele's reference to the 'House of David' provides extra-biblical attestation of his dynasty.
place: Jerusalem

title: The Witch of Endor (1 Samuel 28)
claim: The biblical narrative in which King Saul, on the eve of battle, consults a medium at Endor who summons the spirit of the prophet Samuel, who prophesies Saul's defeat and death.
place: Endor (traditional, Jezreel Valley)

title: The Ark of the Covenant in Axum
claim: That the Ark of the Covenant — the gilded acacia-wood chest of the Hebrew Bible holding the tablets of the Ten Commandments, last attested in Jerusalem before the Babylonian sack of 586 BCE — is currently kept in the Chapel of the Tablet at the Church of Our Lady Mary of Zion in Axum, Ethiopia, seen only by a single guardian monk who may not leave the compound.
place: Axum (Aksum), Tigray Region, Ethiopia — Church of Our Lady Mary of Zion

title: Genealogies as Political Documents
claim: Biblical genealogical lists functioned as political and theological documents: their editors telescoped generations, selected or reordered names, and used schematic numbering to make arguments, so the lists cannot be read as complete literal family trees.
place: Jerusalem (compositional setting of the compiled lists)

title: The burning: one night against witchcraft
claim: The Maqlû ('burning') series — eight tablets of nearly a hundred anti-witchcraft (kišpū) incantations plus a ritual tablet of incipits and directions — records a single complex ceremony performed over one night at the end of the month Abu (July/August), when spirits moved between the netherworld and the living world; figurines of the witch were burned, and the ritual deliberately does not name the witch, trusting the gods to know the target. Mature form early first millennium BCE; performance attested by the exorcist Nabû-nādin-šumi's correspondence with Esarhaddon.
place: Assyria (Nineveh court)

title: Solomon and the First Temple
claim: Solomon (traditional dates c. 970-930 BCE), son of David, built the First Temple in Jerusalem and ruled a united monarchy of Israel and Judah at its greatest extent.
place: Jerusalem (traditional Temple location)

title: Solomon and the First Temple
claim: Solomon (traditional dates c. 970-930 BCE), son of David, built the First Temple in Jerusalem and ruled a united monarchy of Israel and Judah at its greatest extent.
place: Jerusalem (traditional Temple location)

title: The Genesis flood narrative
claim: The Genesis flood narrative (Genesis 6-9) is a composite text — the Priestly and Yahwist sources interwoven — with a final form from the Persian period (5th c. BCE). Its structure (divine warning, ark, pitch caulking, birds released, sacrifice, divine promise) parallels the earlier Mesopotamian flood tradition so closely — down to specific plot sequences (the three-bird release: dove, swallow, raven in Gilgamesh XI vs raven, dove in Gen 8; the post-flood sacrifice and the deity's 'sweet savor' response) — that the scholarly majority holds the Genesis account was composed in literary dependence on the Mesopotamian tradition (Atrahasis/Gilgamesh), circulating via shared scribal culture.
place: Judah/Yehud (composition context)

title: The fravashis: Zoroastrian guardian spirits
claim: The Avesta attests the fravashis (fravartis): guardian spirits — the pre-existing, higher doubles of every living being (humans, animals, even Ahura Mazda and the yazatas themselves) — who protect the soul, warn and admonish it through life, and return to the celestial realm at death. Yasht 13 (the Fravardin Yasht) is the dedicated hymn; the fravashis preside over the 19th day of the Zoroastrian month and the first month (Farvardin), whose feast (farvardin jashan) is kept especially by those who lost kin in the preceding year.
place: Eastern Iran / southern Central Asia (Bactria–Margiana; the Avestan composition zone — disputed)

title: The Pentateuch as a composite work
claim: The Pentateuch (Genesis-Deuteronomy) is a composite work assembled from multiple literary strata and redactional layers over several centuries, not a single composition by Moses in the Late Bronze Age; the classical four-source map (JEDP) is one model of those strata, not a settled document inventory.
place: Jerusalem / Yehud (compositional and redactional setting)

title: The Mesha Stele, Line 31 — the contested 'House of David' reading
claim: Line 31 of the 9th-century BCE Mesha Stele (the Moabite Stone, found 1868 at Dhiban, now in the Louvre) reads 'bt[d]wd' — 'House of [Da]vid' — which would be a second extra-biblical attestation of the Davidic dynasty, older than the Tel Dan stele. The reading is genuinely contested and unresolved.
place: Dhiban (biblical Dibon), Jordan

title: The Tel Dan Stele
claim: A 9th-century BCE Aramaic victory stele from Tel Dan, erected by a king of Damascus (likely Hazael), contains the phrase 'House of David' (bytdwd) — independent evidence for David's dynasty.
place: Tel Dan

title: The Goatherd Kaldi Discovers Coffee (legend)
claim: A 9th-century Abyssinian goatherd named Kaldi discovered coffee when his goats became energetic and 'danced' after eating red berries from a certain shrub; he tasted the berries himself and brought them to a monastery.
place: Kaffa region, Ethiopian highlands (legend's setting)

title: The Carthage Tophet: urns, stelae, and the very young
claim: At Carthage and other Phoenician-Punic settlements, walled precincts called tophets held thousands of urns with cremated infant remains beneath votive stelae dedicated to Tanit and Baal Hammon — a ritual deposition of the very young, c. 800-146 BCE.
place: Salammbo, Carthage (Tunisia) — the Tophet precinct

title: YHWH's courtroom: the Hebrew Bible's own divine council
claim: The Hebrew Bible preserves a working divine council, not a discarded metaphor: Psalm 82 opens 'God stands in the council of El (baʿădat-ʾēl)' and verse 6 declares 'I said, you are gods, sons of the Most High'; 1 Kings 22:19–23 stages a courtroom — 'I saw YHWH sitting on his throne, and all the host of heaven standing beside him on his right and on his left,' debating strategy and commissioning a 'lying spirit'; Job 1:6 and 2:1 show 'the sons of God came to present themselves before YHWH'; Daniel 7:10 has 'a thousand thousands served him, and ten thousand times ten thousand stood before him.' And the Deut 32:8–9 textual variant proves the council concept was live and being edited: 4QDeutj (Dead Sea Scrolls, ~2nd c. BCE) reads 'according to the number of the SONS OF GOD' (bĕnê ʾĕlōhîm), the Septuagint reads 'angels of God,' while the later Masoretic Text reads 'sons of Israel' — two oldest witnesses against the standardized one, with the lectio difficilior ('sons of God') original (Heiser 2001; Skehan 1954; NRSV renders 'according to the number of the gods'). The older reading makes Elyon divide the nations among his divine sons, with YHWH receiving Jacob as his allotted portion.
place: Jerusalem / Judea (textual origin)

title: Manu's flood
claim: Manu's flood: the Shatapatha Brahmana (1.8.1) tells of Manu warned by a fish (the Matsya avatar of Vishnu) of a great flood; he builds a ship, the fish tows it to the northern mountain, and Manu survives to become the progenitor of mankind. One of the earliest non-Mesopotamian flood narratives with the warned-survivor-ship structure (c. 8th-6th c. BCE). It shares the skeleton — warning, vessel, surviving seed of humanity — with the Mesopotamian and Genesis floods, graded as a literary attestation, not a dated event.
place: Kuru-Pancala region (Brahmana composition context)

title: The Greek vowel innovation (8th c. BCE)
claim: In the 8th century BCE the Greeks adapted the Phoenician consonantal abjad by repurposing unused consonant signs as vowels — aleph became alpha, he became epsilon, yod became iota, ayin became omicron — creating the first true alphabet: a writing system that records vowels as well as consonants, and the ancestor of the Latin and Cyrillic scripts.
place: Greece (Dipylon, Athens — the oinochoe's findspot; the adaptation's exact location is unknown)

title: The Indian rope trick as an ancient feat — the legend that began in Chicago
claim: The classic Indian rope trick — a fakir throws a rope into the air, it stays rigid without visible support, a boy climbs it and vanishes at the top, the magician climbs after him and throws down the boy's dismembered limbs, and the boy reappears unharmed — was actually performed as an ancient feat in India.
place: India (where the legend locates the feat)

title: The messengers: mal'akhim, cherubim, seraphim, and the divine council
claim: The Hebrew Bible attests, across textual layers spanning roughly eight centuries, to a populated heaven: mal'akhim ('messengers' — over 200 occurrences, about half human and half heavenly), the mal'akh YHWH who speaks as God himself, cherubim (throne-guardians), seraphim (Isaiah 6 only), the bene elohim and the divine council, named angels only in the latest texts (Gabriel, Michael — Daniel), and ha-satan as a title ('the accuser') becoming a proper name only in the latest text (1 Chronicles 21:1).
place: Ancient Judah (textual origin)

title: The terra-cotta oil lamp: the Mediterranean's light
claim: The terra-cotta oil lamp was the dominant source of artificial light across the Mediterranean world for millennia — a palm-sized clay vessel of oil and a wick, mass-produced in Roman times by named workshops whose stamps survive on the clay.
place: The Mediterranean basin; factory cluster at Mutina (Modena), Italy

title: The Sulba diagonal rule — Baudhayana's general statement, c. 800-500 BCE
claim: The Baudhayana Sulba Sutra — the earliest of the Indian Sulba Sutras, appendices to the Vedas giving rules for constructing sacrificial altars — states the diagonal rule in general form: the rope stretched along the diagonal of a rectangle produces the area which the vertical and horizontal sides produce together. An explicit general statement of the Pythagorean relationship, conventionally dated centuries before Pythagoras.
place: Northern India (Vedic cultural zone — no findspot; textual tradition)

title: 'They burned their own children' — the systematic-sacrifice interpretation of the Tophet
claim: The Carthaginians systematically sacrificed their own live, healthy children — burning firstborns to Baal Hammon and Tanit as a regular rite, not an emergency measure.
place: Salammbo, Carthage (Tunisia) — the Tophet precinct

title: The winged angel: a popular image the text never describes
claim: In the Hebrew Bible, the mal'akhim (angels, 'messengers') are never described as having wings. They appear as men: Abraham feeds three of them lunch in Genesis 18, the men of Sodom mistake two of them for human travelers in Genesis 19, and Hebrews 13:2 preserves the tradition that one might entertain angels unawares. Wings in the Hebrew Bible belong exclusively to two distinct classes — the cherubim (Exodus 25:20, Ezekiel 10) and the seraphim (Isaiah 6:2, 6, 7) — which the texts treat as separate from angels in general. The winged angel of Christmas trees, paintings, and popular imagination is a later artistic convention (early Christian art, 4th century CE onward), not a biblical description.
place: Ancient Judah (textual origin); the image belongs to later Christian art

title: The Bur-Sagale Eclipse — the 15 June 763 BCE anchor
claim: The Neo-Assyrian eponym (limmu) list entry for the year of the official Bur-Sagale records a solar eclipse in the month Simanu; modern retrocalculation identifies it as the total solar eclipse of 15 June 763 BCE (proleptic Julian calendar). This identification is the keystone anchoring the Neo-Assyrian absolute chronology (912–609 BCE).
place: Assur, Assyria (observation point inferred; computed greatest-eclipse point lies east of the Caspian at 38.9N 54.3E — the identification depends on ΔT-corrected visibility at Assur/Nineveh)

title: The Bur-Sagale Eclipse — the 15 June 763 BCE anchor (second pass, 2026-10-16)
claim: The Neo-Assyrian eponym (limmu) list entry for the year of the official Bur-Sagale records a solar eclipse in the month Simanu; modern retrocalculation identifies it as the total solar eclipse of 15 June 763 BCE (proleptic Julian calendar). This identification is the keystone anchoring the Neo-Assyrian absolute chronology (912–609 BCE).
place: Assur, Assyria (observation point inferred; computed greatest-eclipse point lies east of the Caspian at 38.9N 54.3E — the identification depends on ΔT-corrected visibility at Assur/Nineveh)

title: The pyramids of Nubia
claim: The Kingdom of Kush built roughly 255 pyramids in Sudan — at El-Kurru, Nuri, Jebel Barkal, and Meroë (Begrawiya) — from 751 BCE through the Meroitic period (c. 350 CE): steeper (~70°), smaller-footprint royal tombs with attached chapels, numbering more than twice Egypt's 118–138.
place: Meroë / Begrawiya (representative necropolis; El-Kurru, Nuri, Jebel Barkal also pinned)

title: The Olympian assembly: Zeus's council in Homer
claim: Homer's Olympus runs on council procedure: the gods are formally summoned to assembly (Iliad 20.4–30: Zeus bids Themis 'call the gods to council in the starry hall' — the senate of the skies convenes, every god seated on marble thrones, Zeus presiding and announcing his policy), deliberate, and vote by acclaim; the Odyssey opens in council (1.26–95: the gods assembled at Zeus's house, Athena opening the case for Odysseus while Poseidon is absent at the Ethiopians' feast — absence counted, debate recorded); and Iliad 16.433–461 shows the council's limit: Zeus holds the golden scales for Hector but does not overrule fate. The Olympian assembly is the Greek world's picture of how power is exercised among unequals — a constitutional monarchy of gods with Zeus as chairman, not absolute sovereign.
place: Ionia (composition); Mount Olympus (imagined setting)

title: Pazuzu: the demon you hire
claim: The demon Pazuzu — first attested in the late 8th century BCE — was invoked in amulets and healing rituals as protection AGAINST the demoness Lamashtu: Mesopotamians used one feared spirit to ward off another.
place: Assyria/Babylonia

title: The Kushite pharaohs — Egypt's 25th Dynasty
claim: The 25th Dynasty of Egypt (c. 747–656 BCE) was a line of Kushite (Nubian) kings — Piye, Shabaka, Shebitku, Taharqa, Tantamani — who conquered and ruled all of Egypt for ninety-one years, restoring temples, reviving Old and Middle Kingdom art, and being expelled only by the Assyrian Empire.
place: Thebes (representative seat of Kushite rule in Egypt; Napata in Nubia)

title: The Qedarites — the Arab tribal confederacy of the Neo-Assyrian annals, and the biblical Kedar ethnonym
claim: A North Arabian tribal confederation called Qedar (KUR qi-id-ri / qa-da-ri) is attested across Neo-Assyrian royal inscriptions of the 8th–7th centuries BCE: queen Zabibe's tribute to Tiglath-Pileser III (738 BCE, the first explicit mention), Tiglath-Pileser's 733 BCE campaign against queen Samsi south of Damascus, and further attestations under Sennacherib, Esarhaddon, and Ashurbanipal (including the war against Abi-Yate' the Qedarite, RINAP 5 Ashurbanipal 11 IX 36). Assyrian sources name seven Arab queens (Zabibe, Samsi, Yati'e, Apkallatu, Te'elhunu, Tabu'a, Adiya) ruling the Arabs — documented female leadership of a confederacy whose trade routes (Damascus, Tyre, incense aromatics) the empire bargained with. The biblical Kedar (qēdār, 'dark') — second son of Ishmael in Genesis 25:13 — recurs as an ethnonym across the prophetic corpus: the glory of Kedar (Isaiah 21:16–17), the archers and mighty men of Kedar, the tents and flocks of Kedar (Jeremiah 49:28–32), the princes of Kedar trading with Tyre (Ezekiel 27:21), 'I dwell among the tents of Kedar' (Psalm 120:5), 'black as the tents of Kedar' (Song 1:5). The ethnonym Qedar/Kedar is real and independently multiply attested. The kinship frame — 'Kedar, son of Ishmael' — is the biblical tradition's claim about that ethnonym, not the Assyrian record's.
place: North Arabian desert oases, south of Damascus toward the northern Hejaz (traditional)

title: Isaiah 7:14: almah to parthenos
claim: Isaiah 7:14's Hebrew reads ha-almah ('the young woman'); the Septuagint's 3rd-2nd-century-BCE Jewish translators rendered it parthenos ('virgin'); the Gospel of Matthew (1:23) quotes the Greek, not the Hebrew — so the 'virgin birth prophecy' reading enters the record at the translation, centuries after the oracle.
place: Jerusalem (oracle); Alexandria (translation)

title: Hesiod's golden-race daimones: the word's original meaning
claim: In Works and Days (lines 122-126), Hesiod says the men of the golden race, once the earth covered them, became 'pure daimones' dwelling on the earth — kindly guardians of mortal men who roam everywhere 'clothed in mist,' keep watch on judgments and cruel deeds, and give wealth. This is the earliest surviving attestation of daimōn as a class of guardian spirit-beings, and it fixes the word's original semantic range: benevolent, intermediary, never worshipped, never evil.
place: Boeotia (composition); pan-Hellenic circulation

title: The Hanging Gardens at Nineveh (Dalley's relocation)
claim: The 'Hanging Gardens' were built at Nineveh by the Assyrian king Sennacherib (r. 704-681 BCE), a century before Nebuchadnezzar: his prism inscriptions describe an 'unrivalled palace' and a high garden 'a wonder for all peoples' imitating the Amanus mountains, watered by a bronze water-raising screw and the Jerwan aqueduct system.
place: Nineveh (near Mosul, Iraq)

title: The Great Wall of China
claim: The Great Wall of China is a system of fortification walls, trenches, passes, and watchtowers built across northern China by multiple states and dynasties from the 7th century BCE through the Ming dynasty (1368-1644). The first comprehensive archaeological survey (State Administration of Cultural Heritage, 2007-2012) measured 21,196.18 km of wall-related remains across 15 provinces; Ming-era structures alone were preliminarily measured at 8,850 km.
place: Badaling — representative Ming-era section; the system spans 15 provinces, Shanhaiguan to Jiayuguan

title: Lilith: the name's fifteen-century paper trail
claim: The name 'Lilith' has a continuous written trail across ~1,500 years: a single biblical occurrence (Isaiah 34:14, 'night creature' — rendered 'screech owl' in the KJV), the first clear supernatural usage in the Songs of the Sage (4Q510/11, late 1st c. BCE), Talmudic mentions (b. Shabbat 151b; b. Eruvin 18b; b. Niddah 24b), the incantation bowls (Lilith bound by name; Ktar-Lilith iconography), and the medieval Alphabet of Ben Sira — the name's attestation CORROBORATED as belief-phenomenon; the first-wife story is a separate, later claim (see evt-lilith-first-wife-genesis-001).
place: Ancient Judah (textual origin); Qumran; Sasanian Babylonia

title: The shedim: the Jewish tradition's attested demons
claim: The Jewish textual tradition attests across ~1,300 years to a population of harmful spirits called shedim: from the Hebrew Bible (Deuteronomy 32:17; Psalm 106:37 — sacrifices 'to shedim'), through the Testament of Solomon's demon register (1st–3rd c. CE), the Babylonian Talmud's demonology (Pesachim 109b–112a; Gittin 68a–b on Ashmedai; Eruvin 18b on Adam's 130 years), to the late-antique Aramaic incantation bowls that bind named demons — the belief-phenomenon, not the entities.
place: Ancient Judah / Babylonia (textual origin; bowls from the Sasanian east)

title: The Nile's lost branches — Canopic and Pelusiac, and the capital the river abandoned
claim: The Nile Delta once carried a branching distributary network (Herodotus 2.17 counts seven mouths) that has collapsed to essentially two. The Canopic branch — the river of Naukratis, founded in Dynasty 26 (c. 685–525 BCE) at the strategic point within the delta — is now silted up (Pennington & Thomas 2016, via Bunbury et al. 2019), as are others of the former branches (Stanley & Warne 1993). The Pelusiac branch, the easternmost, was traced on the deltaic plain east of the Suez Canal in the 1973 Science survey; its lower reaches died by silting c. AD 25 under prograding beach accretion. Pi-Ramesse (Qantir, built over Avaris), Ramesses II's Delta capital with its chariot workshops and stables, was sited on the Pelusiac branch; when the branch dried, the city was abandoned and its monuments moved to Tanis (21st Dynasty). The delta head itself migrated, first south then north, across the pyramid age (Bunbury et al. 2019).
place: Nile Delta — the defunct Canopic and Pelusiac branches

title: The Library of Ashurbanipal at Nineveh (7th c. BCE)
claim: The Library of Ashurbanipal at Nineveh (7th c. BCE) was the ancient world's oldest organized state library: ~30,000+ cuneiform tablets and fragments gathered by royal acquisition, catalogued with colophons, organized by subject in the South-West and North Palaces, and preserved because the fire that destroyed Nineveh in 612 BCE baked the sun-dried tablets into ceramic.
place: Nineveh (Kuyunjik mound, Mosul, Iraq) — the South-West and North Palaces

title: Thales of Miletus
claim: Thales of Miletus (c. 624-546 BCE) is traditionally regarded as the first Greek philosopher, proposing water as the fundamental principle of nature and reportedly predicting a solar eclipse.
place: Miletus

title: Etemenanki, the ziggurat of Babylon
claim: Etemenanki — 'house of the foundation platform of heaven and earth' — was a seven-stage mudbrick ziggurat at Babylon dedicated to Marduk, rebuilt by Nebuchadnezzar II (604–562 BCE). The Esagila tablet gives its plan as seven stages, 91 meters high on a 91-meter square base; German excavations confirmed a 91.5-meter square base with a triple staircase on the south side.
place: Etemenanki, Babylon (Al Hillah, Iraq)

title: The Hanging Gardens of Babylon (traditional attribution)
claim: The Hanging Gardens — one of the canonical Seven Wonders of the ancient world — stood in the city of Babylon, built by Nebuchadnezzar II (r. 605-562 BCE), traditionally for his Median wife Amytis, as a terraced garden imitating her mountainous homeland.
place: Babylon (traditional location — unattested archaeologically)

title: The 'seventy years' as exact captivity chronology
claim: The Babylonian captivity lasted exactly seventy years — a precise demographic chronology of Judah's exile (the 'seventy years' of Jeremiah 25 and 2 Chronicles 36:21).
place: Babylon (the captivity's location in the tradition)

title: The Book of Daniel — the exile's file, in two stages
claim: The book of Daniel is a two-stage composition: Aramaic court tales (chapters 2-6, plus 7) rooted in the exile/Persian-era storytelling tradition, and visions (chapters 7-12) in their final form from the Maccabean crisis, c. 165 BCE. The dating rests on the ex eventu signature (the 'predictions' are accurate down to Antiochus IV Epiphanes and then fail), the Hebrew/Aramaic language division (Hebrew 1:1-2:4a and 8-12; Aramaic 2:4b-7:28), and Qumran's eight Daniel manuscripts, which put the book in circulation by the mid-2nd century BCE at the latest.
place: Babylon (the book's claimed setting)

title: The Decalogue in two versions: Exodus 20 vs Deuteronomy 5
claim: The Ten Commandments exist on the documentary record in at least two different versions inside the canonical Hebrew Bible itself: Exodus 20:2-17 and Deuteronomy 5:6-21. The versions differ materially: the Sabbath commandment's rationale (Ex 20:11 — God rested after six days of creation; Deut 5:15 — 'remember that you were a slave in the land of Egypt'), the order of the coveting commandment's objects (Ex 20:17: 'your neighbor's house... your neighbor's wife'; Deut 5:21: 'your neighbor's wife... your neighbor's house'), and the wording of the preamble's closing. The 'word-for-word' telling of the Decalogue — one fixed dictation, transmitted unchanged — fails on the documentary record before any archaeology is consulted. The words on the stone, as written, come in two drafts.
place: Mount Sinai (the tradition's own geography for the giving; the comparison is documentary, not excavated)

title: The Tower of Babel was Etemenanki
claim: The tower of Genesis 11:1–9 — built in 'the land of Shinar' at 'Babel' — is the ziggurat Etemenanki at Babylon. This is the mainstream scholarly identification.
place: Etemenanki, Babylon (Al Hillah, Iraq)

title: The Babylonian Exile
claim: Nebuchadnezzar II of Babylon captured Jerusalem (597 BCE; Babylonian Chronicle) and destroyed the First Temple (586/587 BCE; biblical chronology), deporting Judah's elite to Babylon; returns began under Cyrus (538 BCE decree tradition), but Judahite communities persisted in Babylonia and the Temple was not rebuilt until Darius I (516/515 BCE).
place: Babylon (destination of the deportees)

title: The Jehoiachin ration tablets (Babylon, 592 BCE)
claim: Babylonian palace ration tablets from Nebuchadnezzar II's 13th year (592 BCE) record oil rations to 'Ya'ukin, king of the land of Judah' (Yaukin = Jehoiachin), his five sons, and other Judeans — the Babylonian administration's own record of the exiled king, five years after the 597 deportation.
place: Babylon, southern palace area near the Ishtar Gate (findspot)

title: 'Yahweh' — the scholarly reconstruction of the divine-name pronunciation
claim: The scholarly reconstruction of the Tetragrammaton's pronunciation is 'Yahweh' — the best current reading of how ancient Hebrew speakers said YHWH.
place: Jerusalem — locus of the divine-name tradition

title: The 'empty land' telling
claim: The popular reading that Nebuchadnezzar's 586/587 BCE conquest emptied the land of Judah entirely — 'the land enjoyed its sabbaths' (2 Chronicles 36:21) taken as literal demography: everybody deported, nobody left.
place: Mizpah (Tell en-Nasbeh) — Babylonian administrative center after 586 BCE

title: Judaism's formation: from Judahite kingdom to portable religion
claim: Between the 6th century BCE (exile, First Temple destruction) and the 2nd century BCE (Maccabees), Judahite religion transformed into Judaism — a Torah-centered, synagogue-bearing identity carried in exile and diaspora; the word 'Judaism' (Ioudaismos) first appears in print in 2 Maccabees (2:21; 8:1; 14:38), late 2nd century BCE.
place: Jerusalem (with Elephantine at 24.08 N, 32.89 E and Babylon at 32.54 N, 44.43 E as diaspora nodes)

title: The Eclipse of Thales — the battle interrupted, 28 May 585 BCE
claim: A solar eclipse interrupted the battle between the Lydians and the Medes near the Halys river, prompting the armies to break off fighting and make peace (Herodotus 1.74). Modern retrocalculation fixes it to 28 May 585 BCE (proleptic Julian).
place: Battle on the Halys (Kızılırmak) frontier, Anatolia

title: The Eclipse of Thales — the battle interrupted, 28 May 585 BCE
claim: A solar eclipse interrupted the battle between the Lydians and the Medes near the Halys river, prompting the armies to break off fighting and make peace (Herodotus 1.74). Modern retrocalculation fixes it to 28 May 585 BCE (proleptic Julian). The eclipse itself is firm; everything about Thales's foreknowledge is the legend (see evt-thales-001).
place: Battle on the Halys (Kızılırmak) frontier, Anatolia

title: The al-Yahudu archive (Judean exiles in Babylonia, 572-477 BCE)
claim: The al-Yahudu archive — roughly 200 cuneiform tablets (572-477 BCE), 103 published by Pearce & Wunsch (2014) — documents Judean exiles as tenant farmers, taxpayers, litigants, and merchants in Babylonian villages including al-Yahudu ('Judah-town'): an exiled community living ordinary economic lives, not languishing in chains.
place: al-Yahudu ('Judah-town'), Babylonia — actual village location unknown; the tablets are unprovenanced

title: Pythagoras of Samos
claim: Pythagoras (c. 570-495 BCE) founded a religious-philosophical community at Croton; the Pythagorean theorem tradition is attached to his name, though no writings of his survive.
place: Samos (birthplace, traditional)

title: Pythagoras of Samos — the name on the theorem (attribution autopsy)
claim: Pythagoras of Samos (c. 570-495 BCE) founded a religious-philosophical community at Croton; the Pythagorean theorem tradition is attached to his name. The attachment is late doxography: no source within five centuries of Pythagoras connects him to the theorem — the attribution rides Proclus's 5th-century CE commentary on Euclid I.47, citing the lost History of Geometry of Eudemus (4th c. BCE), roughly a thousand years after Pythagoras; the ox-sacrifice-on-discovery legend comes through Apollodorus via Diogenes Laertius 8.12. Plato and Aristotle never connect Pythagoras to the theorem. Burkert's Lore and Science in Ancient Pythagoreanism (1972): the earliest brotherhood was a religious community, and the 'mathematical Pythagoras' is largely later construction. The relationship itself was in working use in Old Babylon ~1,200 years before his birth (evt-pythagorean-triples-babylon-001); Euclid's Elements I.47 (c. 300 BCE) is the earliest fully verifiable proof and does not name Pythagoras.
place: Samos (birthplace, traditional)

title: The Buddha (Siddhartha Gautama)
claim: Siddhartha Gautama, the Buddha, taught the Four Noble Truths and the Eightfold Path in northern India; tradition dates him 563-483 BCE, though modern scholarship favors c. 480-400 BCE.
place: Lumbini (traditional birthplace)

title: Cyrus the Great
claim: Cyrus II of Persia (reigned c. 559-530 BCE) conquered Media, Lydia, and Babylon, founding the Achaemenid Empire. The Jewish return tradition credits Cyrus with a decree permitting the exiles to return (Ezra 1; Aramaic version in Ezra 6); the Cyrus Cylinder itself does not mention Judah or the Jews.
place: Pasargadae (Cyrus's capital)

title: Confucius
claim: Confucius (Kong Qiu, 551-479 BCE) of Lu taught ethics centered on ren (humaneness) and li (ritual propriety); his disciples compiled his sayings in the Analects, which became foundational to East Asian thought.
place: Qufu, Lu state (traditional)

title: The Achaemenid Empire — Persia, 550–330 BCE
claim: The Achaemenid Empire (c. 550–330 BCE), founded by Cyrus the Great, was the largest empire the ancient world had seen — about 5.5 million km² at greatest extent under Darius I and Xerxes I, spanning three continents, administered through satrapies, linked by the Royal Road and a state postal system, and documented in its own trilingual royal inscriptions and tens of thousands of administrative clay tablets.
place: Persepolis, Fars, Iran (empire-wide record; pinned at the ceremonial capital)

title: The Cyrus Cylinder as 'first declaration of human rights'
claim: The Cyrus Cylinder is the world's first declaration of human rights, in which Cyrus the Great freed the Jewish exiles from Babylon and granted religious freedom to all peoples of his empire.
place: Babylon (findspot of the cylinder)

title: The Cyrus edict of return (Ezra's decree tradition)
claim: Cyrus the Great issued a decree in his first year (538 BCE) permitting the Jewish exiles in Babylonia to return to Jerusalem and rebuild the Temple, with royal support.
place: Babylon (where the decree tradition originates)

title: The Boyce thesis: Zoroastrian angelology → Second Temple Jewish angelology
claim: Mary Boyce's thesis: the angelology of post-exilic Judaism — the named, ranked heavenly court of the Second Temple period (the archangels, the watchers) — was developed after the pattern of the Zoroastrian Amesha Spentas and yazatas, under the influence of Persian-period contact (c. 538–332 BCE), when Judah lived under Achaemenid rule and Jews 'entertained warm feelings thereafter for the Persians,' making them receptive to Zoroastrian influence (Boyce, Zoroastrians: Their Religious Beliefs and Practices, 1979; crystallized in Boyce & Grenet, A History of Zoroastrianism vol. 3, 1991, pp. 404–405).
place: Jerusalem / Yehud (the Persian-period Jewish province where the influence is claimed to have landed)

title: The Abrahamic offshoots tree: a shared patriarch, claimed by three traditions
claim: Judaism, Christianity, and Islam each ground their origins in the figure of Abraham — the shared 'Abrahamic' lineage is a genuine feature of each tradition's own foundational texts (Hebrew Bible, New Testament, Qur'an), not a modern scholarly invention. The tree is the map of that shared tradition-claim; it is not a verified genealogy of a verified person.
place: Jerusalem / the shared sacred geography

title: Adon to Adonis: the Semitic root behind the Greek god
claim: The Greek Adonis derives from the Semitic title adon ('lord') — the Byblos cult's god, carried into the Greek world; his explicit resurrection references are largely of the Christian era.
place: Byblos (origin) to the Greek world (transmission)

title: Attis: the Phrygian lament and the argued return
claim: The Phrygian/Gallo-Roman tradition attests Attis as a dying-and-rising figure of the Cybele cult, with the Hilaria festival of March 25 celebrated as his return/rebirth — but the 'resurrection' half of the story is the weakest of the five columns, largely a later Roman reading of an older Phrygian lament tradition.
place: Phrygia (central Anatolia)

title: "Liubo was chess" — the identity claim
claim: Liubo, the Han-dynasty Chinese board game, was an early form of chess (i.e., the same game family, not merely a predecessor or inspiration).
place: Han China (liubo's attested range)

title: Dead Sea Scrolls
claim: ~900 manuscripts / tens of thousands of fragments from eleven Qumran caves (Bedouin discovery of Cave 1's seven scrolls incl. the Great Isaiah Scroll, 1947); c. 250 BCE-68 CE (paleography, stratified archaeology, radiocarbon converge).
place: (varies by record — see sources)

title: Elephantine Papyri
claim: The Judean military colony at Yeb/Elephantine (Upper Egypt) left ~100 Aramaic papyri and ostraca (495-399 BCE), including the Passover letter of 419 BCE (TAD A4.1) and the 407 BCE petitions to rebuild the Yahw temple destroyed in 410 BCE (TAD A4.7/A4.8).
place: (varies by record — see sources)

title: The Deucalion flood
claim: The Greek Deucalion flood: Deucalion and Pyrrha survive a Zeus-sent flood in a chest/ark (larnax), land on Parnassus, and repopulate the world by casting stones ('the bones of the mother'). Attested in Pindar (Olympian 9), Apollodorus (Library 1.7.2), and Ovid (Metamorphoses 1.313-415) — a literary tradition, not a dated event. It shares the ark/bird/landfall skeleton of the Mesopotamian story at a structural level, via the common ancient Near Eastern/Mediterranean flood-memory pool, not direct copying.
place: Mount Parnassus, Phocis (mythic landfall)

title: Ioudaismos First Use
claim: The Greek word Ioudaismos first occurs in surviving literature in 2 Maccabees — 2:21 and 8:1 (the epitomist's preface; admitting to Judas Maccabeus's forces only those 'who had remained in Judaism'), set against Hellenismos; recurs 2 Macc 14:38, 4 Macc 4:26, Galatians 1:13-14. 2 Maccabees dates to the late 2nd c. BCE (c. 124 BCE).
place: (varies by record — see sources)

title: Ketef Hinnom Amulets
claim: Two tiny rolled silver amulets (KH1, KH2) with paleo-Hebrew variants of the priestly blessing (Numbers 6:24-26), excavated 1979 from burial-cave repository 24 at Ketef Hinnom, Jerusalem (Gabriel Barkay's team; first published Biblical Archaeology Review 9.4, 1983).
place: (varies by record — see sources)

title: Mishnah
claim: The Mishnah — 63 tractates in six Sedarim, the earliest systematic rabbinic legal work, redacting Tannaitic traditions; rabbinic tradition attributes redaction to Judah ha-Nasi, c. 200 CE (scholarly consensus ~190-220 CE).
place: (varies by record — see sources)

title: Moses's horns: qaran to cornuta
claim: Exodus 34:29's Hebrew says Moses's face qaran ('was radiant,' 'shone'); Jerome's Vulgate (late 4th c. CE) rendered it cornuta est ('was horned'); Michelangelo's Moses (1513-1515, San Pietro in Vincoli, Rome) wears the Latin's horns — a fifteen-hundred-year-old translation choice, in marble.
place: San Pietro in Vincoli, Rome (the statue); the Hebrew belongs to the Exodus tradition

title: Sacrificed Son Unnamed
claim: The Qur'an names the son Abraham was commanded to sacrifice as Ishmael
place: (varies by record — see sources)

title: The Samaritan temple on Mount Gerizim (5th c. BCE - 110 BCE)
claim: A Yahwistic sanctuary stood on Mount Gerizim's summit from the Persian period (5th century BCE), massively expanded under the Hellenistic kings into a city and sacred precinct, and was destroyed by John Hyrcanus I c. 110 BCE.
place: Mount Gerizim summit, Samaria

title: Yehud Coinage
claim: Small silver fractional coins inscribed YHD (the Achaemenid province 'Judah/Yehud'), many imitating Athenian owl types; Persian-period series mid-4th c. BCE (c. 350-333 BCE), die typology extending to ~30 BCE.
place: (varies by record — see sources)

title: The '300 vs Millions' reading of Thermopylae — DEBUNKED
claim: At Thermopylae, 300 Spartans alone faced millions of Persian soldiers — the pop version of the battle (the school shorthand, Frank Miller's 1998 graphic novel, Zack Snyder's 2007 film): three hundred men against an army counted in the millions.
place: Thermopylae (the Hot Gates), Phthiotis, Greece — the reading is about this pass

title: The Battle of Thermopylae, 480 BCE
claim: In late August/early September 480 BCE, a Greek allied force under the Spartan king Leonidas I held the pass of Thermopylae against the Persian invasion army of Xerxes I for two full days of battle; after the mountain path was betrayed, the rear guard — 300 Spartans, 700 Thespians, and others — was annihilated on the third day and the pass was forced.
place: Thermopylae (the Hot Gates), Phthiotis, Greece

title: The Murasu archive (Judean descendants in Babylonia, 455-403 BCE)
claim: The Murasu archive — roughly 800 legal texts from Nippur (455-403 BCE, excavated 1893) — records the business of a single family across four generations, with some 80 distinctively Judean personal names among its clients: the exiles' descendants, still identifiably Judean a century-plus after the fall, as tenants and entrepreneurs in Persian-period Babylonia. A large Judean community stayed and thrived rather than returning.
place: Nippur (excavation site)

title: The dating of the Jewish-Samaritan 'schism' (the single-break telling)
claim: Jews and Samaritans split at one datable moment: Nehemiah 13:28's priest expelled for marrying Sanballat's daughter, or Josephus's Manasseh-and-Sanballat temple-founding story (Ant. 11.302-347).
place: Mount Gerizim / Jerusalem (the two claimants)

title: The Kingdom of Aksum
claim: That the Kingdom of Aksum — centered on Axum in the Ethiopian highlands, c. 400 BCE–c. 960 CE, at its height spanning the Red Sea into Himyar (Yemen) — was a literate, minting, trading empire: trilingual royal inscriptions (Ge'ez, Sabaean, Greek), giant granite stelae, the first sub-Saharan African minted coinage (gold/silver/bronze), the Red Sea trade hub at Adulis, and the 4th-century CE conversion to Christianity under King Ezana.
place: Axum (Aksum), Tigray Region, Ethiopia

title: Socrates's daimonion: the sign that only ever said no
claim: Plato's Apology (31c-d, 40a-b) and Xenophon's Memorabilia (1.1.2-4) attest that Socrates experienced a daimonion — 'a divine thing,' a voice or sign that came to him since childhood and always held him back from actions he was about to take, never urging him forward. The same charge appears in the indictment at Apology 24b-c ('introducing new daimonia'). The attestation is graded as belief-phenomenon: the texts attest what Socrates reported and what Athens heard, not the sign's metaphysical status.
place: Athens

title: Eros the great daimon: the middle term of the cosmos
claim: In the Symposium (202d-203a), Diotima teaches Socrates that Eros is neither god nor mortal but a 'great daimon' (daimon megas) — an intermediary power whose work is to interpret and convey between gods and men: carrying prayers and sacrifices upward and commands and rewards downward, 'filling the space between' so that the whole is bound together. This is the most explicit classical statement of the daimon as the middle term of the cosmos.
place: Athens (composition); dramatic setting: Agathon's house, Athens

title: Alexander the Great
claim: Alexander III of Macedon (356-323 BCE) conquered the Persian Empire from Greece to India in twelve years, founding cities including Alexandria and spreading Hellenistic culture across three continents.
place: Pella (birthplace and capital of Macedon)

title: The Mieza Royal Gymnasium identified as Aristotle's school where Alexander was tutored (Sept 2026 announcement)
claim: The excavated royal complex at ancient Mieza, northern Greece — the Didaskaleion (teaching area) with lecture rooms and stone benches, a three-part banquet complex with mosaic floors, palaestra, stadium and 200-meter running track — is the royal school where Aristotle tutored the young Alexander (c. 343–340 BCE). The Hellenic Ministry of Culture announced the identification in early September 2026 from the ongoing excavation led by Angeliki Kottaridi (work began 2024 under a Ministry–Municipality of Naoussa agreement). The complex dates to Philip II's reign; its architecture closely resembles Philip's palace at Aigai. Independent scholars (Graham Wrightson, Jeanne Reames) publicly endorsed the identification; Miltiades Hatzopoulos cautioned it is probably right but awaits a peer-reviewed publication of the evidence.
place: Mieza (ancient town; Royal Gymnasium / Didaskaleion complex), near Naoussa, northern Greece — ~43 km from Pella

title: Alexander's consultation of the oracle of Zeus-Ammon at Siwa (331 BCE)
claim: In early 331 BCE, Alexander the Great marched across the Libyan desert from the Mediterranean coast to the Siwa oasis and consulted the oracle of Zeus-Ammon at the Ammoneion (Oracle Temple, Aghurmi), where the priests publicly greeted him as the son of the god.
place: Oracle Temple of Zeus-Ammon (Ammoneion), Aghurmi, Siwa Oasis, Matrouh Governorate, Egypt

title: Alexandria-on-the-Tigris (Charax Spasinou) — location confirmed at Jebel Khayyaber
claim: Alexander the Great founded the port city of Alexandria-on-the-Tigris in 324 BCE on his return from the Indus Valley; the city (later renamed Charax Spasinou) stood at Jebel Khayyaber in southern Iraq, and its location — first proposed by John Hansman in 1965 — was confirmed in early 2026 by the Charax Spasinou Project (Stefan Hauser, University of Konstanz) using aerial/drone photography, caesium-magnetometer geophysics, and over 500 km² of surface survey, revealing a planned grid, harbor/canal works, and residential blocks among the largest in the ancient world.
place: Jebel Khayabir (spelled 'Khayyaber' in some 2026 reporting), Al-Qurna District, Basra Governorate, southern Iraq — the Alexandria-on-the-Tigris / Charax Spasinou site

title: The death of Alexander at Babylon and the lost tomb
claim: Alexander III died at Babylon on 11 June 323 BCE (29 Ajaru), after about ten days of fever, at age 32. The medical cause is unattested: poisoning, malaria, typhoid, West Nile virus, Guillain-Barre syndrome, and pancreatitis are all modern retro-diagnoses from symptom lists written ~400 years later. His body was carried to Memphis then Alexandria by Ptolemy I; the tomb survived into the Roman period (Augustus visited it) and is now lost — the famous 'Alexander Sarcophagus' from Sidon is not his (it belonged to Abdalonymus, king of Sidon).
place: Babylon (death place); Alexandria, Egypt (tomb — location lost)

title: The death of Alexander at Babylon and the lost tomb
claim: Alexander III died at Babylon on 11 June 323 BCE (29 Ajaru), after about ten days of fever, at age 32. The medical cause is unattested: poisoning, malaria, typhoid, West Nile virus, Guillain-Barre syndrome, and pancreatitis are all modern retro-diagnoses from symptom lists written ~400 years later. His body was carried to Memphis then Alexandria by Ptolemy I; the tomb survived into the Roman period (Augustus visited it) and is now lost — the famous 'Alexander Sarcophagus' from Sidon is not his (it belonged to Abdalonymus, king of Sidon).
place: Babylon (death place); Alexandria, Egypt (tomb — location lost)

title: The 300-year source gap behind Alexander's life
claim: No contemporary continuous account of Alexander's life survives. The five surviving full-length ancient narratives — Diodorus (1st c. BCE), Curtius Rufus (1st c. CE), Plutarch (c. 46–c. 120 CE), Arrian (c. 86–160 CE), and Justin's epitome of Pompeius Trogus (2nd/3rd c. CE) — were all written centuries after Alexander's death in 323 BCE, each drawing on lost eyewitness and near-eyewitness works: Callisthenes (court historian), Ptolemy, Aristobulus, Onesicritus, and Nearchus, which survive only as fragments quoted in later authors. The historical Alexander is therefore reconstructed through intermediaries, and every statement about him must be weighted by the distance of its chain.
place: Alexandria, Egypt (composition center of the lost traditions and the Romance; the Library as the symbol of what survived and what burned)

title: The pagan-to-Christianity borrowing claim (dying-and-rising)
claim: Early Christianity borrowed its death-and-resurrection narrative from the pagan dying-and-rising gods of the surrounding world (Osiris, Tammuz/Adonis, Attis, Baal).
place: Eastern Mediterranean (the Hellenistic religious marketplace)

title: The Great Library of Alexandria — the institution
claim: The Great Library of Alexandria was a real institution: part of the Mouseion (Place of the Muses) founded under Ptolemy I Soter and brought to fruition under Ptolemy II Philadelphus, advised by Demetrius of Phaleron, that aggressively acquired scrolls (Galens ship-search account), produced the Pinakes of Callimachus (a 120-book catalogue), and employed Zenodotus, Apollonius of Rhodes, Eratosthenes, Aristarchus of Samothrace, and Hero — with a daughter library established at the Serapeum under Ptolemy III.
place: Alexandria, Egypt (Brucheion royal quarter, traditional; no excavated building securely identified)

title: Manetho's Osarseph account (via Josephus)
claim: The 3rd-century BCE Egyptian priest-historian Manetho wrote an account, preserved in Josephus's Contra Apion (1.26-31), in which a renegade Egyptian priest named Osarseph (Osarsiph) led a group of polluted/lepers who seized Egypt for a time, were expelled, and — at the end of the story — Osarseph took the name Moses.
place: Avaris (Tell el-Dab'a, per Manetho's setting)

title: The Maya hieroglyphic script — deciphered
claim: The Maya hieroglyphic script is a fully functional logosyllabic writing system that records spoken Mayan languages, and it has been substantially deciphered — the great majority of its signs can now be read.
place: Maya lowlands (southern Mexico, Guatemala, Belize, western Honduras, El Salvador)

title: The Samaritan tenth commandment: Mount Gerizim
claim: The Samaritan Pentateuch's Decalogue carries a tenth commandment absent from the Jewish and Christian versions: a commandment to build an altar on Mount Gerizim (commanded, the Samaritan text says, as Moses received it), constructed from the Deuteronomy 27:4 altar-command with 'Gerizim' in place of 'Ebal.' The Samaritan tradition thus holds that the Ten Commandments number ten differently — the same covenant, a different tenth word. The 'word-for-word' telling of the Decalogue fails a second time: the commandments were counted differently by living communities, not only copied differently by scribes.
place: Mount Gerizim (the Samaritan Decalogue's tenth word; the comparison is documentary across living traditions)

title: Saqqara Bird glider claim
claim: The Saqqara Bird (sycamore-wood carving, ~200 BCE) is a model of a glider, proving ancient Egyptians understood aerodynamics.
place: Saqqara necropolis, Egypt (now Egyptian Museum, Cairo)

title: The Translation Rule (VIII.i synthesis)
claim: A claim's evidence grade can turn on a translation choice: the earliest surviving witness to a text is often a translation, and the translation is a new, separately dated claim — so the timeline grades the crossing, not just the source. Where the Hebrew says one thing and the Greek, Latin, or English says another, the grade follows the word.
place: Jerusalem (oracle) / Alexandria (Septuagint) / Bethlehem (Vulgate) — the rule spans the crossings

title: The Pharos of Alexandria (early 3rd c. BCE)
claim: The Pharos of Alexandria — the great lighthouse on the island of Pharos off Alexandria, Egypt — was a purpose-built monumental navigational tower constructed in the early 3rd century BCE (commissioned under Ptolemy I Soter, traditionally completed under Ptolemy II Philadelphus), attributed to the architect Sostratus of Cnidus; it stood in three tiers (square base, octagonal middle, cylindrical top), burned a furnace-fed beacon by night (with a polished-bronze mirror reported for day), endured earthquakes from 956 CE onward with the 1303 Crete quake decisive, and its stones were reused for the Citadel of Qaitbay built on the site in 1477.
place: Island of Pharos, Alexandria, Egypt (site of the Citadel of Qaitbay)

title: Baghdad battery
claim: The 'Baghdad battery' vessels (Khujut Rabu'a, near Baghdad) were ancient electric batteries, proving knowledge of electrochemistry ~2,000 years before Volta.
place: Khujut Rabu'a, northeast of Baghdad, Iraq

title: The three Genesis 5 number traditions
claim: The Adam-to-Noah genealogy's begetting ages differ systematically across the Masoretic Text, the Samaritan Pentateuch, and the Septuagint, yielding three different Adam-to-Flood totals — 1656, 1307, and 2242 years — while the patriarchs' total lifespans mostly agree.
place: Textual tradition: Jerusalem (MT), Samaria (Samaritan Pentateuch), Alexandria (LXX)

title: Eratosthenes measures the Earth (c. 240 BCE)
claim: Around 240 BCE, Eratosthenes of Cyrene — librarian at Alexandria — measured the Earth's circumference using the summer-solstice shadows at Syene and Alexandria: the 7.2° shadow angle (1/50 of a circle) times the 5,000-stadia intercity distance gave ~250,000 stadia.
place: Alexandria (with Syene/Aswan)

title: Jewish reception: almah was the young woman next door
claim: Pre-Christian Jewish reading of Isaiah 7:14 was non-messianic and contemporary: Targum Jonathan renders 'the young woman is pregnant' (Aramaic 'ulaymta, no virginity term) with no messianic language at 7:14 (though it reads 9:5-6 and 11:1 messianically); Rashi reads the almah as Isaiah's own wife ('My wife will conceive this year. This was the fourth year of Ahaz') and rejects the Hezekiah identification on chronology; Ibn Ezra agrees. The 2nd-c. CE Jewish Greek revisers (Aquila, Symmachus, Theodotion) all render neanis ('young woman'), correcting the LXX's parthenos. The 'virgin' reading enters via the Septuagint, which Matthew 1:23 quotes.
place: Jerusalem (oracle); Alexandria (LXX)

title: The Nazca Geoglyphs
claim: The Nazca lines and geoglyphs — ~800 straight lines, 300 geometric figures, and dozens of biomorphic figures (hummingbird, spider, monkey, condor) up to hundreds of meters long on the coastal pampa of southern Peru — are human-made works created by the pre-Incan Nazca culture (c. 200 BCE–700 CE) by clearing dark, sun-oxidized surface stones to expose the pale gypsiferous subsoil beneath; shallow grooves only a few centimeters deep, preserved by the hyper-arid climate.
place: Nazca pampa, Ica region, Peru

title: The oldest extant paper: Fangmatan, early 2nd c. BCE
claim: Paper was already being made in China by the early 2nd century BCE — the Fangmatan Tomb 5 map fragment is the oldest extant sheet of paper on Earth.
place: Fangmatan, near Tianshui, Gansu

title: Parchment was invented at Pergamum under a papyrus embargo
claim: Parchment — prepared animal skin used as a writing surface — was INVENTED at Pergamum in the 2nd c. BCE, when King Eumenes II's scribes, cut off from Egyptian papyrus by Ptolemy's export ban during the Alexandria-Pergamum library rivalry, were forced to invent the material (the 'pergamena' story, from Pliny NH 13.21 citing Varro).
place: Pergamum (Bergama, Turkey) — the claimed site of the invention

title: The Pergamum Library — Alexandria's Hellenistic rival
claim: Pergamum under Eumenes II (197-158 BCE) built the ancient world's great rival to the Alexandrian library — ~200,000 scrolls by literary report, in a library building excavated in the 1880s (Carl Conze's team) with wall niches for the rolls — and the Pergamene workshop refined parchment (pergamena) into a durable, smooth writing surface; the 'Antony gave Cleopatra the 200,000 Pergamene scrolls' episode (Plutarch, Antony 58.9) is single-source and untested.
place: Pergamum (Bergama, Turkey) — the acropolis library building near the sanctuary of Athena

title: The Jewish-internal resurrection lineage (Daniel, 2 Maccabees, Josephus)
claim: Bodily resurrection belief was already documented inside Second Temple Judaism before Christianity: Daniel 12:2 (c. 165 BCE), 2 Maccabees 7 (c. 124 BCE), and Josephus's report of Pharisaic doctrine (Jewish War 2.163) — the proximate, textually chained source of the early Christian resurrection concept.
place: Jerusalem / Judea

title: The cruse of oil: Hanukkah's eight-day miracle telling
claim: When the Temple in Jerusalem was rededicated in 164 BCE, a single cruse of pure oil bearing the High Priest's seal burned for eight days instead of one — the oil miracle is the original account of Hanukkah.
place: Jerusalem — the Temple

title: The Temple rededication of 164 BCE — the festival before the miracle story
claim: In 164 BCE, on the 25th of Kislev, the Maccabees rededicated the Jerusalem Temple after defeating the Seleucids and celebrated for eight days — the festival that became Hanukkah.
place: Jerusalem — the Temple

title: The Nash Papyrus: the oldest Decalogue, and it is not the Masoretic one
claim: The Nash Papyrus (Cambridge University Library, MS Or.233) is a second-century BCE (c. 150-100 BCE) Hebrew manuscript containing the Decalogue followed by the start of the Shema (Deut 6:4-5). Four fragments, 24 lines, acquired from an Egyptian antiquities dealer by W. L. Nash (1898/1902, published by S. A. Cooke 1903); before the Dead Sea Scrolls it was the oldest Hebrew biblical text known. Its Decalogue harmonizes Exodus 20 and Deuteronomy 5, accords closely with the Septuagint's Exodus 20, orders the later commandments Adultery-Murder-Steal (the LXX order, not the Masoretic Murder-Adultery-Steal), and omits the phrase 'house of bondage' (used in both Masoretic versions) — plausibly a reflection of its Egyptian composition setting. The manuscript is not a scroll but a single sheet, likely a phylactery/tefillin extract or a liturgical copy matching the Second-Temple daily recitation (m. Tamid 5:1). The oldest Decalogue we own does not match the Masoretic text in any hymnal.
place: Cambridge University Library, Cambridge, UK (MS Or.233; alleged Fayyum, Egypt provenance fenced)

title: The word-for-word Decalogue transmission telling
claim: The Ten Commandments have been transmitted word-for-word identical from Moses to the present day, with no variation, no alternate versions, and no textual development. FALSE: the documentary record carries the Decalogue in multiple differing versions — Exodus 20 vs Deuteronomy 5 (different Sabbath rationales, different wording), the Nash Papyrus (2nd c. BCE, a harmonized pre-Masoretic text that matches neither), and the Samaritan tenth commandment (Mount Gerizim, absent from Jewish and Christian versions). The 'word-for-word' telling is the 293rd DEBUNKED family: the identical-transmission telling.
place: Jerusalem (textual tradition; witnesses span Egypt, Samaria, Qumran)

title: The Silk Road trade network (c. 130 BCE – c. 1500 CE)
claim: A long-lived, braided network of overland and maritime trade routes connected China, Central Asia, Persia, India, and the Mediterranean world for roughly sixteen centuries — many routes, not one road.
place: Samarkand (the road-city that taxed it)

title: The Aztecs built the pyramids of Teotihuacan
claim: The Mexica (Aztecs) built the pyramids of Teotihuacan — the Pyramid of the Sun, the Pyramid of the Moon, and the Temple of the Feathered Serpent.
place: Teotihuacan, Valley of Mexico

title: Seven years' bad luck for a broken mirror — the Roman attribution
claim: The folklore that breaking a mirror brings seven years of bad luck is said to be Roman in origin — the Romans supposedly believed the gods watched mortal souls through mirrors, and that the body renewed itself every seven years, so the bad luck would expire at the next renewal. The Roman attribution is asserted by modern pop outlets; no primary Latin source is cited by any of them, so it sits one grade below folklore-with-a-trail.
place: Rome (claimed origin; unproven)

title: The gougu rule — China's own right-triangle tradition
claim: The Chinese gougu (勾股) tradition carries the right-triangle relationship under its own name: the Zhou Bi Suan Jing preserves the 3-4-5 triangle and the gou-gu-xian (勾股弦) rule, and Zhao Shuang's 3rd-century CE commentary gives a dissection diagram — right triangles arranged inside a square, areas compared — a visual demonstration of the theorem in a non-Euclidean style.
place: China (textual tradition; no findspot)

title: Jinn in pre-Islamic Arabia: the Palmyrene ginnayê and the poets
claim: Beings named as jinn (or the Aramaic ginnayê) were attested in Arabia before Islam: Palmyrene inscriptions dedicate offerings to the 'good and rewarding gods' ginnayê, and pre-Islamic poetic tradition ascribes poetic inspiration and soothsaying to jinn companions.
place: Palmyra region (inscriptions); the Arabian Peninsula (poetic tradition)

title: Magdala — the archaeology of Mary's hometown
claim: The town of Magdala (Migdal; Josephus's Tarichaea) on the Sea of Galilee's western shore has yielded a first-century Jewish town destroyed in 67 CE (Vespasian's campaign): a synagogue discovered in 2009 with the carved Magdala Stone (its seven-branched menorah, at the time of the IAA excavation report, the earliest known Second Temple-period menorah depiction outside Jerusalem), mosaic floors, mikvaot, and harbor works — and in September-October 2026 the excavation of a second first-century synagogue at the site (University of Haifa), reported as making Magdala the only known site with two Second Temple-period synagogues (the superlative is press framing, fenced; the excavation itself is the graded claim).
place: Magdala/Migdal, Sea of Galilee

title: The Roman lead-pipe water system (the foil)
claim: Roman cities distributed water through lead pipes (fistulae); lead levels in Roman tap water were measurably elevated (about 100 times natural background), though modern sediment-core analysis finds the contamination was unlikely to have been truly harmful.
place: Rome, Italy

title: Teotihuacan, the Classic-period metropolis of central Mexico
claim: Teotihuacan was a vast planned city in the Valley of Mexico, founded c. 100 BCE: at its zenith (c. 150–450 CE) it held 100,000–200,000 people, making it one of the largest cities in the world and the largest in the pre-Columbian Americas; its monumental core — the Pyramid of the Sun, the Pyramid of the Moon, the Avenue of the Dead, the Feathered Serpent Temple — was sacked and systematically burned c. 550 CE, and the city was abandoned by c. 750 CE.
place: Teotihuacan, Valley of Mexico

title: The gladiator's missio — mercy in the arena
claim: A defeated gladiator could appeal for mercy by raising an index finger (ad digitum); the munus's editor then granted or refused 'missio' (release), following the crowd's expressed wishes.
place: Amphitheatres of the Roman world (Colosseum as the type site)

title: The Sepulchre road toward Calvary (Stasolla's hypothesis, 2026)
claim: A broad stepped road uncovered in the Holy Sepulchre excavations, from the early-Roman phase before Hadrian's 2nd-century rebuilding, may have ascended toward the area of Calvary — providing access to a place of public executions. Stasolla's own words: 'One possibility – at present no more than a hypothesis.'
place: Church of the Holy Sepulchre, Jerusalem (traditional)

title: The invention of glassblowing (c. 50–25 BCE, Levant)
claim: Glassblowing was invented in the coastal Levant in the final quarter of the 1st century BCE.
place: Jerusalem (Jewish Quarter excavations)

title: The Library of Alexandria — the single-catastrophic-fire claim
claim: The Great Library of Alexandria was destroyed in a single catastrophic fire (Julius Caesar's fire of 48 BCE being the most-cited candidate).
place: Alexandria, Egypt (Brucheion quarter, traditional)

title: Jesus of Nazareth
claim: Jesus of Nazareth, a Jewish teacher in Roman Galilee and Judea, was crucified under Pontius Pilate (c. 30 CE); his followers proclaimed his resurrection, founding the movement that became Christianity.
place: Nazareth (traditional)

title: The claim that Jesus of Nazareth was born on December 25
claim: Jesus of Nazareth was born on December 25 — that the calendar date of his birth is known and is the 25th of December.
place: Bethlehem (traditional)

title: The James ossuary inscription
claim: The Aramaic inscription 'Ya'akov bar Yosef akhui di Yeshua' (James, son of Joseph, brother of Jesus) on the James ossuary is an authentic 1st-century inscription identifying the family of Jesus of Nazareth.
place: Reported as found near Silwan, Jerusalem (unverifiable — antiquities-market provenance)

title: Cova Dones Roman sanctuary — the Domina inscriptions (announced 2026-10-20)
claim: At Cova Dones (Millares, Valencia, Spain), the DONARQ project has documented at least 120 Latin inscriptions in an underground Roman sanctuary chamber more than 200 m below the surface — the largest Latin cave-inscription corpus known in the Roman Empire, surpassing La Griega (107). Most are dated by the team to the 1st–2nd centuries CE. Five votive inscriptions are dedicated to a goddess reverentially called Domina ('the Lady'), whose specific epithet (possibly water-connected) is still being read; preliminary readings indicate some women inscribed their own vows, and in-situ offerings include spindle whorls, rings, a bracelet, chalice-shaped vessels and a Roman coin of Claudius found in the 2024 campaign.
place: Cova Dones, Millares, Valencia, Spain

title: The folding fan was invented in Japan (~9th c.) and traveled Japan→China
claim: The folding fan (sensu/ōgi) was invented in Japan around the 9th century, in the hi-ogi form of thin cypress slats riveted at one end — and from Japan the folding fan traveled to China, not the reverse.
place: Heian-kyo (Kyoto), Japan

title: Mary Magdalene — the canonical figure
claim: Mary of Magdala is attested in the earliest Christian writings as a follower of Jesus: named among the women who 'provided for them out of their resources' (Luke 8:1-3, with the note that seven demons had gone out of her), named at the crucifixion (Mark 15:40; John 19:25), named at the burial (Mark 15:47), named first at the tomb in all four gospels (Mark 16:1; Matt 28:1; Luke 24:10; John 20:1), and in John 20:11-18 the first person commissioned to carry the resurrection claim ('go to my brothers'). 'Magdalene' is a place-name: Mary of Magdala/Migdal, the fishing town on the Sea of Galilee (Josephus, Jewish War 3.462, Tarichaea).
place: Magdala/Migdal, Sea of Galilee

title: The emergence of Christianity
claim: In the mid-1st century CE, the Jesus movement spread from Judea/Galilee through the eastern Roman Empire as distinct Christian communities, documented by Paul's letters and noted by Roman officials by the early 2nd century.
place: Jerusalem (traditionally the movement's origin)

title: 'Red sky at night, shepherd's delight' (verified folk meteorology)
claim: 'Red sky at night, shepherd's delight; red sky in the morning, shepherd's warning' — a red sunset presages fair weather the next day, and a red sunrise presages foul weather, because mid-latitude weather systems move from west to east.
place: England (mid-latitude saying; biblical and Shakespearean attestations)

title: 'This is my body': the institution narrative, earliest written form (~55 CE)
claim: The words of institution ('this is my body... this cup is the new covenant in my blood') are quadruply attested: 1 Cor 11:23-25 (~55 CE, the earliest written account, already a fixed liturgical formula predating the gospels), Mark 14:22-25, Matt 26:26-29, Luke 22:19-20. Whether ipsissima verba or early-church formulation is debated; an early meal tradition is not in doubt.

title: The Great Fire of Rome, July 64 CE
claim: The Great Fire of Rome broke out in the night of 18–19 July 64 CE (reign of Nero) and burned for six days and seven nights (Tacitus; Dio says nine days), devastating the city.
place: Rome, Italy — the 14 Augustan regions

title: Nero fiddled while Rome burned — the anachronistic legend
claim: Nero fiddled while Rome burned — the popular image of the emperor playing the violin during the Great Fire of Rome (July 64 CE).
place: Rome, Italy — the rumor's claimed scene

title: The Roman persecution of Christians
claim: The Roman state persecuted Christians across three centuries — episodic and regional, never continuous — documented by contemporary and near-contemporary sources: Tacitus on the Neronian scapegoating of 64 CE, the Pliny–Trajan exchange of c. 112 CE, the Decian universal-sacrifice edict and its 45 surviving libelli certificates of 250 CE, and the Diocletianic Great Persecution of 303–311 CE, closed by Galerius's 311 Edict of Toleration and the Milan letters of 313.
place: Rome (Neronian persecution); the phenomenon spans the empire, 64–313 CE

title: Jairus's daughter: 'the child is not dead but sleeping' (triple tradition)
claim: The raising of Jairus's daughter is triple-tradition (Mark 5:21-43; Matt 9:18-26; Luke 8:40-56): Jairus named (Mark/Luke), the daughter twelve years old, Peter/James/John taken inside, the mockers expelled, 'not dead but sleeping' (Mark 5:39), the Aramaic 'talitha koum' (Mark 5:41). The girl herself is NEVER named in any gospel, nor is her mother — the family cannot be traced further. Meier grants the raising stories a claim to historicity on multiple attestation; mainstream form-criticism treats the miracle element with reserve.

title: Joseph of Arimathea: the council member who buried Jesus
claim: Joseph of Arimathea — 'a respected member of the council' (Mark 15:43) — buries Jesus in all four gospels (Mark 15:43-46; Matt 27:57-60; Luke 23:50-53; John 19:38-42) plus the Gospel of Peter. For historicity: Brown/Meier argue via the criterion of embarrassment (an awkward Sanhedrin burial for the early church, a named checkable Jerusalem figure). Against: Crossan/Ehrman argue Mark created him to solve the body-disposal problem, since Roman practice left crucified corpses unburied. A 2004 JSHJ study splits the difference: Mark likely found the name in earlier tradition. Verdict: plausible, not proven. The Grail legends around him (Glastonbury, the blood-cup) are later accretions with no 1st-century root.

title: The women at the tomb: the least convenient, most consistent witnesses
claim: All four gospels agree the first witnesses of the empty tomb were women (Mary Magdalene named in all four; Mark 16:1-8; Matt 28:1-10; Luke 24:1-12; John 20:1-18) — witnesses whose testimony did not count in a first-century court. By the criterion of embarrassment, this is the strongest internal evidence that a memory rather than pure invention sits beneath the narratives: no inventor optimizing for ancient credibility chooses female witnesses.

title: The Murabba'at deeds — the revolt's legal paper trail
claim: The Wadi Murabba'at caves yielded legal documents of the Bar Kokhba administration's own calendar and bureaucracy: land leases dated 'year one / year two of the Redemption of Israel' — e.g. Mur 24E, a five-year tenancy at Herodium dated Shevat 20 of year two (~Jan/Feb 134 CE), 'of the Redemption of Israel by Shimeon ben Kosba, the nasi of Israel' — alongside the revolt-era divorce corpus: the Aramaic 'Masada get' (Joseph son of Naqsan to Miriam daughter of Jonathan, 'year six' = 72 CE, presented at Masada) and the Shelamzion document from Nahal Se'elim ('year three of the freedom of Israel' = 135 CE, naming Bar Kokhba 'nasi of Israel'). A Jewish legal system was operating under the revolt, in Aramaic, in its own year-count.
place: Wadi Murabba'at, ~11 km north of En-Gedi (Judean Desert)

title: 'Nero's sunglasses' — the emerald misreading (DEBUNKED)
claim: The Emperor Nero wore the first sunglasses — he watched the gladiatorial games through an emerald, which corrected or shaded his vision.
place: Rome (the arena Nero watched)

title: Pliny's sapo: soap's first Latin word (77-79 CE)
claim: The Latin word sapo (soap) appears first in a European language in Pliny the Elder's Natural History (77-79 CE): he describes soap manufactured from tallow and ashes as an invention of the Gauls ('Galliarum hoc inventum'), used principally as a hair pomade — and notes, disapprovingly, that among the Gauls and Germans men use it more than women.
place: Gaul (the manufacture Pliny describes)

title: The magnetic compass was invented in China — the Han spoon tradition and the Song nautical needle, ~150 years before Europe's first mention (c. 80 CE - 1088 CE)
