claim: The magnetic compass was invented in China, centuries before any European mention: a lodestone 'south-pointing spoon' (sinan) tradition in the Han era, a magnetized-needle compass for navigation by the Song dynasty, while Europe's first surviving description of the mariner's compass is Alexander Neckam's De naturis rerum, c. 1180-1190 — roughly a century and a half later.
place: Kaifeng / Song China (compass textual tradition)

title: Gamaliel: the historical teacher behind a composed speech (Acts 5)
claim: Gamaliel I is a real historical figure (Mishnah; Josephus Ant. 20; Acts 22:3 as Paul's teacher). But his Acts 5:34-40 speech — the one that freed the apostles from the Sanhedrin — is widely judged Lukan composition: set ~30s CE, it cites the revolt of Theudas BEFORE Judas of Galilee, yet Josephus dates Theudas to 44-46 CE and Judas to 6 CE. The person is historical; the freeing speech is a literary set-piece, not a transcript.

title: The 'Both Genealogies Are Literal Compatible Pedigrees' Telling
claim: Matthew 1 and Luke 3 are both complete, literal, historically compatible family trees of Jesus.
place: Jerusalem (compositional setting of the harmonization question)

title: The 'other disciple known to the high priest' (John 18:15-16)
claim: John 18:15-16 names an 'other disciple who was known to the high priest' who got Peter into the courtyard. Johannine-only attestation. Proposed identifications (Beloved Disciple/John son of Zebedee per Irenaeus — the strongest internal case via John 20:2; the Last Supper householder; an unnamed Jerusalem disciple) are all conjectural; Kok's objection stands (a Galilean fisherman with that social capital is hard to picture). Augustine's verdict holds: Scripture is silent — nothing above speculation.

title: Blood and water from the side (John 19:34-35): attested, read as theology
claim: John 19:34 (the soldier's spear; blood and water flow) with 19:35's explicit eyewitness claim is securely attested. Mainstream scholarship reads it theologically, not forensically: the water as the Holy Spirit given now that Jesus is glorified (cf. John 7:39), the blood as the Passover-lamb sacrificial motif (cf. m. Pesahim 5:3-5 on free-flowing sacrificial blood). Medical readings (pericardial fluid) exist but are secondary; the evangelist's interest is christological.

title: Nicodemus: the Johannine-only ruler of the Jews
claim: Nicodemus — 'a ruler of the Jews' (John 3:1) — appears only in John (3:1-21; 7:50-51; 19:38-42), absent from all three Synoptics. The proposed identification with the Talmudic Nicodemus ben Gurion is rejected by most scholars on dating/age grounds. Majority scholarly view: a representative Johannine figure (the sympathetic-but-secret insider), not an independently attested historical person.

title: The Testimonium Flavianum (Josephus on Jesus)
claim: Josephus's Antiquities of the Jews, Book 18 (written c. 93-94 CE), contains an authentic first-century core mentioning Jesus — his execution under Pontius Pilate and the survival of his followers — with later Christian interpolations overlaid on that core.
place: Rome (where Josephus wrote the Antiquities; the claim's subject is Roman Judea and Galilee)

title: The Babatha archive — a Jewish woman's legal papers, 94–132 CE
claim: A leather pouch holding 35 legal documents — wedding contracts (ketubot), property transfers, land registration, loans, guardianship petitions and summonses — written in Nabatean Aramaic, Judean Aramaic, and Greek and dated c. 94–132 CE, belonged to Babatha bat Shimon, a Jewish woman of Mahoza (Maoza) on the southeastern shore of the Dead Sea (the Nabatean kingdom until 106 CE, then the Roman province of Arabia). She carried the pouch with her when she fled to the Cave of Letters at Nahal Hever with other refugees at the end of the Bar Kokhba revolt (132–135 CE), and hid it in a crevice; she and the others died in the cave. Yigael Yadin's expedition found the pouch in 1961. The documents show a woman litigating, lending, inheriting and registering property under Roman bureaucracy.
place: Cave of Letters, Nahal Hever (Judean Desert); Babatha's Mahoza on the southeastern Dead Sea shore (modern Jordan)

title: The earliest New Testament manuscript fragments
claim: The oldest surviving physical copies of New Testament texts are 2nd–3rd century Greek papyrus fragments from Egypt, headed by P52 (Rylands Gr. P. 457, a fragment of John 18). No autograph — no authorial original — of any New Testament text survives.
place: John Rylands Library, Manchester (current holding; findspot in Egypt unknown)

title: The real history of the padded horse collar: Chinese origin, gradual European adoption
claim: The padded horse collar originated in China (Han-era depictions, documented in Joseph Needham's Science and Civilisation in China research), diffused westward, and was in European use by the High Middle Ages; the European shift from ox to horse draught was then gradual and governed by economics — relative animal prices, fodder (oat) costs, and land regimes (John Langdon, Horses, Oxen and Technological Innovation, 1986) — not a sudden collar-triggered breakthrough.
place: China (Han-era collar origin) → medieval Europe (diffusion, gradual adoption)

title: Cai Lun's 105 CE presentation (the real event)
claim: In 105 CE (the first year of Yuanxing), the Han court official Cai Lun presented an improved papermaking process — using tree bark (likely mulberry), hemp waste, old rags, and fishing nets — to Emperor He, and the court adopted it; the paper was thereafter called 'Cai Hou paper' (Caihou zhi).
place: Luoyang (Eastern Han capital, the imperial court)

title: The Cai Lun invented paper in 105 CE (DEBUNKED)
claim: Paper was invented by the Han court official Cai Lun in 105 CE.
place: Luoyang (Eastern Han capital, where the invention is said to have happened)

title: The Bar Kokhba letters — the revolt's own correspondence, 132–135 CE
claim: Roughly fifteen letters attributed to Shimon bar Kosiba (Bar Kokhba) survive in two groups: a Wadi Murabba'at group (early 1950s, via the antiquities market; published by the de Vaux expedition) and a Nahal Hever Cave of Letters group (1960–61, Yadin expedition, found in a tied bundle in a waterskin). They are addressed to subordinates — Yehonathan ben Be'ayan and Masabala, sitting at En-Gedi — and deal with military discipline, agricultural supplies, taxation, and the movement of people; most are in Aramaic, five in Hebrew, two in Greek; they are not internally dated. They sign the leader 'Shimeon ben Kosba, nasi (prince) of Israel' — the only contemporary voice of the revolt's leadership.
place: Cave of Letters, Nahal Hever (main group); Wadi Murabba'at group ~11 km north of En-Gedi

title: The great inversion: when daimōn became 'demon'
claim: In the 2nd-3rd centuries CE, Christian writers redefined daimones — previously neutral or benevolent intermediary beings in Greek usage — as wholly evil supernatural beings hostile to God and man: Justin Martyr (2 Apology 5) identifies the pagan daimones as the fallen angels of Genesis 6 who enslave mankind; Tatian and Origen (Contra Celsum) carry the identification forward. This is a semantic inversion inside the Christian tradition, not a discovery about the Greek texts: the English word 'demon' descends from the redefined Christian usage, while Hesiod, Plato, and Xenophon attest the earlier, non-evil range. Graded as belief-phenomenon: the redefinition is multiply attested; the beings' status is never adjudicated.
place: Rome, Alexandria, Caesarea (the writers' cities); the Greek texts they redefine are pan-Hellenic

title: The Gospel of Mary — a 2nd-century text about her, not by her
claim: The Gospel of Mary survives in a 5th-century Coptic codex (Papyrus Berolinensis 8502, bought in Cairo 1896, published 1955) plus two 3rd-century Greek fragments (P. Oxyrhynchus 3525; P. Rylands 463): a 2nd-century revelation dialogue in which the risen Savior gives Mary (understood as the Magdalene) private teaching, Peter challenges her authority ('Did he really speak with a woman privately, without our knowledge? Should we turn about and all listen to her?'), and Levi defends her. It was not written by Mary Magdalene and dates a century-plus after the events it describes.
place: Berlin (Papyrus Berolinensis 8502 repository)

title: The Martyrdom of Polycarp
claim: The letter of the church of Smyrna recounting the arrest, trial, and burning of bishop Polycarp in the stadium is a substantially authentic second-century document, not a later forgery. The core narrative is genuine; the dove emerging from the wound appears only in some manuscripts as a later insertion; the exact date (155/156 CE under Antoninus Pius vs. 167 CE under Marcus Aurelius) remains debated among scholars.
place: Smyrna (Izmir), stadium — the execution site per the letter

title: The Scillitan Martyrs (180 CE)
claim: The Acts of the Scillitan Martyrs — the record of the trial and execution of Speratus and six companions at Carthage on 17 July 180 CE — are substantially authentic proconsular court records, the earliest surviving Christian text written in Latin.
place: Carthage — the trial before the proconsul; Scilli the martyrs' home town

title: The Alexander Romance: the legend's literary afterlife
claim: The Alexander Romance (Pseudo-Callisthenes), composed at Alexandria c. 3rd century CE, is a work of fiction about Alexander — opening with the claim that his true father was the Egyptian sorcerer-king Nectanebo, not Philip II — which became the most influential Alexander narrative in the East. It survives in dozens of recensions across some eighty versions (Greek, Latin, Syriac, Arabic, Persian, Armenian, Ethiopic, medieval vernaculars). Byzantine chroniclers (e.g., John Malalas; the Excerpta latina Barbari, 8th c.) treated it as a historical source. As a literary tradition its existence and influence are multiply documented; as a source for the historical Alexander it is graded DEBUNKED.
place: Alexandria, Egypt (composition); recensions across Europe, the Near East, and the Indian Ocean world

title: The Babylonian Talmud — layered corpus, thin manuscript record
claim: The Babylonian Talmud is a layered rabbinic corpus — the Mishnah (redacted c. 200 CE) wrapped in the Babylonian Gemara, whose Amoraic arguments span c. 200–500 CE with Savoraic redaction and Geonic closure (c. 500–650 CE). Its surviving manuscript record is late and thin: the oldest surviving dated copy is Florence, Biblioteca Medicea Laurenziana, Plut. II.1.7–9 (dated 1175 CE), and Munich, Bayerische Staatsbibliothek, Cod.hebr. 95 (1342) is the only complete manuscript of the Babylonian Talmud; earlier witnesses survive only as Cairo Genizah fragments and citations in later works. The printed standard (Vilna/Romm 1880–1886) carries the censor's erasures — the 1553 Roman burnings under Julius III and the Russian expurgations are part of the record's own history.
place: Babylonia (Sura / Pumbedita academies; manuscripts in Florence, Munich, Cairo)

title: The Passion of Perpetua and Felicity (203 CE)
claim: The Passion of Perpetua and Felicity records the imprisonment and execution (7 March 203 CE, Carthage) of the noblewoman Perpetua — whose own prison diary (chapters 3–10) is one of the earliest surviving writings by a Christian woman — alongside her slave Felicity; the framing introduction/conclusion are by a later editor, and the authenticity of the diary portion is the mainstream position.
place: Carthage — prison and amphitheater per the Passio

title: Origen's Hexapla (six-column comparative edition)
claim: Origen of Alexandria compiled at Caesarea Maritima, before c. 240 CE, a six-column comparative edition of the Hebrew Bible: (1) the Hebrew in Hebrew characters, (2) the Hebrew transliterated into Greek (the Secunda), (3) Aquila, (4) Symmachus, (5) the Septuagint with asterisked additions (mainly from Theodotion) marking where the Greek had nothing for the Hebrew and obeloi marking where the Greek had no Hebrew beneath it, (6) Theodotion. The asterisked and obelized differences are openly marked, not silently rewritten.
place: Caesarea Maritima (compilation); surviving witnesses at Cairo and Milan

title: Camel or rope: the kamelos/kamilos variant
claim: In the 'eye of the needle' saying (Matthew 19:24 // Mark 10:25 // Luke 18:25), the mainstream Greek witnesses read kamelos ('camel'); a kamilos ('rope, ship's cable') variant appears in later witnesses, traced to Cyril of Alexandria (5th c. CE); Metzger characterizes it as 'an attempt to soften the rigor of the statement.' The variant is documented transmission-drift; the 'rope was the original' telling is rejected by the manuscript evidence.
place: Jerusalem/Judea (the saying); Alexandria (Cyril's variant)

title: The alchemists' successful transmutation of base metals into gold
claim: Medieval and early-modern alchemists succeeded in transmuting base metals into gold (chrysopoeia) — that they actually produced real gold from lead, iron, copper or mercury by alchemical or chemical means, before the twentieth century.
place: Strasbourg (Sethon projection, July 1602, before Dr Jacob Zwinger); Cologne (August 1603)

title: The 'great horse' study (Ameen et al. 2021) — the bones against the image
claim: The 'great horse' zooarchaeological study (Ameen et al. 2021, published/announced January 2022): 1,965 horse remains from 171 English sites, AD 300–1650 — the first large-scale osteoarchaeological assessment of medieval English horse size, showing medieval horses were markedly smaller than modern riding and draft horses, with the largest animals of the high medieval period reaching about 15–16 hands.
place: England (171 sites; study led by University of Exeter, AHRC-funded)

title: The philosophers' stone as a historical goal
claim: For roughly sixteen centuries, a continuous tradition of practitioners — from Zosimos of Panopolis (c. 300 CE) through the Arabic Jabirian corpus, the Latin Pseudo-Geber Summa perfectionis (c. 1280-1310), the Rosarium philosophorum (1550) to Sendivogius's Novum lumen chymicum (1604) — sought a transmuting agent, the philosophers' stone, that would perfect base metals into gold. The GOAL and the PRACTICE are historically real; only the claimed RESULT is debunked.
place: Panopolis (Akhmim), Roman Egypt — Zosimos's ground

title: The Sogdian Ancient Letters (c. 313 CE)
claim: A cache of personal letters written in Sogdian (an Iranian language of the Samarkand region) by merchants stranded in China, found in a ruined Han watchtower near Dunhuang — the voice of the merchant houses that ran the network: debts, partners, camels, and a lost loan, 3,000 km from home.
place: Dunhuang, Gansu — the Han watchtower where Stein found them

title: The stirrup's Asian origin and westward transmission
claim: The stirrup was invented in East Asia no later than the 4th century CE and reached Europe by the 6th–7th centuries via the steppe peoples (above all the Avars), with Frankish adoption following in the late 8th–early 9th centuries.
place: Nanjing, China (earliest known representation; the transmission runs west across the steppe to the Carpathian Basin)

title: The Eastern Roman Empire (the 'Byzantine' state), 330–1453
claim: A continuous Roman state centered on Constantinople existed from the city's dedication (11 May 330 CE) to the Ottoman conquest of the city (29 May 1453 CE) — an Eastern Roman Empire of eleven centuries, with continuous imperial administration, law, coinage, and historical writing across the span.
place: Constantinople (modern Istanbul)

title: The Rhomaioi: the empire called itself Roman
claim: The people of the Eastern Roman Empire self-identified as Romans (Romaioi/Rhomaioi) and called their state Romania — Romanland — the Empire of the Romans (hê Rhômaíôn Basileía), from Late Antiquity to 1453.
place: Constantinople (modern Istanbul)

title: The first celebration of Christmas on December 25 (Rome, by 336 CE)
claim: By 336 CE, the church at Rome was celebrating Christ's nativity on December 25 — the first undisputed attestation of Christmas on that date.
place: Rome

title: The Aramaic incantation bowls: two thousand buried pleas
claim: In late-antique Babylonia (4th–7th c. CE), Jewish (and Mandaic, and Syriac) households buried earthenware bowls face-down under thresholds, inscribed with Aramaic incantations binding demons — including Lilith and the lilith-classes — quoting the Hebrew Bible, the Targum, and the liturgy. ~2,000 such bowls are known; the published corpora (Montgomery 1913, Nippur; Naveh & Shaked 1985; Naveh & Shaked 1993; Shaked et al. 2013) establish the practice as the material record of lived protective belief.
place: Nippur and Sasanian Babylonia (Iraq)

title: The Indian origin of chess: chaturanga → chatrang → shatranj
claim: Modern chess descends from the Indian game chaturanga (6th century CE), transmitted westward through Persian chatrang and Arab shatranj into medieval Europe.
place: Gupta Empire, northern India (traditional)

title: Nalanda Mahavihara — the ancient university
claim: From c. 427 CE (Gupta foundation under Kumaragupta I) into the late 12th century CE, Nalanda in Magadha (Bihar) was one of the ancient world's great residential universities: a mahavihara complex with multiple monasteries, temples, lecture halls, and a major manuscript library tradition (Dharmaganja), drawing students from across Asia — attested by the Chinese pilgrims Xuanzang (at Nalanda 630–643) and Yijing (675–685), by excavated architecture (ASI campaigns from 1915), and by UNESCO's 2016 World Heritage inscription.
place: Nalanda Mahavihara, Bihar, India (near Rajgir)

title: The sack of Rome by Attila the Hun (the belief that Attila captured and sacked Rome)
claim: Attila the Hun sacked Rome — that is, his Huns captured and sacked the city of Rome itself.
place: Mincio river, near Mantua (meeting site); Rome (the city never taken)

title: The droit du seigneur: the medieval lord's 'right of the first night'
claim: In medieval Europe, feudal lords held a legal right — known as the droit du seigneur or jus primae noctis — entitling them to spend the wedding night with their vassals' brides.
place: Bologna, Italy (Gratian's seat — the seat of medieval canon law, where the right should appear and does not)

title: The medieval non-bather: "medieval people never bathed"
claim: Medieval Europeans (c. 500-1500 CE) rarely or never bathed — regular bathing was essentially unknown in medieval Europe, and public bathhouses were a Roman-era relic that did not exist in medieval cities.
place: Medieval Europe (exemplified by Paris)

title: The spice-covered rot: "medieval cooks used spices to hide rotten meat"
claim: In medieval Europe, cooks used expensive imported spices to disguise or mask the taste of rotten or spoiled meat.
place: Medieval Europe (the schoolbook tradition's setting)

title: Why Teotihuacan fell (the cause of the 6th-century decline)
claim: A specific historical cause explains Teotihuacan's 6th-century decline — the deliberate burning of the civic core c. 550 CE and the city's abandonment by c. 750 CE.
place: Teotihuacan, Valley of Mexico

title: The Birmingham Mingana folios' radiocarbon date (568–645 CE)
claim: The two Birmingham (Mingana Collection) Qur'anic folios — Suras 18–20 in Hijazi script on sheep/goat parchment — were radiocarbon-dated by the Oxford Radiocarbon Accelerator Unit to 568–645 CE at 95.4% probability, making the parchment contemporary with or pre-dating the traditional compilation; the written text matches the standard Qur'anic text with no significant variations.
place: Cadbury Research Library, University of Birmingham, UK (Mingana Collection, acquired from the Middle East)

title: The early Qur'anic manuscript record
claim: A substantial Qur'anic text existed in written form within decades of Muhammad's death: the Birmingham Mingana 1572a folios (parchment radiocarbon-dated 568-645 CE, containing Surahs 18-20 in present-day sequence), the Sanaa palimpsest DAM 01-27.1 (parchment before 671 CE at 99% probability; upper text Uthmanic, lower erased text a non-Uthmanic variant tradition), and the Codex Parisino-petropolitanus (BnF Arabe 328ab, ~45% of the Qur'an, 7th-8th c.) all substantially match the canonical text — while the Sanaa lower text proves textual plurality existed before effective standardization.
place: Sanaa, Yemen (Great Mosque, 1972 find) / Birmingham, UK (Mingana Collection)

title: The early Qur'anic text substantially fixed before 700 CE (rasm closure)
claim: The early Qur'anic text was substantially fixed before 700 CE: the consonantal skeleton (rasm) reached closure by the end of the 7th century — multiple independent lines converge on a single written archetype within decades of the traditional Uthmanic date, while the vocalized/readings layer froze much later.
place: Sanaa, Yemen (Great Mosque, 1972 find) / Birmingham, UK (Mingana Collection) / Paris (BnF)

title: Muhammad
claim: Muhammad (c. 570-632 CE) of Mecca proclaimed the Qur'anic revelation, united the Arabian tribes, and founded the community (umma) at Medina in 622 CE — the event from which the Islamic calendar counts.
place: Mecca (traditional)

title: The 591 conflation: three women fused into one Magdalene
claim: On 21 September 591, Pope Gregory the Great (Homily 33 on the Gospels) identified Mary Magdalene with the 'sinful woman' of Luke 7:36-50 and with Mary of Bethany (John 12): 'she whom Luke calls the sinful woman, whom John calls Mary, we believe to be the Mary from whom seven devils were ejected according to Mark.' The fusion created the penitent-prostitute Magdalene of fourteen centuries of Western art and devotion. No canonical text makes the identification; the Eastern churches never adopted it; the 1969 General Roman Calendar reform (Mysterii Paschalis) separated the celebrations again (July 22, St Mary Magdalene; the Bethany commemoration removed), and in 2016 the July 22 memorial was elevated to a feast, the apostles' own liturgical rank.
place: Rome (Homily 33 preached in Rome)

title: The khipu as the Inca empire's information technology
claim: The khipu — cords of cotton or camelid wool, hung from a primary cord and tied with systematic knots encoding decimal numbers, with information also carried in cord color, fiber type, ply direction, knot type, and attachment position — was the Inca empire's (Tawantinsuyu's) standard system for recording census data, tribute, storehouse accounts, and other administrative information, read and maintained by trained specialists, the quipucamayocs.
place: Cuzco, Peru — imperial capital; khipu use was empire-wide across Tawantinsuyu (~2 million sq km)

title: The origin of Islam
claim: In 7th-century Arabia, the Qur'anic revelation proclaimed through Muhammad founded Islam; within a century of his death the caliphate stretched from Spain to Central Asia, and the Qur'anic text was standardized.
place: Mecca (traditional origin)

title: The Qur'anic attestation of the jinn
claim: The Qur'an attests jinn as created beings distinct from angels and humans: made of smokeless fire, created before Adam, addressed as moral agents (believers and unbelievers among them) alongside humans.
place: Mecca/Hijaz (traditional revelation setting)

title: The 2026 Al-Ma'mala mosque: a first-century-Hijri mosque with a Muhammad-name qibla inscription
claim: The Saudi Heritage Commission's fourth excavation season at Al-Ma'mala (Al-Aqiq Governorate, Al-Baha region, announced 13 September 2026 via the Commission's official channels) uncovered a mosque dated to the first century AH (7th century CE) — dressed-granite construction with mihrab, entrances, and minarets — bearing wall inscriptions including blessings upon 'Muhammad, son of Abdullah' on the qibla wall, plus religious supplications and Quranic passages. The mosque stands in a mining settlement where laboratory analyses date gold, silver, and copper extraction from the late 6th through the 9th century CE.
place: Al-Ma'mala, Al-Aqiq Governorate, Al-Baha region, southwestern Saudi Arabia

title: The 2026 Darb Zubayda inscription: a first-Hijri-century pilgrim graffito quoting Al-Baqarah
claim: The Saudi Heritage Commission documented a first-Hijri-century inscription at Dhali al Nis (south of Samira, Hail region) on the Darb Zubayda, carved on a flat granite rock at a waystation summit: a supplication for forgiveness for an individual named Ibrahim ibn Ziyad, including a quotation from the end of a verse of Surah Al-Baqarah — a documented Kufan Hajj-route waypoint.
place: Dhali al Nis, Darb Zubayda, Hail region (south of Samira)

title: The 2026 Wadi al-Usaylah record: 60+ early Islamic inscriptions on the Iraq Hajj corridor
claim: Wadi al-Usaylah (northeast of Makkah, ~6 km by 2 km), documented by the Royal Commission for Makkah City and Holy Sites in a Saudi Press Agency release of 12 September 2026, preserves more than 60 early Islamic rock inscriptions dated to the 7th–8th centuries CE (1st–2nd c. AH) — evidence for the orthographic and aesthetic development of early Arabic script — plus two surviving historical wells from water infrastructure commissioned by successive Islamic rulers (some Abbasid-era) along the Iraq Hajj corridor; a comprehensive preservation program is now underway.
place: Wadi al-Usaylah, northeast of Makkah

title: The 2026 Al Mahd survey: Umar-name inscriptions in the Madinah desert
claim: The Saudi Heritage Commission's second survey season in Al Mahd Governorate (Madinah region, announced 10 June 2026) documented 1,774 finds across 156 new sites — 461 Islamic inscriptions, 34 Thamudic inscriptions, 1,259 rock art panels, stone structures, palaces, two caravan routes, and four wells — including rock inscriptions in Hijazi script bearing the name of Umar ibn al-Khattab, the second Rashidun caliph (r. 634–644 CE).
place: Al Mahd Governorate, Madinah region (Al Suwayriqiyah, Al Muwayhiyah, Hadhah)

title: The Doctrina Iacobi (July 634 CE) — earliest non-Muslim writing on an Arabian prophet
claim: The Doctrina Iacobi nuper baptizati, a Byzantine Christian-Jewish polemic completed in Carthage before 13 July 634 CE, contains — in a letter from a certain Abraham in Caesarea — the earliest known non-Muslim writing to describe a prophet who 'has appeared among the Saracens': an armed figure proclaiming the advent of the anointed one and claiming the keys of paradise.
place: Carthage (composition); the prophet passage is set at Caesarea Maritima

title: PERF 558 (643 CE) — the oldest dated Arabic document
claim: PERF 558 (P.Vindob. inv. G 39726, Vienna): a bilingual Greek-Arabic tax protocol dated 643 CE (22 AH), issued under 'Abd Allah b. Jabr — the oldest dated Arabic documentary text in the world.
place: Egypt (exact findspot unknown; held Vienna Papyrus Collection)

title: The Zuhayr inscription (24 AH / 644–645 CE)
claim: The Zuhayr graffito from the al-Ula region of the Hijaz — self-dated 'in the year twenty-four' (24 AH / 644–645 CE) and reporting the death of the caliph 'Umar — is the oldest securely dated Arabic inscription of the Islamic era.
place: al-Ula region, Hijaz, Saudi Arabia

title: Pakal's sarcophagus lid ('Palenque astronaut')
claim: The sarcophagus lid of K'inich Janaab' Pakal the Great (603–683 CE) depicts him piloting a spacecraft (the 'Palenque astronaut').
place: Temple of the Inscriptions, Palenque, Chiapas, Mexico

title: The Dome of the Rock inscriptions (72 AH / 691–92 CE)
claim: The Dome of the Rock in Jerusalem, dedicated 72 AH / 691–92 CE, carries about 240 meters of Arabic inscription — including Qur'anic verses and paraphrases — making it the oldest securely dated Qur'anic text in the world: the date belongs to the writing itself, not to the material it is written on.
place: Temple Mount / Haram al-Sharif, Jerusalem

title: The Dhul-Qarnayn identification question
claim: The Qur'an's 'Dhu al-Qarnayn' ('the Two-Horned One,' Surah 18:83–101) — a builder of an iron wall against Gog and Magog — has been traditionally identified with Alexander since the 8th century (al-Tabari and later commentators), drawing on the Syriac Alexander Legend's Christianized Alexander and Pseudo-Callisthenian material; Ferdowsi's Shahnameh (completed 1010) carries the Persian 'Iskandar' further. The identification-tradition is attested across a millennium of texts. Whether the Qur'anic figure IS Alexander is disputed (minority proposals include Cyrus the Great); the identity itself is unresolved and graded SPECULATION.
place: The tradition is textual, not geographic: the Syriac Legend (northern Mesopotamia milieu), al-Tabari (Baghdad), Ferdowsi (Tus, Khorasan)

title: The 'blind Homer wrote the epics' schoolbook picture
claim: The historical Homer was a blind poet who personally composed the Iliad and the Odyssey as written works — the lone blind genius of the schoolroom busts.
place: Chios / Ionia — the traditional homeland of the blind bard (the seven-cities tradition)

title: The Persian panemone — the first practical windmills (700–900 AD)
claim: The first practical windmills were the Persian panemone — vertical-axis machines with lightweight wooden sails on a central vertical shaft, built in the Sistan region (modern Iran/Afghanistan) around 700–900 AD, first for pumping water and later for grinding grain.
place: Sistan, eastern Iran / western Afghanistan; Nashtifan, Razavi Khorasan Province, Iran

title: Tariq ibn Ziyad burned his ships at Gibraltar (711) — DEBUNKED
claim: Tariq ibn Ziyad, after landing in Iberia in 711, burned his ships (or had them scuttled) to deny his men any retreat, then delivered the famous khutba: 'the sea is behind you, the enemy before you.'
place: Gibraltar (Jabal Tariq) — the claimed landing site of the burned fleet

title: Tariq's 711 crossing and the Battle of Guadalete — CORROBORATED
claim: In 711, the Umayyad commander Tariq ibn Ziyad crossed the Strait with about 7,000 men — mostly Berbers — aboard vessels associated with Julian of Ceuta, landed at Gibraltar (Jabal Tariq, 'Mount Tariq'), and defeated the Visigothic king Roderic at Guadalete, opening the Muslim conquest of Iberia.
place: Gibraltar (Jabal Tariq) — the crossing's landing point, named for the commander

title: Charles Martel's cavalry funding and the Church lands
claim: Charles Martel (mayor of the palace 715–741) built Frankish military power in part on mounted warriors and funded it in part through church-land grants (precaria); the documented record shows the reforms and the seizures, but no contemporary source ties either to the stirrup.
place: Tours/Poitiers, Francia (732 — the battle Brunner's thesis keys to)

title: The 2026 al-Juhfah miqat excavation
claim: The Saudi Heritage Commission's first scientific excavation season at Miqat al-Juhfah (2026, with the University of Exeter) documented the Hijrah-era pilgrimage station: 1,700+ artifacts, six pottery kilns, a water channel, and 13 tombstones (some Umayyad/Abbasid), with imported goods from the Levant, Egypt, and Abyssinia — the pilgrimage route's infrastructure in the material record.
place: Miqat al-Juhfah, 187 km NW of Mecca

title: The Donation of Constantine — a forgery
claim: The Constitutum Constantini is an authentic imperial decree issued by Constantine the Great in the 4th century (dated in the document to March 30, consulships naming Constantine's fourth term and Gallicanus), granting Pope Sylvester I and his successors: spiritual supremacy over the four great sees and all churches, the imperial insignia (diadem, tiara, pallium, scepter), the Lateran palace, the city of Rome, and all the provinces, places and cities of Italy and the western regions.
place: Rome (composition: Roman scriptorium, mid-to-late 8th century)

title: The sira transmission gap
claim: The earliest surviving biography of Muhammad — Ibn Hisham's recension (d. 833/834 CE) of Ibn Ishaq's Sirat Rasul Allah (d. 767/768 CE, original lost) — postdates the events it describes by roughly 120–200 years; no biography of Muhammad from the 600s survives, and the Qur'an itself contains no narrative biography (no birth story, no childhood, no year-by-year life).
place: Fustat (Old Cairo), Egypt — where Ibn Hisham produced the recension

title: Cahokia: the earthen city of the Mississippi floodplain
claim: At its peak around 1050-1150 CE, Cahokia — the pre-eminent center of the Mississippian culture (800-1350 CE) — was a city of 10,000-20,000+ people covering ~1,600 hectares with ~120 earthen mounds; Monks Mound, its central pyramid, is the largest prehistoric earthen structure in the New World, and the city ran a solar observatory (Woodhenge) and a continent-spanning trade network. This is the timeline's first pre-Columbian North American record.
place: Cahokia Mounds, Collinsville, Illinois (Monks Mound)

title: 'Lilith was Adam's first wife' (the Genesis claim)
claim: 'Lilith was Adam's first wife' is a biblical statement (Genesis).
place: Medieval Jewish literary culture (textual origin)

title: The Classic Maya 'collapse' — no vanishing, a transformation
claim: The Classic Maya civilization mysteriously vanished — its people disappeared in a single, unexplained collapse.
place: Southern Maya lowlands (Petén, Guatemala; adjacent Chiapas, Belize)

title: The Theology of Aristotle: Plotinus in Arabic dress, shelved under Aristotle for a millennium
claim: The Arabic philosophical text known as the Theology of Aristotle (Uthulujiya Aristu), which circulated for roughly a millennium as a work of Aristotle and shaped Islamic, Jewish, and Christian philosophy, is a creative Arabic paraphrase of Plotinus's Enneads (books IV-VI, on Soul, Intellect, and the One), produced in 9th-century Baghdad in the circle of al-Kindi. Its own preface names the layers: 'the book of Aristotle the philosopher, called in Greek Theologia... The exposition of Porphyry of Syria, translated into Arabic by Ibn Na'ima al-Himsi, and corrected for Ahmad ibn al-Mu'tasim by al-Kindi' - Ahmad being the son of the Abbasid caliph who reigned 833-842, which dates the production to the 830s-840s. The work was the single most important conduit by which Neoplatonism reached the Islamic world, read by al-Kindi, al-Farabi, Avicenna (who wrote comments on it and may have doubted its authenticity), and later by Latin scholastics and Safavid thinkers.
place: Baghdad, Abbasid Iraq (production; al-Kindi's circle)

title: The Varangian (Scandinavian) contribution to the formation of the Rus' polity
claim: The Rus' — the people whose name Russia, Ukraine and Belarus all trace their statehood to — began as a polity whose founding elite and early identity were Scandinavian (Norse/Varangian), arriving via the Baltic–Volga–Dnieper river arteries in the 9th century, before assimilating into the East Slavic majority.
place: Staraya Ladoga and the Volkhov–Dnieper river routes (region: NW Russia / Ukraine)

title: The hardline claim that the Scandinavians played NO role in the formation of the Rus'
claim: The Scandinavians (Varangians/Norse) played NO role in the formation of the Rus' polity — the early Rus' were entirely East Slavic in origin and identity, and any Norse presence was non-existent or historiographically irrelevant.
place: Kiev (the polity the claim is about)

title: Al-Kindi's frequency analysis (c. 850 CE)
claim: Abu Yusuf al-Kindi's treatise Risalah fi Istikhraj al-Mu'amma ('On Deciphering Cryptographic Messages'), written c. 850 CE in Baghdad, is the oldest surviving work describing frequency analysis — the statistical method of breaking substitution ciphers by counting symbol frequencies and matching them against known letter frequencies of the language. It is the first documented systematic method of cryptanalysis: the first time anyone wrote down that a cipher dissolves into arithmetic.
place: Baghdad, Abbasid Caliphate

title: The False Decretals — the forgery's transmission machine
claim: The Pseudo-Isidorian Decretals (the False Decretals), a 9th-century Frankish collection (c. 847-852) of some 100 forged decretals and synodal acts, contains the first surviving witness of the Donation of Constantine; two centuries later the Donation entered Gratian's Decretum (12th century, via a pupil) and thus became part of canon law — the transmission machine that carried the forgery into law.
place: Reims, Francia (Pseudo-Isidorian collection's working milieu)

title: Al-Qarawiyyin of Fez: the 859 foundation and the 'oldest university' dispute
claim: The University of al-Qarawiyyin in Fez, Morocco — founded as a mosque by Fatima al-Fihri in 857-859, later a madrasa, incorporated into Morocco's modern state university system in 1963 — is the oldest existing, continually operating degree-awarding higher learning institution in the world.
place: Fez (Fès), Morocco — the al-Qarawiyyin complex

title: The 'invitation of the Varangians' in 862 (the Chronicle's Rurik narrative)
claim: In the year 862, the East Slavic and Finnic tribes of the northwest (Slovenes, Krivichi, Chud, Ves', Merya) — after expelling their Varangian tribute-takers and falling into internecine strife — sent envoys across the sea inviting the Varangians to rule over them; three brothers came, Rurik, Sineus and Truvor, and Rurik settled at Novgorod, Sineus at Beloozero and Truvor at Izborsk.
place: Novgorod (the Chronicle's settlement of Rurik)

title: The Diamond Sutra of 868 CE — the oldest dated printed book
claim: A woodblock-printed scroll of the Diamond Sutra, printed in China in 868 CE, is the oldest complete printed book in the world that carries a date — printed nearly six centuries before Gutenberg's Bible.
place: Mogao Caves, Dunhuang (Cave 17, the Library Cave)

title: The Bimaristan Hospitals (872-1284 CE)
claim: The bimaristan: the medieval Islamic hospital as an institution — endowed by waqf (charitable trust), free to rich and poor, male and female, Muslim and non-Muslim, with separate wards (surgery, medicine, eye, mental), pharmacies, lecture halls, running water, and paid discharge stipends. Founded first at al-Fustat (c. 872, Ibn Tulun), institutionalized at the Nuri hospital of Damascus (c. 1154, Nur al-Din Zanki), and monumentalized at the Mansuri hospital of Cairo (completed 1284, al-Mansur Qalawun).
place: Damascus (al-Nuri bimaristan, survives); al-Mansuri in Cairo, city precision

title: Alfred's candle clock
claim: Alfred the Great measured his devotional hours with a candle marked in divisions, burning inside an ox-horn lantern — the origin of the 'Alfred invented the candle clock' telling.
place: Wessex (Alfred's court)

title: The medieval Inquisition's actual targets — and its own law on witches
claim: The medieval Inquisition (established 1231 under Gregory IX) was a court directed against heretics — principally Cathars (Albigensians) and Waldensians — and its own law books treated witchcraft skeptically: Canon Episcopi (c. 906, incorporated into Gratian's Decretum c. 1140) declared that belief in night-flight witchcraft was a demonic delusion, not a crime to prosecute.
place: Languedoc, southern France (Cathar inquisition's main theater)

title: Kilwa Kisiwani — the Swahili coast's gold-port city-state
claim: Kilwa Kisiwani, on an island off the Tanzanian coast, was a major Swahili city-state from the 11th–15th centuries, built on customs revenue from the gold trade running from the Zimbabwe plateau via Sofala — minting its own gold coins, building in coral stone, and ranked by Ibn Battuta in 1331 as one of the most beautiful cities he had seen.
place: Kilwa Kisiwani, Lindi Region, Tanzania

title: St Swithin's Day and the forty days (myth)
claim: If it rains on St Swithin's Day (15 July), it will rain for the next forty days; if it is fair, forty days of fair weather follow.
place: Winchester, England (St Swithin's Old Minster — the legend's origin)

title: Al-Zahrawi's Kitab al-Tasrif (c. 1000 CE)
claim: Abu al-Qasim al-Zahrawi (936-c.1013, Cordoba) compiled Kitab al-Tasrif (c. 1000 CE), a 30-treatise medical encyclopedia whose surgical treatise was the first work in Arabic to describe and illustrate surgical instruments — about 200 of them, many of his own design: cauterization irons, lithotrites for bladder stones, obstetrical forceps, catgut absorbable sutures, arterial ligation instruments.
place: Cordoba, Umayyad al-Andalus

title: The Norse settlement at L'Anse aux Meadows, c. 1000 CE
claim: Norse seafarers established a short-lived settlement at L'Anse aux Meadows, on Newfoundland's Great Northern Peninsula, around the year 1000 CE — a European presence in North America roughly five centuries before Columbus.
place: L'Anse aux Meadows National Historic Site, Great Northern Peninsula, Newfoundland

title: Maria Argyropoulina's golden fork at Venice (1004) and Peter Damian's condemnation
claim: In 1004, the Byzantine noblewoman Maria Argyropoulina, marrying into Venice's ruling Orseolo family, refused to touch her food with her fingers and instead ate with a small golden two-pronged fork, scandalizing Venice. The theologian St. Peter Damian (1007-1072) recorded the episode in his letters and condemned her 'artificial metal forks' as decadent luxury, interpreting her early death from plague as divine punishment for that vanity.
place: Venice, Republic of Venice (the Orseolo marriage)

title: The Tale of Genji
claim: The Tale of Genji (Genji Monogatari) — 54 chapters of sustained prose fiction with interior characterization, court intrigue, and psychological realism — was composed by the Heian court lady Murasaki Shikibu (sobriquet; c. 973 – c. 1014/1031) c. 1008–1021, making it the earliest surviving work of extended prose fiction meeting the criteria most literary historians use to define the novel: it predates Cervantes's Don Quixote (1605) by roughly six centuries.
place: Ishiyamadera temple, Otsu (traditional composition site per legend) / Heian-kyo (Kyoto), Japan — the legend puts the first inspiration at Ishiyamadera; the court life it describes is Heian-kyo

title: Bi Sheng's movable type (1041–1048 CE)
claim: Bi Sheng, a commoner of the Northern Song dynasty, invented movable type printing using fired-clay characters, more than four centuries before Gutenberg — described in detail by his contemporary Shen Kuo in the Dream Pool Essays (~1088).
place: Yingshan County, Hubei (Bi Sheng's home; invention in the Song capital region)

title: The East–West Schism of 1054: the excommunications that did not, by themselves, split Christianity
claim: The Christian Church divided into two churches — Roman Catholic (West) and Eastern Orthodox (East) — in a single event in 1054, when Cardinal Humbert laid a bull of excommunication on the altar of Hagia Sophia and Patriarch Michael Cerularius was excommunicated in return.
place: Hagia Sophia, Constantinople (Istanbul)

title: The Maine penny (Norse coin in a Maine midden)
claim: The Maine penny — a Norwegian silver coin of Olaf Kyrre's reign (1067–1093) — was found in 1957 in the pre-Columbian Goddard-site midden at Naskeag Point, Maine: genuine Norse object in a New England context.
place: Goddard site, Naskeag Point, Penobscot Bay, Brooklin, Maine

title: The Bayeux comet — the earliest known European depiction of Halley's Comet
claim: The Bayeux embroidery's comet panel (scenes 32, under the Latin caption ISTI MIRANT STELLA — 'these men marvel at the star') depicts the April 1066 apparition of what is now called Halley's Comet — and is the earliest known European pictorial depiction of the comet.
place: Bayeux Museum, Normandy, France (the panel); the apparition observed over England, April 1066

title: The Bayeux Tapestry — the artifact
claim: The Bayeux 'Tapestry' (c. 1070) is a ~70-meter embroidered linen cloth depicting the events of 1066 — the Norman Conquest of England — made in England to a Norman brief (traditionally attributed to Bishop Odo's commission, Canterbury workshop) as a piece of Norman propaganda.
place: Musée de la Tapisserie de Bayeux, Normandy, France (long-term home; the work is named for the city it resides in, not where it was made)

title: The Bayeux Tapestry is not a tapestry
claim: The Bayeux Tapestry — the famous ~70-meter 11th-century depiction of the 1066 Norman Conquest — is a tapestry (a textile whose images are woven into the cloth on a loom).
place: Musée de la Tapisserie de Bayeux, Normandy, France (the examined object)

title: The Domesday Book (1086) — the first great count
claim: The Domesday Book (1086) is a real, surviving, comprehensive survey of landholding in England — the largest single record of its kind from the Middle Ages, and the foundation of medieval English demography.
place: The National Archives, Kew, England (holding institution); survey coverage: England

title: Shen Kuo's Dream Pool Essays (~1088) — the first clearly-dated, named-author account of magnetic declination, four centuries before Europe wrote it down
claim: Shen Kuo (1031-1095), in his Mengxi Bitan (Dream Pool Essays, compiled c. 1086-1088), wrote the first clearly-dated, named-author account of magnetic declination: the magnetized needle 'is always displaced slightly east rather than pointing due south.' Europe did not document the phenomenon until roughly four centuries later.
place: Dream Torrent Garden, Runzhou (modern Zhenjiang), Song China — where Shen Kuo compiled the essays

title: The University of Bologna's 1088 founding date
claim: The University of Bologna was founded in the year 1088, as a dated and documented founding event.
place: Bologna, Italy

title: The Two Deaths That Weren't: 'al-Ghazali/Mongols Ended Islamic Science'
claim: The popular two-cause story: Islamic scientific research effectively ENDED with (a) al-Ghazali's critique of philosophy (Tahafut al-Falasifa, 1095; d. 1111) and/or (b) the Mongol sack of Baghdad (1258) — so that nothing significant in science happened in the Islamic world after those events.
place: Maragha, East Azerbaijan, Iran (site of the observatory founded 1259, one year after the sack of Baghdad — the fact that falsifies the claim)

title: The 'Dutch invented the windmill' myth (DEBUNKED)
claim: The Dutch invented the windmill.
place: Netherlands (the claimed origin)

title: The 'cathedral glass flows' myth (DEBUNKED)
claim: Medieval cathedral window glass has flowed downward over the centuries — old panes are thicker at the bottom because glass is a slow-moving liquid.
place: European cathedrals (Westminster Abbey, Sainte-Chapelle studied)

title: Great Zimbabwe — the Shona stone city
claim: Great Zimbabwe, on the Zimbabwe plateau, was a stone-built African city and capital of a gold-trading state, constructed in the 11th–15th centuries CE by the ancestors of the Shona/Karanga people — the largest ancient stone construction south of the Sahara.
place: Great Zimbabwe, Masvingo, Zimbabwe

title: Medieval European public bathhouses
claim: Medieval European cities had public bathhouses — licensed, guilded establishments operating across the 12th-16th centuries.
place: Paris (the 1268 étuviers guild statutes)

title: Spices as medieval status: the pepper that meant money
claim: In medieval Europe, imported spices functioned primarily as luxury goods consumed for social display — elite dining used expensive spices the way a modern household uses a luxury car: as a public statement of wealth.
place: Medieval Europe (the elite table)

title: The Bologna studium: Europe's first university corporation
claim: In the 12th century Bologna developed the first European studium in the corporate sense: Irnerius's law school and the glossators, imperial protection of wandering scholars, and the student guilds (universitates/nations) that became the university.
place: Bologna, Italy (the law schools; the Authentica issued at the Diet of Roncaglia)

title: Angkor Wat — the temple and its continuous life
claim: Angkor Wat — the world's largest religious complex (162.6 hectares, ~401.8 acres) — was built between c. 1113 and c. 1150 CE during the reign of the Khmer king Suryavarman II as a Hindu state temple dedicated to Vishnu (likely also his mausoleum), and has remained in continuous religious use ever since, converting to Theravada Buddhist use from the late 13th century onward into the present day.
place: Angkor Wat, Siem Reap, Cambodia

title: Gratian's Decretum: the medieval law books and what they do not contain
claim: Gratian's Decretum (Concordia discordantium canonum, compiled c. 1140 at Bologna) founded medieval canon law; the glossators' Corpus Juris Canonici (completed 1582) regulated marriage, clergy, heresy, and procedure for four centuries — and this entire corpus, thousands of canons and glosses, contains no droit du seigneur, no jus primae noctis, and no seigneurial wedding-night right of any kind.
place: Bologna, Italy (Gratian's school; the manuscripts live in the Biblioteca dell'Archiginnasio and across Europe)

title: Angkor Wat was never abandoned — the continuous-use record
claim: Angkor Wat was never abandoned: it converted to Theravada Buddhist use from the late 13th century onward and has remained a continuously active religious center into the present day — the Khmers never 'lost' it.
place: Angkor Wat, Siem Reap, Cambodia

title: No blood-of-Christ relic has verified 1st-century provenance
claim: No blood-of-Christ relic anywhere has verified 1st-century provenance. The Bruges Holy Blood has a 1150 tradition (Thierry of Alsace) but no documentary record before 1256; most historians link it to the 1204 sack of Constantinople, and the crystal tube is a Byzantine perfume bottle. The Mantua relic's chain is likewise medieval. The claim of a 1st-century blood relic is therefore DEBUNKED as a provenance claim — what exists are medieval devotional objects.

title: The Trabia itriyya industry — pasta in Sicily before Polo
claim: By 1154, the town of Trabia near Palermo (Sicily) produced thread-like dried pasta (itriyya) in industrial quantities and exported it by ship to Calabria and to Muslim and Christian lands — 141 years before Marco Polo's return from China.
place: Trabia, Sicily

title: Henry II's Assize of Clarendon (1166) — the jury of presentment
claim: Henry II's Assize of Clarendon (1166) established the jury of presentment: twelve lawful men of each hundred and four of each vill, sworn to report under oath those accused or notoriously suspect of robbery, murder, or theft. This jury of twelve — plus the civil-assize recognitions (novel disseisin, mort d'ancestor, darrein presentment) — is the documented seed of the English jury system, forty-nine years before Magna Carta.
place: Clarendon, Wiltshire, England (traditional site of the council)

title: Alexander Neckam's De naturis rerum (c. 1180-1190) — the earliest surviving European description of the mariner's compass, recorded as existing seamen's practice
claim: Alexander Neckam (1157-1217), in De naturis rerum (book ii, ch. 89/98 'De vi attractiva,' written c. 1180-1190), gives the earliest surviving European literary description of the mariner's compass: sailors in cloudy weather 'touch the magnet with a needle,' which 'whirls round in a circle until, when its motion ceases, the point looks direct to the north.' Neckam describes it as existing seamen's practice, not his own invention.
place: Oxford / St Albans, England — Neckam's teaching world; the sailors he describes are the Channel seamen

title: The blood-catching Grail is a ~1200 literary invention (Robert de Boron)
claim: The Holy Grail as a vessel of Christ's blood originates in literature, not 1st-century tradition: Chrétien de Troyes' Perceval (~1190) has a graal as a serving dish — no blood, not holy. Robert de Boron's Joseph d'Arimathie (~1190-1200) is FIRST to make it the Last Supper cup used to catch Christ's blood. Wolfram von Eschenbach's Parzival (~1210) makes the grail a stone (lapsit exillis), not a cup at all. The blood-catching grail is twelve centuries younger than the Last Supper.

title: The Pray Codex's shroud image (c. 1192–1195)
claim: The Hungarian Pray Codex (c. 1192–1195, the first book in Hungarian, National Széchényi Library, Budapest) contains an Entombment illumination showing a burial cloth with distinctive marks — including an L-pattern resembling the Shroud of Turin's burn holes, a long narrow cloth, hands crossed over the body without visible thumbs — attesting a Shroud-like image-tradition roughly 160 years before the Shroud's first undisputed documentation at Lirey (c. 1355).
place: Budapest (National Széchényi Library)

title: The 'libraries burned for months' claim (Nalanda)
claim: After Bakhtiyar Khilji's 1193 sack of Nalanda, the university's manuscript libraries (Dharmaganja) burned continuously for months — told as three months, six months, nine months, or 'several' months depending on the telling, often paired with 'nine million manuscripts'.
place: Nalanda Mahavihara, Bihar, India

title: The 1190s–1200s sack of the Bihar monasteries (Khilji)
claim: In the 1190s–1200s CE, the Turkic general Bakhtiyar Khilji's campaigns in Bihar sacked the great Buddhist monastic universities — Nalanda, Vikramashila, and Odantapuri — killing many monks and damaging the institutions; the near-contemporary Persian chronicle Tabaqat-i Nasiri (Minhaj-i Siraj, c. 1260) describes the Bihar campaign's assault, the killing of the shaven-headed inhabitants, and the discovery of the great book collections.
place: Nalanda / Bihar monastic belt, India

title: The torture was the procedure: the law-of-proof thesis
claim: Continental Europe's judicial torture was not lawless cruelty but a formal, rule-bound evidentiary stage of the Romano-canonical inquisitorial procedure: the law of proof required two eyewitnesses or the accused's confession for conviction, so torture existed to produce the confession — permitted only on 'half proof' (one eyewitness or sufficient circumstantial indicia), governed by codified safeguards (the Carolina 1532, the ordonnance criminelle 1670), and it died when the law of proof was reformed rather than when a book was read.
place: Regensburg (the Carolina, Diet of 1532); the procedure's theater is the Empire and France

title: Al-Jazari's Book of Ingenious Devices (1206 CE)
claim: Ismail al-Jazari (d. 1206), chief engineer at the Artuqid court of Diyar Bakr (Amid), compiled al-Jami' bayn al-'ilm wa al-'amal al-nafi' fi sina'at al-hiyal ('The Book of Knowledge of Ingenious Mechanical Devices', presented 1206): 50+ illustrated machines including the elephant clock, castle clock, musical automata with programmable peg-and-cam mechanisms, the double-action suction pump, the camshaft, and the crankshaft with crank-slider mechanism — the rotary-to-reciprocating conversion at the heart of every modern engine.
place: Amid (Diyarbakir), Artuqid Diyar Bakr

title: The Mongol Empire at its greatest extent (c. 1279–1294) — the largest contiguous land empire in history
claim: At its greatest extent, around 1279–1294, the Mongol Empire was the largest contiguous land empire in history: roughly 23.5–24 million square kilometers (~9.1 million square miles), about 17.8% of Earth's land surface, with on the order of 110 million subjects — about a quarter of humanity under one administration.
place: Karakorum (capital 1235–1271); the empire at height stretched from the Sea of Japan to Eastern Europe and the Levant

title: Magna Carta, Clause 39 (the 'peers' clause)
claim: Clause 39 of the 1215 Magna Carta, sealed at Runnymede (15 June 1215), provides that no free man shall be seized, imprisoned, stripped of rights or possessions, outlawed, exiled, or destroyed except by the lawful judgment of his equals or by the law of the land. The clause's actual historical content is a baronial guarantee against arbitrary royal action — judgment by fellow barons in the feudal court — not a grant of trial by jury to the population.
place: Runnymede, Surrey, England (traditional site of the sealing)

title: The claim that Magna Carta created trial by jury
claim: Magna Carta (1215) created, invented, or first granted the right to trial by jury — that before Runnymede there was no jury, and the charter gave England (and by inheritance, America) the jury as a new institution.
place: Runnymede, Surrey, England (the myth's alleged birthplace)

title: The end of the ordeal in England (1215–1219) — how the jury got its courtroom
claim: In 1215, the Fourth Lateran Council (Canon 18) forbade clergy to take part in trials by ordeal — priests could no longer bless the water or the iron. With the rite's divine machinery removed, England abandoned the ordeal: the plea rolls contain no trial by ordeal after 1219, when Henry III's regency issued instructions to the itinerant justices ordering a new method of proof — the jury. The ordeal-to-jury turn was papal-and-crown work, not the charter's.
place: London, England (seat of the 1219 instructions; the ordeal-to-jury turn)

title: The Wandering Jew (1228) is not Cain
claim: The 'wandering man who cannot die' legend first recorded in 1228 (Roger of Wendover's Flores Historiarum, via an Armenian archbishop at St Albans; incorporated into Matthew Paris's Chronica Majora) concerns Cartaphilus, Pilate's doorkeeper — not Cain. Christ's sentence, 'I will go, but thou shalt remain waiting until I come,' launched 800 years of folklore (renamed Ahasuerus the cobbler in the 1602 German chapbook). Conflating this figure with Cain is a popular error; the legend says nothing about Cain at all.
place: St Albans (recording); Jerusalem (narrative)

title: Ibn al-Nafis Describes Pulmonary Circulation (1242 CE)
claim: In his Sharh Tashrih al-Qanun ('Commentary on the Anatomy of the Canon of Avicenna', c. 1242 CE), the Damascus physician Ibn al-Nafis (1213-1288) described the pulmonary circulation: blood passes from the right ventricle through the lungs to the left ventricle, explicitly denying Galen's 'invisible pores' in the interventricular septum; he also described the coronary arteries and predicted small passages (manafidh) between pulmonary artery and vein — about 300 years before Servetus and Harvey.
place: Damascus (Ibn al-Nafis's city; he later headed the al-Mansuri hospital in Cairo)

title: The Tusi Couple's Road to Copernicus
claim: Late Islamic astronomical devices — above all Nasir al-Din al-Tusi's 'Tusi couple' (Tadhkira fi 'ilm al-hay'a) and the planetary models of the 14th-century Damascene astronomer Ibn al-Shatir — appear inside Nicolaus Copernicus's De revolutionibus orbium coelestium (1543), used by Copernicus in his reformulation of mathematical astronomy.
place: Maragha, East Azerbaijan, Iran (observatory site); the devices travel to Copernicus via routes still debated (Byzantine, Hebrew, Iberian)

title: The Mongol Sack of Baghdad (1258)
claim: The Mongol army under Hülegü besieged Baghdad in January 1258, took the city in February, massacred its population over roughly a week, and killed the Abbasid caliph al-Musta'sim — ending the Abbasid Caliphate's five centuries as a territorial power.
place: Baghdad, Iraq (Abbasid capital)

title: The ink-black Tigris: Baghdad 1258's legendary river
claim: After the Mongol sack of Baghdad in 1258, so many books from the House of Wisdom were thrown into the Tigris that the river's water ran black with ink (and, in some tellings, red with blood).
place: Baghdad, Tigris River

title: The House of Wisdom Destroyed (1258)
claim: The Bayt al-Hikma (House of Wisdom) — Baghdad's grand Abbasid institution of translation and learning — was destroyed by the Mongols in the 1258 sack, its library burned and its books thrown into the Tigris.
place: Baghdad, Iraq (Abbasid capital)

title: The Tigris Ran Black with Ink (1258)
claim: During the 1258 Mongol sack of Baghdad, so many books and manuscripts were thrown into the Tigris River that its waters ran black with ink (and, in the paired version, red with the blood of the slain).
place: Baghdad — the Tigris at the city

title: The Turin Shroud linen
claim: The linen of the Turin Shroud is the burial cloth of Jesus of Nazareth, woven in the 1st century CE.
place: Turin Cathedral, Italy (cloth kept; sample taken 1988)

title: The invention of eyeglasses in Italy, c. 1268–1289 (anonymous)
claim: Eyeglasses were invented in Italy, between about 1268 and 1289, by a maker whose name the record does not preserve; the art spread by the early 14th century.
place: Pisa / Venice, Italy (the two documented early centers)

title: 'Jehovah' as the original pronunciation of the divine name
claim: 'Jehovah' is the original pronunciation of the Hebrew divine name — the way ancient Israelites spoke YHWH.
place: Jerusalem — locus of the divine-name tradition

title: The fall-blade's two-century head start: Halifax and the Scottish Maiden
claim: Fall-blade beheading machines predated the 1792 French guillotine by centuries: the Halifax Gibbet (England) and the Scottish Maiden (Edinburgh, 1564) are documented precedents.
place: Halifax, West Yorkshire (Gibbet); Edinburgh Mercat Cross (Maiden) — pins carried jointly, region precision for the pair

title: Venice confines glassmaking to Murano (8 November 1291)
claim: On 8 November 1291, Venice confined most of its glassmaking industry to the island of Murano.
place: Murano, Venetian Lagoon

title: The Ottoman Empire (c. 1299–1922)
claim: The Ottoman Empire existed as a continuous state from c. 1299 (Osman I) until 1 November 1922 (the Grand National Assembly's abolition of the sultanate) — roughly six hundred and twenty years, one of the longest-lived states in recorded history.
place: Istanbul (seat of the Sublime Porte; founded as Ottoman state in Bithynia, northwestern Anatolia)

title: The fibula (14th c. BCE) — the safety pin's ancestor
claim: The ancient fibula is the safety pin's ancestor: the Mycenaean violin-bow fibula (14th c. BCE) combined a single wire, a spring, a sharp point, and a hooked catch — the same four elements as Hunt's 1849 Dress-Pin — and the type ran for millennia through the Roman bow fibulae.
place: Greek Peloponnese (Mycenaean heartland; violin-bow fibula introduction)

title: The 'died at thirty' myth
claim: The typical (average) person in medieval Europe died at about age 30 — most medieval people were dead by their thirties.
place: England (the IPM data's coverage)

title: The predecessor's Atlantic expedition
claim: Mansa Musa's predecessor equipped a first fleet of 200 ships, then 2,000 ships (1,000 for men, 1,000 for water and provisions) to cross the Atlantic Ocean, and never returned; Musa became king after the fleet vanished.
place: West African Atlantic coast (departure point uncertain)

title: 'Mansa Musa, the richest man in history'
claim: Mansa Musa was the richest person in history — worth about $400 billion in modern money.
place: Niani, Mali Empire (capital)

title: The Kebra Nagast as 14th-century compilation
claim: That the Kebra Nagast (The Glory of the Kings) — the Ge'ez national epic narrating the Queen of Sheba (Makeda), Solomon, their son Menelik I, and the migration of the Ark of the Covenant to Ethiopia — is a 14th-century CE compilation written to legitimize the restored Solomonic dynasty, not an eyewitness account from the 10th century BCE.
place: Axum (Aksum), Tigray Region, Ethiopia — composition circle

title: The Kebra Nagast as ancient eyewitness account (DEBUNKED)
claim: That the Kebra Nagast is an ancient text — an eyewitness-era account reaching back to the 10th century BCE, contemporary with Solomon and the Queen of Sheba — whose antiquity vouches for the Ark's migration to Ethiopia as recorded history.
place: Axum (Aksum), Tigray Region, Ethiopia — composition circle

title: Mansa Musa's Hajj of 1324
claim: In 1324, Mansa Musa, ruler of the Mali Empire (r. c. 1312–1337), traveled from his capital to Mecca with a vast caravan, distributing such quantities of gold in Cairo that the gold price there fell.
place: Cairo, Egypt

title: The Black Death (1347–1352): Yersinia pestis and the 30–50% toll
claim: The Black Death pandemic of 1347–1352 — the first and most lethal wave of the second plague pandemic — was caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis (the bubonic-plague pathogen), entered the Mediterranean in 1347 on trade ships from the Black Sea, and killed an estimated 30–50% of Europe's population (~25–30 million people; the literature ranges 25–60% depending on region).
place: Lake Issyk-Kul, Chu Valley, Kyrgyzstan (origin of the source strain, Spyrou et al. 2022) — spread to all of Europe 1347–1352

title: The forty days that gave the world 'quarantine'
claim: The word 'quarantine' comes from the Venetian Republic's forty-day (quaranta giorni) isolation of suspect ships.
place: Lazzaretto Nuovo, Venetian Lagoon

title: Jikji (1377) — the oldest extant book printed with movable metal type
claim: The Korean Buddhist anthology Jikji, printed in 1377 at Heungdeoksa temple in Cheongju, is the oldest surviving book printed with movable metal type — 78 years before Gutenberg's Bible.
place: Cheongju, Korea (Heungdeoksa temple site); volume held in Paris

title: The Mamluk 52-Card Pack — Europe's Deck Ancestor
claim: The European 52-card pack descends from the Islamic world's Mamluk cards: a 52-card deck in four suits (cups, coins, swords, polo sticks) with ten pip cards and three court cards — malik (king), na'ib malik (viceroy), thani na'ib (second viceroy) — the 'na'ib' being the probable origin of the early Italian word naibi for playing cards.
place: Istanbul, Türkiye (Topkapi Palace)

title: The 1378 iconoclast: al-Maqrizi's account of the Sphinx's nose
claim: The Great Sphinx's nose was chiseled off in 1378 CE by Muhammad Sa'im al-Dahr, a Sufi iconoclast who was angered by local villagers making offerings to the Sphinx; he was seized and killed by the same villagers after the act.
place: Great Sphinx of Giza, Giza Plateau, Egypt

title: The Chinese bristle toothbrush (15th century, conventionally)
claim: A toothbrush with hog bristles set into a bone or bamboo handle was in use in China by the 15th century; European travelers carried the design west in the 17th century.
place: China (Ming context, conventionally)

title: The treasure ships: '44 zhang' (400-foot) claim
claim: Zheng He's largest 'treasure ships' (baochuan) were 44.4 zhang long and 18 zhang wide — roughly 400+ feet, with nine masts — the largest wooden ships ever built.
place: Nanjing, China (Longjiang treasure-shipyard site; 1962 rudder-post find)

title: Zheng He's seven treasure voyages (1405–1433)
claim: Between 1405 and 1433 the Ming court dispatched seven large maritime expeditions under the eunuch admiral Zheng He, sailing from Nanjing through Southeast Asia and the Indian Ocean to Calicut (India), Hormuz and the Persian Gulf, the Red Sea, and the east coast of Africa (Malindi) — the largest wooden fleets assembled before the industrial age, on tribute-diplomacy and trade missions.
place: Nanjing, China (Longjiang shipyard, departure point)

title: Machu Picchu
claim: An Inca settlement on a mountain ridge at ~2,430 m above the Urubamba River, built c. 1420-1450 and occupied until the 1530s; the majority scholarly reading (Rowe; Burger) is that it was a royal estate of the Inca ruler Pachacuti (reigned c. 1438-1471), housing some 500-750 people including Pachacuti's lineage, religious specialists, and skilled yanacona artisans. The Spanish never found or plundered it.
place: Machu Picchu ridge, Urubamba Province, Peru

title: Gutenberg's integrated printing system
claim: In Mainz in the 1440s-1450s, Johannes Gutenberg built the first integrated European printing system: reusable metal type cast in a hand mold, a suitable metal alloy, oil-based ink, and an adapted screw press — and with it produced the 42-line Bible (completed late 1455).
place: Mainz, Electorate of Mainz

title: Valla's 1440 proof: the philologist who broke the Donation
claim: In 1439-1440 Lorenzo Valla, in his Declamatio 'De falso credita et ementita Constantini donatione' (dedicated to Alfonso V of Naples), proved by philological analysis that the Constitutum Constantini could not have been written in the 4th century: the Latin carries vocabulary impossible for a 4th-century imperial chancery, and the document's own internal dating is self-contradictory.
place: Naples (Valla wrote in the service of Alfonso V of Aragon)

title: "Gutenberg invented printing"
claim: Johannes Gutenberg of Mainz invented printing — the first person in the world to develop a method of printing text.
place: Mainz (Holy Roman Empire)

title: The Tarot as a 15th-Century Milanese Game
claim: The tarot deck began as a 15th-century northern-Italian aristocratic card game (tarocchi) — 78 cards: 56 suit cards plus 22 trump cards — documented by surviving hand-painted luxury decks made for the Milanese court.
place: Milan, Italy

title: The First Documented Coffee Drinking — Yemeni Sufi monasteries, 15th century
claim: Coffee as a brewed drink is first documented in the Sufi monasteries of Yemen in the mid-15th century; the earliest named adopter is Sheikh Jamal al-Din al-Dhabhani, mufti of Aden (d. 1470), reported as the first to take up the drink c. 1454.
place: Aden, Yemen

title: Flavio Gioja 'invented the compass at Amalfi in 1302' — the inventor who was a misplaced comma (legend killed at the Latin)
claim: That Flavio Gioja (Gioia) of Amalfi invented the magnetic compass in 1302 — the schoolbook 'inventor' of the mariner's compass. The claim is an attribution legend built on a 16th-century Latin misreading; the person most likely never existed.
place: Amalfi, Italy — the attributed invention place (the statue stands there)

title: The 'millions burned as witches' — the nine-million figure
claim: Millions of people were executed as witches during the Middle Ages, primarily by the medieval Inquisition — the popular "millions burned as witches" figure (often nine million).
place: Europe (witch-hunt era 1450-1750); myth's birthplace: 19th-century Germany and the United States

title: Orban's great bombard, 1452-1453
claim: The Hungarian iron-founder Orban (d. 1453), after offering his services to Constantine XI in 1452, cast a giant bronze bombard for Mehmed II at Adrianople — an approximately 8-meter gun firing stone shot of around half a ton to over a ton — which was dragged some 150 miles to Constantinople by teams of oxen and pounded the Theodosian walls through the 53-day siege.
place: Adrianople (Edirne) — the casting; the gun was dragged to Constantinople

title: The Fall of Constantinople, 29 May 1453
claim: On 29 May 1453, after a 53-day siege (6 April - 29 May), the Ottoman army of Sultan Mehmed II stormed Constantinople, ending the Eastern Roman Empire's eleven-century continuous existence and making the city the Ottoman capital.
place: Constantinople (modern Istanbul)

title: The Marble Emperor legend (Constantine XI)
claim: Constantine XI Palaiologos did not die when Constantinople fell on 29 May 1453; instead an angel rescued him, turned him into marble, and hid him in a cave beneath the Golden Gate of Constantinople, where he sleeps awaiting God's call to awaken and reconquer the city for Christendom.
place: Constantinople — the Golden Gate (Yedikule) of the legend

title: Columbus's real error: the size of the Earth, not its shape
claim: The learned opposition to Columbus's 1492 plan was not about the Earth's shape — which everyone at the table knew was round — but about its size: Columbus argued the Ocean Sea was crossable because he had shrunk the planet by roughly a quarter; the experts were right and he was wrong.
place: Salamanca, Spain (the examining faculty)

title: The real shinobi of Iga and Kōka
claim: Professional shinobi existed: Iga and Kōka families produced trained intelligence and infiltration operatives hired by daimyō in 1485–1581; the Tenshō Iga War (1579/1581) destroyed the Iga sōkoku ikki as an independent power; survivors served Tokugawa Ieyasu; the craft was codified in the Bansenshukai (1676).
place: Iga (Mie Prefecture) — the Iga sōkoku ikki

title: Aixa's "weep like a woman" rebuke to Boabdil (1492)
claim: As Boabdil departed into exile in 1492, pausing at the hill called El Suspiro del Moro to look back at Granada, his mother Aixa (Aisha al-Hurra) rebuked him with words to the effect of "Weep like a woman for what you could not defend as a man" (Spanish: "Llora como mujer lo que no supiste defender como hombre").
place: El Suspiro del Moro, near Padul, Granada (traditional site of the alleged scene)

title: The claim that Columbus discovered the Americas in 1492
claim: Christopher Columbus discovered the Americas in 1492 — i.e., he was the first European to reach them.
place: San Salvador Island, Bahamas (traditional Guanahani landfall, 12 Oct 1492)

title: The surrender of Granada (2 January 1492)
claim: Muhammad XII of Granada (Boabdil) surrendered the Nasrid kingdom — the last Muslim polity of Iberia — to Ferdinand of Aragon and Isabella of Castile on 2 January 1492, under the Capitulations of Santa Fe signed 25 November 1491. He received a fief at Laujar de Andarax in the Alpujarras, which he sold in 1493 before crossing to Fez.
place: The Alhambra, Granada

title: The 1492 'transfusion' of Pope Innocent VIII
claim: Pope Innocent VIII (Giovanni Battista Cybo/Cibo, d. 25 July 1492) received the first recorded blood transfusion in history — the blood of three young boys transfused into the dying pontiff on the suggestion of a Jewish physician.
place: Rome, Vatican

title: The post-1492 depopulation of the Americas (the Great Dying)
claim: In the century after 1492, European colonization and introduced disease caused a massive demographic collapse in the Americas — roughly 90% of the pre-contact population died by ~1600 — on a scale that left ~56 million hectares of farmland to revert to forest.
place: The Americas (hemisphere-wide claim)

title: The 'pristine wilderness' myth of the Americas in 1492
claim: The belief that in 1492 the Americas were a sparsely populated wilderness, 'a world of barely perceptible human disturbance' — an almost untouched, Edenic land untrammeled by man.
place: The Americas (the claim covers the hemisphere)

title: The "toothbrush was invented in China in 1498" telling
claim: The toothbrush was invented in China in 1498, during the reign of the Hongzhi Emperor.
place: China (Hongzhi reign, 1488–1505, conventionally)

title: Letterlocking — the letter as its own envelope
claim: Before cheap pre-made envelopes, letters were routinely folded, secured, and sent without any envelope at all — the technique of 'letterlocking' — used alongside handmade envelopes for centuries.
place: Early modern Europe (exemplars in European archives)

title: The pointed personal knives that came before the table knife
claim: Before the table knife, the European dining knife was a pointed personal implement — each diner carried his own sharp knife, used it to cut what he had seized with his hand, and the same point served as toothpick, lance for the mouth, and occasional weapon.
place: Europe (dining practice)

title: The Venetian mirror monopoly
claim: In the 16th century, Venetian glassmakers on Murano mastered glass backed with a tin-mercury amalgam, giving Europe's only crystal-clear mirrors — and a Venetian export monopoly lasting ~150 years, guarded by laws forbidding glassmakers from leaving and by trade-secrets oaths enforced on penalty of death.
place: Murano, Venice, Italy

title: The scale of the transatlantic slave trade: 12.5 million embarked, 10.7 million disembarked
claim: Between 1501 and 1867, slaving vessels embarked about 12.5 million African captives on the transatlantic crossing; about 10.7 million disembarked alive in the Americas. About 1.8 million died in the Middle Passage. Just 4% of the embarkations were destined for what became the United States.
place: the Atlantic crossing corridor (Africa to the Americas)

title: 'Here be dragons' — the convention that never existed
claim: 'Here be dragons' (hic sunt dracones) was a standard warning that medieval and Renaissance cartographers inscribed on unexplored or dangerous regions of their maps.
place: New York Public Library, Rare Book Division, New York City (the phrase's surviving habitat)

title: The Lenox Globe — the apple with dragons
claim: The Hunt–Lenox Globe (c. 1508–1510) is the second-oldest known terrestrial globe after Martin Behaim's Erdapfel (1492); a hollow red-copper engraved globe, ca. 112 mm in diameter, housed in the NYPL Rare Book Division; and the only accepted historical object bearing the inscription 'HC SVNT DRACONES' ('here be dragons'), placed just below the equator on the eastern coast of Asia.
place: New York Public Library, Rare Book Division (Stephen A. Schwarzman Building)

title: Luther Nailed the 95 Theses to the Church Door
claim: On 31 October 1517 (the eve of All Saints' Day), Martin Luther nailed his 95 Theses on indulgences to the door of All Saints' Church (the Schlosskirche) in Wittenberg — the dramatic hammer scene that popular tradition holds to be the first act of the Reformation.
place: All Saints' Church (Schlosskirche), Wittenberg, Germany

title: The Theses Went Viral on the Press
claim: Luther's 95 Theses were printed and spread across Germany and beyond within weeks and months of October 1517 — Nuremberg (December 1517), Leipzig and Basel (January 1518), with a German translation in January 1518 — largely without Luther's involvement: the printing press, not the hammer, made the theses famous.
place: Wittenberg to Nuremberg, Leipzig, Basel — the early print corridor

title: The handful-of-conquistadors myth
claim: Hernán Cortés conquered the Aztec Empire with about five hundred Spaniards — a handful of Europeans toppling a great empire by their own arms.
place: Tenochtitlan (present-day Mexico City)

title: The siege of Tenochtitlan, 1521
claim: From late May to 13 August 1521, a Spanish–indigenous coalition besieged and took Tenochtitlan, the Triple Alliance capital, after a smallpox epidemic had devastated the city; Cuauhtémoc was captured on 13 August 1521 and the Mexica state fell.
place: Tenochtitlan (present-day Mexico City)

title: The 'Catherine de' Medici introduced the fork to France in 1533' myth
claim: Catherine de' Medici introduced the table fork to France when she traveled there in 1533 to marry the future Henri II, acting as the fork's emissary to the French court.
place: The French court, Paris (the alleged introduction)

title: The Goree Door-of-No-Return throughput: 15-20 million through one house
claim: Fifteen to twenty million enslaved Africans passed through the House of Slaves on Goree Island, Senegal, through its 'Door of No Return,' on the way to the Americas — making the house the trade's principal departure point.
place: Goree Island, Senegal — House of Slaves

title: The deathbed copy: the legend and the one letter
claim: A finished printed copy of De revolutionibus reached Nicolaus Copernicus on the day of his death (24 May 1543) — the legend of the dying astronomer presented with his book as he lay on his deathbed. The ENTIRE claim rests on one primary source: a letter from Canon Tiedemann Giese to Rheticus, written weeks after the death (recorded via Koestler 1963, citing Prowe 1883-84, vol. 1, pt. 2, p. 554): 'For many days he had been deprived of his memory and mental vigour; he only saw his completed book at the last moment, on the day he died.' Christie's catalog states 'a finished copy of the De revolutionibus only reached Copernicus on the eve of his death, his reaction to this addition is unknown.' Jagiellonian classics scholar Jacek Partyka (2023) calls it 'legend' and wryly doubts Copernicus could have approved anything. Copernicus was apoplectic and possibly unconscious; what he actually perceived is unknown.
