place: Frauenburg (Frombork), Poland — Copernicus's death

title: De revolutionibus (1543): the book as printed
claim: Nicolaus Copernicus's De revolutionibus orbium coelestium was printed at Nuremberg by Johannes Petreius in 1543. Rheticus delivered the manuscript in 1542 and supervised the printing, then left for a Leipzig mathematics professorship before completion; Andreas Osiander took over. Osiander added the unsigned instrumentalist preface Ad lectorem ('To the Reader Concerning the Hypotheses of this Work' — 'these hypotheses need not be true nor even probable; if they provide a calculus consistent with the observations, that alone is enough') without Copernicus's authorization: the standard scholarly position is that it was added unsigned and long mistaken for Copernicus's own (evidence: Rheticus crossed it out in his copy and would 'rough up the fellow' if he knew; Giese protested to the Nuremberg city council; Schreiber's note; Praetorius learned of Osiander's authorship from Rheticus and wrote his name in the margin; Kepler methodically exposed Osiander as the author in the 1609 introduction to Astronomia nova). Owen Gingerich's census located 269 surviving copies and estimates the print run at 400-500 copies — usual for the period. The book was 'suspended until corrected' by the Index Decree of 5 March 1616.
place: Nuremberg (Johannes Petreius's press, 1543)

title: The Ottoman 'continuous decline' thesis
claim: The Ottoman Empire entered a continuous, unbroken decline starting in the late 16th century (after Suleiman the Magnificent's death in 1566), decaying steadily in military, fiscal, and administrative power for ~350 years until 1922 — the traditional 'decline thesis.'
place: Istanbul (historiographical debate centered on the Porte's archive and European Orientalist historiography)

title: 'The Byzantine Empire' — the name is 1557, not 330
claim: The empire we call 'Byzantine' called itself 'Byzantine' — that 'the Byzantine Empire' was its own name and it was a civilization separate from Rome.
place: Augsburg (publication place of Wolf's Corpus, Germany)

title: Shakespeare of Stratford wrote the canon — the documentary case
claim: William Shakespeare of Stratford-upon-Avon (1564-1616) wrote the plays and poems attributed to him.
place: Stratford-upon-Avon & London (the Globe), England

title: Gesner's 1565 lead-holder: the first pencil drawing
claim: In 1565, Conrad Gesner (Conrad von Gesner) published, in his book on fossils, a drawing of a strip of graphite held inside a tube of wood — the first depiction of a lead-holder / wood pencil.
place: Zurich, Switzerland

title: The Delft tower experiment, 1586 — the documented drop Galileo never did
claim: In 1586, Simon Stevin and Jan Cornets de Groot (the father of Hugo de Groot) carried two lead balls - one ten times heavier than the other - up the Nieuwe Kerk tower in Delft, dropped them 30 feet onto a wooden platform, and heard a single bang: the balls fell at the same rate, disproving Aristotle's weight-proportional fall theory.
place: Nieuwe Kerk, Delft, Netherlands

title: The Leaning Tower drop — the experiment Galileo never ran
claim: Galileo Galilei, while professor of mathematics at the University of Pisa (c. 1589-1592), publicly dropped balls of different weights from the Leaning Tower of Pisa to demonstrate that they fall at the same rate, disproving Aristotle in front of his colleagues and students.
place: Leaning Tower of Pisa, Pisa, Italy

title: The tine evolution: two tines to three to four
claim: The European table fork evolved from two tines to three to four. The two-prong fork dominated through the 17th century (the earliest two-prong fork bearing an English hallmark, engraved with the Earl of Rutland's coat of arms, dates to 1632 and is held by the V&A). Between the 17th and 18th centuries the tines increased from two to three and then to four — the widely spaced two-prong fork could not spear peas and grains, and from the late 17th to mid-18th century the fork's profile changed from flat to slightly curved to accommodate scooping. The four-tine design became current in the early 19th century; two-tine forks nevertheless lasted in British common usage into the 20th century.
place: London, England (the V&A's 1632 hallmarked fork)

title: The 'wampum was Indian money' telling
claim: The popular telling that wampum — the white and purple shell beads of the Eastern Woodlands — was 'Indian money', a currency of Indigenous societies, is false. In Munsee, Haudenosaunee, and neighboring societies the beads were not used as money: they served spiritual and ceremonial purposes, signified authority, sealed diplomacy, and were woven into belts whose designs acted as mnemonic devices for history, law, and tradition. The currency reading is the colonists' projection, not the makers' practice.
place: Eastern Woodlands / coastal New England and New Netherland

title: Cawdrey's Table Alphabeticall, 1604 — the first English dictionary
claim: In 1604 the schoolmaster Robert Cawdrey published A Table Alphabeticall in London: the first monolingual English dictionary — 120 pages, 2,543 headwords with brief (often single-word) definitions, written 'for the benefit and help of ladies, gentlewomen, or any other unskillful persons.'
place: London, England (published 1604; Cawdrey was living in Coventry)

title: Don Quixote was the first novel ever written
claim: Don Quixote by Miguel de Cervantes — first part published 1605, second part 1615 — was the first novel ever written.
place: Madrid, Spain (1605 first-part printing, Juan de la Cuesta)

title: DEBUNKED: 'Galileo invented the telescope'
claim: The textbook sentence 'Galileo invented the telescope' is false. Galileo Galilei never claimed to have invented the telescope — he learned of the Dutch device from his friend Paolo Sarpi in Venice (who received the Hague newsletter in November 1608), built his own improved instruments from August 1609 (up to ~20-30x), and was the FIRST to turn a telescope to systematic astronomical observation: the four moons of Jupiter (January 1610), the mountains of the Moon, the phases of Venus — published in Sidereus Nuncius (March 1610). The device demonstrably predates his first build by documented months; the States-General Acts show it already being copied in Middelburg before he had heard of it. Twenty-eighth DEBUNKED family.
place: Middelburg, Netherlands (where the device was made); Venice, Italy (where Galileo learned of it, Nov 1608)

title: The first documented telescopes: Lipperhey's 1608 States-General patent bid
claim: The first documented telescopes were made in the Netherlands in 1608: Hans Lipperhey, a spectacle-maker of Middelburg, petitioned the States General for a patent on an instrument 'for seeing things far away as if they were nearby' on 2 October 1608; the assembly tested it (4 Oct), paid him 900 florins (6 Oct), and ordered binocular versions (15 Dec) — denying the patent because Jacob Metius filed a competing application weeks later and the knowledge was already widespread. Lipperhey is the first DOCUMENTED claimant; the original Dutch design (convex objective + concave eyepiece, ~3x) spread across Europe within months. This is the timeline's first early-modern-optics record.
place: Middelburg, Zeeland, Netherlands (Lipperhey's shop; States-General proceedings at The Hague)

title: The compound microscope before Leeuwenhoek (documented by 1619)
claim: Compound microscopes — two-lens tubes — existed and were publicly demonstrated by 1619 at the latest, well before Antonie van Leeuwenhoek's first publications in the 1670s.
place: London (Drebbel's 1619 demonstration); Rome/Florence (Galileo's occhiolino)

title: The expulsion of the Moriscos (1609-1614)
claim: Philip III of Spain, at the instigation of the Duke of Lerma and Archbishop Juan de Ribera of Valencia, ordered the expulsion of the Moriscos (baptized descendants of Iberian Muslims) between 1609 and 1614. Contemporary accounts put the number expelled at roughly 270,000-300,000 people.
place: Valencia (first embarkations, 1609)

title: January 1610 — the moons of Jupiter (what Galileo really proved with a real instrument)
claim: In January 1610, Galileo Galilei observed four points of light near Jupiter with his ~20x telescope, tracking them night after night (7-15 January) as they changed position relative to the planet; they were moons orbiting Jupiter. Published March 1610 in Sidereus Nuncius ('The Starry Messenger').
place: Padua, Italy (observations); Venice (publication)

title: The 'seven candles of the Temple' telling
claim: The Temple menorah is pictured in modern retellings as 'seven candles' — the Temple lit by seven wax candles.
place: Jerusalem (the Temple); the retelling lives in modern illustration

title: The 1621 Plymouth Harvest Feast
claim: In autumn 1621, after the first successful harvest at Plymouth, Governor William Bradford's colonists held a three-day feast attended by Massasoit and about ninety Wampanoag men; wildfowl was served, and the Wampanoag guests contributed five deer they hunted themselves.
place: Plymouth, Massachusetts

title: Wampum as colonial legal tender (1637–1661)
claim: After contact, European colonists made wampum a currency by law: Massachusetts declared it legal tender in 1637 (6 white or 3 black beads per penny, sums under 1 shilling; extended 1643 to sums up to 40 shillings), the Dutch used it as the colony's circulating medium for half a century, and it remained legal tender in New England until 1661 (New York to 1673, North Carolina briefly 1710). European mass-manufacturing then inflated its value roughly a hundredfold and killed it as money — a documented commodity-currency collapse.
place: Massachusetts Bay / New Netherland (Boston, New Amsterdam)

title: Harvey describes the circulation of the blood (1628)
claim: William Harvey published the experimental demonstration that blood circulates — pumped by the heart through arteries, returning through veins — in Exercitatio Anatomica de Motu Cordis et Sanguinis in Animalibus (Frankfurt, 1628).
place: London (experiments); Frankfurt (publication)

title: The Loudun possessions, 1632–1634: the trial that burned a priest
claim: In 1632–1634 in Loudun, Kingdom of France, the nuns of the Ursuline convent reported demonic possession. The parish priest Urbain Grandier was accused of causing the possessions by sorcery, tried by a royal commission (Cardinal Richelieu's), convicted — on the evidence of the nuns' own demonic identifications (including the 'Astaroth' testimony) and a presented pact with the Devil — tortured without confessing, and burned at the stake on 18 August 1634. Public exorcisms of the nuns continued for years after his death (to c. 1638), drawing crowds. Most modern commentators (Jules Michelet, Aldous Huxley, historians of European witchcraft) read the case as a politically motivated persecution led by Richelieu.
place: Loudun, Poitou, Kingdom of France

title: The Taj Mahal: Shah Jahan's 1632-1653 marble mausoleum at Agra
claim: The Taj Mahal is the marble mausoleum on the Yamuna at Agra commissioned by the fifth Mughal emperor Shah Jahan (r. 1628-1658) for his wife Mumtaz Mahal (died 1631 giving birth to their fourteenth child); construction ran c. 1632-1648 with the surrounding complex finished c. 1653, under the principal direction of the court architect Ustad Ahmad Lahauri, using Makrana marble and pietra-dura inlay.
place: Taj Mahal, Agra, Uttar Pradesh, India

title: The 1633 sentence: what the Inquisition actually wrote
claim: The Roman Inquisition's sentence of 22 June 1633 found Galileo Galilei guilty not of formal heresy but of 'vehement suspicion of heresy' — a technical canon-law category short of the most serious crime (Finocchiaro, The Galileo Affair). He abjured, cursed, and detested heliocentrism kneeling before the Congregation; the Dialogue was banned; he was ordered to recite the seven penitential psalms weekly for three years. The formal sentence condemned him 'to prison at the pleasure of the Sacred Congregation' — but this was commuted the next day to house arrest, which he served the rest of his life: first the Tuscan Embassy and Villa Medici in Rome, then Archbishop Piccolomini's residence in Siena (five months), then his own Villa Il Gioiello at Arcetri. He was never tortured (the 21 June 1633 deposition records only a verbal threat — 'otherwise one would have recourse to torture' — which Von Gebler describes as never leaving the ordinary judgment hall) and never entered a dungeon (during proceedings he occupied a five-room suite in the Holy Office palace with his own valet). The 16 June 1633 minutes ordered interrogation 'even with the threat of torture'; the threat was the instrument, not the act.
place: Convent of Santa Maria sopra Minerva, Rome (site of the 22 June 1633 abjuration and sentencing)

title: Tulip mania, winter 1636–1637 — the futures trade and its February collapse
claim: In the winter of 1636–1637, Dutch merchants and skilled craftsmen traded tulip-bulb futures contracts at rapidly rising prices; in February 1637 buyers defaulted on their promises and the market for those contracts collapsed.
place: Amsterdam / Haarlem, Dutch Republic

title: Torricelli invents the barometer — and the vacuum (1643–44)
claim: In 1643, Evangelista Torricelli — Galileo's former assistant — invented the mercury barometer: a 6-foot glass tube filled with mercury, inverted in a dish, retaining 30 inches (760 mm) of column against air pressure — and in the space above the column created the first artificial vacuum (the Torricellian vacuum).
place: Florence

title: The Old Deluder Satan Act of 1647
claim: In 1647 the Massachusetts General Court passed the 'Old Deluder Satan' school law: every township with 50 or more households had to hire and maintain a teacher for reading and writing; towns of 100 or more families had to establish a grammar school preparing students for the university; towns neglecting the order for over a year paid 5 pounds per annum to the next school. The act's first line frames the project as thwarting 'that old deluder, Satan' in keeping men from the knowledge of the Scriptures.
place: Boston, Massachusetts (seat of the Massachusetts General Court)

title: The 'Genesis 5 fixes Creation to 4004 BCE' telling
claim: Read literally, the Genesis 5 genealogy yields one consistent chronology that fixes Creation to 4004 BCE — Archbishop Ussher's famous date — as the text's own calendar.
place: Textual tradition (Jerusalem/MT; Samaria; Alexandria/LXX)

title: Walking the plank as a Golden Age pirate punishment
claim: Pirates during the Golden Age of Piracy (c. 1650–1726) forced prisoners to walk a plank extending from the ship's side into the sea as a characteristic method of execution.
place: Caribbean Sea (the Golden Age's theater)

title: Huygens builds the first pendulum clock (25 December 1656)
claim: On 25 December 1656, Christiaan Huygens completed the first working pendulum clock — built by Salomon Coster, patented 1657, described in Horologium (1658) — cutting daily error from ~15 minutes to ~15 seconds and making the pendulum clock the world's most accurate timekeeper for 300 years.
place: The Hague (Huygens; built by Coster)

title: The Zhou-dynasty (3,000-year) Chinese magnetic compass — the 1658 Jesuit conflation of the mechanical south-pointing chariot with the magnetic needle
claim: That China had the magnetic compass as early as the Zhou dynasty (3,000+ years ago) — the reading that credits the Yellow Emperor / Zhou Gong with the compass, treating the mechanical 'south-pointing chariot' (zhinanche) as a magnetic instrument. The claim is a 17th-century conflation, not ancient history.
place: Zhou China (claimed antiquity); the conflation was born in Jesuit Rome/Munich (Martini's publication world)

title: The Puritan ban on Christmas (Massachusetts Bay, 1659-1681)
claim: In 1659 the Massachusetts Bay Colony made it a crime to observe Christmas — five shillings fine per offense — and the ban stood for 22 years until its repeal in 1681.
place: Boston, Massachusetts Bay Colony

title: The rounded-tip table knife's French standardization
claim: The blunt/rounded-tip table knife became the European standard through a gradual 17th-century French development — the fork's spread removed the need for a pointed table knife, and French court etiquette standardized the blunt form (commonly associated with Louis XIV's reign, with 1669 and 1699 royal-edict variants in the telling).
place: France (court tradition)

title: Christopher Merret's 1662 Royal Society paper: the documented sparkling-wine method
claim: In December 1662, the English scientist and physician Christopher Merret presented a paper to the Royal Society documenting the deliberate addition of sugar and molasses to finished wine to make it 'brisk and sparkling' — the technique that became the basis of champagne production.
place: London, England (Royal Society)

title: Lower's dog-to-dog transfusions (1665)
claim: Richard Lower performed the first successful documented blood transfusions between animals: in 1665 he bled a dog nearly to death and revived it by transfusing the blood of a second dog through a tied artery, demonstrating the technique on circulation's new map.
place: Oxford / London (Royal Society)

title: Newton's fluxions: the unprinted calculus of 1665–1666
claim: Isaac Newton developed his own method of infinitesimals (the method of fluxions) independently in 1665–1666 during the plague years, circulated it in manuscript (De analysi, 1669, via Barrow and Collins; De methodis, 1671), and communicated results to Leibniz through the 1676 epistolae (via Henry Oldenburg), but did not publish his calculus until decades later — well after Leibniz's 1684 publication.
place: Cambridge (Trinity College), England

title: The Great Fire of London, 2–6 September 1666, and the law written in its ashes
claim: The Great Fire of London burned 2–6 September 1666, destroying ~13,200 houses, 89 parish churches, and St Paul's Cathedral, leaving ~80,000 Londoners homeless — and wrote the law in its ashes: the Rebuilding Act 1667 (the first modern building code) and Barbon's Fire Office 1680 (the world's first fire-insurance company).
place: Pudding Lane, City of London (the street no longer exists — built over after the fire)

title: The Great Fire 'burned out' the plague — the schoolbook one-liner
claim: The Great Fire of London (2–6 September 1666) burned out the Great Plague of London — that is, the fire ended the epidemic, and without the fire the plague would have continued.
place: City of London (the fire burned ~436 acres — the suburbs, where later plague cases were found, were untouched)

title: Denys's 1667 transfusions and the 150-year ban
claim: Jean-Baptiste Denys (physician to Louis XIV) performed the first documented animal-to-human blood transfusions: 15 June 1667, lamb's blood into a 15-year-old boy; then a laborer; in December 1667 into Antoine Mauroy, who died. Denys was tried for murder in 1668 and acquitted; the Paris Faculty of Medicine condemned the practice (1668) and the French Parliament banned it (1670), opening the ~150-year hiatus in transfusion.
place: Paris

title: Dom Pérignon's real craft: blending and white wine from black grapes
claim: Dom Pérignon (1638–1715), cellar master of the Abbey of Saint-Pierre d'Hautvillers from 1668, made genuine contributions to winemaking: he mastered the technique of producing white wine from black/red grapes (gentle pressing of clear juice, blending across vineyards), contributing substantially to the development of champagne as it is known today.
place: Abbey of Saint-Pierre d'Hautvillers, Champagne, France

title: The rushlight as the poor's light
claim: For centuries, the rushlight — dried rush pith soaked in fat or grease — was the common artificial light of poor people in the British Isles, costing almost nothing to make.
place: British Isles

title: Leeuwenhoek's animalcules (1674–1723)
claim: Antonie van Leeuwenhoek discovered and documented microorganisms ('animalcules') in 1674–1723, the first human observation of microbial life — reported in letters to the Royal Society, published in Philosophical Transactions (1677), and independently verified at the time.
place: Delft, Dutch Republic (Leeuwenhoek's workshop; Berkelse Mere nearby)

title: The myth: Leeuwenhoek invented the microscope
claim: Antonie van Leeuwenhoek invented the microscope — i.e., that he was the instrument's inventor, and that the microscope dates to his 1670s work.
place: Delft, Dutch Republic (Leeuwenhoek's workshop; the instruments)

title: Leibniz's calculus: independent invention, first publication (1684)
claim: Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz developed the differential and integral calculus independently in Paris in 1674–1675 (his October 1675 manuscripts contain the differential notation dy/dx and the integral sign, extended form), and published first: the Nova Methodus pro Maximis et Minimis in the Acta Eruditorum of Leipzig, October 1684. His notation — dy/dx, the long-s integral sign, the differentiation rules — is the notation mathematics still uses; Newton's dot notation for fluxions is obsolete.
place: Leipzig, Saxony (Acta Eruditorum printing)

title: The 'Salvino D'Armati invented eyeglasses' claim (DEBUNKED)
claim: Salvino D'Armati (or degli Armati) of Florence invented eyeglasses in the 13th century — the named inventor on the Florence plaque and in the schoolbook histories.
place: Florence, Italy (Church of Santa Maria Maggiore — the claimed, obliterated tomb)

title: Denner invents the clarinet (c. 1700, Nuremberg)
claim: Johann Christoph Denner of Nuremberg invented the clarinet around the turn of the 18th century by modifying the chalumeau — adding a register (speaker) key that forced the instrument to overblow at the twelfth, creating the upper 'clarion' register (named for a trumpet style) that gave the instrument its name.
place: Nuremberg (Denner's workshop; born Leipzig, 1655)

title: The idiom-origin audit (method)
claim: An idiom's history is graded on two separate claims: the earliest printed attestation (the anchor, graded on its documentation) and the origin story that explains the phrase (a separate claim, graded on its own evidence). The most confidently told origin stories are the ones that fail at the dates.
place: English-language print culture (London anchor)

title: TELLING (DEBUNKED): 'rule of thumb' = wife-beating law
claim: TELLING (DEBUNKED): the phrase 'rule of thumb' originates from an English common-law rule permitting a husband to beat his wife with a stick no thicker than his thumb.
place: London (legal and fencing print culture)

title: Dom Pérignon invented champagne (4 August 1693)
claim: The Benedictine monk Dom Pérignon invented champagne (sparkling wine) on 4 August 1693 at the Abbey of Saint-Pierre d'Hautvillers, exclaiming 'Come quickly, I am drinking the stars!'
place: Abbey of Saint-Pierre d'Hautvillers, Champagne, France (the legend's theater)

title: The Cornish wreckers' false lights (the systematic-luring legend)
claim: Cornish wreckers in the 18th and 19th centuries routinely and systematically lured ships onto the rocks with deliberately displayed false lights (the 'lights tied to donkeys' tails' image) as an organized criminal industry — wrecking as deliberate murder-by-deception.
place: Cornwall, England (Mounts Bay sample)

title: The real Cornish wrecking economy (1700-1860)
claim: Cornish wrecking in 1700-1860 was a real, multi-faceted coastal salvage economy: (1) rare direct attack and plunder of vessels, (2) the frequent 'harvesting' of wrecked goods from beaches and shorelines, and (3) salvage of goods washed ashore from wrecks that might lie many miles over the horizon — governed by a developing wreck law (the right to salvage goods washed on shore) and carried out by poor and gentry alike, with lifesaving activity far more common in the record than violence.
place: Cornwall, England

title: Cristofori invents the piano (documented 1700; named 1711)
claim: Bartolomeo Cristofori invented the piano in Florence around 1700 — first documented in the 1700 Medici instrument inventory ('arpicimbalo... newly invented by Bartolomeo Cristofori,' a harpsichord-like instrument with hammers and dampers), and first named 'pianoforte' in Scipione Maffei's 1711 article ('gravicembalo col piano, e forte').
place: Florence (the Medici court)

title: The black-clad ninja assassin
claim: Historical Japanese ninja (shinobi) wore distinctive all-black outfits (the classic black shinobi shōzoku) and fought primarily as stealth assassins relying on thrown shuriken.
place: Edo/Tokyo — the theater district where the image was born

title: The phonetic-khipu claim: were khipus writing?
claim: Inca khipus encoded spoken language phonetically — a logosyllabic writing system in which pendant cords represent syllables — rather than recording numbers only.
place: San Juan de Collata, Peruvian Andes (approximate; highland village context)

title: The 1712/1713 verdict against Leibniz: a verdict that invalidates itself
claim: The Royal Society's 1712/1713 report, the Commercium Epistolicum (published 8 January 1713), fairly adjudicated the calculus priority dispute between Newton and Leibniz and stands as valid evidence that Leibniz plagiarized Newton.
place: London, Royal Society

title: Newcomen's atmospheric engine (1712): the first successful steam engine
claim: Thomas Newcomen's first commercially successful atmospheric steam engine was erected in 1712 at the Conygree Coalworks near Dudley (Tipton, in the West Midlands) to pump water from a flooded coal mine — the practical steam engine that pumped the mines of the early 18th century.
place: Conygree Coalworks, Tipton, West Midlands (near Dudley Castle)

title: The 'prompt £20,000 prize' version of the Harrison story
claim: John Harrison's marine chronometer H4 won the longitude problem, and the Board of Longitude promptly awarded him the full £20,000 Longitude Prize under the 1714 Longitude Act.
place: Greenwich / London (Board of Longitude, Royal Observatory, Parliament)

title: The world's first lightship: the Nore, 1731-1732
claim: The world's first lightship — a floating lighthouse — was moored at the Nore sandbank at the mouth of the Thames Estuary in 1731-1732: the private venture of Captain Robert Hamblin (shipowner of King's Lynn), the vessel built by David Avery, operating on a 1730 patent from George II; Trinity House revoked the original patent as an infringement of its powers, and the Admiralty allowed tolls to be levied while the vessel became Trinity House property.
place: The Nore sandbank, Thames Estuary, England (approx station area)

title: 'Lightships were safe — they never dragged, never sank'
claim: Lightships were a safe, uneventful duty: anchored vessels that sat quietly on station and were never in serious danger — the romantic assumption that the boats just sat there.
place: South Goodwin Sands, off Deal, Kent (LV-90 loss, Nov 1954)

title: Norden's 1737 plates: the Sphinx already noseless
claim: Frederic Louis Norden's Egypt plates — drawn in Egypt in 1737, engraved and published posthumously in 'Voyage d'Egypte et de Nubie' (Copenhagen, 1755) — constitute a dated eyewitness image record of the Sphinx that predates both the Napoleonic myth (1798) and photography (1840s), and functions as documentary evidence: the 1737 plate shows the Sphinx already noseless.
place: Great Sphinx of Giza, Giza Plateau, Egypt (the plate's subject)

title: Prussia 1754: the first abolition of judicial torture
claim: Frederick II of Prussia abolished judicial torture by cabinet order in 1754 — the first European abolition of the practice, a decade before Beccaria's book.
place: Berlin, Prussia (the cabinet orders)

title: Celsius's 1742 paper: the reversed scale and the birth of pressure-calibrated thermometry
claim: In 1742, Anders Celsius's paper 'Observations of two persistent degrees on a thermometer' established a mercury thermometer calibrated on two fixed points — with the melting point of ice shown to be essentially pressure-independent and the boiling point of water calibrated at the mean barometric pressure at mean sea level.
place: Uppsala, Sweden (Celsius's observatory; the 1742 paper)

title: The myth: Celsius invented the Celsius scale as we use it (0 freezing, 100 boiling)
claim: Anders Celsius invented the Celsius temperature scale with 0° representing the freezing point of water and 100° representing the boiling point of water — the scale as it hangs on every classroom wall.
place: Uppsala, Sweden (Celsius's observatory; the 1742 paper)

title: Jonas Hanway popularizes the umbrella in London (c. 1750-1786)
claim: Jonas Hanway (1712-1786) was the first Englishman who habitually carried an umbrella in London rain — beginning c. 1750 and persisting for about thirty years despite public mockery, notably from hackney coachmen who saw umbrellas as a threat to their fares; by his death umbrellas were commonplace in London, and men even called their umbrellas a 'Hanway'.
place: London

title: 'The first stapler was made for King Louis XV' — DEBUNKED
claim: The telling that 'the first stapler was made in the 18th century for King Louis XV of France, with handmade staples each inscribed with the insignia of the royal court.'
place: Versailles, France — where the telling places the stapler

title: The Encyclopédie (1751–1772): the Enlightenment's printing war
claim: Denis Diderot and Jean le Rond d'Alembert's Encyclopédie, ou dictionnaire raisonné des sciences, des arts et des métiers (1751–1772) — 28 folio volumes (17 of text, 11 of plates), some 72,000 articles — systematically organized all human knowledge with the mechanical arts given the same dignity as the liberal ones, was suppressed in 1759, and was completed anyway: the Enlightenment's masterwork and its printing war.
place: Paris, France (Le Breton's print shop; the volumes were printed in Paris and Neuchâtel)

title: The Liberty Bell (State House Bell)
claim: The Liberty Bell — originally the Pennsylvania State House bell — was ordered in 1751 by Assembly Speaker Isaac Norris from the London firm of Lester and Pack (later the Whitechapel Bell Foundry), cast with the inscription 'Proclaim LIBERTY Throughout all the Land unto all the Inhabitants Thereof' (Leviticus 25:10). It arrived in Philadelphia in September 1752, cracked on its first test strike, and was twice recast in 1753 by Philadelphia workmen John Pass and John Stow, whose surnames appear on the bell. It hung in the State House (now Independence Hall) steeple, was used to summon lawmakers and mark proclamations, weighs about 2,080 pounds, was dubbed the 'Liberty Bell' by abolitionist societies in the 1830s, and today stands in the Liberty Bell Center, Independence National Historical Park.
place: Liberty Bell Center, Independence National Historical Park, Philadelphia, Pennsylvania

title: Schönbrunn 1752 — the zoo that predates London
claim: Tiergarten Schönbrunn (Vienna), founded 1752, is the oldest zoo in the world still in operation.
place: Tiergarten Schönbrunn, Vienna (coordinates via map.geocode, FULL_ADDRESS match)

title: Beccaria's book did not end judicial torture — the single-cause myth
claim: Cesare Beccaria's 1764 book 'On Crimes and Punishments' (Dei delitti e delle pene) ended judicial torture in Europe — the single-book origin story of the abolition.
place: Europe (the abolition century: Prussia 1754 → Milan 1764 → France 1780/1788)

title: Johnson's Dictionary, 1755 — the nine-year monument that wasn't the first
claim: On 15 April 1755 Samuel Johnson published A Dictionary of the English Language: the product of nine years' work — about 2,300 pages, close to 43,000 entries, and the first English dictionary built on extensive literary quotations (over 100,000) from Shakespeare, Milton, Swift, Pope and others. The standard English dictionary until the OED, 150 years later.
place: London, England (published 15 April 1755)

title: The myth of the first English dictionary: not Johnson, but Cawdrey (1604)
claim: Samuel Johnson wrote the first English dictionary — that no English dictionary existed before Johnson's A Dictionary of the English Language, and that the English dictionary tradition begins with Johnson's 1755 work.
place: London, England (Johnson's Dictionary published 1755; Cawdrey's Table Alphabeticall published 1604, while Cawdrey lived in Coventry)

title: The lunar-distance rival method
claim: The lunar-distance method — measuring the Moon's position against known stars and comparing with tabulated predictions to recover Greenwich time — was a genuine, workable rival solution to the longitude problem, championed by Astronomer Royal Nevil Maskelyne, with Tobias Mayer's lunar tables at its core; the Board of Longitude paid Mayer's widow £3,000 and Leonhard Euler £300 for the lunar-table work, and Maskelyne's Nautical Almanac (from 1767) put the method in sailors' hands.
place: Greenwich Observatory (Royal Observatory, home of the Nautical Almanac)

title: "E pur si muove" — the whisper that wasn't
claim: After abjuring heliocentrism before the Roman Inquisition on 22 June 1633, Galileo Galilei muttered "E pur si muove" ("And yet it moves") — the defiant whisper under the recantation. No contemporary source contains it. The earliest documented print attribution is 115 years later: Giuseppe Baretti's The Italian Library (London, 1757), which presents a garbled version ("stamping with his foot, in a contemplative mood") alongside claims the trial documents themselves refute (six years' imprisonment, torture). Vincenzo Viviani, Galileo's own disciple and first biographer (1655-56), never mentions it; the Inquisition trial record never mentions it. A 1911 '1643 painting' showing the words was exposed as a near-copy of an 1837 painting. Scholars treat the whisper as an 18th-century invention.
place: Santa Maria sopra Minerva, Rome (site of the 22 June 1633 abjuration — where the whisper allegedly happened)

title: 'Melvil Dewey invented the index card' — DEBUNKED
claim: The telling that 'Melvil Dewey invented the index card in 1876' — that the index card began with Dewey and the American library movement.
place: Amherst, Massachusetts — where the telling places the invention (Dewey's 1876 pamphlet)

title: Linnaeus's paper slips (mid-1760s) — the card before the catalog
claim: Carl Linnaeus used standardized, unbound paper slips (~7.5x13 cm) in the mid-1760s for organizing taxonomic data — a paper tool functionally identical to modern index cards.
place: Uppsala, Sweden — Linnaeus's home; the slips survive in Stockholm collections

title: The H4 Jamaica trial, 1761–1762
claim: On the Board of Longitude's official sea trial from Portsmouth to Kingston, Jamaica (HMS Deptford, 18 November 1761 – 19 January 1762, 81 days 5 hours), John Harrison's H4 lost approximately 5.1 seconds after correction for its known daily rate — a longitude error of 1.25 minutes (about one nautical mile), far inside the half-degree (30 nautical miles) required by the 1714 Longitude Act for the £20,000 reward.
place: Kingston, Jamaica (arrival; the voyage ran Portsmouth → Kingston)

title: Prussian schools were designed to produce obedient soldiers
claim: The Prussian school system was designed — from Frederick the Great's 1763 Generallandschulreglement onward — to produce obedient soldiers: a factory-model education 'deliberately designed to produce mediocre intellects... and to ensure docile and incomplete citizens' (Gatto), the template for modern schooling's bells, rows, and 45-minute periods.
place: Berlin, Prussia

title: Rousseau's 'great princess' and the brioche (1765)
claim: In his Confessions, Book 6 (first six books written c. 1765, published posthumously 1782), Jean-Jacques Rousseau recounts that an unnamed 'great princess,' told that the peasants had no bread, replied 'Qu'ils mangent de la brioche' ('Then let them eat brioches') — the true paper trail of the 'let them eat cake' anecdote.
place: Paris, France (where Rousseau set the anecdote and wrote the manuscript)

title: "James Watt invented the steam engine"
claim: James Watt (1736–1819) invented the steam engine.
place: Britain (the schoolbook tradition's setting)

title: Watt's separate condenser, Patent No. 913 (5 January 1769)
claim: On 5 January 1769 James Watt received UK Letters Patent No. 913 for the separate condenser — 'A New Invented Method of Lessening the Consumption of Steam and Fuel in Fire Engines' — the improvement that kept the working cylinder hot while condensing steam in a separate chamber, cutting fuel consumption by roughly two-thirds and making the steam engine a general-purpose industrial power source.
place: Great Britain (patent enrolled at the Patent Office, London; developed at Glasgow)

title: The 'eraser was invented in 1770' telling — DEBUNKED by bread
claim: The telling that the eraser was invented in 1770 — that Nairne's rubber cube was the beginning of erasing — is false. Erasing predates rubber by centuries. Before rubber erasers, tablets of wax were used to erase lead or charcoal marks from paper; bits of rough stone such as sandstone or pumice removed small errors from parchment or papyrus written in ink; and crustless bread was the standard pencil-mark eraser — a Meiji-period (1868–1912) Tokyo student recalled: 'Bread erasers were used in place of rubber erasers, and so they would give them to us with no restriction on amount.' The bread-crumb eraser is itself the probable source of Nairne's 'accidental pickup' tradition. What 1770 invented was the rubber eraser — not the eraser.
place: London (telling's home market)

title: Nairne's widely marketed rubber eraser, 1770
claim: In 1770 the English optician and scientific instrument maker Edward Nairne developed the first widely marketed rubber eraser — natural-rubber cubes sold at three shillings per half-inch cube from his shop opposite the Royal Exchange. The event is documented in Joseph Priestley's footnote of 15 April 1770: 'I have seen a substance excellently adapted to the purpose of wiping from paper the mark of black-lead-pencil. ... It is sold by Mr. Nairne, Mathematical Instrument-Maker, opposite the Royal-Exchange.' Until then the material was known as gum elastic or caoutchouc; the word 'rubber' was in general use in 1770 for anything used to rub and attached to the new material sometime between 1770 and 1778.
place: Royal Exchange, London (Nairne's shop)

title: The Jenner-was-first myth (DEBUNKED)
claim: Edward Jenner was NOT the first person to use cowpox to protect against smallpox. The documented predecessors include Benjamin Jesty (1774, Dorset — 22 years before Jenner), Peter Plett (1791, Holstein — 5 years before), and others named in the literature (Bose 1769, Fewster's 1760s observations, Sevel, Jensen, Rendall).
place: Berkeley, Gloucestershire, England (Jenner's 1796 experiment)

title: Benjamin Jesty's 1774 cowpox inoculation
claim: In 1774, Dorset farmer Benjamin Jesty inoculated his wife Elizabeth and his two eldest sons, Robert (3) and Benjamin (2), with cowpox lymph taken from a cow at Chetnole — twenty-two years before Jenner's 1796 experiment.
place: Chetnole / Worth Matravers, Dorset, England

title: The deleted anti-slavery paragraph of the Declaration
claim: Thomas Jefferson's original draft of the Declaration of Independence contained a full paragraph condemning the slave trade — arraigning George III for forcing "that execrable commerce" on the colonies — and Congress deleted the entire paragraph in the Committee of the Whole on July 3-4, 1776, at the objection of South Carolina and Georgia (with the northern states, Jefferson noted, also "pretty considerable carriers" of enslaved people).
place: Independence Hall, Philadelphia, Pennsylvania

title: Ned Ludd — real person or figurehead?
claim: Ned Ludd — Captain/General/King Ludd — was a real historical person: an Anstey, Leicestershire weaver's apprentice who, in 1779, smashed two stocking frames in a fit of rage after being whipped for idleness (or taunted by youths), and whose name the 1811–1813 frame-breakers adopted as their leader.
place: Anstey, Leicestershire, England

title: William Addis and the mass-produced toothbrush (1780)
claim: In 1780, William Addis of England made a bone-handled toothbrush with swine bristles (the prison-prototype story) and, after release, began mass-producing toothbrushes in England; the family firm (Wisdom Toothbrush) continued into the 1990s.
place: London, England

title: The Tarot as the Egyptian 'Book of Thoth'
claim: The tarot deck is an ancient Egyptian artifact — the 'Book of Thoth,' the esoteric wisdom of the Egyptian temples preserved in card form and carried to Europe by the Romani people.
place: Paris (publication site)

title: The Washington dentures: the materials record
claim: George Washington's surviving dentures were constructed from hippopotamus, walrus, and probably elephant ivory; cow, horse, and human teeth; and lead, brass, silver, and gold alloys — with no wood as a tooth material.
place: Mount Vernon, Virginia (the surviving complete set); New York Academy of Medicine (Greenwood 1789 set)

title: The first free flight — Pilatre de Rozier and d'Arlandes, 21 November 1783
claim: On 21 November 1783, Jean-Francois Pilatre de Rozier and the Marquis d'Arlandes made the first untethered crewed balloon flight — the first confirmed human flight of any kind — in a Montgolfier hot-air balloon, taking off from the garden of the Chateau de la Muette in the Bois de Boulogne (Paris) and flying ~25 minutes, ~9 km, to the Butte-aux-Cailles, before a crowd that included Louis XVI and Benjamin Franklin.
place: Chateau de la Muette, Bois de Boulogne → Butte-aux-Cailles, Paris

title: The Bramah Challenge Lock stood unpicked for 67 years (VERIFIED)
claim: Joseph Bramah's Challenge Lock stood unpicked for 67 years — from the 1784 patent to Alfred Charles Hobbs's opening of it at the Great Exhibition of 1851.
place: 124 Piccadilly, London (shop window); opened at the Great Exhibition, Crystal Palace, Hyde Park

title: Franklin's bifocals, 1784
claim: Benjamin Franklin invented bifocals — lenses with two optical powers in one frame — describing the invention in a 1784 letter from Passy to George Whatley.
place: Passy (Paris), France — where Franklin wrote the 1784 letter

title: The 1784 ledger: nine teeth, 122 shillings
claim: In 1784, Washington's plantation ledger records a cash payment of 122 shillings (£6.10) to several enslaved people for nine teeth, on account of the French dentist Jean-Pierre Le Mayeur.
place: Mount Vernon plantation, Virginia (the ledger)

title: The Bastille's 'hundreds of political prisoners' (myth)
claim: The popular claim that the Bastille held hundreds of political prisoners, liberated by the storming of 14 July 1789.
place: Place de la Bastille, Paris

title: The storming of the Bastille, 14 July 1789
claim: On 14 July 1789 a Parisian crowd stormed the Bastille fortress; the garrison surrendered, governor Bernard-René de Launay was killed by the mob, roughly 100 people died in the fighting, and the fortress's seven prisoners were freed.
place: Place de la Bastille, Paris (fortress demolished 1789–1790; site marked by the Colonne de Juillet)

title: Bligh's open-boat voyage to Timor, April–June 1789 (the foil)
claim: Cast adrift on 28 April 1789, Bligh navigated the Bounty's 23-foot launch some 3,600 nautical miles over 47 days to Coupang, Timor, arriving 14 June 1789 — without charts, by dead reckoning and sextant — one of the great feats of open-boat navigation. One man, John Norton, was killed by islanders at Tofua days into the voyage; the other 18 survived.
place: Coupang (Kupang), Timor — the landing; voyage began near Tofua, Tonga

title: The mutiny on HMS Bounty, 28 April 1789 (the foil)
claim: On 28 April 1789, near Tofua in the Tonga group, Fletcher Christian and disaffected crewmen seized HMS Bounty — 23 days out from Tahiti — and set William Bligh and 18 loyal men adrift in the ship's 23-foot launch.
place: Near Tofua, Tonga

title: The namesake who never invented it — Dr. Guillotin and the machine that stole his name
claim: Joseph-Ignace Guillotin invented the guillotine — the machine as his personal invention.
place: Paris (where Guillotin made his December 1789 Assembly motion, Louis designed the machine, and Schmidt built it; first use at the Place de Grève, 25 April 1792)

title: DEBUNKED: Marie Antoinette said 'Let them eat cake'
claim: Marie Antoinette, queen of France, when told that the French peasants had no bread, replied "Let them eat cake" (French: "Qu'ils mangent de la brioche") — the remark that became the universal shorthand for aristocratic indifference on the eve of the Revolution.
place: Versailles, France (where the claim sets the remark)

title: The makers: Louis's design, Schmidt's build, Pelletier's morning — 25 April 1792
claim: Antoine Louis designed and Tobias Schmidt built the French guillotine; its first public use was the execution of Nicolas-Jacques Pelletier at the Place de Grève, Paris, on 25 April 1792.
place: Place de Grève (now Place de l'Hôtel-de-Ville), Paris — first use, 25 April 1792

title: Chappe's optical telegraph (1791–1794)
claim: Claude Chappe (1763–1805), with his brothers, invented the optical semaphore telegraph; the first public demonstration ran on 2 March 1791 (Brûlon to Parcé, 16 km); the Legislative Assembly adopted the machine in 1792; Chappe was appointed ingénieur-télégraphiste and built the Paris–Lille line (230 km), which carried official military dispatches in 1794.
place: Brûlon, Sarthe, France (the 1791 demonstration site; Paris–Lille line terminals)

title: The revolutionary playing-card catalog (1791) — a million cards to Paris
claim: During the French Revolution, officials cataloged libraries confiscated from aristocrats and clergy on blank-backed playing cards — over a million cards sent to Paris within three years — a national card catalog before the term existed.
place: Paris, France — the Bureau de Bibliographie, destination of the cards

title: The Pandora pencil: 1791, already mechanical
claim: The earliest extant datable example of a mechanical pencil was recovered from the wreckage of HMS Pandora, which sank in 1791 — a working propelling pencil predating the 1822 patent by 31 years.
place: Great Barrier Reef, Australia (wreck region)

title: The death of Mozart, 5 December 1791
claim: Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart died in Vienna on 5 December 1791, at age 35, after a short final illness marked by fever, rash, and severe swelling (edema).
place: Vienna, Austria

title: 'Napoleon invented the semaphore' — the authorship myth
claim: Napoleon Bonaparte invented the semaphore (optical) telegraph — the 'Napoleonic semaphore' label as an authorship claim.
place: Paris (the popular telling's home — where the Assembly adopted Chappe's machine in 1792, seven years before the 18 Brumaire coup)

title: Peter Plett's 1791 Holstein cowpox vaccinations
claim: In 1791, Holstein teacher Peter Plett vaccinated the three children of his employer Martini at Hasselburg with cowpox lymph — five years before Jenner's experiment — and reported the success to the Kiel medical faculty.
place: Hasselburg (Gut Wittenberg), East Holstein

title: Salieri and Mozart: the documented courtesy
claim: Whatever their professional rivalry, Salieri and Mozart behaved as collegial Viennese court composers: Mozart rode with Salieri to The Magic Flute in October 1791 and Salieri praised it number by number, and after Mozart's death Salieri taught composition to Mozart's son.
place: Vienna, Austria

title: The legend that Salieri poisoned Mozart
claim: Antonio Salieri poisoned Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart out of professional jealousy, as depicted in Peter Shaffer's 1979 play Amadeus and Milos Forman's 1984 film.
place: Vienna, Austria — the rumor's city and the play's stage

title: The death the machine never dealt him — Guillotin, 1814, of a carbuncle
claim: Joseph-Ignace Guillotin was executed by the guillotine — killed by the machine that bears his name.
place: Père-Lachaise Cemetery, Paris — Guillotin's burial; the myth dies at the graveside

title: The 'Captain Bligh the sadistic tyrant' reading (DEBUNKED)
claim: William Bligh, captain of HMS Bounty, was a sadistic tyrant whose cruelty drove his crew to mutiny on 28 April 1789.
place: Near Tofua, Tonga — where the mutiny's story was born

title: Conté's 1795 recipe: clay, graphite, and the hardness dial
claim: In 1795, Nicolas-Jacques Conté patented the process of making pencil lead from powdered graphite mixed with wet clay, shaped into rods and fired — the mixture ratio controlling the lead's hardness — freeing continental pencil-makers from dependence on British graphite.
place: Paris, France

title: Paris 1794 — the first public scientific zoo
claim: The Ménagerie du Jardin des Plantes in Paris, officially inaugurated in 1794, was the first modern public scientific zoo.
place: Ménagerie du Jardin des Plantes, 75005 Paris (coordinates via map.geocode, FULL_ADDRESS match)

title: The Paris–Lille line's first dispatch (1794)
claim: The first military dispatches over the Paris–Lille semaphore line carried news of the French recapture of Condé-sur-l'Escaut from the Austrians in 1794 — the victory known in Paris less than an hour after it occurred.
place: The Paris–Lille semaphore line (230 km); news terminus Condé-sur-l'Escaut (~50.45N, 3.59E)

title: Edward Jenner's 1796 experiment and the 1798 Inquiry (the foil)
claim: On 14 May 1796, Edward Jenner inoculated 8-year-old James Phipps with cowpox matter from the hand of the dairymaid Sarah Nelmes; on 1 July he challenged Phipps with smallpox matter and no disease followed. He self-published An Inquiry into the Causes and Effects of the Variolae Vaccinae in 1798 after the Royal Society declined the paper, named the method 'vaccination' (from vacca, cow), and drove its global adoption — earning £10,000 (1802) and £20,000 (1807) from Parliament.
place: Berkeley, Gloucestershire, England

title: Phrenology (skull-bump faculty mapping)
claim: The shape of the skull reveals the strengths of the mind: 27 (later 35) mental faculties can be read from the bumps on a person's cranium, allowing diagnosis of character and ability by palpation.
place: Vienna, Austria (Gall's lecture halls)

title: The rival 'first skyscraper' candidates: the 93-year candidate map
claim: The 'first skyscraper' title has at least four documented earlier or rival candidates, each holding a different 'first' under a different definition: the Ditherington Flax Mill (1797), Oriel Chambers (1864), the Equitable Life Building (1870), and the Rand McNally Building (1890).

title: Napoleon's soldiers shot off the Sphinx's nose (1798)
claim: Napoleon Bonaparte's soldiers shot the nose off the Great Sphinx of Giza with cannon fire during the French invasion of Egypt in 1798.
place: Great Sphinx of Giza, Giza Plateau, Egypt

title: The Mount Sapo naming legend (soap's false etymology)
claim: Soap takes its name from Mount Sapo (or Sappo), a supposed Roman hill where animals were sacrificed to the gods; rain washed the sacrifices' fat and ashes down the slope into the Tiber, where laundresses discovered the mixture cleaned their clothes.
place: Rome (the legend's claimed setting — no such place)

title: The 'Richelieu invented the table knife' telling
claim: Cardinal Richelieu (1585-1642) invented the blunt-tipped table knife around 1637 — the schoolbook telling that he ordered all table knives' points ground off at his own table after seeing a dinner guest pick his teeth with a pointed knife.
place: Paris (the telling's claimed setting)

title: The 'valid firman' defense of the Elgin removal
claim: Lord Elgin held a valid Ottoman firman (royal decree) that legally authorized the removal of the Parthenon sculptures from the Parthenon itself — that the surviving document authorizes taking statues and reliefs off the building, not merely drawing, casting, measuring, and excavating around it.
place: The Parthenon, Athenian Acropolis

title: The Parthenon sculptures' removal and 1816 purchase
claim: Sculptures from the Parthenon on the Athenian Acropolis (carved c. 447-432 BCE) were removed between 1801 and 1812 by agents of Thomas Bruce, 7th Earl of Elgin; the collection was sold to the British Parliament in 1816 for 35,000 pounds and has been held in the British Museum since.
place: The Parthenon, Athenian Acropolis (sculptures now in the British Museum, London)

title: Luke Howard names the clouds (December 1802)
claim: In December 1802, the London pharmacist and amateur meteorologist Luke Howard presented 'On the Modification of Clouds' to the Askesian Society, establishing the Latin cloud nomenclature — cirrus, cumulus, stratus (and nimbus) — that remains the basis of cloud classification today.
place: London (the Askesian Society)

title: The 'short Napoleon' myth
claim: Napoleon Bonaparte was unusually short — about 5 feet 2 inches (English measure).
place: London (caricature press) / Paris (measurement origin)

title: Beaufort devises the wind force scale (1805)
claim: In 1805, Francis Beaufort — then a Royal Navy officer serving aboard HMS Woolwich — devised the Beaufort wind force scale: thirteen classes (0–12) describing wind strength by its effects on a frigate's sails, from 'just sufficient to give steerage' to 'that which no canvas sails could withstand.'
place: Aboard HMS Woolwich (at sea)

title: Chancel's chemical matches (1805) — the dipping predecessor
claim: In 1805, Paris, Jean-Louis Chancel produced the first chemical match in commercial form: a splint tipped with potassium chlorate, sulfur, sugar, and rubber, ignited by dipping it into a bottle of concentrated sulfuric acid (the oxy-muriatic or 'dipping' chemical match). Walker was already making variations on Chancel's matches for local hunters before his friction-match accident.
place: Paris, France (Chancel's workshop)

title: Frederic Tudor's ice trade (VERIFIED)
claim: Frederic Tudor of Boston created the global natural-ice trade, shipping New England ice to the Caribbean from 1806 and to India from 1833.
place: Boston, Massachusetts (origin); Martinique; Calcutta, India

title: The British Orders in Council (1807–1812)
claim: Britain's 1807 Orders in Council — retaliatory trade restrictions requiring neutral shipping to clear British ports — strangled American commerce with Europe; they were suspended 16 June 1812, two days before the United States declared war on 18 June 1812, and provisionally repealed 23 June 1812, the news reaching Madison only on 12 August 1812.
place: London, England (Parliament — the acts and their suspension)

title: The tin can (Durand, 1810)
claim: English merchant Peter Durand patented the tinplate food can in 1810 (British Patent 3,372, 25 August 1810), adapting Nicolas Appert's heat-preservation process to iron canisters coated in tin; Donkin, Hall & Gamble bought the rights and opened the world's first commercial cannery in London in 1813.
place: London (patent enrolled; first cannery at Bermondsey, opened 1813)

title: The Luddite movement, 1811–1817
claim: The Luddite movement (1811–1817) was a protest movement of English textile workers — framework knitters in Nottinghamshire/Leicestershire/Derbyshire, croppers in the West Riding of Yorkshire, handloom weavers — who conducted organized, often nocturnal raids to destroy specific textile machinery they held responsible for cutting wages, de-skilling work, and breaking standard labor practices; the movement began at Arnold, Nottinghamshire, on 11 March 1811, spread to Yorkshire and Lancashire in 1812, and was suppressed by legal and military force culminating in the York Special Commission of January 1813.
place: Arnold, Nottinghamshire, England

title: 'The Luddites were anti-technology'
claim: The Luddites were opposed to technology itself — blind enemies of progress who smashed machines because they feared or hated machinery, the modern dictionary-shorthand meaning of 'luddite'.
place: Arnold, Nottinghamshire, England

title: 'The French burned Moscow'
claim: The French army set the 1812 Moscow fire as policy — that is, Napoleon or his commanders ordered the burning of the city.
place: Moscow

title: 'General Winter defeated Napoleon'
claim: The Grande Armée was destroyed in 1812 primarily by the Russian winter — that is, the extreme cold, rather than hunger, disease, desertion, and the Russian army, was the main cause of the army's destruction.
place: Western Russia (Niemen to Moscow to Berezina)

title: The destruction of the Grande Armée, 1812
claim: The 1812 Russian campaign destroyed the Grande Armée as a fighting force: of the several hundred thousand men who crossed the Niemen in June 1812, only tens of thousands recrossed in fighting condition by December — the largest army Europe had yet seen, annihilated.
place: Western Russia (Niemen to Moscow to Berezina)

title: The Burning of Moscow, September 1812
claim: Moscow burned 14-18 September 1812 (Old Style 2-6 September), beginning the day French troops entered the evacuated city; roughly three-quarters of the mostly wooden city was destroyed over five days.
place: Moscow

title: The War of 1812
claim: The United States declared war on Great Britain on 18 June 1812; the war ended with the Treaty of Ghent (signed 24 December 1814, ratified 16 February 1815), with the Battle of New Orleans fought 8 January 1815 — after the treaty was signed.
place: United States / British North America / the Atlantic (war theater); Ghent, Belgium (treaty)

title: 'The War of 1812 was fought to stop impressment'
claim: The War of 1812 was fought primarily to stop the British practice of impressment — that is, impressment was the war's principal cause.
place: Washington, D.C. (war message, declaration) / Ghent (treaty)

title: 'The Star-Spangled Banner has always been the national anthem'
claim: The Star-Spangled Banner has always been the national anthem of the United States — since the founding era, effectively from 1776 onward.
place: Washington, D.C. (Congress, 3 March 1931)

title: Key writes 'Defence of Fort M'Henry' (The Star-Spangled Banner), 13–16 September 1814
claim: On the morning of 14 September 1814, after watching the British bombardment of Fort McHenry from detention aboard a British vessel, Francis Scott Key wrote the poem 'Defence of Fort M'Henry' — the words that became 'The Star-Spangled Banner' — setting them to the tune 'To Anacreon in Heaven' (commonly attributed to John Stafford Smith, c. 1770).
place: Fort McHenry, Baltimore, Maryland (written aboard a detained cartel vessel in the Patapsco during the bombardment)

title: Cambronne's 'La Garde meurt, elle ne se rend pas!'
claim: When the British called on the last square of the Imperial Old Guard to surrender at Waterloo, General Pierre Cambronne answered with the noble sentence 'La Garde meurt, elle ne se rend pas!' ('The Guard dies, it does not surrender!').
place: Waterloo battlefield, Walloon Brabant, Belgium

title: Cambronne's one-word reply — 'le mot de Cambronne'
claim: When the British insisted on the surrender of the last Old Guard square at Waterloo, General Cambronne answered with a single scatological word: 'Merde!'
place: Waterloo battlefield, Walloon Brabant, Belgium

title: The Tambora-year motive for the Laufmaschine
claim: Karl Drais invented the Laufmaschine in response to the horse-feed crisis of the Year Without a Summer (1816), when the April 1815 eruption of Mount Tambora caused crop failures that starved horses across Europe.
place: Mannheim / the Baden crisis of 1816

title: The Battle of Waterloo (18 June 1815)
claim: On 18 June 1815, near Waterloo in present-day Belgium, Napoleon Bonaparte's Armée du Nord was defeated by the Anglo-Allied army under the Duke of Wellington and the Prussian army under Gebhard von Blücher; it was Napoleon's last battle, and he abdicated four days later.
place: Waterloo battlefield, Walloon Brabant, Belgium

title: The Laufmaschine's first ride (12 June 1817)
claim: Karl Drais rode the first documented two-wheeled steerable vehicle — the Laufmaschine — from Mannheim to the Schwetzinger Relaishaus (Rheinau) and back on 12 June 1817, about 7 km each way, the round trip in a little more than an hour, establishing the two-wheeler principle basic to the bicycle and the motorcycle.
place: Mannheim, Grand Duchy of Baden

title: Blundell's human-to-human transfusions (1818)
claim: James Blundell (British obstetrician) performed the first documented successful human-to-human blood transfusions: 1818, for postpartum hemorrhage — the patient's husband as donor, about four ounces, delivered by syringe. Between 1825 and 1830 he performed ten transfusions, five of which he reported as beneficial, publishing the results and devising transfusion instruments.
place: London (Guy's Hospital)

title: Fresnel's lighthouse lens: invented 1819-1822, first lit at Cordouan 25 July 1823
claim: Augustin-Jean Fresnel invented the stepped annular lighthouse lens for the French Commission des Phares (1819-1822): his lentilles a echelons replaced the parabolic reflectors then in use; the revolving eight-panel first-order apparatus passed its official public test atop the unfinished Arc de Triomphe on 20 August 1822 (witnessed by Louis XVIII and his entourage from 32 km away); the world's first lighthouse Fresnel lens was lit at the Cordouan lighthouse on 25 July 1823. The invention carried a documented 74-year prehistory: Buffon had proposed a stepped lens in 1748 (for burning glasses, single piece), Condorcet had suggested assembling annular sections separately on a frame in 1790, Rogers had focused a lighthouse beam with a conventional lens at Portland Bill in 1789, and Brewster had advocated a Condorcet-style lens for British lighthouses by 1820.
place: Cordouan lighthouse, Gironde estuary, France

title: Starke's Travels on the Continent (1820) — the first modern travel guide
claim: Mariana Starke's Travels on the Continent, written for the use and particular information of travellers, published by John Murray in 1820, was the first modern travel guide — practical itineraries, journey times, inn and restaurant assessments (the 'daggers of admiration' ratings), maps and archaeological plans, updated across editions.
place: London (John Murray, publisher)

title: Napoleon's actual height
claim: Napoleon Bonaparte's height was approximately 169 cm (about 5 feet 6 to 5 feet 7 inches in English measure), average to slightly above average for French men of his era.
place: Longwood, Saint Helena

title: DEBUNKED: 'no one proposed the stepped lens before Fresnel'
claim: The stepped/annular lighthouse lens — the Fresnel lens — was entirely Augustin-Jean Fresnel's own unanticipated idea: no one had proposed a stepped lens before him. (The ex nihilo lone-genius version of the invention.)
place: Paris, France (the telling's home)

title: The telling that died: 'the mechanical pencil is modern' (234th family)
claim: DEBUNKED: the mechanical pencil is a 20th-century invention — killed twice: (1) the 1822 British patent (Mordan & Hawkins, #4742) is a documented 203-year-old propelling-pencil patent with manufactured, hallmarked survivors; (2) the 19th century ran a whole propelling-pencil industry — 160+ British patents 1822–1874, the 1877 spring-loaded mechanism, and the 1791 Pandora example — before the 20th-century brands existed.
place: London, England

title: The 1822 patent: the mechanical pencil's birthday
claim: In 1822, Sampson Mordan and John Isaac Hawkins filed in Great Britain the first patent for a refillable metal pencil with an internal mechanism for propelling the graphite lead forward during use (the 'ever-pointed pencil'); Mordan bought out Hawkins and manufactured the pencils with Gabriel Riddle (1823–1837, SMGR hallmark), then as S. Mordan & Co. into the 20th century.
place: London, England

title: Walker's friction match (1826/1827) — the first practical friction match
claim: John Walker of Stockton-on-Tees invented the first practical, commercially successful friction match in 1826 (accidental ignition: a dipped stick scraped against his hearth), and sold the first recorded box on 7 April 1827 — recorded in his sales ledger as 'Sulphurata Hyper-Oxygenata Frict', batch 'No. 30', to a Mr. Hixon, a solicitor. The splints were sulfur-dipped, tipped with antimony trisulfide and potassium chlorate in gumwater, sold 1s 2d per 100 with a tin and a folded piece of sandpaper. Walker never patented the invention ('I doubt not it will be a benefit to the public, so let them have it'), despite encouragement from Michael Faraday; Samuel Jones of London copied the design in 1829 as 'Lucifers'. Walker died 1 May 1859 in Stockton, uncredited in his lifetime.
place: Stockton-on-Tees, County Durham, England (59 High Street chemist's shop)

title: The 'Victorian secret language of the fan' myth
claim: Victorian (and Regency) women communicated through a codified, widely-used secret 'language of the fan' — a fixed system of fan positions and gestures carrying specific messages ('fan in the left hand in front of the face = I desire your acquaintance', 'touching the handle to the lips = kiss me', etc.).
place: Paris and London (the alleged practice)

title: Poenaru's 1827 fountain-pen patent
claim: Petrache Poenaru registered a French patent on 25 May 1827 (brevet no. 3208) for a 'plume portable sans fin, qui s'alimente elle-meme avec de l'ancre' — a portable pen that recharges itself with ink, built from a large swan's quill used as an ink reservoir.
place: Paris, France — where Poenaru studied at the École Polytechnique and registered the invention

title: 'The match is a Swedish invention' — DEBUNKED (225th family)
claim: The claim that the match is a Swedish invention is DEBUNKED as a blanket statement. The friction match was English: John Walker's Stockton-on-Tees matches were on sale from 7 April 1827, seventeen years before Gustaf Erik Pasch's 1844 Swedish safety-match patent — and Chancel's Paris chemical matches (1805) preceded both. What Sweden genuinely contributed was the SAFETY match: Pasch's 1844 separated design (red phosphorus on the striking surface, not in the head) plus the Lundström brothers' commercial manufacture from Jönköping (1845–47 development, 1855 Paris award). 'Swedish match' is a brand and an industrial monopoly (Jönköpings & Vulcans Tändsticksfabriks AB 1903 → Swedish Match), not an invention credit for the match itself.
place: Stockholm, Sweden (the myth's home — Pasch's city; the fiction belongs where the truth was partial)

title: The claim that Columbus sailed to prove the Earth was round
claim: Christopher Columbus sailed west to prove the Earth was round, against scholars and churchmen who believed it was flat.
place: Salamanca, Spain (the 1486-87 commission)

title: Joseph Henry's wire: the science before the patent (1828–1835)
claim: Joseph Henry — at the Albany Academy, 1826–1832 — built the scientific core the telegraph ran on: the high-intensity multi-turn insulated electromagnet (1828), the 1831 'magnetic telegraph' demonstration ringing a bell through a mile of wire, and the 1835 mercury-dipping electrical relay. He refused to patent, choosing open science.
place: Albany, New York (the Albany Academy)

title: 'Elias Howe invented the sewing machine' — the sole-invention telling
claim: Elias Howe alone invented the sewing machine — the 1846 lockstitch patent (U.S. 4,750) was the invention of the sewing machine itself, with no prior inventors of working sewing machines.
place: United States (the popular telling)

title: Thimonnier's sewing machine: the first functional machine and the tailor riot
claim: French tailor Barthélemy Thimonnier patented a working sewing machine in 1830; his chain-stitch machine (barbed needle, foot treadle, spring return) was put into production in a Paris workshop making army uniforms, and the machines were destroyed by a mob of tailors fearing for their livelihoods.
place: Paris, France (Thimonnier's workshop)

title: 'Morse invented the telegraph' — the sole-inventor myth
claim: The electric telegraph was invented single-handedly by Samuel F. B. Morse — one man, one invention, c. 1832–1844.
place: Washington, D.C. (the Capitol rotunda, where the 1844 line terminated and the stamp's version of the story begins)

title: White phosphorus, phossy jaw, and the 1906 Berne Convention
claim: White phosphorus — the active ingredient of most strike-anywhere matches from the 1840s to the 1910s (Charles Sauria's 1831 French substitution of white phosphorus for antimony sulfide in the Walker formula started the industry) — poisoned its workforce. The first case of phossy jaw (phosphorus necrosis of the jaw) was diagnosed in 1839 by Vienna physician Friedrich Wilhelm Lorinser in a Viennese matchstick maker; in 1844 he reported 22 cases and established white phosphorus's toxicity in matches. The disease fed the London matchgirls' strike of 1888 (Bryant & May); William Booth and the Salvation Army opened a red-phosphorus match factory in 1891. The International Convention respecting the Prohibition of the Use of White (Yellow) Phosphorus in the Manufacture of Matches — the Berne Convention — was concluded 26 September 1906 and entered into force 1 January 1912, banning manufacture, import, and sale; it remains in force for 48 states (Switzerland depositary). Edward J. Phelan later said the ILO 'may in one sense be traced to the Berne Convention of 1906'.
place: Bern, Switzerland (Berne Convention, 1906)

title: Walter Hunt's 1834 lockstitch machine: built, never patented
claim: New York inventor Walter Hunt built a working lockstitch sewing machine in 1834 — the first American lockstitch machine, with an eye-pointed needle and shuttle interlocking two threads — but never patented it, reportedly fearing it would put seamstresses out of work.
place: New York City, USA (Hunt's workshop)

title: The Liberty Bell's crack is NOT from its first ringing
claim: The famous crack visible on the Liberty Bell today dates to the bell's first ringing — i.e., the bell has carried the same crack since it was first struck in Philadelphia in 1752.
place: Liberty Bell Center, Independence National Historical Park, Philadelphia, Pennsylvania

title: 'Liebig invented the mirror in 1835' — the quiz telling
claim: The telling that 'Justus von Liebig invented the mirror in 1835' — repeated in quiz formats and trivia — is false: glass mirrors existed centuries before Liebig (14th-century Italy; the Venetian tin-mercury mirrors of the 16th century). Liebig's 1835 contribution was the chemical silvering PROCESS, not the mirror.
place: Giessen, Germany (Liebig, 1835)

title: Liebig's 1835 chemical silvering
claim: In 1835, the German chemist Justus von Liebig developed a process for depositing metallic silver on glass by reducing ammoniated silver nitrate with an aldehyde/sugar — the chemical silvering that replaced poisonous tin-mercury amalgam mirror-making and made the modern looking glass cheap.
place: Giessen, Germany (Liebig's university)

title: The Great Moon Hoax of 1835 — six days of lunar life in the New York Sun
claim: The New York Sun published six articles, 25–31 August 1835, reporting lunar life — bison, blue single-horned goats, miniature zebras, unicorns, bipedal tail-less beavers, and the winged Vespertilio-homo — discovered by Sir John Herschel at the Cape of Good Hope with a 24-foot, 7-ton lens, ostensibly written by his fictitious companion Dr. Andrew Grant and reprinted from the Edinburgh Journal of Science.
place: New York City — the Sun's office (claim); Cape of Good Hope (the fictional observatory)

title: The legend that nobody questioned the Moon Hoax
claim: The 1835 Moon Hoax fooled New York wholesale: nobody questioned the articles, the public believed them entirely, and the hoax permanently doubled the Sun's circulation, establishing it as the world's most-read paper.
place: New York City — the city that supposedly was fooled whole

title: The mythicist hypothesis (the Christ-myth theory)
claim: Jesus of Nazareth never existed as a historical person: the Gospel Jesus is a wholly mythic construction — assembled from Jewish scripture, dying-and-rising god motifs, and early Christian theology — with no human core (the 'Christ myth' or mythicist position).
place: Berlin (Bauer's 1841 Christ-myth writings)

title: Poe's own moon hoax — 'Hans Pfaall,' June 1835
claim: Edgar Allan Poe published 'The Unparalleled Adventure of One Hans Pfaall' — the first installment of his own moon hoax — in the June 1835 Southern Literary Messenger, a month before Locke's Sun series, and afterward charged that the Sun's hoax plagiarized his story.
place: New York (the Sun) and Richmond (the Southern Literary Messenger)

title: The Marsh test for arsenic (1836)
claim: In 1836 the Scottish chemist James Marsh published a sensitive test for arsenic: the sample is treated with arsenic-free zinc and sulphuric acid, any arsenic present forming arsine gas, which is led through a heated tube where it decomposes, leaving a mirror-like deposit of metallic arsenic on a cold porcelain or glass surface. The test could detect minute traces in exhumed matter and became forensic toxicology's first decisive instrument.
place: Royal Arsenal, Woolwich, London (Marsh's workplace; paper published in Edinburgh)

title: Cooke & Wheatstone: the first commercial telegraph (1837–1839)
claim: Cooke & Wheatstone's electric telegraph — patented 10 June 1837, trialed Euston–Camden 25 July 1837 — produced the world's first commercial telegraph line: Paddington to West Drayton (13 miles), opened July 1839 on the Great Western Railway.
place: Paddington Station, London (the 1839 line's London terminus)

title: Horace Mann invented the public school
claim: Horace Mann (1796-1859) invented the American public school — that is, before Mann's reforms as Secretary of the Massachusetts Board of Education (1837-1848), there were no public schools in America, and the public school is his invention.
place: Boston, Massachusetts

title: Horace Mann's common-school reforms (1837-1848)
claim: Horace Mann, as first Secretary of the Massachusetts Board of Education (1837-1848), campaigned for free, tax-funded, non-sectarian common schools open to all children: he established the first public normal school (Lexington, 1839) to train teachers, pushed standardized curricula, age-graded classrooms, written examinations and report cards, founded The Common School Journal (1838), and wrote 12 annual reports that carried the common-school model nationwide; most U.S. states adopted a version of the Massachusetts system.
place: Boston, Massachusetts

title: The Morse system: the single wire that won the world (1837–1844)
claim: The Morse/Gale/Vail single-wire telegraph system — dots-and-dashes code, practical hand key, embossing receiver — was developed 1837–1844 and connected Washington to Baltimore on 24 May 1844 ('What hath God wrought'), becoming the system that won the world.
place: Baltimore, Maryland (the 24 May 1844 line: Washington, D.C. → Baltimore)

title: Vulcanization: Goodyear's process, Hancock's patent, the band's enabling science
claim: Vulcanization — heating natural rubber with sulfur to make it durable, elastic, and temperature-stable — was discovered by Charles Goodyear (1839) and patented by him in the US (patent 3,633, 15 June 1844); Thomas Hancock independently developed the process and patented it in Britain about eight weeks before Goodyear filed there, and is credited today as an independent co-inventor. The Goodyear Tire & Rubber Company (founded 1898 by Frank Seiberling in Akron, Ohio) was named for Goodyear, never founded by him; he died 1 July 1860 about $200,000 in debt.
place: Connecticut — the Lower Naugatuck Valley rubber works (Goodyear's manufacturing ground); the 1839 stove incident is traditionally placed at Woburn, Massachusetts

title: 'Paperweights are an ancient art' — the myth
claim: Glass paperweights — the glass dome weight as a desk object — are an ancient art, with the object itself dating back to antiquity (ancient Egypt, Rome, or the old world).
place: Paris, France — the trade center of the 1840s paperweight boom

title: The 1840 Lafarge arsenic trial at Tulle
claim: Marie Lafarge was convicted of murdering her husband Charles by arsenic poisoning at the Tulle assizes on 19 September 1840, in a trial dominated by forensic chemistry: the Marsh test for arsenic, applied by Mathieu Orfila as the deciding expert. The trial is widely described as the first murder trial decided by forensic toxicological evidence.
place: Tulle, Corrèze, France (assize court; crime at Le Glandier)

title: The Penny Black (1 May 1840)
claim: The Penny Black was the world's first adhesive postage stamp used in a public postal system, issued in the United Kingdom on 1 May 1840 (valid for use from 6 May). It bore the profile of the young Queen Victoria, was printed by Perkins Bacon (68,808,000 printed), and was the instrument of Rowland Hill's 1837 postal reform: a flat rate of one penny per half-ounce regardless of distance, prepaid by the sender — replacing the old system under which the recipient paid, charged by the sheet and by distance travelled.
place: London, United Kingdom (issue; Perkins Bacon printing)

title: "Pyramids are Egypt's monopoly"
claim: Pyramids are an Egyptian monopoly: Egypt has the most pyramids in the world, and the pyramid-building tradition belongs to Egyptian civilization alone.
place: The claim is a global belief about pyramid distribution; pin carried at Meroë, the counter-evidence's representative site

title: The recipient-pays root: before 1840, the addressee paid
claim: Before Rowland Hill's 1840 uniform penny postage, recipients — not senders — usually paid for the post. Britain's prepaid-postage revolution (the Penny Black, issued 1 May 1840, valid from 6 May) flipped the default so the sender paid. Business reply mail and the international reply coupon are therefore the formalized return of the older recipient-pays idea: a prepaid-reply instrument lets the party expecting the reply bear the cost, inside a system where sender-pays is now the default.
place: London, United Kingdom — 1840 postal reform

title: 'Thomas Cook invented tourism' (myth)
claim: Thomas Cook invented tourism — the 5 July 1841 Leicester–Loughborough excursion created the travel and leisure industry.
place: Leicester, England (the 'birthplace of tourism' claim's origin point)

title: De Moleyns's 1841 patent — the lamp's birth certificate
claim: In 1841, Frederick de Moleyns of England was granted the first patent for an incandescent lamp: a design using powdered charcoal heated between two coils of platinum wire in vacuo.
place: London, England (British patent register)

title: Mackay 1841 — the popularizer of the tulip-mania ruin narrative
claim: Charles Mackay's 1841 book Extraordinary Popular Delusions and the Madness of Crowds created the popular form of the tulip-mania story — the version every subsequent popular account descends from: all levels of society swept in, fortunes ruined, Dutch commerce shocked.
place: London (publication)

title: 1841: Poe's 'Rue Morgue' founds detective fiction
claim: Edgar Allan Poe's "The Murders in the Rue Morgue" (Graham's Magazine, April 1841) is the first detective story — the founding document of detective fiction, with the locked-room murder, the eccentric reasoning detective (C. Auguste Dupin), and the admiring narrator as the genre's DNA.
