place: Philadelphia (Graham's Magazine) / Paris (the story's fictional setting)

title: 'Slocum invented the stapler in 1841' — DEBUNKED
claim: Samuel Slocum of Poughkeepsie, New York, received U.S. Patent 2,275 on September 30, 1841, for a 'machine for sticking pins in paper' — and this machine is often misidentified as the first stapler.
place: Poughkeepsie, New York — Slocum's pin works

title: Cook's first railway excursion, 5 July 1841
claim: On 5 July 1841, Thomas Cook chartered a special train from the Midland Counties Railway and carried some 485–500 members of the Leicester Temperance Society from Leicester Campbell Street station to Loughborough and back for one shilling each — the first publicly advertised special railway excursion.
place: Leicester, England (Campbell Street station)

title: The tulip crash that bankrupted a nation — the ruin reading of 1637
claim: The 1637 collapse of tulip prices devastated the economy of the Dutch Republic — ruining fortunes across the nation and inflicting a severe, years-long shock on Dutch commerce.
place: The Dutch Republic (claim) vs the archive (Amsterdam/Haarlem)

title: The showman, minus the sentence — Barnum's documented career
claim: Phineas Taylor Barnum (1810–1891) was the American showman of the American Museum in New York (1842–1865 fire), the admitted humbug-promoter (the Feejee Mermaid, Joice Heth, Tom Thumb, Jumbo), and the man who built and exhibited his own replica of the Cardiff Giant in 1869–1870 after David Hannum refused to sell.
place: New York City — Barnum's American Museum (1842–1865); the Cardiff Giant replica exhibited here 1869–1870

title: Crawford Long's ether surgeries, 1842 (published 1849)
claim: On 30 March 1842, in Jefferson, Georgia, surgeon Crawford W. Long removed a tumor from the neck of James M. Venable under inhaled sulfuric ether — with earlier 'ether frolic' observation (pain-free bruises while inhaling) as the insight, and further ether operations through 1842 (a second tumor operation 6 June, a toe amputation 3 July). He published the account in the Southern Medical and Surgical Journal in December 1849.
place: Jefferson, Georgia (Long's office)

title: Poe's 'Balloon-Hoax' — the Atlantic crossing that never happened (13 April 1844)
claim: Edgar Allan Poe's 'Balloon-Hoax' — printed as a news extra in the New York Sun on 13 April 1844 with the headline 'THE ATLANTIC CROSSED IN THREE DAYS!' — reported that Monck Mason's steering balloon 'Victoria' had crossed the Atlantic in 75 hours and landed on Sullivan's Island, South Carolina. No such flight occurred: the Victoria never existed, the passengers were invented (the real novelist William Harrison Ainsworth was listed among them), and the Sun printed a retraction on 15 April 1844.
place: New York Sun building (publication); purported landing at Sullivan's Island, South Carolina

title: Rynd's hollow needle: the first known hypodermic injection (1844)
claim: On 3 June 1844, Dublin surgeon Francis Rynd used a thin hollow needle to inject a solution of morphine (fifteen grains of acetate of morphia in one drachm of creosote) under the skin of Margaret Cox, a 59-year-old neuralgia patient at the Meath Hospital, to the supra-orbital, temporal, malar and buccal nerves — the first known hypodermic injection.
place: Meath Hospital, Dublin, Ireland

title: Pasch's safety match (1844) — the separated design
claim: Swedish chemist Gustaf Erik Pasch (1788–1862), professor at the Karolinska Institute and student of Berzelius, was granted the first patent on the safety match in 1844. His design moved the phosphorus from the match head to a specially prepared striking surface: the head contained only potassium chlorate (no phosphorus), and ignition required striking on the red-phosphorus surface. Manufacturing at J.S. Bagge & Co.'s chemical factory in Stockholm failed — the striking surface was poor quality and red phosphorus was prohibitively expensive — and production ceased.
place: Stockholm, Sweden (J.S. Bagge & Co.'s chemical factory)

title: Horace Wells: nitrous oxide 1844, the failed Boston demo, and the 1848 death
claim: On 11 December 1844 (the day after witnessing Samuel Cooley's painless bruised leg at a Gardner Quincy Colton laughing-gas exhibition), Hartford dentist Horace Wells had his own wisdom tooth painlessly extracted under nitrous oxide, used the gas on 12–15 dental patients, and in January 1845 demonstrated it publicly in Boston before John Collins Warren and medical students — the demonstration failed when the gas was removed too soon and the patient groaned, earning cries of 'humbug.' Wells died by suicide under chloroform in New York's Tombs Prison on 24 January 1848; the ADA (1864) and AMA (1870) later declared him the real discoverer of anesthesia.
place: Hartford, Connecticut (Wells's practice); Boston demonstration at MGH

title: Bigaglia's first glass paperweight (1845, credited)
claim: Pietro Bigaglia, a member of an old Venetian family of glass artists, manufactured the first glass paperweight in 1845.
place: Venice, Italy — Pietro Bigaglia's manufactory

title: The Hill & de la Rue envelope-folding machine, 1845
claim: Edwin Hill (brother of postal reformer Rowland Hill) and Warren de la Rue received the first British patent for an envelope-folding machine in 1845 — a steam-driven machine that creased and folded pre-cut diamond sheets into envelopes — and exhibited an improved version at the London Great Exhibition of 1851.
place: London, England — patent registered; improved machine exhibited at the Crystal Palace, 1851

title: The food that kept leaving (1845–1852)
claim: Throughout the Great Famine, Ireland continued to export food — grain, livestock, dairy, and other produce shipped to Britain — and London refused to bar those exports, as it had done on previous occasions of dearth. The exports are honestly bounded: they were significantly reduced compared to pre-famine years, imports exceeded exports after 1846, and the exported grain would have compensated for only about one-seventh of the potatoes destroyed by the blight (Ó Gráda 1999).
place: Dublin and the Irish ports — the export manifests; the decision at Westminster

title: The Franklin expedition, 1845-1848 - the voyage that never came home
claim: In May 1845 Sir John Franklin sailed from England with HMS Erebus and HMS Terror and 129 officers and men to complete the charting of the Northwest Passage. The ships were beset in the ice off King William Island from September 1846; Franklin died on 11 June 1847; the 105 survivors abandoned the ships on 22 April 1848 and attempted a march south toward Back's Fish River (the Great Fish River). None survived.
place: Off the north-west coast of King William Island, Nunavut (beset position 5 leagues NNW of Point Victory)

title: The French classic period of glass paperweights (1845–1860)
claim: From about 1845 to about 1860 — the collectors' 'classic period' — the French glasshouses Baccarat, Saint-Louis, and Clichy (with Monot's Cristallerie de Pantin and lesser lights such as Grenelle and Saint-Mandé) produced the finest glass paperweights in the world: millefiori canes and lampwork flowers under domed crystal, exhibited to acclaim at the 1851 Crystal Palace Great Exhibition, after which the art all but disappeared for some eighty years.
place: Lorraine, France — Baccarat and Saint-Louis glassworks; Paris — Clichy

title: The Great Irish Famine, 1845–1852
claim: The Great Irish Famine (An Gorta Mór) ran 1845–1852: potato blight destroyed the staple crop across successive seasons, roughly one million people died of starvation and famine-related disease, and over one million more emigrated; Ireland's population fell from ~8.5 million on the eve of the famine to ~4.4 million by 1901, and has never recovered to its pre-famine level. 1847 — 'Black '47' — was the worst year.
place: Ireland — island-wide; worst in the western counties (Connacht, west Munster)

title: DEBUNKED: the famine was caused solely by the potato blight
claim: The Irish Potato Famine (1845–1852) was caused solely by the potato blight — that is, the million deaths and mass emigration were a pure natural disaster with no significant human or political causes.
place: Ireland — the telling is about the whole island; the evidence is the British policy record at Westminster and Dublin Castle

title: 'Stephen Perry invented the rubber band alone' — DEBUNKED
claim: The telling that 'Stephen Perry invented the rubber band alone in 1845' — that the rubber band began with one man, Perry, and the 1845 patent is his alone.
place: London, England — where the telling places the solo invention (Perry's city)

title: The Perry & Daft rubber-band patent (17 March 1845)
claim: British Patent 13880/1845 — sealed 17 March 1845 — granted jointly to Stephen Perry of St John's Wood, Middlesex, and Thomas Barnabas Daft of Birmingham, for 'improvements in springs to be applied to girths, belts, and bandages, and improvements in manufacture of elastic bands.' The elastic bands were cut as narrow rings from vulcanized rubber tube and sold by Perry's firm, Messrs Perry and Co., Rubber Manufacturers of London, advertised as useful for holding 'papers, letters, etc.'
place: London, England — Messrs Perry and Co., Rubber Manufacturers of London

title: HERB-1: the blight strain identified (1845)
claim: The potato crop failures of 1845–1852 were caused by potato late blight, the oomycete Phytophthora infestans — and the exact historical strain is now identified: HERB-1, a unique 19th-century genotype distinct from all modern strains (including the long-suspected US-1), which spread from North America to Europe in 1845 from a Mexican Toluca Valley origin. The 1845 harvest was cut roughly in half; by 1846 it had fallen to about a quarter.
place: County Cork, Ireland — first Irish reports, summer 1845; the strain's origin: Toluca Valley, Mexico

title: The Lundström safety match (1845–1858) — Sweden's commercial match
claim: The Lundström brothers of Jönköping, Sweden — Johan Edvard (1815–1888) and Carl Frans (1823–1917) — took Pasch's separated safety-match design and made it commercially successful: experimenting from 1845, a production plant on Lake Vättern by 1847, a prize-winning exhibit at the 1855 Paris World Exhibition, ~12 million matchboxes in 1858, and a path to the Jönköping match monopoly (Jönköpings & Vulcans Tändsticksfabriks AB, 1903; later Swedish Match). Johan Edvard Lundström left the business in 1863 and spent 1875–77 as a government inspector in the match industry, working to prevent and forbid the use of dangerous white phosphorus.
place: Jönköping, Sweden (Lundström match factory; original factory now a museum)

title: Adolphe Sax patents the saxophone (28 June 1846) — and the twenty-year patent war
claim: Adolphe Sax invented the saxophone — a conical brass body with a single-reed mouthpiece, bridging brass power and woodwind agility — patented 28 June 1846 in France for use in orchestras and military bands; he then spent over twenty years in patent litigation that bankrupted him three times, and died in poverty in Paris in 1894 without ever hearing the jazz the instrument would define.
place: Paris (Sax's workshop; born Dinant, Belgium, 1814)

title: DEBUNKED: 'Ether Day was the first ever surgical anesthesia'
claim: The 16 October 1846 Ether Dome demonstration was the first ever use of inhaled anesthesia in surgery — the moment pain was abolished.
place: Boston (the monument and the dome)

title: Ether Day — the 16 October 1846 Ether Dome demonstration
claim: On 16 October 1846, in the Bulfinch Building's surgical amphitheater at Massachusetts General Hospital (Boston), dentist William T. G. Morton administered sulfuric ether to patient Edward Gilbert Abbott, after which surgeon John Collins Warren painlessly removed part of a tumor from Abbott's neck before a medical audience — the event known as Ether Day, and the first successful public demonstration of surgical ether anesthesia.
place: Massachusetts General Hospital (Bulfinch Building), Boston

title: The 'First Thanksgiving' National-Origin Myth
claim: That the 1621 Plymouth harvest feast was 'the first Thanksgiving' and the founding of an annual national tradition leading directly to the American Thanksgiving holiday.
place: Plymouth, Massachusetts (site of the retrojected claim)

title: Howe's 1846 lockstitch patent (U.S. 4,750)
claim: On 10 September 1846, Elias Howe Jr. of Massachusetts was granted U.S. Patent No. 4,750 for an improvement in sewing machines using a lockstitch design — eye-pointed needle, shuttle beneath the cloth forming the lockstitch, automatic feed — sewing about 250 stitches per minute.
place: Boston / Spencer, Massachusetts, USA (Howe's shop and patent filing)

title: TELLING (DEBUNKED): 'crap' = Thomas Crapper's name
claim: TELLING (DEBUNKED): the word 'crap' (excrement) derives from the surname of Thomas Crapper (1836-1910), the Victorian plumber — and Crapper invented the flush toilet, so his name became the word.
place: London (Victorian plumbing and English print culture)

title: Lipman's eyelet paper-binding method
claim: Philadelphia stationer Hymen Lipman — of the 1858 pencil-eraser patent and the first U.S. envelope company — devised an eyelet paper-binding method that, per the Smithsonian's account of his career, 'preceded the stapler by two decades.'
place: Philadelphia, Pennsylvania — Lipman's stationery business

title: The Gregory clause (June 1847)
claim: The Poor Law Extension Act of June 1847 carried the quarter-acre (Gregory) clause: no occupier of more than a quarter acre of land could receive poor relief. Cottiers had to surrender their holdings — their potato ground, their only subsistence — to qualify for the workhouse, and the clause drove a wave of evictions and 'voluntary' surrenders across the west.
place: Ireland — the Poor Law unions; worst in Connacht

title: Semmelweis's chlorine hand disinfection, Vienna 1847
claim: Mandatory hand disinfection with chlorinated lime by physicians and students at Vienna General Hospital's First Obstetrical Clinic, ordered by Ignaz Semmelweis in 1847, cut maternal mortality from puerperal (childbed) fever from roughly 18% to roughly 1-2%, a level matching the midwives' Second Clinic.
place: Allgemeines Krankenhaus (Vienna General Hospital), Vienna

title: Simpson's chloroform, 1847 — and Victoria's 1853 confinement
claim: On 8 November 1847, Edinburgh's Professor of Midwifery James Young Simpson introduced chloroform as an obstetric (and general) anesthetic, after the famous dinner-party self-experiment with assistants Keith and Duncan (waking under the mahogany table). On 7 April 1853, John Snow administered chloroform to Queen Victoria for the birth of Prince Leopold — 'that blessed chloroform... soothing, quieting and delightful beyond measure' — which made obstetric anesthesia respectable across Britain.
place: Edinburgh (Simpson); London/Buckingham (Snow, Victoria)

title: The Victory Point note - the only words the expedition left behind
claim: The Victory Point note is the single written record the Franklin expedition left behind: a pre-printed Admiralty form written in two parts. The first, dated 28 May 1847 and signed by Lt. Graham Gore and Mate Charles Des Voeux, reports the ships wintered in the ice and 'All well.' The second, added in the margins on 25 April 1848 and signed by Capt. James Fitzjames and Capt. Francis Crozier, records that the ships were deserted on 22 April 1848 after being beset since 12 September 1846, that Sir John Franklin died on 11 June 1847, that deaths had reached nine officers and fifteen men, and that the 105 survivors under Crozier would start the next day for Back's Fish River. It was found in May 1859 by Lt. William Hobson of McClintock's Fox expedition in a cairn at Point Victory on the north-west coast of King William Island - originally deposited in James Clark Ross's 1830 Victory Point cairn four miles north.
place: Point Victory, north-west coast of King William Island, Nunavut

title: The word 'zoo', c. 1847
claim: The word 'zoo' dates to about 1847, as an abbreviation of the London Zoological Society's 'Zoological Gardens'.
place: London Zoo, Regent's Park, London (coordinates via map.geocode, FULL_ADDRESS match)

title: The Seneca Falls Convention, July 1848
claim: On 19–20 July 1848, about 300 people gathered at the Wesleyan Chapel in Seneca Falls, New York, at the convention organized by Elizabeth Cady Stanton and Lucretia Mott — the first formal women's rights convention in the United States — and adopted the Declaration of Sentiments, modeled on the Declaration of Independence, including the contested ninth resolution demanding women's elective franchise; Frederick Douglass's North Star backed the resolution and Douglass's speech is credited with carrying the vote.
place: Seneca Falls, New York (Wesleyan Chapel)

title: "Hunt invented the safety pin" (1849) — the invention telling
claim: Walter Hunt invented the safety pin in 1849.
place: Greek Peloponnese (Mycenaean violin-bow fibula find region, 14th c. BCE)

title: The $400 sale — Hunt sells the safety pin forever
claim: Walter Hunt sold all rights to the safety-pin patent (U.S. 6,281) in 1849 for $400 — reportedly to settle a $15 debt — and never earned another penny from it, while later rights-holders made millions.
place: New York City (sale of the patent rights)

title: Hunt's Dress-Pin patent (1849) — the modern safety pin
claim: Walter Hunt's 1849 "Dress-Pin" (U.S. Patent No. 6,281, granted April 10, 1849) is the documented modern safety pin: a single length of brass wire, coiled at the center to act as a spring, with one end sharpened to a point and the other formed into a clasp that shields the point.
place: New York City (Walter Hunt's workshop; patent filed at the U.S. Patent Office)

title: Meucci's teletrofono — the 1871 caveat, the lapsed renewal, the 2002 recognition
claim: Antonio Meucci developed a 'teletrofono' (speaking telegraph): conceived in Havana c. 1849, demonstrated in New York in 1860, U.S. patent caveat filed December 28, 1871, lapsed after 1874 when he could not pay the $10 renewal; on June 11, 2002 the U.S. House of Representatives passed H. Res. 269 acknowledging his work in the invention of the telephone.
place: Clifton, Staten Island, New York

title: Rowley's independent safety-pin patent (October 1849)
claim: Charles Rowley of Birmingham, England independently patented a similar safety pin in October 1849 — the same year as Hunt — which fences the single-inventor version of the safety-pin story.
place: Birmingham, England

title: Semmelweis's professional rejection and death in the asylum
claim: Semmelweis's discovery was not adopted by the medical establishment in his lifetime: his 1849 reappointment as assistant at Vienna's First Obstetrical Clinic was not granted, and he died in the Oberdöbling (Döbling) asylum in Vienna in 1865, fourteen days after commitment.
place: Vienna (Allgemeines Krankenhaus, then Oberdöbling asylum)

title: The Sewing Machine War and the 1856 Combination (first U.S. patent pool)
claim: Elias Howe's lockstitch patent (4,750, 1846) was so broad that nearly every later machine infringed it; Howe sued Isaac Singer and others (litigation ~1849-1854), won in 1854, collected up to $25 per machine in royalties; then on 24 October 1856 the Albany Agreement formed the Sewing Machine Combination (Howe, Wheeler & Wilson, I.M. Singer & Co., Grover & Baker) — the first patent pool in U.S. history, with nine patents pooled (lockstitch, four-motion feed, vertical needle/horizontal surface), Howe taking $5 per domestic machine and $1 per export until his patent expired in 1867 (roughly $2 million, 1860s dollars).
place: Albany, New York, USA (the 1856 Agreement)

title: 'Lightning never strikes the same place twice' (myth)
claim: Lightning never strikes the same place twice — once a particular spot has been hit by lightning, it will not be hit again.
place: Empire State Building, New York (the canonical counter-example)

title: The 'Mere Conduit' Myth of Medieval Islamic Medicine — DEBUNKED
claim: 'Medieval Islamic medicine produced nothing original — it was merely a conduit for Greek texts, a translation project between Galen and the European Renaissance, contributing no new knowledge of its own.'
place: Damascus (nominal pin for the historiographical claim; the evidence lives in Cairo, Cordoba, and Diyarbakir)

title: Joseph Swan's carbon-filament lamp — the priority the legend skipped (evidence chain corrected)
claim: Joseph Swan built and publicly demonstrated a working carbon-filament incandescent lamp before Edison — public demonstrations at Newcastle on 18 December 1878 (Chemical Society lecture), 17 January 1879 (repeat lecture, lamp shown in operation), and 3 February 1879 (Literary and Philosophical Society theatre, audience 700+, Sir William Armstrong presiding); British Patent No. 4933 granted 27 November 1880; installations followed at his Gateshead home, the Lit & Phil Library (20 October 1880), and the Savoy Theatre, London (December 1881).
place: Newcastle upon Tyne / Gateshead, England — the February 1879 lecture demonstration; Swan's Gateshead home, the first home lit by electric light

title: Hobbs picked the Chubb detector lock in 25 minutes, 1851 (CORROBORATED)
claim: At the Great Exhibition of 1851, the American locksmith Alfred Charles Hobbs picked the Chubb six-lever detector lock — the lock designed to seize up when picked incorrectly — in about 25 minutes.
place: Crystal Palace, Hyde Park, London (Great Exhibition, 1851)

title: Howe's 1851 clothing closure — patented, never marketed
claim: Elias Howe patented an 'automatic, continuous clothing closure' in 1851 — a device similar to the later zip — but never marketed it; he was occupied with the sewing machine, and the closure never reached the market.
place: Boston, Massachusetts (Howe's base)

title: The Canterbury Hall opens, 17 May 1852 — Morton's purpose-built hall
claim: On 17 May 1852 Charles Morton and Frederick Stanley opened the 700-seat Canterbury Hall at the Canterbury Arms, Upper Marsh, Lambeth — the purpose-built hall that became the model for the music-hall boom, described by historians as 'the most significant date in all the history of music hall'.
place: Canterbury Arms / Canterbury Hall, Upper Marsh, Lambeth, London, England

title: The electric fire alarm telegraph, Boston 1852 (VERIFIED)
claim: On 28 April 1852, the first municipal electric fire alarm system — call boxes with automatic signaling indicating the location of a fire — was placed into operation in Boston, Massachusetts, invented by William F. Channing and Moses G. Farmer; the first alarm was received 29 April 1852 at 8:25 p.m.
place: Boston, Massachusetts (original system: three box circuits, three bell circuits, forty boxes, sixteen alarm bells)

title: Samuel Fox's Paragon rib patent (1852): the modern umbrella frame
claim: Samuel Fox patented the 'Paragon' umbrella rib in 1852 — a thin steel strip rolled into a U (trough) section, combining lightness with strength, inspired by the tubular construction of the Menai bridge; the Paragon frame became the industry standard for umbrella ribs. Fox founded Fox Umbrella Frames Ltd at Stocksbridge, Sheffield, in 1842, and became the world's largest umbrella-frame manufacturer.
place: Stocksbridge, Sheffield, England

title: 'Charles Morton invented the music hall' — the invention credit, corrected
claim: Charles Morton invented the music hall — he was the inventor of music-hall entertainment as a form.
place: Canterbury Hall, Upper Marsh, Lambeth, London, England (the telling's location)

title: Pravaz's syringe: the Lyon half of the 1853 twin invention
claim: In 1853, Charles-Gabriel Pravaz of Lyon built a working hypodermic syringe — graduated glass cylinder, screw-driven piston, silver construction — and used it to inject coagulating solutions (perchloride of iron/mercury) via trocar into aneurysms, in sheep and then in practice — independently of Alexander Wood's same-year Edinburgh work, with no channel of transmission between the two.
place: Lyon, France

title: The myth: Alexander Wood invented the hypodermic syringe (sole inventor, 1853)
claim: Alexander Wood was the sole inventor of the hypodermic syringe in 1853 — the lone genius of the glass tube.
place: Edinburgh, Scotland (Wood's practice, 19 Royal Circus)

title: Wood's real achievement: the all-glass syringe and the 1855 neuralgia paper
claim: In 1853, Alexander Wood of Edinburgh built an all-glass hypodermic syringe with a hollow needle, and in 1855 published 'A New Method of Treating Neuralgia by the Direct Application of Opiates to the Painful Points' (Edinburgh Medical and Surgical Review) — the first practical method of subcutaneous morphine injection for neuralgia, which Wood argued had 'a far wider application' beyond narcotics.
place: 19 Royal Circus, Edinburgh, Scotland

title: The Inuit testimony - the witnesses the searchers kept ignoring
claim: Inuit oral testimony is a primary evidentiary source for the Franklin expedition's fate: Inuit witnesses continuously located the expedition and its ships from the 1850s onward. Charles Francis Hall's 1869 witness In-nook-poo-zhe-jook described a ship sunk off the west coast of King William Island - the account that matches Terror Bay, where HMS Terror was found in 2016. John Rae's 1854 report (the £10,000 Admiralty-reward report) rested on Inuit accounts of starving white men near the Back River. Louie Kamookak of Gjoa Haven spent decades compiling Inuit oral history into a search geography that Parks Canada's teams credit as decisive in locating HMS Erebus in 2014. The testimony was repeatedly discounted by Victorian and modern searchers in favor of their own theories - and was right.
place: King William Island and the Queen Maud Gulf region, Nunavut

title: Göbel's 1854 lamp — the priority claim the courtroom killed
claim: Heinrich Göbel built a working incandescent electric lamp with a carbonized bamboo filament in New York in 1854 — beating Swan and Edison by decades.
place: New York, New York — the claimed site of the 1854 lamp (no contemporary site documentation)

title: The first can opener (Yeates, 1855)
claim: The first patented can opener was Robert Yeates's (also rendered Yates in the key specialist source) lever-type opener, British Patent No. 1577, dated 13 July 1855 — a curved-blade lever knife for 'cutting or ripping open preserved provision cases', from Trafalgar Place West, Hackney Road, London.
place: Trafalgar Place West, Hackney Road, London

title: The cannonballs in the road at Crimea
claim: Roger Fenton's 'Valley of the Shadow of Death' (Crimea, April 1855) exists in two plate variants — cannonballs on the road in one, off the road in the other — because Fenton's team moved the cannonballs onto the road for the more dramatic exposure.
place: Valley of the Shadow of Death, near Sevastopol, Crimea

title: The real 19th-century life of 'lions led by donkeys'
claim: The 'lions led by donkeys/asses' image predates the First World War by more than half a century, appearing in the Crimean War, the Franco-Prussian War, the Boxer Rebellion, and in print as early as 1855 — it was a 19th-century commonplace, not a 1914 German verdict.
place: Western Europe — the phrase's 19th-century print trail (London, Paris, Sevastopol)

title: The Yellow River's 1855 avulsion — a river that changed seas
claim: On 1 August 1855 (19th day of the 6th month, Xianfeng 5), the Yellow River breached its northern bank at Tongwaxiang in present-day Lankao, Henan, diverting its course from the Yellow Sea (via the Huai system, Jiangsu) to the Bohai Sea via the old Daqing/Ji River course in Shandong. The 1855 event ended the river's 1128–1855 southern course (itself a man-made diversion of 1128, when the river captured the Huai); the 1855 shift was natural. The new delta has since migrated repeatedly (six large natural diversions 1889–1934, four artificial 1953–1996).
place: Tongwaxiang, Lankao, Henan — the 1855 breach point

title: The anti-Stratfordian claim — 'Shakespeare didn't write Shakespeare'
claim: William Shakespeare of Stratford-upon-Avon did not write the plays and poems attributed to him; a hidden aristocrat or courtier (Francis Bacon, Christopher Marlowe, Edward de Vere, Mary Sidney, Queen Elizabeth I, or another candidate) wrote them and used his name as a front.
place: Stratford-upon-Avon, England (the claim is about Stratford; the evidence is London's archives)

title: Scott's 1860 phonoautogram — the first recorded human voice
claim: On 9 April 1860, a Parisian inventor's machine recorded a human voice on soot-covered paper — the singer singing a fragment of the French folk song 'Au Clair de la Lune' — and that physical trace survives, dated, and was played back audibly in 2008: the earliest recognizable recording of a human voice, made seventeen years before Edison's phonograph.
place: Paris, France (phonoautograph patent; phonautogram papers at the French Academy of Sciences / Paris patent office)

title: Lipman's pencil-with-eraser patent, US 19,783 (March 30, 1858)
claim: On March 30, 1858, Philadelphia stationer Hymen L. Lipman (born Kingston, Jamaica, 1817; America's first envelope manufacturer) was granted U.S. patent 19,783 for the 'Combination of Lead-Pencil and Eraser' — the first patent for a pencil with an attached eraser. Lipman sold the patent in 1862 to Joseph Reckendorfer for $100,000. Important design note: Lipman's patent was not the glued-on pink cap of modern memory — the specification embeds a groove of prepared india-rubber inside the pencil wood, exposed by cutting/sharpening the end, so a soiled point could be renewed 'as in the ordinary lead-pencil.'
place: Philadelphia, Pennsylvania

title: Warner's can opener (US 19,063, 1858)
claim: Ezra J. Warner of Waterbury, Connecticut received US Patent 19,063 on 5 January 1858 for a can opener — a curved-handle tool combining a piercing 'bayonet' and a sawing 'sickle' blade that cut a jagged line around the can lid, kept from penetrating too deep by a metal guard.
place: Waterbury, Connecticut, USA

title: The Carrington Event, 1–2 September 1859 (VERIFIED)
claim: On 1–2 September 1859, the Carrington Event — the most intense geomagnetic storm in recorded history — set telegraph systems sparking and pushed auroras to the tropics.
place: London, England (observation); global (storm effects)

title: The Crown's storm-glass distribution to fishing villages
claim: After the Royal Charter storm of October 1859, the Crown distributed storm glasses — 'FitzRoy's storm barometers' — to many small fishing communities around the British Isles, as part of FitzRoy's program to put forecasting instruments in working hands.
place: British Isles coastal fishing communities

title: The Suez Canal opens (1869)
claim: On 17 November 1869, a 164 km sea-level waterway opened through the Isthmus of Suez, connecting the Mediterranean at Port Said to the Red Sea at Suez — built 1859–1869 by Ferdinand de Lesseps's Compagnie Universelle du Canal Maritime de Suez.
place: Isthmus of Suez, Egypt (Port Said → Suez)

title: The crystal skulls (ancient-artifact claim)
claim: Life-size quartz crystal skulls are genuine pre-Columbian (Aztec or Maya) artifacts, thousands of years old.
place: Eugène Boban's Paris curio shop (first appearance); British Museum / Smithsonian (the lab verdicts)

title: 'Edison made the first sound recording' — the misattributed superlative
claim: Thomas Edison made the first sound recording — the claim that the human voice was first captured in 1877 on Edison's tin-foil phonograph, and that Edison stands as the 'father of recorded sound' by virtue of the first recording.
place: Paris, France (the 1860 phonautogram's archive)

title: Mouhot 'discovered' Angkor Wat — the discovery reading
claim: Henri Mouhot, the French naturalist, 'discovered' Angkor Wat in 1860 — he was the first person to find the lost temple in the jungle.
place: Angkor Wat — the temple whose 'discovery' is the claim

title: The Pony Express (April 1860 – October 1861)
claim: The Pony Express was an American express mail service using relays of horse-mounted riders between St. Joseph, Missouri and Sacramento, California, operated by the Central Overland California and Pikes Peak Express Company (founders Alexander Majors, William B. Waddell, William H. Russell). It ran from 3 April 1860 to 26 October 1861 — about eighteen months. The ~1,900-mile route used relay stations every 10-15 miles (riders changed horses at stations, fresh riders every 75-100 miles), delivering mail in about ten days at an initial rate of $5 per half-ounce. Despite a heavy subsidy it was not a financial success: it went bankrupt within eighteen months, never winning the hoped-for U.S. government postal contract, and was made obsolete by the completion of the first transcontinental telegraph on 24 October 1861.
place: St. Joseph, Missouri (headquarters; eastern terminus of the route)

title: The long-lived Pony Express (myth)
claim: The popular image of the Pony Express as a long-running American mail institution — years or decades of lone heroic riders carrying the West's mail as a great national success — rather than what it was: an eighteen-month relay service that went bankrupt.
place: St. Joseph, Missouri (headquarters; the myth's eastern terminus)

title: The secession declarations' own words
claim: The seceding states of the Lower South stated their reasons for secession in formal written declarations, and those declarations name slavery and hostility to slavery as their cause.
place: Charleston, South Carolina (the convention that adopted the first declaration)

title: The storm glass predicts the weather (myth)
claim: The storm glass (the camphor-liquid 'FitzRoy storm barometer') predicts the weather — its crystallization patterns foretell storms, frost, and fair weather.
place: London (Meteorological Office / Tomlinson's tests)

title: Joseph Swan's carbon-filament lamp — the priority the legend skipped
claim: Joseph Swan built and demonstrated a working carbon-filament incandescent lamp before Edison — British patent 1878, public demonstration February 1879, commercial and public-building lighting thereafter.
place: Newcastle upon Tyne / Gateshead, England — the February 1879 lecture demonstration; Swan's Gateshead home, the world's first home lit by electricity

title: Localization of function (the genuine heir of phrenology's question)
claim: Cognitive functions are localized in distinct regions of the cerebral cortex: damage to a specific region produces a specific deficit — the lesion logic that built modern neuroscience.
place: Paris, France (Broca's 1861 presentation)

title: FitzRoy's storm-warning service, February 1861
claim: In February 1861, Vice-Admiral Robert FitzRoy's Meteorological Department of the Board of Trade issued the first telegraphed storm warnings to British harbor towns — cones and drums hoisted on warning masts — the origin of the shipping forecast and the longest-running national forecasting service in the world.
place: London (Board of Trade Meteorological Department)

title: Reis's 'Telephon' — the 1861 public demonstrations
claim: In 1861, German physics teacher Johann Philipp Reis publicly demonstrated his 'Telephon' — an apparatus that converted sounds to electrical signals and transmitted speech, imperfectly — the first use of the word 'telefon/telephone' for such a device; he demonstrated widely but never sought a patent.
place: Frankfurt am Main, Germany

title: The 'states' rights, not slavery' cause claim
claim: The American Civil War (1861-1865) was fought mainly over 'states' rights' and not mainly over slavery.
place: Charleston, South Carolina (the Secession Convention, December 1860)

title: Lipman founds America's first envelope company
claim: Philadelphia stationer Hymen Lipman (1817-1893) founded the first envelope company in the United States — three years after he sold his 1858 pencil-with-attached-eraser patent to Joseph Reckendorfer for $100,000 (1862). The Smithsonian account adds that Lipman put adhesive on the back flap, devised an eyelet paper-binding method that preceded the stapler by two decades, and sold the first blank postcards in the US in 1873.
place: Philadelphia, Pennsylvania

title: The Emancipation Proclamation as issued
claim: President Abraham Lincoln's Emancipation Proclamation (preliminary Sept 22, 1862; final Jan 1, 1863) declared free all persons held as slaves in the states then in rebellion, authorized the enlistment of Black men in the Union armed forces, and turned emancipation into a war aim — but did not end slavery nationally (that took the Thirteenth Amendment, ratified December 1865).
place: Washington, D.C. (the White House, where Lincoln signed it)

title: The Lincoln portrait that is really Calhoun
claim: The popular 1860s full-length standing portrait of Abraham Lincoln — Lincoln in frock coat and shawl beside a table of documents — is a composite image: Lincoln's head set on John C. Calhoun's body.
place: New York (printmaker William Pate)

title: The staged Gettysburg sharpshooter
claim: Alexander Gardner's 'Home of a Rebel Sharpshooter' (Gettysburg, July 1863) is an unmanipulated documentary record: the dead Confederate soldier lies exactly where he fell.
place: Devil's Den, Gettysburg battlefield, Pennsylvania

title: Who wrote the Bixby letter: Lincoln or Hay
claim: Abraham Lincoln personally composed the November 21, 1864 condolence letter to Mrs. Bixby.
place: Executive Mansion, Washington, D.C.

title: The Bixby letter's premise: five sons lost
claim: Lydia Bixby, the Boston widow addressed in the November 21, 1864 condolence letter, had lost five sons fighting for the Union — the letter's own premise ('a statement of the Adjutant General of Massachusetts that you are the mother of five sons who have died gloriously on the field of battle').
place: Boston, Massachusetts

title: The Bixby letter (Nov 21, 1864)
claim: A condolence letter signed 'A. Lincoln,' dated at the Executive Mansion November 21, 1864, was issued to Mrs. Lydia Bixby of Boston, Massachusetts; Massachusetts Adjutant General William Schouler delivered it to her on November 24, 1864, and its full text appeared in the Boston Evening Transcript's afternoon second edition of November 25, 1864.
place: Boston, Massachusetts

title: 'McGill invented the brass fastener' — the first-inventor telling
claim: George W. McGill invented the brass paper fastener in 1866 — that the round-head brad with two split legs originated with him and his US 56,587 patent.
place: Washington, D.C. — McGill's residence at filing

title: McGill's 1866 paper-fastener patent (US 56,587)
claim: George W. McGill of Washington, D.C. received U.S. Patent 56,587 in 1866 (antedated January 24, 1866) for 'small, bendable paper fasteners' — brass fasteners inserted one at a time, the documented beginning of the modern American stapler's paper trail.
place: Washington, D.C. — McGill's residence at filing

title: McGill's 1867 staple press (US 67,665)
claim: George W. McGill's follow-on patent US 67,665 (August 13, 1867) describes a spring-plunger press — hammer, punch, and clinching base — built specifically to attach his 1866 brass paper-fastener to papers by punching holes and hammering the shanks down.
place: Washington, D.C. — McGill's residence at filing

title: 'Burlesque was always about stripping'
claim: American burlesque was, from its beginning, essentially the striptease — the 'always about stripping' telling.
place: New York City, USA (the burlesque houses)

title: The giant that was carved in Chicago — the Cardiff Giant hoax, 1868–1869
claim: The Cardiff Giant — unearthed near Cardiff, New York, in October 1869 — was a genuine petrified prehistoric man (or an ancient statue of a giant).
place: Cardiff, New York — the Newell farm where the gypsum figure was buried and 'discovered' in October 1869

title: The anonymous Ether Monument, 1868
claim: The Ether Monument (Boston Public Garden, unveiled 1868 — the first statue erected in the Public Garden) is a 40-foot Gothic memorial topped by a Good Samaritan sculpture that names NO discoverer of anesthesia — no Morton, no Wells, no Jackson, no Long — only biblical quotations about relieving pain ('Neither shall there be any more pain'). The anonymity was the settlement of a credit war no committee could decide.
place: Boston Public Garden

title: Haeckel's embryo drawings were doctored
claim: Ernst Haeckel's embryo drawings (Anthropogenie, 1874) were doctored: he resized embryos to a common scale (erasing up to 10-fold size differences), eliminated limb buds and heart bulges, and omitted species names to exaggerate similarity — documented contemporaneously by Rütimeyer (1868) and forensically by Richardson et al. (1997, Anatomy and Embryology 196:91–106, photographic comparison across 39 species).
place: Jena, Germany (Haeckel's chair, 1865–1909)

title: The 'Jonas Hanway invented the umbrella' telling
claim: Jonas Hanway (1712-1786), the London merchant and philanthropist, invented the umbrella — the schoolbook-and-quiz telling that credits him with the umbrella's invention.
place: London (the telling's claimed setting)

title: Lydia Thompson's British Blondes open in New York, 28 September 1868
claim: On 28 September 1868 Lydia Thompson's British Blondes opened at Wood's Museum and Metropolitan Theatre, New York, in F. C. Burnand's burlesque 'Ixion' — the arrival that made American burlesque a commercial force.
place: Wood's Museum and Metropolitan Theatre, Broadway and 31st Street, New York City, USA

title: The QWERTY layout, 1868-1878
claim: The QWERTY keyboard arrangement emerged between 1868 and 1878 through documented, gradual iteration: Sholes's November 1868 first TypeWriter (28 keys, alphabetical, piano-style) built with Glidden, Soule and Densmore in Milwaukee and shipped to Edward Payson Porter's Telegraph College in Chicago; the April 1870 38-key machine built with Matthias Schwalbach; the August 1872 Scientific American engraving showing a four-row keyboard with a second row beginning QWE.TY; the 1873 sale of manufacturing rights to E. Remington & Sons; the Remington No. 1 (1874, commercially successful); and the Remington No. 2 (1878), which stabilized the modern QWERTY layout. The arrangement was shaped by feedback from early professional users — principally telegraph operators — not by a single design decision.
place: Milwaukee, Wisconsin (Sholes's workshop; machines shipped to Chicago)

title: The line the showman never said — Barnum and 'a sucker born every minute'
claim: P. T. Barnum said 'There's a sucker born every minute.' — the most famous sentence in show business, as his own philosophy.
place: New York City (Barnum's American Museum and the 1869–1870 Cardiff Giant affair); Syracuse, New York (Hannum's exhibit)

title: The myth: Wood's wife was the first morphine addict, killed by his syringe
claim: Rebecca Massey Wood — wife of Alexander Wood — was the first known intravenous morphine addict, and she died of a morphine overdose delivered by her husband's invention.
place: Dean Cemetery, Edinburgh (Wood family grave)

title: The transcontinental railroad completed at Promontory Summit, 10 May 1869 — VERIFIED
claim: On 10 May 1869 at Promontory Summit, Utah Territory, the Central Pacific and Union Pacific railroads were joined, completing the first continuous transcontinental railroad across the United States; the ceremony centered on the driving of the 'Last Spike' — a golden spike — with the moment signaled nationwide by telegraph.

title: The Chicago Water Tower survived the 1871 fire (CORROBORATED; the 'only survivor' telling corrected)
claim: The Chicago Water Tower (designed 1869 by W. W. Boyington, built of Lemont limestone) survived the Great Chicago Fire of 8-10 October 1871 and stands today at 880 North Michigan Avenue — one of the few pre-fire structures still standing.
place: 880 North Michigan Avenue, Chicago (Michigan Avenue and East Pearson Street)

title: The Kansas cattle towns' body count
claim: The five Kansas railhead cattle towns (Abilene, Ellsworth, Wichita, Caldwell, Dodge City) recorded 45 homicides across 15 town-years of peak cattle-trading seasons; Dodge City during its 1876-1886 cattle-trading period (with the open carry of sidearms banned) averaged fewer than two violent deaths per year; Dodge's most homicidal year had 5 killings, Deadwood's 4, Tombstone's 5.
place: Dodge City, Kansas (with Abilene, Ellsworth, Wichita, Caldwell as comparison set)

title: The rotary opener that reached the kitchen (Lyman, 1870)
claim: William W. Lyman of Meriden, Connecticut patented the first practical domestic rotary can opener on 12 July 1870 (US Patent 105,346) — pierce the lid's center, set the butterfly-screw wheel, cut around; the design Baumgarten & Co. put into production from 1890 and that American kitchens actually held.
place: Meriden, Connecticut, USA

title: The lawless Wild West (constant gunfights)
claim: The frontier towns of the American West, c. 1870-1890, were lawless places where gunfights in the streets were a daily or near-daily occurrence — the Hollywood version: every disagreement settled at high noon.
place: Dodge City, Kansas (control sample; Abilene, Ellsworth, Caldwell, Wichita as the comparison set)

title: The Great Chicago Fire (8-10 October 1871)
claim: The Great Chicago Fire burned 8-10 October 1871, destroying some 17,000-18,000 buildings across about 3.3 square miles, killing approximately 300 people, and leaving about 100,000 of the city's 300,000 residents homeless — one of the most devastating urban fires of the 19th century.
place: Chicago, Illinois (fire began at the O'Leary barn, DeKoven Street, Near West Side)

title: The foreign builders of Great Zimbabwe — the colonial myth
claim: Great Zimbabwe was built by non-African foreigners: Phoenicians, Arabs, the Queen of Sheba's people from the biblical Ophir, Egyptians, Vikings, Atlanteans — 'more civilized races' than the Africans who lived around it.
place: Great Zimbabwe, Masvingo, Zimbabwe

title: The O'Leary cow that started the Great Chicago Fire (DEBUNKED)
claim: Mrs. Catherine O'Leary's cow kicked over a lantern while being milked in the O'Leary barn on the night of 8 October 1871, starting the Great Chicago Fire.
place: The O'Leary barn, DeKoven Street, Chicago (the fire's origin point, per the 1871 Board)

title: Schliemann's excavation of Troy at Hisarlik (1871–1890)
claim: Heinrich Schliemann excavated the mound of Hisarlik in the Troad (1871–1890), identified it as the Troy of Homer's Iliad, and the site is broadly accepted as ancient Troy (Ilios/Ilion).
place: Hisarlik (Troy), Tevfikiye, Çanakkale Province, Turkey

title: The gladiatorial 'thumbs down' death signal
claim: In the Roman arena, the crowd signaled death for a defeated gladiator with a thumbs-down gesture (thumbs-up meaning spare him).
place: The Colosseum (Flavian Amphitheatre), Rome

title: Troy II as Homer's Troy — Schliemann's 'burnt city'
claim: Troy II — Schliemann's 'burnt city,' the layer from which 'Priam's Treasure' came — is the Troy of Homer's Iliad, the city besieged in the Trojan War.
place: Hisarlik (Troy), Tevfikiye, Çanakkale Province, Turkey

title: 'Priam's Treasure' — Schliemann's 1873 gold hoard
claim: The gold hoard Heinrich Schliemann reported discovering on 31 May 1873 at Troy is the personal treasure of Homer's King Priam — one single find, in the ruins of Homeric Troy, photographed on Sophia Schliemann and smuggled out in her shawl.
place: Hisarlik (Troy), Tevfikiye, Çanakkale Province, Turkey

title: Reckendorfer v. Faber (92 U.S. 347, 1875) — the Supreme Court kills the eraser patent
claim: In Reckendorfer v. Faber, 92 U.S. 347 (1875), the U.S. Supreme Court declared Lipman's pencil-with-eraser patent invalid. The ruling: the patent was 'merely the combination of two things, without a new use' — 'A combination, to be patentable, must produce a different force, effect, or result in the combined forces or processes from that given by their separate parts... A combination, therefore, which consists only of the application of a piece of rubber to one end of the same piece of wood which makes a lead pencil is not patentable.' Lipman kept the $100,000 he got from Reckendorfer; Reckendorfer was left with nothing.
place: Washington, D.C. (U.S. Supreme Court)

title: 'Mr. Watson, come here' — the first intelligible telephone transmission, March 10, 1876
claim: On March 10, 1876, at 5 Exeter Place, Boston, Alexander Graham Bell transmitted the first intelligible sentence by telephone to his assistant Thomas Watson in the next room — 'Mr. Watson, come here, I want to see you!' — as recorded in Bell's laboratory journal.
place: 5 Exeter Place, Boston, Massachusetts

title: Alexander Graham Bell alone invented the telephone (the sole-inventor myth)
claim: That Alexander Graham Bell alone invented the telephone — the single-inventor reading of the telephone's origin carried by textbooks and popular history.
place: Boston, Massachusetts (the myth's home city)

title: US Patent 174,465 — Bell's telephone patent, granted March 7, 1876
claim: United States Patent No. 174,465, titled 'Improvement in Telegraphy,' was granted to Alexander Graham Bell on March 7, 1876, covering an apparatus for 'transmitting vocal or other sounds telegraphically... causing electrical undulations.'
place: Washington, D.C. (U.S. Patent Office)

title: Bell's telephone offered to Western Union, fall 1876 (and declined)
claim: In the fall of 1876, Gardiner Hubbard, Alexander Graham Bell's chief backer, brought Bell's inventions to the Western Union Telegraph Company and its president William Orton, and Western Union declined to buy them.
place: New York City (Western Union headquarters)

title: Dewey's real achievement: the standardized, commercialized card (1876)
claim: Melvil Dewey's 1876 work and the Library Bureau made the index card the American library industry's agreed unit — standardization and commercialization, not invention.
place: Boston, Massachusetts — the Library Bureau's home

title: The 'Mask of Agamemnon' (Mycenae, 1876)
claim: The gold funeral mask found at Mycenae in 1876 is the death mask of Homer's King Agamemnon — the face Schliemann claimed in his telegram to have gazed upon.
place: Mycenae, Argolis, Greece (Grave Circle A)

title: The Valentine's Day race — Bell's application and Gray's caveat, February 14, 1876
claim: On February 14, 1876, Bell's lawyer filed Bell's telephone patent application and Elisha Gray's lawyer filed Gray's telephone caveat on the same day at the U.S. Patent Office — Bell's the fifth entry of the day, Gray's the thirty-ninth; both documents incorporated a liquid transmitter.
place: Washington, D.C. (U.S. Patent Office)

title: 'An electrical toy' — the Western Union dismissal quote (misquotation)
claim: That Western Union president William Orton, on being offered Bell's telephone patent in 1876, dismissed it with the words 'an electrical toy' (in some tellings 'nothing but a toy') — the famous attributed quote of the Western Union telephone story.
place: New York City (the attributed scene)

title: The real doctor behind Holmes: Doyle's 1892 letter to Joseph Bell
claim: Sherlock Holmes's analytical method was modeled on the real Edinburgh surgeon Joseph Bell — Arthur Conan Doyle himself named Bell as Holmes's model in writing.
place: Edinburgh Royal Infirmary / Royal College of Surgeons of Edinburgh (letter archive)

title: Edison's tin-foil phonograph, December 1877 — the first machine that talked back
claim: In December 1877 Thomas Edison's shop built the first practical machine capable of BOTH recording and reproducing sound: the tin-foil cylinder phonograph — Edison speaking 'Mary had a little lamb' into the mouthpiece and the machine playing his words back — demonstrated at Scientific American's offices (reported 22 December 1877), patent filed 24 December 1877, granted 19 February 1878 as U.S. Patent 200,521.
place: Menlo Park, New Jersey (Edison's laboratory; Scientific American demonstration at the magazine's New York offices)

title: The name "Silk Road" (and the single-road idea)
claim: The "Silk Road" is a single ancient trade road whose name dates to antiquity — the ancients knew it as one road under that name.
place: Berlin (publication place of Richthofen's China vol. 1, 1877)

title: The telephone war of 1877-78 and the 1879 settlement (the foil)
claim: After declining Bell in 1876, Western Union built its own telephone operation — hiring Elisha Gray and Thomas Edison to develop rival telephony — fought Bell for the telephone business in 1877-78, and settled in 1879 by withdrawing from telephony, with Bell acquiring the Edison carbon-microphone technology from Western Union's camp. The rejection had a documented price.
place: New York / the Bell vs Western Union litigation

title: The QWERTY slowdown myth
claim: The QWERTY keyboard layout was deliberately designed to slow typists down, so that the typewriter's typebars would not jam.
place: Milwaukee, Wisconsin (geography of the claim's subject — the 1870s design work)

title: Edison 'invented' the light bulb — the solo-inventor reading
claim: Thomas Edison invented the (incandescent) light bulb — he was the first person to create a working electric incandescent lamp.
place: Menlo Park, New Jersey — the laboratory where the legend was written, not where the lamp began

title: Edison 'invented' the light bulb — the solo-inventor reading (evidence chain corrected)
claim: Thomas Edison invented the (incandescent) light bulb — he was the first person to create a working electric incandescent lamp.
place: Menlo Park, New Jersey — the laboratory where the legend was written, not where the lamp began

title: Edison's Menlo Park system — the real achievement the legend mislabels
claim: Edison's real achievement was the first practical, complete incandescent electric lighting system — long-life lamp plus generators, distribution, and wiring — demonstrated at Menlo Park in December 1879 and commercialized with Pearl Street Station, New York, in September 1882.
place: Menlo Park, New Jersey (demonstration, Dec 1879); Pearl Street, New York (station, Sep 1882)

title: The French Panama effort, 1882–1889
claim: Ferdinand de Lesseps's Compagnie Universelle du Canal Interocéanique de Panama (founded 1879; construction 1882–May 1889) attempted the Panama Canal before the United States: a sea-level design stubbornly kept until the October 1887 conversion to a lock canal; by the 1889 bankruptcy the company had spent ~Fr 1.18 billion (≈ $235 million), excavated ~50–53 million cubic meters — about two-fifths of the final total — and lost roughly 20,000–22,000 workers, mostly to yellow fever and malaria.
place: Isthmus of Panama (Colon → Panama City)

title: The Selden patent monopoly (1903–1911) and Ford's courtroom win
claim: The Selden patent (US 549,160, filed 8 May 1879, issued 5 November 1895) gave its holders — the Electric Vehicle Company and the Association of Licensed Automobile Manufacturers (ALAM, founded March 1903) — a working monopoly claim over gasoline automobiles in the United States from 1903 until the 9 January 1911 Second Circuit decision in Ford's favor, which held the patent valid only for Brayton-type two-stroke engines that the industry no longer used.
place: Rochester, New York (Selden's residence and filing origin)

title: The "America built the Panama Canal alone" myth
claim: The United States built the Panama Canal from scratch and on its own — the canal was an entirely American achievement, with no foreign effort before it and American hands doing the digging.
place: Isthmus of Panama (Colon → Panama City)

title: The 1883 Edison & Swan merger — the lawsuit that became a company
claim: After the British Edison Company sued Swan's company for incandescent-lamp patent infringement, the British suit was dropped in favor of a negotiated merger — creating the Edison and Swan United Electric Light Company in 1883 to exploit the two firms' complementary patents.
place: London, England — the joint company's formation; the British suit was dropped, not decided

title: The day of two noons — US standard time, 18 November 1883
claim: The American railroads adopted standard time at noon on 18 November 1883 — William F. Allen's five-zone plan (Intercolonial, Eastern, Central, Mountain, Pacific) approved by the General Time Convention in Chicago on 11 October 1883 — a full year before the International Meridian Conference met; the day was called 'the day of two noons' because cities reset their clocks at the new standard noon after having already observed local noon.
place: Chicago (General Time Convention, Grand Pacific Hotel, 11 Oct 1883)

title: 'The 1884 conference created the world's time zones'
claim: The 1884 International Meridian Conference created the world's time zones in a single meeting — that 41 delegates in Washington drew the zone system the world now uses.
place: Washington, D.C. (the conference that did not draw them)

title: The Home Insurance Building's hybrid frame: iron-dominant, steel-incorporating, bolted
claim: The Home Insurance Building's frame was a metal skeleton incorporating structural steel alongside wrought and cast iron; the frame carried the floors and helped carry the exterior walls — but masonry walls still carried some of the weight, and the metal frame was bolted rather than riveted.
place: LaSalle & Adams Streets, Chicago, Illinois (demolished 1931)

title: The International Meridian Conference of 1884
claim: The International Meridian Conference assembled at Washington, D.C. in October 1884 — 41 delegates from 25 nations (26 invited, Denmark absent) — and on 13 October 1884 adopted Resolution II: the meridian through the centre of the transit instrument at the Greenwich Observatory would be the initial meridian for longitude, by 22 votes to 1 (San Domingo against), with Brazil and France abstaining. The conference also recommended a universal day — a mean solar day beginning at mean midnight at Greenwich — expressly for purposes 'for which it may be found convenient,' with no interference to local or standard time, and all resolutions were framed as proposals to the governments represented, not binding acts.
place: Washington, D.C. (Meridian Conference)

title: Waterman's 1884 three-fissure feed
claim: Lewis Waterman's first pen-related patent, granted 12 February 1884, was for the 'three fissure feed' — a capillary-action ink feed that let air into the reservoir through narrow channels so ink flowed steadily without flooding; Waterman took over Frank Holland's abandoned 1883 pen company and fitted its pens with this feed, which is what made the Waterman pen the first reliably non-leaking, commercially dominant fountain pen.
place: New York City, USA — where Waterman assembled and sold the pens (behind a cigar shop, with a five-year guarantee)

title: 'Waterman invented the fountain pen' — the myth
claim: Lewis Waterman invented the fountain pen in 1884.
place: New York City, USA — where Waterman's pen company was founded

title: The 'first skyscraper' was the Home Insurance Building (1885) — the definition-dependent title
claim: The Home Insurance Building in Chicago (designed by William Le Baron Jenney, completed 1885) was the world's first skyscraper — the unqualified textbook form of the claim.
place: LaSalle & Adams Streets, Chicago, Illinois (demolished 1931)

title: The hyper-radial order: the largest lighthouse lens ever put into use (Makapu'u Point, 1909)
claim: The hyper-radial order of Fresnel lens (focal length 1330 mm) is the largest lighthouse-lens size ever put into use: made from 1885 (Barbier test lens for the South Foreland trials; Chance Brothers' first in 1887), installed in about two dozen major landfall beacons worldwide; the Makapu'u Point hyper-radial (lit 1909) is the only such lens in U.S. service and has been the largest lens in U.S. service since 1909 — 12 feet tall, over a thousand prisms, displayed at the 1893 Chicago World's Fair before installation.
place: Makapu'u Point Light, Oahu, Hawaii, USA (the flagship hyper-radial)

title: Smith's conductor's punch (1885)
claim: In 1885, Benjamin Smith of Massachusetts invented the 'conductor's punch' — a single-hole punch for train conductors, using effort-relieving levers, with a collector at the bottom for gathering the cut confetti.
place: Massachusetts, United States (Smith's conductor's punch)

title: The 'Soennecken invented the hole punch' telling
claim: Friedrich Soennecken invented the hole punch in 1886 — he was the first inventor of the device.
place: Bonn, Germany (Soennecken's city; the telling attaches to the German patent tradition)

title: Benz's DRP 37435 (1886) — the automobile's birth certificate
claim: Carl Benz's DRP 37435 — 'vehicle with gas engine operation', filed 29 January 1886 at the Imperial Patent Office in Berlin — is the documentary birth certificate of the automobile: a purpose-built gasoline automobile (the Benz Patent-Motorwagen), distinct from a motorized carriage.
place: Berlin, Germany (Imperial Patent Office, filing)

title: 'Henry Ford invented the automobile' — the misattributed superlative
claim: Henry Ford invented the automobile — the claim that the automobile originates with Ford's work (the Ford Quadricycle of 1896, the Ford Motor Company of 1903, or the Model T of 1908) and that Ford is the automobile's inventor.
place: Berlin, Germany (filing location of DRP 37435)

title: Soennecken's Papierlocher (1886)
claim: On 14 November 1886, Friedrich Soennecken filed a German patent for the Papierlocher für Sammelmappen — a two-hole paper punch for binders — the device Google celebrated with its 131st-anniversary Doodle on 14 November 2017.
place: Bonn, Germany (Soennecken's company and city)

title: The Statue of Liberty as a Working Lighthouse (1886–1902)
claim: The Statue of Liberty was a working federal lighthouse from 1886 to 1902: at its dedication President Grover Cleveland placed the statue and pedestal under the U.S. Lighthouse Board, which lit the torch with electric arc lamps (first lit 22 November 1886) and tended it with a dedicated lighthouse keeper, Albert E. Littlefield — making it the first electric lighthouse in the United States. The light was judged ineffective for navigation and was extinguished when care passed to the War Department on 1 March 1902.
place: Bedloe's (now Liberty) Island, New York Harbor

title: Edison's real anti-AC campaign, 1887–1890 — the foil the Topsy myth misdates
claim: In 1887–1890 Edison's interests ran a genuine propaganda campaign against alternating current: Harold P. Brown's public animal electrocutions (including the July 1888 Columbia College demonstration killing a dog with AC), the coinage of 'Westinghoused' as a verb for electrocution, and lobbying that put AC into New York's first electric chair (William Kemmler, Auburn, 6 August 1890).
place: New York City (campaign); West Orange, NJ (Edison laboratory); Auburn, NY (Kemmler execution)

title: The 1888 Figaro obituary mix-up
claim: After Alfred Nobel's brother Ludvig died in Cannes (12 April 1888), Le Figaro mistakenly published an obituary of Alfred on 15 April 1888 — 'A man who can only with the utmost difficulty be considered a benefactor of mankind has died yesterday at Cannes. It is Mr. Nobel, inventor of dynamite. Mr. Nobel was Swedish' — and retracted it the next day. Alfred knew about the mix-up: a surviving letter from his friend Juliette Adam-Lambert expressing relief the rumor was false is the best archival evidence he did.
place: Paris (Le Figaro); Cannes (Ludvig's death)

title: The 'merchant of death' headline (the questioned text)
claim: The mistaken 1888 obituary of Alfred Nobel ran under the headline 'Le marchand de la mort est mort' ('The merchant of death is dead') and declared that 'Dr. Alfred Nobel, who became rich by finding ways to kill more people faster than ever before, died yesterday.'
place: Paris (claimed newspaper)

title: The obituary that supposedly created the Nobel Prize
claim: Alfred Nobel established the Nobel Prizes because he read the mistaken 1888 obituary and was horrified at the 'merchant of death' reputation it promised him — the obituary shock caused the 1895 will.
place: Paris

title: The Forth Bridge (VERIFIED)
claim: The Forth Bridge — the cantilever railway bridge across the Firth of Forth, Scotland, designed by John Fowler and Benjamin Baker, built 1883–1890 and opened in 1890 — is the span behind the idiom 'like painting the Forth Bridge.'
place: Firth of Forth, Scotland (South Queensferry ↔ North Queensferry)

title: The Gem paper clip: anonymous invention, commercial by ~1900
claim: The loop-within-a-loop paper clip — the Gem — was already in widespread commercial use by about 1900, produced by the Gem Manufacturing Co. in England (possibly from the 1870s), was never itself patented, and its inventor is anonymous.
place: England (Gem Manufacturing Co.; Middlebrook filed from Waterbury, Connecticut, US)

title: The 1890 Chicago Tribune hoax that invented the rope trick
claim: In 1890, Chicago Tribune city editor John E. Wilkie wrote a hoax story about the Indian rope trick that launched the modern legend; the newspaper later admitted in print that the story was false.
place: Chicago, Illinois (the Tribune's newsroom)

title: Judson's Clasp Locker (1893) — the idea, not the teeth
claim: Whitcomb L. Judson invented the first metal slide fastener, the 'clasp locker' — a hook-and-eye shoe fastener patented 1891-1893 and debuted at the 1893 Chicago World's Fair; it was cumbersome and popped open unexpectedly, and was never a commercial success.
place: Chicago, Illinois (Columbian Exposition)

title: The 1892 Rosenau/Library Bureau vertical-filing prototype
claim: In 1892, Dr. Rosenau, secretary of a Buffalo, New York charity organization, took his vertical-filing idea to the Library Bureau's Chicago office, which built a prototype — the earliest documented vertical filing cabinet.
place: Chicago, Illinois (Library Bureau Chicago office)

title: The 'Ferris invented the Ferris wheel' myth (DEBUNKED)
claim: George Washington Gale Ferris Jr. invented the Ferris wheel — the rotating passenger wheel was his original invention for the 1893 World's Columbian Exposition.
place: Chicago, Illinois, USA (World's Columbian Exposition)

title: Ferris's 1893 Chicago wheel (VERIFIED)
claim: George Washington Gale Ferris Jr.'s wheel at the 1893 World's Columbian Exposition in Chicago was 264 feet tall, carried 36 cars of 60 passengers each (2,160 per revolution), opened to the public in June 1893, and carried over a million paying customers during the fair.
place: Chicago, Illinois, USA (World's Columbian Exposition, Midway)

title: The Mendenhall Order of 1893: metric standards become the fundamental standards of the United States
claim: In 1893, by the Mendenhall Order issued by T. C. Mendenhall (Superintendent of the U.S. Coast and Geodetic Survey), the United States adopted the international meter and kilogram as the fundamental standards for length and mass; the customary units — the yard, the pound, and their relatives — have been defined in relation to the meter and the kilogram ever since.
place: Washington, D.C., United States (the Mendenhall Order was an administrative act of the U.S. Coast and Geodetic Survey, not a place-bound event)

title: "Edwin Seibels invented the vertical filing cabinet in 1893"
claim: Edwin Seibels, an insurance salesman, invented the vertical filing cabinet in 1893 — first and alone.
place: Chicago, Illinois (the 1892 Library Bureau prototype — the evidence that predates the claim)

title: 'America never adopted the metric system': the myth that mistakes the road signs for the statute books
claim: The United States has NEVER adopted the metric system — that metric units have never been the legally fundamental measurement standards of the country.
place: United States (a legal-fact claim, not a place-bound event)

title: The Dickson Experimental Sound Film (1894/95) - the first known sound film
claim: The Dickson Experimental Sound Film, made by W.K.L. Dickson in late 1894 or early 1895 at Edison's Black Maria studio, is the first known film with live-recorded sound - Dickson playing a violin into a wax-cylinder recording horn while two men dance to the music; selected for the National Film Registry in 2003.
place: Black Maria studio, West Orange, New Jersey (city precision)

title: The Dreyfus Affair: arrest, trials, degradation, exoneration (1894-1906)
claim: The Dreyfus Affair (1894-1906): French artillery captain Alfred Dreyfus, an Alsatian Jew, was arrested in October 1894 on suspicion of passing military secrets to Germany, convicted of treason by a Paris court-martial on 22 December 1894, publicly degraded (5 January 1895) and deported to Devil's Island; in 1896 the new head of the army's intelligence Statistical Section, Georges Picquart, identified Major Ferdinand Walsin Esterhazy as the real author of the incriminating bordereau; after Zola's 'J'Accuse' (13 January 1898), the exposure of Colonel Henry's forged evidence (August 1898), a second court-martial at Rennes (August-September 1899) that still found Dreyfus guilty 'with extenuating circumstances,' a presidential pardon (19 September 1899), the Court of Cassation annulled the conviction on 12 July 1906, reinstated Dreyfus as a major, and awarded him the Legion of Honour.
place: Paris, France (court-martial, degradation, J'Accuse); Devil's Island, French Guiana (imprisonment); Rennes (1899 retrial)

title: The Dreyfus guilty verdict: the bordereau was Esterhazy's, the evidence was forged
claim: Captain Alfred Dreyfus was guilty of the treason for which he was convicted on 22 December 1894 — that he personally authored the bordereau (the torn-up memorandum found in the German military attache's wastebasket) offering French military secrets to Germany.
place: Paris, France

title: Edison 'invented the movies' — the solo-inventor reading
claim: Thomas Edison invented motion pictures — he was the sole inventor of the movies.
place: West Orange, New Jersey — the laboratory where the legend was written

title: The Kinetoscope — 1894, the first commercially viable motion-picture system (peep-show, not projection)
claim: The Edison-lab Kinetograph/Kinetoscope system (1889–1894): William K.L. Dickson's motion-picture camera and peep-show viewer, first commercially exhibited 14 April 1894 at the Holland Brothers' parlor in New York City — the first commercially viable motion-picture system, single-viewer, not projected.
place: Broadway, New York City — the first Kinetoscope parlor

title: The Browne Issue System (1895)
claim: Nina E. Browne, librarian at the Library Bureau in Boston, devised the first widely adopted card-and-pocket library charging system by 1895: each borrower's ticket and each book's card were filed together in date trays at checkout, the date was stamped in the book, and on return the borrower's card was handed back and the book card replaced in the book — after which no record of the transaction remained.
place: Library Bureau, Boston, Massachusetts

title: The 'Einstein failed math' myth
claim: Albert Einstein failed mathematics in school — he was a poor student of math as a child.
place: Aarau, Switzerland (Aargau Cantonal School); Zurich (ETH)

title: The Lumière first paid public screening — 28 December 1895
claim: The first paid public film projection in history took place on 28 December 1895 at the Salon Indien du Grand Café, Paris — the Lumière brothers' Cinématographe screening of ten short films before a paying audience.
place: Salon Indien du Grand Café, 14 Boulevard des Capucines, Paris

title: 'Cinema is an invention without a future' — the Louis Lumière attribution
claim: Louis Lumière told Georges Méliès that the cinema was 'an invention without a future' (the famous 1895–96 warning, usually in the form: 'Jeune homme, remerciez-moi. Mon invention n'est pas à vendre... elle n'a aucun avenir commercial').
place: Paris — the legend's claimed scene

title: Nobel's 1895 will
claim: On 27 November 1895, at the Swedish-Norwegian Club in Paris, Alfred Nobel signed his last will and testament, directing that the bulk of his estate (about 94% after taxes and individual bequests) be converted into a fund whose interest would be distributed annually as prizes to 'those who, during the preceding year, shall have conferred the greatest benefit to mankind' — in physics, chemistry, physiology or medicine, literature, and peace. Nobel died 10 December 1896 in Sanremo, Italy, leaving no public explanation for the bequest.
place: Swedish-Norwegian Club, Paris

title: The train panic — audiences fled the Lumière screening in terror
claim: When the Lumières projected 'L'Arrivée d'un train en gare de La Ciotat,' the audience panicked — leapt up, ducked, fled the room in terror at the train rushing toward them (the founding legend of cinema's power, usually dated to the 28 December 1895 premiere).
place: Salon Indien du Grand Café, Paris — the legend's claimed scene

title: Hubert's company and the 'Ever Ready' brand
claim: Conrad Hubert's American Electrical Novelty and Manufacturing Company commercialized the flashlight, built the 'Ever Ready' brand (1905), and became the Eveready of the battery aisle.
place: New York City

title: Why they were called 'flash' lights
claim: The word 'flashlight' (American) / 'torch' naming comes from the devices' first decade: weak zinc-carbon batteries and carbon-filament bulbs could only produce brief flashes of light, not sustained beams.
place: New York City

title: The coal-bunker fire theory — the Maine's most probable cause
claim: The USS Maine was destroyed by an internal explosion: a spontaneous fire in a coal bunker — burning bituminous coal, prone to spontaneous combustion — ignited the adjacent 6-inch reserve magazines, which detonated the forward magazines on the night of 15 February 1898.
place: Havana Harbor, Cuba

title: The destruction of the USS Maine
claim: On the evening of 15 February 1898, the American battleship USS Maine (ACR-1) exploded and sank in Havana Harbor, Cuba, killing 266 of the 350 men aboard when her forward magazines detonated. She had been sent to Havana three weeks earlier, moored at buoy 4, to protect American interests during the Cuban War of Independence. The wreck was raised within a cofferdam in 1911 and re-sunk with military honors in deep water north of Havana in 1912; her main mast stands as a memorial at Arlington National Cemetery.
place: Havana Harbor, Cuba (moored at buoy 4)

title: The Spanish mine that never was — 'Remember the Maine, to hell with Spain'
claim: Spain — a Spanish-placed mine, a Spanish-ordered sabotage — destroyed the battleship USS Maine in Havana Harbor on 15 February 1898, and the 'Remember the Maine — to hell with Spain!' war cry named the true culprit.
place: Havana Harbor, Cuba

title: David Misell's tubular flashlight, 1898-1899
claim: English inventor David Misell designed and patented the first practical tubular dry-cell flashlight, 1898-1899.
place: New York City

title: Seibels's 1898 prototype, the 1899 Globe-Wernicke cabinets, and the denied patent
claim: Edwin Seibels, an insurance salesman, built a vertical-filing prototype in 1898; a year later the Cincinnati company Globe-Wernicke produced five vertical filing cabinets, one of which survives in the Smithsonian Institution's National Museum of American History collection; Seibels's patent application was denied on the grounds that it described a system that was an idea, not a device.
place: National Museum of American History, Washington, DC (holds one of the five 1899 Globe-Wernicke cabinets)

title: The invention of bushido
claim: Bushido was the ancient, timeless code of honor followed by the samurai class throughout Japan's feudal history.
place: Tokyo — the samurai tradition the doctrine claims to describe

title: The "Conrad Hubert invented the flashlight" telling
claim: Conrad Hubert invented the flashlight.
place: New York City

title: The 'Johan Vaaler invented the paper clip' myth
claim: Johan Vaaler, a Norwegian inventor, invented the paper clip — filing his patent in 1899 and receiving German (DRP 121,067) and US patents in 1901 — and the modern paper clip is his invention.
place: Sandvika, Norway (the 1989 monument site; Vaaler was an Oslo clerk)

title: Cows lying down means rain (myth)
claim: Cows lying down in a field is a sure sign that rain is on the way — cattle can sense approaching rain and lie down in anticipation.
place: England (UK Met Office survey — over 60% of the British public believe it)

title: MYTH: John Cotton Dana invented the library's card-and-pocket checkout system
claim: The popular telling that John Cotton Dana invented the library book-card checkout — that the card-and-pocket system (book pocket, book card, date slip, borrower's card) began with Dana's Newark system about 1900, with no predecessor.
place: Newark Public Library, Newark, New Jersey (the telling's home; the refutation's geography is Boston 1895)

title: The giant destrier — the draft-horse-sized medieval war horse
claim: The medieval knight's war horse — the destrier — was a huge animal, the size of a modern draft horse (17–18 hands high at the withers), a mount built to carry an armored man like a small tank.
place: England (171 excavated sites, AD 300–1650 — the study sample that killed the image)

title: The Flannan Isles keepers' disappearance, December 1900
claim: Three lighthouse keepers — James Ducat, Thomas Marshall and Donald McArthur — vanished from the Flannan Isles lighthouse (Eilean Mòr, Outer Hebrides) between the last written log entries of 13 December and the arrival of the relief tender Hesperus on 26 December 1900; the steamer Archtor had already noted the light unlit on 15 December. Their bodies were never found.
place: Eilean Mòr, Flannan Isles, Outer Hebrides, Scotland

title: TELLING (DEBUNKED): 'posh' = Port Out, Starboard Home
claim: TELLING (DEBUNKED): 'posh' is an acronym of 'Port Out, Starboard Home' — the Peninsular & Oriental Steam Navigation Company stamped wealthy Britain-India passengers' tickets P.O.S.H. for the cooler (more expensive) cabins.
place: London (P&O shipping and English print culture)

title: Landsteiner's ABO blood groups (1900–1901)
claim: Karl Landsteiner discovered the human ABO blood groups (A, B, O) — 1900 serum-mixing experiments, published 1901 — establishing the compatibility rules that made transfusion safe; AB followed (Decastello & Sturli, 1902); Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine 1930.
place: Vienna

title: The Newark Charging System (~1900)
claim: John Cotton Dana's Newark Public Library introduced its card-based circulation system about 1900: each book carried a book pocket with a book card (4"x2"), each checkout was stamped on a date slip pasted in the book, and the book card was filed in charging trays by date and call number against the borrower's registration — replacing ledger-based circulation and becoming, by the 1913 ALA survey, the most common named charging system in American libraries.
place: Newark Public Library, Newark, New Jersey

title: Stage versions of the rope trick — the legend's children, not its ancestors
claim: Twentieth-century stage magicians performed rope-rising effects — a rope made to stand or rise apparently without support — inspired by the Indian rope trick legend, not as survivals of an ancient classic feat.
