place: India and the Western stage (the legend's two homes)

title: Conklin's 1901 crescent filler — the first reliable self-filler
claim: Roy Conklin's US patent 685,258 (granted October 1901) covered the crescent filler: an internal rubber sac compressed by a pressure bar running through a slot in the barrel, attached to an external crescent-shaped hump; pressing and releasing the hump drew ink in without a separate dropper — the first reliable self-filling fountain pen. Conklin had founded the Self-Filling Fountain Pen Company (1898, with C. B. Gundy), renamed the Conklin Pen Manufacturing Co. (1901); Mark Twain lent his name to the pens; crescent fillers were produced through 1930.
place: Toledo, Ohio, USA — Conklin Pen Manufacturing Co.

title: Marconi's 1901 transatlantic 'S' (the contested reception)
claim: On 12 December 1901, at Signal Hill, St. John's, Newfoundland, Guglielmo Marconi received three faint clicks — the Morse letter 'S' — transmitted from his station at Poldhu, Cornwall, the first wireless reception across the Atlantic.
place: Signal Hill, St. John's, Newfoundland

title: "Elementary, my dear Watson" — the line Doyle never wrote
claim: Sherlock Holmes said "Elementary, my dear Watson" in Sir Arthur Conan Doyle's original published stories (the canon of 56 short stories and four novels, 1887–1927).
place: London (221B Baker Street — the fictional setting) / the canon as published

title: The 'Brontosaurus never existed' myth
claim: The popular claim 'Brontosaurus never existed — it was a scientific error from the start.' The animal was always real: Riggs 1903 performed a taxonomic sinking (synonymy under the priority rule), not a fraud exposure, and the type skeleton sat in museums throughout; the 2015 peer-reviewed reinstatement of the genus makes the 'never existed' version false twice over.
place: Como Bluff, Wyoming — the animal's type locality; the myth lived in textbooks and on a postage stamp

title: The myth: Edison electrocuted Topsy to win the War of Currents
claim: Thomas Edison personally ordered the 1903 electrocution of the elephant Topsy as an anti-AC demonstration during the War of Currents against George Westinghouse.
place: Luna Park, Coney Island, Brooklyn, New York

title: The execution of Topsy the elephant, 4 January 1903
claim: On 4 January 1903 at Luna Park, Coney Island, New York, the female Asian elephant Topsy was publicly executed by electrocution on the orders of her owners, park proprietors Frederick Thompson and Elmer Dundy; the event was filmed by the Edison Manufacturing Company as 'Electrocuting an Elephant.'
place: Luna Park, Coney Island, Brooklyn, New York

title: The Wrights' first powered, controlled flights, December 17, 1903
claim: At Kill Devil Hills, North Carolina, on December 17, 1903, Orville and Wilbur Wright made four sustained, powered, controlled, man-carrying flights (12 seconds/120 feet to 59 seconds/852 feet), photographed at the moment of liftoff and reported by telegram the same day — the first such flights in history. This is the timeline's first aviation record.
place: Kill Devil Hills, North Carolina (Wright Brothers National Memorial)

title: The 1906 San Francisco Earthquake
claim: On 18 April 1906 at 05:12 local time, a ~Mw 7.9 strike-slip earthquake ruptured ~296 miles of the San Andreas Fault, shaking northern California from Eureka to the Salinas Valley at up to Mercalli XI (Extreme).
place: San Andreas Fault, northern California (epicenter debated; most recent USGS estimate near Mussel Rock, Daly City)

title: Santos-Dumont's 14-bis: the first officially observed powered flights in Europe, 1906
claim: On October 23 and November 12, 1906, Alberto Santos-Dumont flew his 14-bis at Bagatelle field, Paris — officially observed, publicly announced powered flights, taking off under its own power without a launch rail — the first powered, man-carrying flights in Europe and the first to be widely witnessed by the public and sporting authorities of their day.
place: Bagatelle field, Bois de Boulogne, Paris

title: The 1906 San Francisco Firestorms
claim: The three-to-four-day firestorms after the 18 April 1906 earthquake — 30+ fires from ruptured gas mains, overturned stoves, and dynamited firebreaks — destroyed roughly 25,000-28,000 buildings on ~490 city blocks, doing at least 80% (some estimates up to ~95%) of the disaster's total destruction, with the death toll now put at ~3,000+ against the official 498.
place: San Francisco, California (burned district: ~490 city blocks)

title: The 'Earthquake Destroyed the City' Telling (1906)
claim: The telling that the 1906 San Francisco earthquake's ground shaking destroyed the city — i.e., that the shaking, not the subsequent fires, did the vast majority of the destruction.
place: San Francisco, California

title: The 1907 international reply coupon — the world's first prepaid-reply instrument
claim: The Universal Postal Union's 1906 congress in Rome created the International Reply Coupon: a small paper document (UPU form C22, later CN 01) sold by post offices against cash payment, which the buyer could send to any UPU country so the recipient could exchange it for postage stamps (initially stamps valued at 25 gold centimes) to pay return postage. The proposal came from the British Colonies of Australasia, which wanted a domestic reply-prepayment practice extended worldwide. The first coupons were put on sale on 1 October 1907 (UPU International Bureau). Seven design types have followed; the U.S. discontinued sales on 27 January 2013 and Royal Mail on 31 December 2011, but exchange remains mandatory for UPU members.
place: Bern, Switzerland — UPU headquarters (resolution at the Rome 1906 congress)

title: Marie Lloyd's 'Let her through, girls' picket-line quip to Belle Elmore
claim: During the 1907 music-hall strike, Marie Lloyd — on picket duty — spotted Belle Elmore crossing the picket line and shouted 'Let her through, girls — she'll close the place faster than we can.' Belle Elmore was Cora Crippen, later murdered by her husband Dr. Hawley Crippen.
place: London (the Bedford picket, per the tradition)

title: Marie Lloyd 'led' the 1907 music-hall strike
claim: That Marie Lloyd — the 'Queen of the Music Hall' — led the 1907 music-hall strike, as the popular shorthand runs.
place: London

title: The 1907 Music Hall Strike (the Music Hall War)
claim: In January–February 1907, London music-hall performers, musicians and stagehands struck across 22 theatres, organized by the Variety Artistes' Federation (founded 18 February 1906), ending in arbitration chaired by George Askwith with a resolution broadly favourable to the performers — national agreements on codes of conduct, contracts and dispute resolution.
place: London — Holborn Empire, Scala Theatre, Surrey Theatre, 22 picketed halls

title: The twenty-six-year detention of Mary Mallon
claim: Mary Mallon was confined on North Brother Island from 1907 to 1910 and again from 1915 until her death in 1938 — the only identified typhoid carrier detained indefinitely.
place: North Brother Island, East River, New York City

title: The 'only carrier' legend of Typhoid Mary
claim: Mary Mallon was the only healthy typhoid carrier — the one dangerous exception among well people.
place: New York City (identification, confinement on North Brother Island)

title: Frederick Cook's 1908 North Pole claim — the pole that wasn't reached (claimed 21 April 1908, disproven 21 December 1909)
claim: Frederick A. Cook claimed that he reached the North Pole on 21 April 1908, traveling by dogsled across the polar ice cap, and announced the achievement in September 1909 — days before Robert Peary announced his own 6 April 1909 claim. No verifiable proof of Cook's arrival at the Pole has ever been produced.
place: North Pole (claimed arrival point)

title: Peary's 1909 North Pole claim — the expedition is documented; the exact point stays contested (6 April 1909)
claim: Robert E. Peary claimed he reached the North Pole on 6 April 1909, traveling by dogsled from the Roosevelt with Matthew Henson and four Inughuit men. The expedition itself is documented to the day; whether his party stood at the exact point 90 degN remains contested by serious scholarship.
place: North Pole (claimed arrival point, vicinity)

title: Sheaffer's 1908 lever filler
claim: Walter A. Sheaffer patented the lever-filling fountain pen in August 1908: a slim metal lever on the barrel depressed the internal ink sac directly, filling the pen from the ink bottle with a single stroke — eliminating the eye-dropper. The first Sheaffer-marked pens were produced in 1912; the W.A. Sheaffer Pen Company was incorporated 1 January 1913 at Fort Madison, Iowa ($35,000 capital), and the lever became the industry-standard filler, displacing Conklin's crescent.
place: Fort Madison, Iowa, USA — the back room of Sheaffer's jewelry store, then the Sheaffer factory

title: The 1910 Halley cyanogen panic (DEBUNKED)
claim: When Earth passed through Halley's tail on 18–19 May 1910, the cyanogen gas in the tail would poison the atmosphere and kill all life.
place: New York, USA (panic epicenter); global (tail passage)

title: Amundsen reaches the South Pole, 14 December 1911 — VERIFIED
claim: Roald Amundsen's Norwegian party reached the geographic South Pole on 14 December 1911 — the first humans to do so — beating Robert Falcon Scott's British Terra Nova party (which arrived c. 17 January 1912 and perished on the return) by roughly five weeks. This is the Race to the Pole, settled by the logs.
place: South Pole, Antarctica — the 1911 marker site (Polheim); longitude undefined at the pole

title: The 'lost city discovered by Bingham, 1911' — the Machu Picchu discovery myth
claim: Machu Picchu was a lost city, unknown to the world until Yale explorer Hiram Bingham III discovered it on 24 July 1911.
place: Machu Picchu ridge, Urubamba Province, Peru

title: The fictional Flannan logbooks and the supernatural explanations
claim: The famous 'dramatic log entries' of the Flannan Isles keepers (12 Dec: severe winds and McArthur crying; 13 Dec: storm still raging, all three praying; 15 Dec: 'Storm ended, sea calm. God is over all') are authentic contemporary records, and the keepers were taken by supernatural means (a sea serpent, the Phantom of the Seven Hunters, arranged escape, or foreign spies).
place: Eilean Mòr, Flannan Isles, Outer Hebrides, Scotland

title: The whole nine yards: attestation (1946-1962)
claim: The phrase 'the whole nine yards' is attested in American print from the mid-20th century: 1946-51 in a Lexington, Kentucky newspaper; July 1956 and January 1957 in Kentucky Happy Hunting Ground (Kentucky Dept. of Fish and Wildlife Resources); 1962 in Michigan's Voices and a Car Life letter. A 1912 Kentucky 'whole six yards' variant shows the number was never fixed — it is a reified-number idiom, not a measurement.
place: Lexington / Kentucky print culture

title: Titanic's wireless room: the distress calls that brought the Carpathia (1912)
claim: On the night of 14-15 April 1912, RMS Titanic's wireless operators Jack Phillips and Harold Bride transmitted distress calls — first Marconi's CQD, then also the international SOS at Bride's suggestion — that reached RMS Carpathia 58 miles away; the Carpathia altered course and rescued the survivors in the lifeboats (705). The disaster led to the Radio Act of 1912 mandating round-the-clock wireless watches aboard ships.
place: North Atlantic, Titanic wreck position (distress position transmitted was ~41°46'N 50°14'W, ~13 miles east of the actual wreck)

title: Death Valley's 134°F (1913) as the reliable world record (disputed)
claim: The highest air temperature ever reliably measured on Earth is 134°F (56.7°C), recorded at Greenland Ranch, Death Valley, California, on 10 July 1913.
place: Greenland Ranch (Furnace Creek), Death Valley, California

title: The Palace Theatre's slow exit from vaudeville, 1927–1952
claim: New York's Palace Theatre (opened 24 March 1913, the flagship of American vaudeville — 'playing the Palace' the industry's pinnacle) played straight vaudeville until July 1932 — five years after The Jazz Singer — then a mixed vaudeville-before-film policy (last vaudeville accompaniment 12 November 1932), converted to a movie palace under RKO, flipped back to vaudeville-before-film on 7 January 1933, alternated formats for two years, showed films almost exclusively 1935–1949, and hosted vaudeville revivals in the 1950s (Judy Garland, 16 October 1951, 19 weeks).
place: Palace Theatre, 160 West 47th Street, New York City

title: The Christmas Truce of 1914
claim: In late December 1914, on the Western Front in Flanders, soldiers of the British Expeditionary Force and the Imperial German Army initiated a series of localized, unofficial truces: singing carols across the lines on Christmas Eve, meeting in no-man's-land on Christmas Day, exchanging gifts and food, posing for photographs together, and organizing joint burial parties for the dead. The truces were not universal (fighting continued in other sectors), were unofficial (high commands disapproved and issued anti-fraternization orders afterward), and made no difference to the war's course.
place: Frelinghien / Messines / Ploegsteert sector, Western Front, French-Belgian border

title: The Christmas Truce Kickabouts (December 1914)
claim: During the Christmas truce of December 1914, in multiple sectors of the Western Front, British and German soldiers engaged in informal football kickabouts in no-man's-land — improvised games with real or makeshift balls (bully-beef tins, straw-stuffed sandbags), caps for goalposts, frozen ground, dozens to hundreds of men joining in, no teams, no officials, no kept score.
place: Western Front, French-Belgian border sectors (Frelinghien, Messines, Ploegsteert among the documented areas)

title: The Legend of the Organized Christmas Truce Football Match
claim: During the Christmas truce of 1914, British and German soldiers played an organized, regulation football fixture — eleven players a side, ninety minutes, officials, a definitive final score — the great Germany-3-2-England 'match' of popular legend.
place: Western Front, Flanders — the legendary fixture is placed variously and vaguely across the truce sectors

title: The Endurance expedition and the all-28-survived rescue — VERIFIED
claim: The Imperial Trans-Antarctic Expedition (1914–1917): the Endurance was beset in the Weddell Sea pack ice in January 1915, abandoned 27 October 1915, and sank 21 November 1915; the 28 men of the Weddell Sea party drifted on ice floes, reached Elephant Island 15 April 1916, and were all — every one of the 28 — brought home alive after Shackleton's James Caird open-boat voyage to South Georgia (24 April–10 May 1916) and the Chilean Yelcho's rescue on 30 August 1916.
place: Endurance wreck site, Weddell Sea (found 5 March 2022 by Endurance22 at ~3,000 m; consistent with the drift account)

title: Gallieni's taxis: the requisition and the run, 6–7 September 1914
claim: On the night of 6–7 September 1914, General Joseph Gallieni, military governor of Paris, requisitioned approximately 600–630 Paris taxis (chiefly Renault AG1 Landaulets, many from the G7 company) to transport roughly 3,000–6,000 soldiers of the French 7th Division (103rd and 104th Infantry Brigades) from Les Invalides to Nanteuil-le-Haudouin (~50 km). The drivers were paid by the meter; the French war ministry put the total bill at about 70,102 francs.
place: Les Invalides, Paris → Nanteuil-le-Haudouin (49.14033, 2.81303), ~50 km

title: The Taxis of the Marne decided the battle and saved Paris (the 'miracle' reading)
claim: The Paris taxis of September 1914 were decisive in the Allied victory at the First Battle of the Marne — the reinforcements they carried saved Paris and decided the battle.
place: Nanteuil-le-Haudouin — where the taxis arrived; the battle's decision happened elsewhere

title: Niemann's 3-2 Game at Frelinghien
claim: Lieutenant Johannes Niemann of the 133rd Saxon Infantry Regiment, opposite Scottish troops (Seaforth or Argyll & Sutherland Highlanders) at Frelinghien, described a football game during the Christmas truce: a Tommy arrived with a football, caps were laid down to mark the goals, the teams organized on the frozen ground, and 'the Fritzes beat the Tommies 3-2' — a real game with a claimed score, attested by one man.
place: Frelinghien, Western Front (opposite the British/Scottish line)

title: The Assassination at Sarajevo (28 June 1914)
claim: On the morning of 28 June 1914, in Sarajevo, Gavrilo Princip — a 19-year-old Bosnian Serb nationalist and one of seven conspirators armed by Serbian military intelligence — shot and killed Archduke Franz Ferdinand of Austria, heir to the Austro-Hungarian throne, and his wife Sophie, Duchess of Hohenberg, when their motorcar stopped on Franz Josef Street in front of Moritz Schiller's delicatessen.
place: Sarajevo — corner of Appel Quay and Franz Josef Street, in front of Moritz Schiller's delicatessen

title: The Sarajevo Motorcade Route and the Wrong Turn (28 June 1914)
claim: Franz Ferdinand's published motorcade route ran along the Appel Quay, with conspirators stationed along it; after Nedeljko Cabrinovic's grenade bounced off the Archduke's car (10-second fuse; it exploded under the following car), the plan changed — the drivers, not briefed on the change, continued on the original route, and at the corner with Franz Josef Street the chauffeur took the wrong turn, corrected on Governor Potiorek's orders, bringing the car to a halt directly in front of Schiller's delicatessen, where Princip was standing outside (having spoken with his friend Mihajlo Pusara) on the original route — the position he should have held all along.
place: Sarajevo — Appel Quay / Franz Josef Street corner

title: Shackleton's 'Men wanted for hazardous journey' advertisement — DEBUNKED
claim: Ernest Shackleton placed a famous newspaper recruitment advertisement for his Antarctic expedition reading: 'Men wanted for hazardous journey. Low wages, bitter cold, long hours of complete darkness. Safe return doubtful. Honour and recognition in event of success.' (Often said to have drawn ~5,000 applications.)
place: London, England — the claimed placement venue (the ad is about this city's newspapers)

title: What Mata Hari's information was actually worth
claim: The intelligence Mata Hari actually transmitted — to Germany, and to France — was of negligible military value: she took German money (autumn 1915, ~20,000 francs, codename H21) and she did work for the French Deuxième Bureau, but no operation, battle, or casualty has ever been documented as a consequence of her information, and the case against her rested substantially on circumstantial and tampered evidence.
place: Madrid, Spain (German embassy station, Major Arnold Kalle) and Paris

title: The Sykes-Picot Agreement, May 1916
claim: In May 1916, Britain and France secretly agreed to partition the Ottoman Arab lands into zones of direct control (blue/French, red/British) and spheres of influence (A/French, B/British), with Palestine as an international (brown) zone — the Sykes-Picot Agreement.
place: The Ottoman Arab provinces (the Levant and Mesopotamia covered by the 1916 map)

title: The claim that Sykes-Picot drew the modern Middle East's borders
claim: The borders of today's Middle Eastern states were drawn by the 1916 Sykes-Picot Agreement — the lines on the modern map are essentially the lines Sykes and Picot drew on their 1916 map.
place: The Ottoman Arab provinces (the Levant and Mesopotamia as partitioned in the 1916 map)

title: Mata Hari: arrest, trial, and execution (1917)
claim: Margaretha Geertruida Zelle (born 7 August 1876, Leeuwarden, Netherlands), performing as the exotic dancer Mata Hari, was arrested in Paris on 13 February 1917 on suspicion of spying for Germany, tried by a French military court on 24 July 1917, convicted, and executed by firing squad at Vincennes on 15 October 1917.
place: Fort de Vincennes, Paris, France

title: Mata Hari the 'master spy' who killed 50,000 men
claim: Mata Hari was a master German spy (agent H21) whose treason caused the deaths of at least 50,000 French soldiers — the charge on which she was convicted at her 24 July 1917 trial.
place: Paris, France (the court-martial)

title: The Mae Dix 'accident' at the National Winter Garden, 1917
claim: In 1917, on a hot night at the Minsky brothers' National Winter Garden on Houston Street, chorus performer Mae Dix walked offstage while still removing her costume — and when the crowd cheered she returned and kept removing it; the Minskys' first raid followed, and the 'accident' became the house's founding striptease legend.
place: National Winter Garden theatre, Houston Street at 2nd Avenue, New York City, USA

title: Zimmermann's admission: 'I cannot deny it. It is true.' (March 1917)
claim: Confronted with the published Zimmermann telegram, Foreign Secretary Arthur Zimmermann publicly admitted it was genuine: at a press conference on 3 March 1917 he told an American journalist, 'I cannot deny it. It is true,' and on 29 March 1917 he admitted it before the Reichstag — ending the Hearst-press and pro-German lobby's forgery defense in a single sentence.
place: Berlin (press conference, then the Reichstag)

title: 'The telegram alone brought America into the war' — the sole-cause myth
claim: The Zimmermann telegram, by itself, brought the United States into World War I — i.e., without the telegram the US would not have declared war in April 1917.
place: Washington, D.C. (Congress, declaration of war)

title: The Zimmermann telegram, 16 January – 1 March 1917
claim: On 16 January 1917 German Foreign Secretary Arthur Zimmermann sent a coded telegram to Heinrich von Eckardt, the German minister in Mexico City, proposing a German-Mexican military alliance in the event the United States entered WWI: 'make war together, make peace together, generous financial support and understanding on our part that Mexico is to reconquer the lost territory in Texas, New Mexico and Arizona.' It also announced the 1 February resumption of unrestricted submarine warfare and instructed Eckardt to invite Japan to adhere via the Mexican president. The British Admiralty's Room 40 intercepted and decoded it on 17 January 1917 (Nigel de Grey, with William Montgomery; German diplomatic code 13040). After a cover story that it had been 'stolen in deciphered form in Mexico,' the text was published 1 March 1917.
place: Berlin (origin) → intercepted at Room 40, London (51.50, -0.13) → delivered to Eckardt, Mexico City (19.43, -99.13)

title: Sundback's Separable Fastener (1917) — the modern zipper
claim: Gideon Sundback's 1917 'Separable Fastener' (US patent 1,219,881) — the interlocking-tooth slide fastener with slider — is the modern zipper: the first cheap, reliable, mass-producible design.
place: Meadville, Pennsylvania (Hookless Fastener Company; Talon from 1937)

title: The 'female Cher Ami' myth (DEBUNKED by 2021 DNA)
claim: Cher Ami, the famous WWI homing pigeon, was female (a hen).
place: Smithsonian National Museum of American History, Washington D.C. (where the bird is displayed)

title: Cher Ami's flight for the Lost Battalion (4 October 1918)
claim: On 4 October 1918, the homing pigeon Cher Ami carried Major Whittlesey's message from the surrounded Lost Battalion 25 miles to division headquarters in 25 minutes, despite being shot through the breast, blinded in one eye, and nearly losing the leg carrying the message — and the message halted the friendly-artillery barrage, contributing to the relief of the battalion's survivors.
place: Argonne Forest, France (Charlevaux ravine to division HQ)

title: The Smithsonian's claim that Langley's 1903 Aerodrome was the first flight-capable man-carrying aircraft
claim: That the Smithsonian Institution was correct (1918-1942) to display Langley's Great Aerodrome as the first man-carrying aeroplane capable of free flight — i.e., that Langley's 1903 machine, as Langley built and launched it, had been demonstrated capable of sustained powered flight before the Wrights' December 1903 flights.
place: Smithsonian Institution, Washington, D.C. (site of the 1918-1942 display and the 1942 retraction)

title: The 19th Amendment ratified, August 1920
claim: The Nineteenth Amendment to the United States Constitution — 'The right of citizens of the United States to vote shall not be denied or abridged by the United States or by any State on account of sex' — passed the Senate on 4 June 1919 (56–25), was ratified by Tennessee as the 36th state on 18 August 1920 (the House carried it by a single vote, 49–47, after 24-year-old Rep. Harry T. Burn switched at his mother Febb Burn's urging), and was certified in effect on 26 August 1920 by Secretary of State Bainbridge Colby.
place: Nashville, Tennessee (state capitol; final ratifying vote)

title: The first artificial transmutation — Rutherford 1919
claim: In 1919 Ernest Rutherford achieved the first artificial transmutation of one element into another: bombarding nitrogen-14 with alpha particles produced oxygen-17 and a proton (alpha + 14N -> 17O + p) — the experiment that actually did what the alchemists had promised for sixteen centuries.
place: University of Manchester, England — the 1917-19 alpha-bombardment experiments

title: The tribunal dockets as measured denominator
claim: When a regime loses a war intact and its archives are seized whole, the denominator is measured, not guessed. The Nuremberg IMT published 42 volumes of transcript with prosecution document books built from the regime's own captured files; the Tokyo IMTFE left ~48,000 pages of transcript; the victor's archivists catalogued what the defeated had filed while they expected to win. Against that measured baseline, systematic silence reads as VIII.f-pattern: what a regime documented when it thought it would never answer for it is the expectation, and the gaps are the evidence. The Constantinople courts-martial of 1919–20 are the counter-exhibit: the empire that tried the Armenian massacres dissolved, its archives scattered across three continents, and the baseline there stays a guess — VIII.d retains jurisdiction. The tribunal dockets are the VIII.g rule's regime-baseline measured at full strength.
place: Nuremberg, Palace of Justice (regime-baseline exhibit); Constantinople (scattered-baseline exhibit)

title: Versailles Article 231 — the clause itself
claim: Article 231 of the Treaty of Versailles (signed 28 June 1919; Part VIII, Section I, 'Reparation — General Provisions') is the opening clause of the treaty's reparations section. Its text: 'The Allied and Associated Governments affirm and Germany accepts the responsibility of Germany and her allies for causing all the loss and damage to which the Allied and Associated Governments and their nationals have been subjected as a consequence of the war imposed upon them by the aggression of Germany and her allies.' The clause contains no word 'guilt'; it names 'Germany and her allies' (not Germany alone); and it sits immediately above Article 232, which recognizes that Germany's resources are inadequate for complete reparation — i.e. Article 231 establishes legal liability while Article 232 limits the financial obligation.
place: Palace of Versailles, Versailles, France

title: The Treaty of Versailles (1919)
claim: A peace treaty between Germany and the Allied and Associated Powers, signed in the Hall of Mirrors at Versailles on 28 June 1919 and entering into force on 10 January 1920, imposing territorial, military, economic, and reparations terms.
place: Hall of Mirrors, Palace of Versailles

title: The 'war guilt clause' reading of Article 231 (myth)
claim: Article 231 of the Treaty of Versailles assigned sole moral blame ('war guilt') to Germany alone for World War I.
place: Hall of Mirrors, Palace of Versailles

title: The 'war guilt clause' reading of Versailles Article 231
claim: Article 231 of the Treaty of Versailles — commonly called the 'war guilt clause' — formally required Germany to confess sole moral guilt for starting World War I.
place: Quai d'Orsay, Paris, France (Paris Peace Conference drafting)

title: The 'all women got the vote in 1920' reading
claim: The 19th Amendment gave all American women the right to vote in 1920 — the universal version of the suffrage victory story.
place: United States (national scope)

title: The Coso artifact (500,000-year-old spark plug claim)
claim: The Coso artifact — a device found inside a 500,000-year-old geode at Olancha, California, in 1961 — is an ancient or advanced-technology object (Atlantis, ancient astronauts, time travelers).
place: Olancha, California (reported find site)

title: The Great Wall visible from the Moon / from space with the naked eye
claim: The Great Wall of China is visible with the naked eye from the Moon — and/or is the only man-made structure visible from space with the naked eye.
place: The claim is about the Wall seen from afar; pin carried as Badaling representative section

title: 'KDKA made the first radio broadcast' (2 Nov 1920) — DEBUNKED
claim: Pittsburgh's KDKA made the first radio broadcast in history on 2 November 1920, when it transmitted the Harding-Cox presidential election returns.
place: East Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania (Westinghouse plant shack)

title: The 1920-1926 settlement that actually drew the Middle East's borders
claim: The Middle East's modern state borders were drawn by the 1920-1926 settlement — the San Remo Conference (April 1920) assigning the League of Nations mandates (British Palestine and Mesopotamia; French Syria and Lebanon), the Treaty of Sevres (August 1920, superseded), the Cairo Conference (1921), the Treaty of Ankara (1921) fixing the Franco-Turkish frontier, the Treaty of Lausanne (July 1923) fixing Turkey's borders, and the 1926 Mosul settlement attaching the vilayet of Mosul to Iraq — not by the 1916 Sykes-Picot map.
place: The post-Ottoman Middle East (the Levant, Mesopotamia, and Anatolia's frontier)

title: The Vinland Map as a pre-Columbian artifact
claim: The Vinland Map is a genuine 15th-century map depicting Norse exploration of North America (Vinland) before Columbus.
place: Beinecke Rare Book & Manuscript Library, Yale University, New Haven, Connecticut (current holding)

title: The 1921 Nobel Prize (photoelectric effect, not relativity)
claim: Albert Einstein's 1921 Nobel Prize in Physics was awarded 'for his services to Theoretical Physics, and especially for his discovery of the law of the photoelectric effect' — not for the theory of relativity.
place: Stockholm (the award)

title: The 'Nobel for relativity' myth
claim: Albert Einstein won the Nobel Prize in Physics for his theory of relativity.
place: Stockholm (the award); myth carried globally

title: The name 'zipper' (B.F. Goodrich, 1923)
claim: The B.F. Goodrich Company coined the name 'zipper' in 1923, applying Sundback's fastener to rubber galoshes: the 'Mystik Boot' was renamed the 'Zipper Boot,' and the name — from the 'zip' sound of the slider — stuck to the fastener itself.
place: Akron, Ohio (B.F. Goodrich)

title: 'Marie Lloyd died on stage' — the compressed ending, corrected
claim: Marie Lloyd, the 'Queen of the Music Hall,' died on stage in 1922 — she collapsed and died before an audience, the great performer dying in harness on the boards.
place: London, England (the telling's location; the real death was at home, not on stage)

title: Marie Lloyd's final week, 4–7 October 1922
claim: In the first week of October 1922 Marie Lloyd — the 'Queen of the Music Hall' — gave her last performances: on 4 October, against her doctor's advice, she appeared at the Empire Music Hall, Edmonton, North London, sang 'I'm One of the Ruins That Cromwell Knocked About a Bit', was unsteady and fell over on stage while the audience laughed, believing it part of the act; on 7 October she was taken ill on stage at the Alhambra Theatre and found in her dressing room crippled with pain and stomach cramps; she returned home that evening, where she died of heart and kidney failure, aged 52.
place: Empire Music Hall, Edmonton, North London, England

title: Alliance Rubber (1923): the rubber band's mass-production era
claim: William H. Spencer founded the Alliance Rubber Company on 7 March 1923 in Alliance, Ohio — buying rejected Goodyear inner tubes at auction in Akron, cutting them by hand into rubber bands in a boarding-house garage, and persuading the Akron Beacon Journal to wrap its newspapers with bands so they would not come apart and blow across lawns. Spencer moonlighted with the Pennsylvania Railroad for 14 years; in 1937 the company began extruding its own tubing; a second plant opened in Hot Springs, Arkansas, in 1944. The company remains family-owned (president Bonnie Spencer Swayze, the founder's daughter).
place: Alliance, Ohio — the boarding-house garage; later Hot Springs, Arkansas

title: Phonofilm (1923) - sound-on-film reaches the theaters
claim: Lee de Forest's Phonofilms (1923-1924) were commercial theatrical sound-on-film shorts - vaudeville acts, singers, comedians, and Max Fleischer cartoons - using Theodore Case and Earl Sponable's optical sound system; by 1924, 20 Phonofilm outfits were giving roadshows in theaters.
place: New York City theatrical roadshows (city precision)

title: Don Juan (1926) - the first feature with a synchronized soundtrack
claim: Don Juan (1926), starring John Barrymore, premiered on 6 August 1926 at Warner's Theatre, New York, as the first feature-length film released with a synchronized soundtrack - a Vitaphone sound-on-disc musical score and sound effects, with English intertitles and no spoken dialogue.
place: Warner's Theatre, Times Square, New York City (approximate venue pin)

title: The Einstein–Szilard refrigerator (VERIFIED)
claim: Albert Einstein co-invented a refrigerator with Leó Szilárd in 1926 — an absorption machine with no moving parts, US patent 1,781,541 granted 11 November 1930.
place: Berlin, Germany

title: The Vitaphone–Movietone format war (1926–1931)
claim: Sound-on-film (Fox-Case Movietone, then RCA Photophone) defeated sound-on-disc (Western Electric's Vitaphone) in a competitive 'format war' for the talkie market — a contest of corporate licensing systems as much as of engineering, fought 1926–1931.
place: Hollywood / New York — the studio-and-laboratory corridor (Warner Bros. Burbank, Western Electric, Fox, RCA)

title: The 'overnight' Vitaphone death (1928–1929) — a compression debunked
claim: The common shorthand that Hollywood abandoned sound-on-disc 'overnight' as soon as sound-on-film proved itself (1928–1929) — the instant format-war ending.
place: Hollywood / New York — the studio-and-laboratory corridor

title: Farnsworth's first all-electronic TV transmission (7 Sept 1927)
claim: On 7 September 1927, at his laboratory at 202 Green Street, San Francisco, 21-year-old Philo Farnsworth transmitted the first all-electronic television image: his image-dissector camera aimed at a glass slide with a single painted line, the line appearing live on a cathode-ray-tube receiver in the next room — and rotating when the slide was rotated.
place: 202 Green Street, San Francisco, California

title: 'The Jazz Singer was the first sound film'
claim: The Jazz Singer (1927) was the first motion picture with synchronized sound - that no film before October 1927 carried synchronized sound of any kind.
place: Warner's Theater, Times Square, New York City (the premiere that owns the myth)

title: The Jazz Singer premieres — the talkie era's conventional start
claim: The Jazz Singer premiered on 6 October 1927 at Warner's Theater, New York City, as the first feature-length film with sequences of synchronized spoken dialogue (Vitaphone sound-on-disc) — the conventional marker of the talkie era's beginning.
place: Warner's Theater, Times Square, New York City (approximate venue pin)

title: The 'talkies killed vaudeville overnight' myth
claim: The arrival of the talkies (synchronized-sound film, from The Jazz Singer's October 1927 premiere) killed American vaudeville overnight — that live vaudeville effectively ended in 1927–1928.
place: Palace Theatre, New York City (venue of the five-year evidence gap)

title: US Business Reply Mail introduced in 1928
claim: The U.S. Post Office Department introduced Business Reply Mail (together with bulk mail) in 1928: a permit system under which a mailer distributes reply cards, envelopes, self-mailers, cartons, or labels pre-printed with the 'BUSINESS REPLY MAIL' legend, a permit imprint, and a unique ZIP+4; the customer returns them with no postage affixed, and the permit holder pays postage plus a per-piece fee only on the pieces actually returned. The 1928 introduction is attested in the Winton M. Blount Postal History Symposium presentation by Diane DeBlois and Robert Dalton Harris (Smithsonian National Postal Museum, 8 December 2022): 'Business Reply & Bulk Mail introduced 1928.'
place: Washington, D.C. — U.S. Post Office Department

title: The Italia airship disaster, 25 May – 12 July 1928
claim: On 25 May 1928, the Italian N-class semi-rigid airship Italia (N-4, designed by Umberto Nobile) crashed on the Arctic pack ice northeast of Svalbard while returning from the North Pole. The control car was smashed open and torn from the keel; nine survivors and one dead crewman were left on the ice, while the envelope rose again with six men aboard and was never found. The survivors dyed their 2.4×2.4 m silk tent red for visibility, radio operator Giuseppe Biagi transmitted SOS from 25 May, the signal was picked up on 3 June by a 21-year-old Soviet radio amateur (Nikolai Schmidt, Vokhma, on a home-made receiver), and after 48 days on the ice the remaining survivors were rescued — Nobile by the Swedish pilot Einar Lundborg on 23 June, the rest by the Soviet icebreaker Krasin on 12 July. Roald Amundsen disappeared on 18 June in the French Latham 47 while flying to join the rescue. Seventeen people died (crew and rescuers); eight survived.
place: Arctic pack ice ~120 km northeast of Nordaustlandet, Svalbard (crash site; the ice drifted during the 48 days on it)

title: 'No postage necessary' means free — DEBUNKED
claim: The legend 'NO POSTAGE NECESSARY' on business reply mail means the mail travels free — that nobody pays for the postage. This is false. In the United States, the USPS Domestic Mail Manual (DMM 505) requires the BRM permit holder to guarantee payment of the applicable First-Class or Priority Mail postage, plus a per-piece fee, on ALL returned BRM — including incomplete, blank, or empty cards and envelopes — and to pay an annual permit fee. Under Royal Mail's Business Reply and Freepost services the licensee is billed per returned item (Freepost Standard/Plus, Business Reply Standard/Plus, Freepost Name licences). The Dutch antwoordnummer system bills the recipient the costs plus a fee; New Zealand freepost bills only when the permit number and recipient address match. In every system, 'no postage necessary' is a sender-facing instruction about affixing stamps, not a statement about who pays.
place: United States (USPS system; Royal Mail, Dutch PostNL, NZ Post analogues cited)

title: The 'Nobile abandoned his men' charge, 1928 (myth)
claim: Umberto Nobile cowardly abandoned his men in June 1928 by having himself rescued first from the Italia crash site — deserting them on the ice.
place: The Red Tent crash site, Arctic pack ice northeast of Svalbard (where the rescue priority was decided)

title: The Parry-Lord oral-formulaic thesis: the song before the book
claim: The Homeric epics were composed in the oral tradition using a system of traditional formulae — poems tens of thousands of lines long made without writing.
place: Yugoslavia (Bosnia) — the 1933–1935 Parry–Lord fieldwork with the guslars

title: The 1929 crash (Black Thursday to Black Tuesday)
claim: In late October 1929 the New York stock market collapsed in a run of record selling days — Black Thursday (24 October) and Black Tuesday (29 October) — driven by forced selling of margin positions, wiping out much of the decade's paper gains and opening the financial chapter of the Great Depression.
place: New York Stock Exchange, 11 Wall Street, New York City

title: The Wall Street suicide wave of 1929 (myth)
claim: The popular image of a mass epidemic of ruined Wall Street brokers and speculators throwing themselves from office windows in the days and weeks after the October 1929 crash.
place: Wall Street financial district, Manhattan, New York City (geography of the claim)

title: The Salt March (Dandi March), March–April 1930
claim: From 12 March to 6 April 1930, M.K. Gandhi led 78 volunteers on a 240-mile (387 km) march from Sabarmati Ashram to Dandi, Gujarat, where on the morning of 6 April he broke the British salt laws by making salt from seawater — inaugurating the Civil Disobedience Movement; the ensuing satyagraha saw 60,000+ Indians jailed.
place: Dandi, Gujarat, India (march terminus; route Sabarmati Ashram, Ahmedabad → Dandi)

title: 'The Salt March ended the salt tax' — the seventeen-year gap
claim: Mahatma Gandhi's 1930 Salt March ended the British salt tax in India — the tax was abolished as a result of the march.
place: Dandi, Gujarat, India (where the reading locates the victory)

title: Dord, the ghost word (1934–1947): the dictionary that printed a word that never existed
claim: For thirteen years (1934–1947), Webster's New International Dictionary, Second Edition, contained the word 'dord' — a ghost word, a non-word accidentally created when a chemistry editor's 3x5 slip reading 'D or d, cont./density.' was misread as the single word 'dord' (headwords were typed with spaces between letters). It appeared on page 771 defined as a noun meaning 'density' in physics and chemistry; an editor caught it on 28 February 1939, and it was excised in 1947.
place: Springfield, Massachusetts (G. and C. Merriam Company)

title: The workers entombed in Hoover Dam's concrete
claim: Construction workers who fell into wet concrete during Hoover Dam's construction (1931-1936) were left there, entombed in the dam's structure.
place: Hoover Dam, Black Canyon, Arizona-Nevada border

title: Hoover Dam built, 1931-1936
claim: Hoover Dam (authorized as Boulder Dam) was built in Black Canyon on the Arizona-Nevada border by Six Companies, Inc. under a 1931 contract: roughly 3.25 million cubic yards of concrete poured in interlocking blocks, dedicated by President Franklin D. Roosevelt on 30 September 1935, completed 1936; 96 workers died during construction per the official count.
place: Hoover Dam, Black Canyon, Arizona-Nevada border

title: The Vitaphone disc's afterlife (1931–mid-1930s)
claim: After the format war, sound-on-disc lived on as an exhibition medium: Warner Bros. recorded and edited optically from mid-1931 but dubbed the finished soundtracks to discs for theaters with Vitaphone projection equipment, and most Hollywood studios pressed dubbed disc sets for disc-only houses into the mid-1930s.
place: United States exhibition circuit — the disc-only small-town and late-converting houses

title: The Polish break of Enigma (1932) and the Pyry transfer (1939)
claim: In December 1932 (between Christmas and New Year, per Rejewski's account), Marian Rejewski of the Polish Cipher Bureau (Biuro Szyfrow) reconstructed the internal wiring of the German military Enigma machine using permutation theory plus German cipher documents obtained by French intelligence (Captain Gustave Bertrand's source inside the German cipher office, Hans-Thilo Schmidt, 'Asche'). With Jerzy Rozycki and Henryk Zygalski, the Poles then read German military Enigma traffic daily from ~January 1933, building the cyclometer, Zygalski's perforated sheets, and the electromechanical bomba kryptologiczna (Nov 1938). On 25 July 1939 at Pyry, south of Warsaw — five weeks before WWII — Poland handed Britain (Alastair Denniston, Alfred Dillwyn Knox, Humphrey Sandwith) and France (Bertrand, Braquenie) the full documentation, the cryptanalytic machines, and Enigma replicas. Britain, which had concluded Enigma unbreakable and made zero pre-war progress, began reading Enigma within months of the war's outbreak, on Polish foundations.
place: Pyry, south of Warsaw (Biuro Szyfrow facility); Warsaw

title: DEBUNKED: 'Alan Turing single-handedly broke the Enigma'
claim: The popular version — most concentrated in the 2014 Oscar-nominated film 'The Imitation Game' — that Alan Turing single-handedly broke the Enigma code is false. The military Enigma was first broken by Marian Rejewski and the Polish Cipher Bureau in December 1932 — seven years before Bletchley Park's wartime program began — and Poland handed Britain the complete solution (documentation, machines, replicas) at Pyry on 25 July 1939, when Britain had made zero pre-war progress. Turing's genuine, major contributions — the Bombe (built with Gordon Welchman's diagonal board), Banburismus, and the breaking of naval Enigma (Shark) — belong to the wartime industrial phase of a break that already existed. Colossus (the Lorenz-cipher machine) belongs to Bill Tutte, Max Newman, and Tommy Flowers, not Turing. Twenty-ninth DEBUNKED family.
place: Bletchley Park, UK (where the myth is set); Warsaw/Pyry (where the break happened)

title: The Akron rubber workers' sit-downs (1934–36) — the tactic Flint inherited
claim: In early 1936, Akron, Ohio's rubber workers carried out some of the first major sit-down strikes in the United States — the tactic pioneered at General Tire in 1934, used at Firestone in January 1936 and Goodyear in February 1936 — proving the tactic and making the Flint sit-down possible.
place: Akron, Ohio — the rubber plants

title: The RCA–Farnsworth patent interference (1934–1939)
claim: In 1934 the Radio Corporation of America brought patent interference proceedings (Interference No. 64,027) against Philo Farnsworth's television patents, asserting Vladimir Zworykin's priority; the U.S. Patent Office decided the interference for Farnsworth in February 1935, RCA's 1936 appeal failed, and in 1939 RCA took a license to Farnsworth's patents — paying him about $1 million in royalties — before launching television to the public at the New York World's Fair.
place: Washington, D.C. (U.S. Patent Office, Interference No. 64,027)

title: 'YKK invented the zipper' — the manufacturer, not the inventor (DEBUNKED)
claim: The Japanese company YKK — the letters stamped on most of the world's zippers — invented the zipper. The documents say otherwise: YKK (Yoshida Kogyo K.K.) was founded January 1, 1934 by Tadao Yoshida in Tokyo as a zipper MANUFACTURER, seventeen years after Sundback's 1917 separable-fastener patent and eleven years after Goodrich coined the name. YKK overtook the inventor's own company (Talon, the former Hookless Fastener Co.) for the American market in the 1970s-80s; it conquered zipper MANUFACTURE, not zipper INVENTION.
place: Tokyo, Japan (YKK headquarters; founded in Nihonbashi, Tokyo)

title: The 1937 New York City burlesque license-kill
claim: In April 1937, a police raid on Abe Minsky's New Gotham Theater in Harlem — a stripper caught working without a G-string — gave New York City License Commissioner Paul Moss the criminal conviction he needed, and he then refused to renew the licenses of all of New York City's burlesque theaters, driving them to close.
place: New York City, USA (the burlesque houses; the April 1937 raid at the New Gotham Theater, Harlem)

title: The 'Invented Once, in the Fertile Crescent' Claim
claim: Agriculture was invented exactly once in human history — in the Fertile Crescent — and then spread outward from that single origin to every other farming society in the world.
place: The Fertile Crescent (the claimed single hearth)

title: The Berlin Olympic Games, 1936
claim: The Games of the XI Olympiad were held in Berlin 1–16 August 1936, with 3,963 athletes from 49 nations; American sprinter Jesse Owens won four gold medals — 100 metres, 200 metres, long jump, and 4x100 metre relay — in Adolf Hitler's Berlin.
place: Olympiastadion, Berlin, Germany

title: The Dvorak-superiority claim
claim: The Dvorak Simplified Keyboard is scientifically proven to be faster than QWERTY, and QWERTY's survival is therefore proof of an inefficient market lock-in.
place: Washington, DC (US Patent Office, 1936 patent; Navy and GSA studies)

title: The Flint sit-down strike (1936–37) — the 44 days that unionized the auto industry
claim: The Flint sit-down strike — autoworkers occupying General Motors' Fisher Body plants in Flint, Michigan — ran from 30 December 1936 to 11 February 1937 (44 days), and ended with GM formally recognizing the United Automobile Workers as the collective bargaining representative, the victory that unionized the American auto industry.
place: Flint, Michigan — the Fisher Body plants

title: The Hitler–Owens 'Snub' at Berlin 1936
claim: Adolf Hitler personally snubbed Jesse Owens at the 1936 Berlin Olympics — deliberately refusing to meet, greet, or congratulate him because he was Black.
place: Olympiastadion, Berlin, Germany

title: The '10% of the brain' myth
claim: Human beings use only 10 percent of their brains; 90 percent of the brain's tissue is unused and available to be unlocked.
place: Cambridge, Massachusetts (Harvard — James's lecture halls; Thomas's attribution point)

title: Han van Meegeren's forged Vermeers
claim: Between 1936 and 1943 the Dutch painter Han van Meegeren (1889–1947) produced a series of forged 'Vermeer' paintings — including The Supper at Emmaus (1936–37) and Christ with the Woman Taken in Adultery (1941–42) — on genuine 17th-century canvases, using period pigments hardened with 20th-century phenol-formaldehyde resin, and sold them as rediscovered Vermeers.
place: Amsterdam, Netherlands (arrest, demonstration painting, trial)

title: The Atanasoff–Berry Computer (1937–1942)
claim: The Atanasoff–Berry Computer (ABC), built by John Vincent Atanasoff and Clifford Berry in the basement of the physics building at Iowa State College (1937–1942), was a working electronic digital computer — binary arithmetic, vacuum-tube switching, regenerative capacitive memory kept separate from computation — and the documented prior art from which the ENIAC inventors derived the automatic electronic digital computer. John Mauchly visited Ames for five days in June 1941 as Atanasoff's houseguest, studied the machine in detail with the schematics, and helped Berry work on it.
place: Basement of the physics building, Iowa State College, Ames, Iowa

title: 'La Guardia's 1937 ban killed burlesque'
claim: La Guardia's 1937 action against burlesque was a ban that killed burlesque — the form died in 1937.
place: New York City, USA (the telling's home address; the form survived elsewhere)

title: The Supper at Emmaus as a genuine Vermeer
claim: The Supper at Emmaus — bought by Museum Boijmans (Rotterdam) in 1937 for 520,000 guilders after Abraham Bredius authenticated it in The Burlington Magazine as 'the masterpiece of Johannes Vermeer of Delft' — is a genuine painting by Johannes Vermeer (1632–1675).
place: Rotterdam, Netherlands (Museum Boijmans Van Beuningen)

title: The Roman-chariot-rut origin of standard gauge — DEBUNKED
claim: The world's standard railroad gauge of 1,435 mm (4 ft 8 1/2 in) descends from the ruts left by Roman chariots and war wagons — the story that George Stephenson's gauge, and the whole modern railway system, preserves the Roman wheel standard through two millennia of road vehicles that kept running in the same ruts.

title: The nylon toothbrush (1938) — the end of animal bristles
claim: In 1938, DuPont introduced the first toothbrush with synthetic nylon bristles (Dr. West's Miracle-Tuft Toothbrush), ending the centuries-long dependence on animal-hair bristles.
place: Wilmington, Delaware, USA (DuPont)

title: The Molotov-Ribbentrop Pact (23 August 1939)
claim: The German-Soviet Nonaggression Pact — the Molotov-Ribbentrop Pact — was signed in Moscow on 23 August 1939 by German Foreign Minister Joachim von Ribbentrop and Soviet Foreign Minister Vyacheslav Molotov, with Stalin present, committing both parties to ten years of nonaggression.
place: Moscow, Kremlin

title: 'RCA invented television' (the Sarnoff claim)
claim: Electronic television was invented by RCA — David Sarnoff's Radio Corporation of America — and specifically by RCA's engineer Vladimir Zworykin, the 'father of television'; the independent inventor Philo Farnsworth contributed nothing original to electronic TV.
place: Flushing Meadows, Queens, New York (1939 World's Fair RCA pavilion)

title: The Secret Additional Protocol (23 August 1939)
claim: On 23 August 1939, alongside the public Molotov-Ribbentrop Pact, Ribbentrop and Molotov signed a Secret Additional Protocol dividing Eastern Europe into German and Soviet spheres of influence: the Baltic states (Finland, Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania) with Lithuania's northern boundary as the sphere line; Poland along the Narew-Vistula-San rivers; and Bessarabia noted as a Soviet interest — the document to be treated as 'strictly secret'.
place: Moscow, Kremlin (applies to Eastern Europe as the mapped region)

title: The fifty-year denial of the secret protocol (1939-1989)
claim: The secret protocol of 23 August 1939 never existed — it was a Western forgery, and the Soviet Union's official position denying its existence (maintained from 1939 to 1989) was correct.
place: Moscow (the denial's issuing authority)

title: Aeroelastic flutter: the mechanism that killed Galloping Gertie
claim: The destructive final oscillation of the Tacoma Narrows Bridge on 7 November 1940 was aeroelastic flutter: the slender 8-foot plate-girder deck, displaced by the wind, shed motion-induced vortices whose aerodynamic forces fed energy back into the twist — a self-excited oscillation with effectively negative damping, in a fundamental antisymmetric torsion mode that had not manifested until ~45 minutes before the collapse. The wind (42 mph) was far in excess of the velocity required for incipient flutter.
place: Tacoma Narrows, Washington, USA

title: The Katyn Forest massacre, April-May 1940
claim: In April-May 1940 the NKVD shot approximately 21,857 Polish prisoners - officers, police, and intelligentsia held in the Kozelsk, Starobelsk and Ostashkov camps and in prisons of western Ukraine and Belarus - pursuant to Lavrenty Beria's 5 March 1940 memorandum (No. 794/B) and the Politburo's same-day shooting order (protocol No. 13); burials at Katyn forest (4,421), Kharkov (3,820), Kalinin/Mednoye (6,311), and Ukraine/Belarus prisons (7,305).
place: Katyn forest district, near Smolensk, Russia

title: The paper clip as Norway's WWII resistance symbol
claim: During the German occupation of Norway (1940–1945), Norwegians wore paper clips on their lapels as a quiet symbol of national unity and non-violent resistance — beginning with students at Oslo University in autumn 1940 after the occupiers banned buttons and badges bearing the exiled King Haakon VII's initials.
place: Oslo, Norway (Oslo University; the reported origin point)

title: The Tacoma Narrows Bridge collapses (7 November 1940)
claim: The first Tacoma Narrows suspension bridge ('Galloping Gertie'), opened 1 July 1940, collapsed into Puget Sound on the morning of 7 November 1940 after violent torsional oscillations in ~42 mph winds; the center span fell around 11:00–11:10 AM. No people died; the only casualty was Tubby, a cocker spaniel left in a car on the deck. The collapse was filmed (Barney Elliott, Harbine Monroe) and studied by a Federal Works Agency commission in 1941.
place: Tacoma Narrows, Washington, USA

title: The Tacoma Narrows 'resonance' explanation (the textbook myth)
claim: The Tacoma Narrows Bridge collapsed on 7 November 1940 because the wind's frequency matched the bridge's natural resonant frequency — i.e., the cause was externally forced mechanical resonance, the textbook 'swing-pushed-at-the-right-moment' story.
place: Tacoma Narrows, Washington, USA

title: The 1941 flight-strip program (CORROBORATED)
claim: The Defense Highway Act of 1941, Section 108, created a flight-strip program: the Army Air Force and the Public Roads Administration operated landing strips near (not on) highways for military use — the documented historical root from which the Interstate landing-strip myth grew.
place: United States (flight strips near the wartime highway network)

title: De Mestral invents the hook-and-loop fastener (1941–1954)
claim: Swiss engineer George de Mestral conceived the hook-and-loop fastener in 1941 after burdock burrs clung to his clothes and his dog's fur and he studied them under a microscope; after years of development he filed for Swiss patent protection in 1951 (first Swiss patent issued 16 March 1954), and named the product Velcro from the French 'velours' (velvet) + 'crochet' (hook).
place: Switzerland (Swiss Alps walk; Swiss patent jurisdiction)

title: The 'Alexander son of Simon' ossuary (1941 Kidron find; the Simon-of-Cyrene identification pressed October 2026)
claim: A limestone ossuary discovered in a Jerusalem (Kidron Valley) tomb in 1941 carries the inscriptions 'Alexander' and 'Simon' — including 'Alexander, son of Simon' — with a lid inscription read by some as 'QRNYT' (Cyrene). Biblical Archaeology Review contributor Tom Powers (2003) and onomastics specialist Tal Ilan argued the names match Mark 15:21's Simon of Cyrene and his son Alexander; in October 2026 press coverage, New Testament scholar Jeremiah Johnston called the Simon-of-Cyrene-family identification 'very plausible, if not likely' — 'high probability' — while cautioning that Simon was the most common Jewish name of the period, Alexander common too, the Cyrene reading disputed, and no Rufus ossuary among the tomb's eleven boxes. The 1941 ossuary is a documented artifact; the Simon-of-Cyrene identification is a scholarly hypothesis, not a provenance.
place: Kidron Valley tomb, Jerusalem (1941 find; approximate)

title: The curse of Tamerlane: opening the tomb in June 1941 unleashed the invasion of the USSR
claim: Opening Timur's tomb in June 1941 released a supernatural curse — announced by the inscribed warning 'whomsoever opens my tomb shall unleash an invader more terrible than I' — that caused Nazi Germany's invasion of the Soviet Union (Operation Barbarossa) on 22 June 1941; the curse was lifted when Timur was reburied in November 1942, before Stalingrad.
place: Gur-e Amir mausoleum, Samarkand, Uzbekistan (the legend's scene)

title: The 1941 Soviet exhumation of Timur's tomb at the Gur-e Amir (Samarkand)
claim: In June 1941, a Stalin-ordered Soviet scientific expedition led by anthropologist Mikhail Gerasimov opened Timur's tomb at the Gur-e Amir mausoleum in Samarkand, examined his remains, and — after confirming key details of his appearance and injuries — reburied him with Islamic rites in November 1942.
place: Gur-e Amir mausoleum, Samarkand, Uzbekistan

title: The Soviet attribution of Katyn to Nazi Germany (1944-1990)
claim: The Katyn Forest massacre of Polish officers in 1940 was committed by Nazi Germany in the fall of 1941 - the Soviet state's official position from 1943 to 1990, established by the Burdenko Commission (January 1944) and carried into the Nuremberg indictment.
place: Katyn forest district, near Smolensk, Russia

title: The Venona Project
claim: From 1 February 1943 to 1 October 1980, the US Army's Signal Intelligence Service (later the NSA) ran a counterintelligence program at Arlington Hall that decrypted and translated approximately 2,900–3,000 Soviet intelligence cables (NKVD/KGB/GRU, mostly 1942–1946), revealing extensive Soviet espionage in the United States during and after World War II. The decrypts were declassified and publicly released beginning 11 July 1995.
place: Arlington Hall, Virginia (project headquarters)

title: DEBUNKED: 'ENIAC was the first electronic computer'
claim: The claim that ENIAC (Electronic Numerical Integrator and Computer) was the first electronic computer is false. The invention of the automatic electronic digital computer was legally assigned by a federal court to John Vincent Atanasoff, whose Atanasoff–Berry Computer predates ENIAC by years; John Mauchly examined Atanasoff's machine in detail during a five-day visit to Ames, Iowa, in June 1941, three years before ENIAC's construction began. Seventy-third DEBUNKED family.
place: Moore School of Electrical Engineering, University of Pennsylvania, Philadelphia (where the claim was built); U.S. District Court, Minneapolis (where it was unmade)

title: TELLING (DEBUNKED): the whole nine yards = WWII ammo belt
claim: TELLING (DEBUNKED): 'The whole nine yards' comes from the length of a World War II fighter plane's machine-gun ammunition belt — nine yards of belt, hence 'give 'em the whole nine yards.'
place: Kentucky print culture (where the phrase is documented)

title: The cryptonym caveat
claim: A decrypted Venona cable names a person. The NSA's cryptanalysts assigned real names to the Soviet cryptonyms, and the identifications are settled. (The methodological caveat every historian of Venona must carry: the transcripts identify about 349 Americans with a covert relationship to Soviet intelligence, but fewer than half have been matched to real-name identities; the cryptonym-to-person match is a method, not a conviction.)
place: Arlington Hall, Virginia (the identifications' working room)

title: The 'peaceful handover' myth of decolonization
claim: The European empires ended peacefully — independence was granted by the colonizers rather than taken by the colonized, without war or systematic violence on the colonizers' part.
place: Cape Town, South Africa (the 'Wind of Change' speech, 3 Feb 1960 — the myth's emblematic telling; the claim itself spans the decolonizing world, 1947-1990)

title: The withheld 1948 Peace Prize (Gandhi)
claim: The Nobel Peace Prize was not awarded in 1948, the year Mohandas Gandhi was assassinated (30 January 1948); the Norwegian Nobel Committee stated that 'there was no suitable living candidate.' The non-award is understood as the withheld Gandhi prize — posthumous award was possible at the time (Dag Hammarskjold received the 1961 Peace Prize posthumously), and the formal ban on posthumous awards came only in 1974.
place: Oslo

title: The 1949 Roland Doe case: the best-documented possession dossier
claim: From January to April 1949, a fourteen-year-old boy from Cottage City, Maryland (later moved to St. Louis), documented under the pseudonyms 'Roland Doe' and 'Robbie Mannheim', was the subject of a series of Catholic exorcisms authorized by Archbishop Joseph Ritter and performed by Jesuit priests including Fr. William S. Bowdern, with Fr. Raymond J. Bishop keeping a diary (reportedly ~26 pages). The family's Lutheran minister referred them to Catholic help; forty-eight witnesses are said to have observed episodes, nine of them Jesuits (per Thomas B. Allen). Mid-1949 newspapers printed anonymous reports of the case. William Peter Blatty used the events in The Exorcist (1971). In December 2021, The Skeptical Inquirer reported the boy's identity as Ronald Edwin Hunkeler (1935–2020). Fr. Walter H. Halloran, one of the last surviving eyewitnesses, refused to go on record affirming a possession.
place: Cottage City, Maryland (family home); St. Louis, Missouri (St. Louis University Hospital; Alexian Brothers Hospital)

title: Dogon Sirius knowledge (Sirius Mystery)
claim: The Dogon people of Mali possessed inexplicable knowledge of Sirius B (invisible companion, ~50-year orbit, extreme density) — evidence of extraterrestrial contact (Robert Temple, The Sirius Mystery, 1976).
place: Bandiagara plateau, Mali (Dogon country)

title: The Fermi paradox (the argument, not the evidence)
claim: In 1950, over lunch at Los Alamos, Enrico Fermi asked 'Where is everybody?' — pointing at the tension between the high estimated number of habitable planets and the absence of observed extraterrestrials. The argument was formalized by Michael Hart ('An Explanation for the Absence of Extraterrestrials on Earth', 1975) and Frank Tipler (1980). It is a reasoning tool about scale versus silence, not evidence for or against extraterrestrial life.
place: Los Alamos, New Mexico (origin of the anecdote)

title: Bette Nesmith Graham invents correction fluid (Mistake Out / Liquid Paper)
claim: Bette Nesmith Graham, an executive secretary at the Texas Bank and Trust in Dallas, invented correction fluid in the early 1950s: a white tempera-paint mixture mixed in her kitchen blender, first called 'Mistake Out' and renamed 'Liquid Paper' in 1958.
place: Dallas, Texas

title: The 1952 Cuyahoga River fire (the big one)
claim: The 1952 Cuyahoga River fire was a genuinely large blaze — the biggest of the river's documented fires — causing over $1.3 million (some accounts say $1.5 million+) in damage. It is the fire whose photographs the nation actually saw: Time's 1 August 1969 article about the 1969 fire illustrated it with this blaze's picture.
place: Cuyahoga River, Cleveland, Ohio

title: The Ipuwer-as-Exodus-plagues telling
claim: The Admonitions of Ipuwer (Papyrus Leiden I 344) are an Egyptian eyewitness record of the ten plagues of Exodus: 'the river is blood' describes the first plague, and the text's chaos imagery corroborates the biblical narrative. (Claim form; adjudicated.)
place: Egypt (the text's setting; the claim concerns the plagues' geography)

title: Blake's betrayal of the Berlin Tunnel (1953)
claim: George Blake, the MI6 officer assigned to the tunnel's planning side, informed his KGB handler of the tunnel plan in the autumn of 1953 — before construction began. Moscow faced a choice between exposing the tunnel (and protecting Soviet communications) and protecting Blake; it chose Blake. The KGB deliberately withheld knowledge of the tap even from the Soviet military users of the lines, let the tunnel operate for its full eleven months, and only staged its 'discovery' after Blake was transferred in 1955.
place: London (the SIS briefings and Blake's KGB handler meetings)

title: Wheeler's 'Massacre' at Mohenjo-daro
claim: Sir Mortimer Wheeler's 1953 interpretation that 37 skeletons found at Mohenjo-daro were the victims of an invading army that massacred the city's inhabitants in a single violent event — 'Indra stands accused' of destroying the Harappan civilization.
place: Mohenjo-daro, Sindh, Pakistan

title: Bernice Eddy's ignored 1954 warning (August 1954)
claim: In August 1954 — eight months before the Cutter Incident — NIH scientist Dr. Bernice Eddy, testing a submitted Cutter vaccine sample, found that it had given polio to a test monkey: the supposedly killed-virus vaccine contained live, infectious virus. She reported her findings, with photographs of the paralyzed monkeys, to her superiors — William Workman, head of the Laboratory of Biologics Control, and NIH director William Sebrell Jr. The warning was set aside; Eddy was removed from polio-vaccine safety work.
place: Bethesda, Maryland (National Institutes of Health)

title: Operation Gold — the Berlin Tunnel
claim: In 1954–55 the CIA and MI6 (Operation Gold / Operation Stopwatch) dug a ~450-meter tunnel from Rudow in the American sector of Berlin, under the sector boundary, to Altglienicke in the Soviet sector, where a vertical shaft tapped three Soviet military trunk cables. The tap ran from May 1955 until the night of 21–22 April 1956, recording on the order of 50,000 reels of tape (~40,000 hours of telephone conversations), of which some 443,000 conversations were fully transcribed, producing about 1,750 intelligence reports; the backlog was processed into 1958.
place: Rudow (US sector) → Altglienicke (Soviet sector), Berlin — beneath the sector boundary

title: The Bandung Conference, April 1955
claim: The Asian-African Conference met at Bandung, Indonesia, 18-24 April 1955: delegations from 29 Asian and African states, convened at the invitation of the five Colombo powers (Burma, Ceylon, India, Indonesia, Pakistan), condemned colonialism in its final communiqué, and adopted unanimously the ten-point 'Dasasila Bandung' (Ten Principles of Bandung) declaration on world peace and cooperation.
place: Gedung Merdeka (Merdeka Building), Bandung, Indonesia

title: The Cutter Incident (April–May 1955)
claim: In April 1955, production lots of Cutter Laboratories' Salk polio vaccine contained live poliovirus despite passing the required safety tests. On April 27, 1955, the Epidemic Intelligence Service determined that two Cutter production pools — about 120,000 doses — contained live virus; the same day, U.S. Surgeon General Leonard Scheele ordered all Cutter vaccine recalled. On May 6, 1955, the national polio vaccination program was suspended pending investigation of every manufacturer.
place: Berkeley, California (Cutter Laboratories)

title: The Cutter Incident's aftermath: blame, law, and the quiet Wyeth cases (1955–1960)
claim: After the Cutter Incident, the June 1955 congressional inquiry concluded that Cutter's production methods were sound and that the failure lay primarily with the NIH's Laboratory of Biologics Control for inadequate scrutiny of the lots. Oveta Culp Hobby (HEW secretary), William Sebrell Jr. (NIH director), and William Workman (Lab of Biologics Control chief) lost their positions; a jury found Cutter not negligent but liable for breach of implied warranty (Gottsdanker v. Cutter, 1960); and the federal biologics oversight system was rebuilt (Division of Biologics Standards, 1955). Meanwhile Wyeth's vaccine also caused vaccine-associated polio (the Nathanson expert report described 37 cases) — known to a handful of officials, never released to the public — so the 'Cutter alone' verdict is incomplete.
place: Washington, D.C. (congressional hearing, June 1955)

title: The Cutter Incident's toll (April–December 1955)
claim: The Cutter lots' live virus infected the children they were meant to protect: about 40,000 developed abortive (non-paralytic) poliomyelitis; 51–56 developed paralytic poliomyelitis, of whom five died. Because polio is contagious, the recipients' infections seeded secondary spread: a further 113 people in their families and communities developed paralytic polio, and five of them died.
place: California, Idaho, Arizona and other states receiving Cutter lots (Berkeley manufacture)

title: The flawless-1955-launch myth (DEBUNKED)
claim: The Salk polio vaccine's rollout after its April 12, 1955 licensing was a smooth, flawless triumph — no vaccine-caused polio outbreak occurred during the launch of America's first polio vaccine.
place: Berkeley, California (Cutter Laboratories)

title: The Dartmouth Summer Research Project on Artificial Intelligence (1956)
claim: The Dartmouth Summer Research Project on Artificial Intelligence (June–August 1956) at Dartmouth College, Hanover, New Hampshire, was the event that named artificial intelligence as a field — the proposal behind it introduced the term and set the research agenda.
place: Dartmouth College, Hanover, New Hampshire

title: The 'AI was invented at Dartmouth 1956' myth
claim: Artificial intelligence was invented at the 1956 Dartmouth Summer Research Project — the field's working invention happened there, and the first AI programs and research originated at the workshop.
place: Dartmouth College, Hanover, New Hampshire (the workshop's site)

title: The staged 'discovery' of the Berlin Tunnel (April 1956) — the accident that was scheduled
claim: The claim that the Berlin Tunnel's unearthing on the night of 21–22 April 1956 was a genuine accident — a maintenance crew stumbling onto the American tap by luck (in the popular version, after heavy rains flooded the tunnel and exposed the wires).
place: Altglienicke, East Berlin (the tap chamber, south of the sector boundary)

title: The Interstate Highway System, 1956 (CORROBORATED)
claim: The Federal-Aid Highway Act of 1956 (signed by President Dwight D. Eisenhower, 29 June 1956) authorized the National System of Interstate and Defense Highways: 41,000 miles of limited-access highways, 90 percent federally funded through the Highway Trust Fund (fuel taxes), built by the states to a single national design standard.
place: United States (the Interstate Highway System)

title: The 'NASA invented Velcro' myth
claim: NASA (the US National Aeronautics and Space Administration) invented Velcro, the hook-and-loop fastener.
place: Switzerland (de Mestral's filing jurisdiction; NASA founded in the United States)

title: The eradication of smallpox (VERIFIED)
claim: Smallpox was eradicated by human effort — the last natural case in 1977, global eradication certified by the World Health Assembly in May 1980. The only human disease ever eradicated.
place: Merca, Somalia (last natural smallpox case, 26 October 1977)

title: Baran's RAND memos on distributed survivable communications (1960-64)
claim: Paul Baran's RAND Corporation memoranda (1960-64, published as 'On Distributed Communications,' 1964) proposed a distributed, packet-switched communications system designed to remain operational under nuclear attack — in the Air Force secure-voice context. This is the genuine survivability work whose rationale the ARPANET nuclear myth later grafted onto the wrong network.
place: RAND Corporation, Santa Monica, California

title: The SETI search record (1960–present): sixty years of listening, zero confirmed artificial signals
claim: A continuous, documented scientific search for extraterrestrial technosignatures has run since 1960 (Project Ozma, Frank Drake, Green Bank) through Ohio State's Big Ear all-sky surveys, Harvard's META/BETA, Project Phoenix (1995–2004), SERENDIP, SETI@home (1999–2020, ~5 million volunteers), and Breakthrough Listen (launched 2015, $100M). As of 2026, no confirmed artificial signal has been detected.
place: Green Bank, West Virginia (origin point; programs span many sites)

title: The Stevenson reincarnation case literature
claim: The University of Virginia's Division of Perceptual Studies holds a documented body of ~2,500-3,000 cases of children reporting spontaneous memories of previous lives, assembled by psychiatrist Ian Stevenson (1920-2007) and continued by Jim Tucker: the case files exist, the 'solved' cases name verifiable details checked against the previous person's records, and the birthmark/birth-defect correspondence claims are published in the peer-reviewed and university-press literature.
place: Charlottesville, Virginia (University of Virginia, Division of Perceptual Studies)

title: The severed hands: Shah Jahan mutilated the Taj Mahal's artisans to keep it unrepeatable
claim: After the Taj Mahal was completed, the Mughal emperor Shah Jahan ordered the hands of the artisans and workers who built it to be cut off (or otherwise mutilated — killed, blinded, imprisoned) so that they could never build another monument like it.
place: Taj Mahal, Agra, Uttar Pradesh, India (the legend's scene)

title: NASA adopts Velcro for Apollo — the myth's honest root
claim: NASA adopted hook-and-loop fasteners for Apollo-era spaceflight in the 1960s to secure tools, food pouches, and equipment in weightlessness; the aerospace industry was Velcro's first serious market, and the visible space use popularized the fastener on Earth — this genuine association is the honest root of the 'NASA invented Velcro' myth.
place: United States (NASA/Apollo program)

title: The origin of the genetic code: cracked, not authored
claim: No scientific consensus exists for why the genetic code maps 64 codons to 20 amino acids as it does. The mapping itself is the most-tested lookup in biology (cracked 1961-1966); the origin of the assignment - frozen accident, co-evolution, or stereochemistry - is unattested by any experiment.
place: Bethesda, Maryland, USA (NIH - Nirenberg's lab)

title: 'Lions led by donkeys' as a real German generals' remark
claim: The phrase 'lions led by donkeys' was a genuine remark made by German generals in World War I — Erich Ludendorff saying 'The English soldiers fight like lions,' and Max Hoffmann replying 'True. But don't we know that they are lions led by donkeys,' in a conversation published in the memoirs of German chief of staff Erich von Falkenhayn.
place: London — where 'The Donkeys' was published and where the attribution was first printed

title: The 'resolved by resolve alone' reading of the Cuban Missile Crisis
claim: The popular reading that the Cuban Missile Crisis was resolved PURELY by the American naval quarantine and U.S. resolve — with no American concessions — is false. The settlement of 28 October 1962 contained two American concessions: the public no-invasion pledge against Cuba (in Kennedy's 27 Oct letter) and the secret pledge to remove the Jupiter missiles from Turkey within months (delivered by Robert Kennedy to Dobrynin on the evening of 27 Oct, kept secret ~25 years). The resolve-only reading survived in textbooks and film precisely because the trade was secret; the declassifications of 1987–1989 killed it.
place: Washington D.C. (the settlement); the myth lived in textbooks and film

title: The Cuban Missile Crisis (14–28 October 1962)
claim: The October 1962 Cuban Missile Crisis — the thirteen-day confrontation of 14–28 October 1962 over Soviet SS-4/SS-5 nuclear missiles in Cuba (discovered by U-2 photography on 14 October), met by Kennedy's naval 'quarantine' announced 22 October, Khrushchev's two letters of 26 and 27 October, and the announced settlement of 28 October — was the documented near-miss it is remembered as: on 'Black Saturday' 27 October a U-2 was shot down over Cuba (Maj. Rudolf Anderson killed) and a second U-2 strayed over Soviet Chukotka, prompting the secret back-channel settlement that ended the crisis the next morning.
place: Cuba (deployment sites); Washington D.C. (ExComm)

title: The Kennedy secret White House tapes (1962–1963)
claim: In the summer of 1962 President John F. Kennedy had a secret taping system installed in the White House — Tandberg reel-to-reel recorders (obtained from the U.S. Army Signal Corps by Secret Service Agent Robert Bouck) wired to concealed microphones in the Oval Office and the Cabinet Room — which recorded some 248 hours of meetings plus more than 17 hours of telephone conversations between July 1962 and November 1963 without the knowledge of the participants (probably except Robert Kennedy). The tapes preserve the real-time, unguarded deliberations of the ExComm during the October 1962 Cuban Missile Crisis, and were first deeded to the John F. Kennedy Presidential Library in 1975; crisis transcripts were published in May & Zelikow, 'The Kennedy Tapes' (1997).
place: The White House, Washington D.C. (Oval Office, Cabinet Room)

title: The secret Jupiter-missile trade (27 October 1962)
claim: The Cuban Missile Crisis was settled by a SECRET American concession: on the evening of 27 October 1962, at President Kennedy's instruction, Attorney General Robert Kennedy told Soviet Ambassador Anatoly Dobrynin that the United States would remove its Jupiter nuclear missiles from Turkey within a few months — on the condition that the concession remain secret and never be treated as a public quid pro quo. Khrushchev announced the Soviet withdrawal from Cuba the next morning (28 Oct); the Jupiters were removed from Turkey by April 1963 (Operation Pot Pie). The secrecy held for roughly 25 years — the assurance stayed unpublished until the 1987–1989 disclosures.
place: Washington D.C. (Justice Department — RFK–Dobrynin meeting); Izmir/Cigli, Turkey (Jupiter bases)

title: The claim that the stirrup created feudalism
