claim: Lynn White Jr.'s 1962 thesis (Medieval Technology and Social Change): the stirrup's 8th-century arrival in Europe enabled true mounted shock combat, and Charles Martel — seeing this — built a cavalry army funded by confiscating Church lands, thereby creating feudalism.
place: Oxford, England (publication of the thesis, 1962)

title: The claim that the horse collar caused the medieval agricultural revolution
claim: Lynn White Jr.'s 1962 thesis (Medieval Technology and Social Change), chapter 'The Discovery of Horse-Power': the padded horse collar — which White dated to roughly 10th-century Europe — together with the nailed horseshoe, unlocked the horse as a draught animal, displaced the ox, and thereby CAUSED the medieval agricultural revolution: oat cultivation, the three-field rotation, the resulting food surplus, population growth, and the northward shift of Europe's civilizational center.
place: Oxford, England (publication of the thesis, 1962)

title: The mutual lifting of the 1054 excommunications, 7 December 1965
claim: On 7 December 1965, Pope Paul VI and Ecumenical Patriarch Athenagoras I simultaneously lifted the excommunications of 1054 — read aloud at a public session of the Second Vatican Council in Rome and at a special ceremony at the Patriarchate in Istanbul — 'committing them to oblivion' in the words of the Joint Declaration.
place: St. Peter's Basilica, Rome & the Patriarchal Church, Istanbul (simultaneous)

title: The Fisher Space Pen AG-7 (1965–1967)
claim: Paul C. Fisher independently developed the AG-7 pressurized-cartridge space pen (US Patent 3,285,228, filed 19 May 1965); after ~2 years of NASA testing it flew on Apollo 7 (Oct 1968), and NASA purchased ~400 pens at $2.95 each in 1967.
place: Boulder City, Nevada (Fisher Pen Company)

title: NASA's $128.89 mechanical pencils (1965)
claim: In 1965 NASA ordered 34 mechanical pencils from Houston's Tycam Engineering Manufacturing, Inc. for $4,382.50 — $128.89 per pencil — sparking a public outcry; pencils were then found hazardous in spacecraft (flaking graphite tips drifting in microgravity, flammable wood in the post-Apollo-1 cabin), and the agency moved away from them.
place: Houston, Texas (NASA Manned Spacecraft Center / Johnson Space Center)

title: 'Lead poisoning caused the fall of Rome'
claim: Lead poisoning caused the decline and fall of the Roman Empire — lead exposure from the Romans' lead water pipes (fistulae) and lead-sweetened wine (sapa/defrutum) was a primary cause of the Empire's collapse.
place: Rome, Italy (myth's supposed locus)

title: 'Walt Disney was cryogenically frozen' (DEBUNKED)
claim: Walt Disney was cryogenically frozen after his death in December 1966 (in some versions, only his head, stored under Disneyland's Pirates of the Caribbean or Cinderella Castle).
place: Forest Lawn Memorial Park, Glendale, California

title: The 'Stevenson proved reincarnation' telling
claim: Popular tellings present Ian Stevenson's case research as having PROVED reincarnation — the claim that the documented cases constitute proof that consciousness survives death and is reborn.
place: Charlottesville, Virginia (the telling cites UVA's Division of Perceptual Studies)

title: Honeywell v. Sperry Rand: the courtroom that unmade ENIAC (19 October 1973)
claim: On 19 October 1973, U.S. District Judge Earl R. Larson of the District of Minnesota decided Honeywell Inc. v. Sperry Rand Corp. (180 U.S.P.Q. 673; Case 4-67 Civ. 138), invalidating the 1964 ENIAC patent (U.S. Patent 3,120,606, filed 1947) on four grounds — including derivation: 'Eckert and Mauchly did not themselves first invent the automatic electronic digital computer, but instead derived that subject matter from one Dr. John Vincent Atanasoff.' The trial ran 1 June 1971 – 13 March 1972 with 77 witnesses and ~33,000 exhibits; the suits were filed 26 May 1967 (Honeywell's filing minutes earlier). The ruling placed the invention of the electronic digital computer in the public domain; it was never appealed. The news was largely buried: the Saturday Night Massacre broke the next day, 20 October 1973.
place: U.S. District Court for the District of Minnesota, Minneapolis

title: The first undisputed North Pole arrivals over the surface — Plaisted 1968 (snowmobile), Herbert 1969 (on foot)
claim: The first expedition to reach the North Pole over the surface with an undisputed, independently verifiable arrival was Ralph Plaisted's 1968 snowmobile expedition — Plaisted and three companions arrived at the Pole in April 1968. The first to reach it the traditional way, on foot with dog teams, was Sir Wally Herbert's 1968-69 British Trans-Arctic Expedition, which crossed the entire Arctic from Point Barrow, Alaska to Svalbard over 476 days and reached the Pole on 6 April 1969 — the 60th anniversary of Peary's claimed arrival.
place: North Pole

title: The 'Nazca Runways' Claim
claim: The claim (popularized by Erich von Däniken's 'Chariots of the Gods?', 1968) that the long straight lines and trapezoid shapes on the Nazca pampa were built as runways or landing strips for aircraft — ancient or extraterrestrial.
place: Nazca pampa, Ica region, Peru

title: The 'Nazca Runways' Claim
claim: The claim (popularized by Erich von Däniken's 'Chariots of the Gods?', 1968) that the long straight lines and trapezoid shapes on the Nazca pampa were built as runways or landing strips for aircraft — ancient or extraterrestrial.
place: Nazca pampa, Ica region, Peru

title: The first AI winter (c. 1974–1980)
claim: The first AI winter (c. 1974–1980) was a real funding-and-credibility collapse in artificial intelligence research, triggered by the Lighthill report (1973) and DARPA's subsequent cutbacks to academic AI research.
place: Washington, D.C. (DARPA) / London (Science Research Council) — the funding rooms

title: The Apollo Moon landings, 1969-1972
claim: Between July 1969 and December 1972, six crewed Apollo missions (Apollo 11, 12, 14, 15, 16, 17) landed on the Moon, and twelve astronauts walked on its surface — beginning with Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin in Mare Tranquillitatis on 20-21 July 1969.
place: Mare Tranquillitatis (Apollo 11 site; hardware and astronaut footpaths visible in LRO imagery)

title: The ARPANET and the first message ('LO', 29 October 1969)
claim: The ARPANET — the first packet-switched computer network, funded by ARPA (later DARPA) — went live in 1969 with the stated purpose of letting researchers share scarce, expensive time-sharing computers. The first host-to-host transmission ran 29 October 1969 at 22:30 PST: UCLA graduate student Charley Kline, supervised by Leonard Kleinrock, typed 'login' on the UCLA SDS Sigma 7 host (Boelter Hall room 3420) toward Bill Duvall's SRI SDS 940 host — the SRI machine crashed after the letters 'l' and 'o', and the full login succeeded about an hour later. The first permanent ARPANET link followed 21 November 1969; the initial four-node network (UCLA, SRI, UCSB, Utah) was complete by 5 December 1969.
place: UCLA, Boelter Hall room 3420, Los Angeles, California (transmission origin)

title: The 1969 Cuyahoga River fire
claim: On the morning of Sunday, 22 June 1969, an oil slick on the Cuyahoga River at Cleveland caught fire — probably from sparks off a passing railcar — burning about 24–30 minutes, damaging railroad bridges spanning the river, costing roughly $50,000, and extinguished by land-based battalions and a city fireboat. The thirteenth and last of the river's documented fires.
place: Cuyahoga River, Cleveland, Ohio

title: The legend of the catastrophic 1969 Cuyahoga fire
claim: The June 1969 Cuyahoga River fire was a massive, catastrophic, singular blaze — a towering inferno that burned for hours or days, caused enormous damage, was the river's first fire, and was photographed in dramatic full color — the apocalyptic spark that woke the nation.
place: Cleveland, Ohio — the myth's home, not the fire's scale

title: The Soviet Fisher pen purchase (1969)
claim: In 1969 the Soviet space program purchased 100 Fisher Space Pens (with 1,000 ink cartridges) for use on all future missions — Soviet cosmonauts had used pencils and grease pencils on plastic slates, and, like NASA, adopted the Fisher pressurized pen.
place: Moscow, USSR (Soviet space program procurement)

title: Pazuzu the possessor is the film's invention
claim: William Peter Blatty's novel The Exorcist (1971) and William Friedkin's film (1973) made Pazuzu a possessing demon — the entity inside Regan MacNeil, named outright in Exorcist II: The Heretic (1977). In the cuneiform tradition Pazuzu was the wind-demon king invoked APOTROPAICALLY against Lamashtu (evt-pazuzu-001, CORROBORATED; Heeßel 2002): the film inverted the tradition's hired protection into its possessor. The possession reading is modern fiction, not ancient religion.
place: Assyria (the tradition's geography; the inversion happened in Hollywood, 1971–1973)

title: The Leonardo bicycle sketch (Codex Atlanticus)
claim: Leonardo da Vinci designed a bicycle (a two-wheeled, chain-driven machine) circa 1500, as shown in a sketch in the Codex Atlanticus.
place: Biblioteca Ambrosiana, Milan (the Codex Atlanticus)

title: The ozone hole and the Montreal Protocol (VERIFIED)
claim: Human-made CFCs depleted stratospheric ozone, creating the Antarctic ozone hole (discovered 1985); the 1987 Montreal Protocol banned them and the layer is recovering.
place: Antarctica (ozone hole); Montreal, Canada (treaty)

title: The 'Wite-Out came first' myth
claim: Wite-Out was the first correction fluid — the brand that invented (or originated) the correction-fluid product category.
place: United States (category origin: Dallas, Texas; Wite-Out's own origin not dated this pass)

title: 'The Moon landings were faked'
claim: The Apollo program's crewed Moon landings (1969-1972) never happened — NASA staged them on Earth, in a studio or a remote desert, to fool the public.
place: The claim is about fabrication on Earth, not a place; pin carried at the stated landing site (Mare Tranquillitatis) for reference

title: The Wow! signal (15 August 1977)
claim: On 15 August 1977, Ohio State University's Big Ear radio telescope recorded a 72-second narrowband signal near 1420 MHz (the hydrogen line), strong enough that astronomer Jerry Ehman circled it on the computer printout and wrote 'Wow!' in the margin. It has never been repeated.
place: Ohio State Radio Observatory (Big Ear), Delaware, Ohio — demolished 1998

title: The Wow! signal (15 August 1977)
claim: On 15 August 1977, Ohio State University's Big Ear radio telescope recorded a 72-second narrowband signal near 1420 MHz (the hydrogen line), strong enough that astronomer Jerry Ehman circled it on the computer printout and wrote 'Wow!' in the margin. It has never been repeated.
place: Ohio State Radio Observatory (Big Ear), Delaware, Ohio — demolished 1998

title: The Wow! signal (15 August 1977) — 2026 evidence state
claim: On 15 August 1977, Ohio State University's Big Ear radio telescope recorded a 72-second narrowband signal near 1420 MHz (the hydrogen line), strong enough that astronomer Jerry Ehman circled it on the computer printout and wrote 'Wow!' in the margin. It has never been repeated.
place: Ohio State Radio Observatory (Big Ear), Delaware, Ohio — demolished 1998

title: Double Eagle II — the first real Atlantic crossing by balloon (11–17 August 1978)
claim: The first successful transatlantic balloon flight: Ben Abruzzo, Maxie Anderson, and Larry Newman flew the helium balloon Double Eagle II from Presque Isle, Maine (lift-off 8:42 pm, 11 August 1978) to Miserey, France (landing 17 August 1978) — 137 hours 6 minutes, ~5,001 km, the 14th known attempt, ending the 134-year wait that began with the Montgolfier flights.
place: Presque Isle, Maine → Miserey, France (Irish coast crossed evening of 16 August 1978)

title: The 1979 Gillette sale of Liquid Paper
claim: In 1979 Bette Nesmith Graham sold the Liquid Paper Company to the Gillette Corporation for $47.5 million (plus a royalty on every bottle); she died in 1980, leaving half her fortune to her son Michael Nesmith (of the Monkees) and half to philanthropic foundations.
place: Dallas, Texas

title: The '24-chromosome blood of Christ' claim (Ron Wyatt) fails basic biology
claim: Ron Wyatt's claim (from 1982) of Christ's blood found under the crucifixion site — '24 chromosomes' (23 from Mary + 1 Y from the Father), allegedly rehydrated 'living' after 2,000 years — has no peer-reviewed publication, no documented lab, no verifiable sample. It fails basic biology: viable human blood has 46 chromosomes, and 2,000-year-old 'living' blood cells are impossible. Graded DEBUNKED.

title: 'It never happened': the urban-legend dismissal of the Atari burial, killed by the 2014 dig
claim: Atari never buried any unsold E.T. cartridges in the New Mexico desert — the whole story is just an urban legend that never happened.
place: Alamogordo landfill, Otero County, New Mexico

title: The Atari burial, September 1983: the inventory that went into the desert and the dig that found it
claim: In September 1983, Atari, Inc. buried a large quantity of unsold video-game cartridges, consoles, and other equipment in a landfill in Alamogordo, New Mexico.
place: Alamogordo landfill, Otero County, New Mexico

title: The Orion correlation theory (Giza 'mirrors Orion's Belt')
claim: The 'Orion correlation theory' (Robert Bauval, 1983/1994, popularized in The Orion Mystery) holds that the layout of the Giza pyramids mirrors the stars of Orion's Belt and that the 'airshafts' point at specific stars — evidence of astronomically precise, supposedly impossible knowledge. The theory was never published in a peer-reviewed archaeology or astronomy venue; Egyptologist-archaeoastronomers (notably Juan Belmonte's survey work) showed the fit fails: the belt stars' brightness order does not match the pyramids' size order, the southern 'shaft' angles do not hold across the measured stellar positions at 2500 BCE, and the theory treats the pyramids as an isolated cipher rather than a 4th-Dynasty royal necropolis with a documented construction context.
place: Giza plateau

title: The lead in the Franklin sailors' bones
claim: The crewmen of the 1845 Franklin expedition (HMS Erebus and HMS Terror) carried high body lead burdens, far above modern background levels.
place: Beechey Island, Nunavut

title: The claim that lead-poisoned tinned food destroyed the Franklin expedition
claim: Lead poisoning — from the lead solder sealing the expedition's tinned-food provisions — was the principal cause of the death and disintegration of the 1845 Franklin expedition.
place: Beechey Island, Nunavut

title: LTEE reaches 75,000 generations (2026 milestone)
claim: Richard Lenski's Long-Term Evolution Experiment (LTEE) — twelve replicate E. coli populations founded 1988 — passed 75,000 generations in 2026; the frozen 'fossil record' (samples every 500 generations) continues to make evolution replayable: the Ara-3 citrate innovation (~gen. 31,500, Blount/Borland/Lenski 2008) remains the headline innovation, with Blount's follow-up work (2026) sequencing citrate-transporter variants to map the physiological and ecological consequences of the innovation and its counterfactuals.
place: Michigan State University, East Lansing — Lenski lab

title: LTEE reaches 80,000 generations (2024 milestone); lab moves MSU → UT Austin
claim: Richard Lenski's Long-Term Evolution Experiment (LTEE) — twelve replicate E. coli populations founded 1988 at UC Irvine, run at Michigan State University from 1991 — passed 80,000 generations in 2024, with the populations at all-time peak fitness and no plans to end the experiment; the LTEE now continues at the University of Texas at Austin under Dr. Jeffrey Barrick. The frozen 'fossil record' (samples every 500 generations, -80°C) continues to make evolution replayable: the Ara-3 citrate innovation (~gen. 31,500, Blount/Borland/Lenski 2008) remains the headline innovation, six of the 12 populations had become hypermutators by 50,000 generations, and adaptation has continued indefinitely without plateauing in a constant environment.
place: University of Texas at Austin — Barrick lab (LTEE since the ~2024–2025 MSU handoff; founded 1988 UC Irvine, MSU 1991–2024)

title: The Quebec blackout, 13 March 1989 (VERIFIED)
claim: On 13 March 1989, a geomagnetic storm collapsed Quebec's entire power grid in 92 seconds, leaving 6 million people without power for up to 9 hours.
place: Quebec, Canada (grid collapse); global (storm effects)

title: The OOPArt autopsy method
claim: Out-of-place artifacts are adjudicated object-by-object: a lab test (tool marks under magnification, materials analysis, abrasive identification, dating where possible) plus a provenance chain (first appearance, dealer or finder, every transfer). The method separates genuine ancient objects (the Iron Pillar of Delhi, the Diquis spheres) from modern fabrications (the crystal skulls, the Coso artifact) and from genuine objects with contaminated find contexts (the Maine penny).
place: The lab bench — British Museum Scientific Research / Smithsonian NMNH (the method's home, not the objects')

title: The scholarly consensus that the Tel Dan Stele attests the Davidic dynasty
claim: By 2006-2007 the scholarly field had settled the question of whether an extra-biblical 'House of David' existed: the Tel Dan Stele's bytdwd is widely read as a 9th-century BCE Aramaic reference to the Judahite royal house, ending the argument that David was a purely literary invention; the live argument moved to the kingdom's scale, not the dynasty's existence.
place: The published literature (Tel Dan stele at the Israel Museum, Jerusalem)

title: The Pray Codex 'proves' the Shroud of Turin existed in 1192
claim: Apologetic tellings present the Pray Codex's shroud illumination as a 'fingerprint' or 'DNA match' that PROVES the Shroud of Turin existed in Constantinople before 1192 — i.e., the illumination is treated as a positive identification of the cloth as the Shroud of Turin.
place: Budapest (National Széchényi Library)

title: Assmann's counterhistory: the Exodus as deliberate inversion
claim: Jan Assmann's thesis that the biblical Exodus narrative functions as a 'counterhistory' — a deliberate literary inversion of the Egyptian account preserved by Manetho (via Josephus): expulsion becomes liberation, the expelled become the chosen, the kings become the slaves, the lepers/polluted become the elect. Assmann developed this in Moses the Egyptian (Harvard UP, 1997) and later works; mnemohistory studies the remembered past, not the past as such.
place: Heidelberg (Assmann's university; the thesis, not the events)

title: Deep Blue defeats Kasparov, 1997
claim: The 1997 Deep Blue–Kasparov rematch (3–11 May 1997, Equitable Center, New York City) ended 3½–2½ to IBM's Deep Blue — the first defeat of a reigning world chess champion by a computer under standard tournament time controls.
place: Equitable Center, New York City

title: The 'Deep Blue thought like a human' myth
claim: Deep Blue defeated Garry Kasparov in 1997 by out-thinking him — playing and thinking like a human chess player, demonstrating machine intelligence in the human sense.
place: Equitable Center, New York City (the match's site)

title: The pine cone as hygrometer (verified folk instrument)
claim: Pine cones open their scales when good (dry) weather is coming and close them when wet weather approaches — the cone is a working hygrometer.
place: Freiburg, Germany (livMatS biomechanics research; folk use universal in temperate pine regions)

title: The Toba bottleneck hypothesis (1998) — the causality question
claim: The volcanic-winter bottleneck hypothesis (Ambrose 1998, Journal of Human Evolution): the Youngest Toba Tuff (~74 ka) triggered years of global cooling — a volcanic winter — that collapsed the human population to a few thousand breeding individuals, creating the genetic bottleneck read in the mitochondrial and Y-chromosome coalescences.
place: Lake Toba (the cause); the claimed effect is global

title: The 1998 Lancet MMR-autism fraud (DEBUNKED)
claim: MMR vaccination causes autism (the claim built on Wakefield et al.'s 1998 Lancet paper).
place: Royal Free Hospital, Hampstead, London (Wakefield's 1998 research base)

title: The 2001 NORC Media Recount of Florida 2000
claim: The 2001 NORC media recount of Florida's 2000 presidential ballots showed George W. Bush would have kept Florida under every recount strategy Al Gore actually pursued — and that Al Gore could only have won under a full statewide recount of all uncounted ballots (undervotes plus overvotes) that was never requested and never happened.
place: Florida, USA (statewide; 67 counties)

title: The Interstate 'one mile in five' landing-strip rule (DEBUNKED)
claim: The United States Interstate Highway System was designed so that one mile in every five is straight, for use as emergency landing strips for airplanes in wartime.
place: United States (the Interstate Highway System)

title: The category rehabilitated: dying-and-rising gods before Christianity
claim: The category 'dying-and-rising gods' names a real, pre-Christian phenomenon of attested death-and-return narratives in the ancient Near East — Osiris, Dumuzi/Tammuz, Baal, Melqart attested; Adonis and Eshmun probable — rehabilitated by Mettinger (2001) against the 1990s consensus ('they died but did not return'), which overstated its case. The category is a scholarly instrument graded on the columns, and the claim that early Christianity borrowed a ready-made 'resurrection template' from it remains unattested transmission — CLAIMED, not evidence.
place: Lund, Sweden (Mettinger's chair; historiographical anchor — the map pins the argument, not a place)

title: 'Like painting the Forth Bridge' — the never-ending job (DEBUNKED)
claim: Painting the Forth Bridge is a never-ending task — a job that must begin again the moment it is finished, because by the time one end is painted the other end already needs a fresh coat.
place: Firth of Forth, Scotland

title: The '1421' thesis: Zheng He's fleet discovered America
claim: Gavin Menzies' 2002 thesis (1421: The Year China Discovered the World): that during or after Zheng He's sixth voyage, detached Chinese fleets circumnavigated the globe, reached the Americas, Australia, and Antarctica, mapped them, and returned — so China 'discovered' America ~70 years before Columbus and the world ~100 years before Magellan.
place: Beijing (publication/imperial-center anchor of the claim)

title: The Sarajevo Sandwich Myth (the lunch-hour coincidence)
claim: The telling that Gavrilo Princip only happened to be standing outside Moritz Schiller's delicatessen because he had stepped in to buy a sandwich — and that the Archduke's car stopped right in front of him by outrageous coincidence, so that 'no sandwich, no shooting; no shooting, no war.'
place: Sarajevo — Moritz Schiller's delicatessen, Franz Josef Street

title: The Semmelweis 'persecuted martyr' narrative (popular version)
claim: The popular 'persecuted martyr' narrative — that Ignaz Semmelweis was mocked and ridiculed by a closed medical establishment that refused to look at his evidence, and that he was driven into an asylum and to his death by their persecution — is an exaggeration of the real record, largely assembled by later popularizers (notably Nuland's The Doctor's Plague, 2003).
place: Vienna (the historiographic claim's origin point)

title: ABC News 2004 poll: 64% say Moses parted the Red Sea 'literally true word-for-word'
claim: In an ABC News poll of 1,011 American adults (Feb 6-10, 2004), 64% said the story of Moses parting the Red Sea was 'literally true, meaning it happened that way word-for-word'; about 30% said the Bible stories are meant as lessons, not to be taken literally.
place: United States (national poll)

title: Ingredient delivery: returned asteroid/comet samples contain life's building blocks
claim: Pristine samples returned from carbonaceous asteroids and a comet contain the molecular building blocks of life — amino acids, nucleobases, sugars, phosphate — demonstrating that the ingredients were widespread in the early solar system before life existed on Earth. Delivery of ingredients is demonstrated; the mechanism of life's origin is not.
place: NASA Johnson Space Center, Houston (Bennu sample curation); JAXA Sagamihara (Ryugu)

title: The Ark-Encounter/Creation-Museum-exhibit-as-evidence telling (dino-human coexistence)
claim: The dioramas, animatronics, and placards at Answers in Genesis's Creation Museum (Petersburg, KY) and Ark Encounter (Grant County, KY) — the 'dragons were dinosaurs' exhibit, dinosaur animatronics in cages, dinosaurs standing with Adam and Eve in the Garden of Eden, dinosaurs aboard the Ark — constitute historical evidence that humans and non-avian dinosaurs lived at the same time. FALSE: a diorama is a claim in three dimensions, and the claim it makes is the young-earth telling — Day-6 creation, juveniles on the Ark, post-Flood climate extinction — which the evidence record (evt-dino-human-coexistence-001, DEBUNKED; evt-paluxy-mantracks-001, DEBUNKED) already kills. The exhibits are the 292nd DEBUNKED family: the museum-exhibit-as-evidence telling.
place: Ark Encounter, Grant County, Kentucky, USA

title: Venona 'vindicates' McCarthy
claim: The Venona decrypts prove Senator Joseph McCarthy's accusations were right — that the evidence shows he was justified in his zeal in exposing those he believed to be Soviet spies or communist sympathizers (the form in which the Texas State Board of Education proposed revising high school history curricula in 2009).
place: Austin, Texas (Texas State Board of Education, 2009)

title: Pew 2010: 72% identify Moses as the Exodus leader; the non-religious know the most
claim: In Pew Research Center's U.S. Religious Knowledge Survey (fielded May 19-June 6, 2010, among 3,412 U.S. adults by landline and cell phone, in English and Spanish), 72% correctly identified Moses — not Job, Elijah, or Abraham — as the biblical figure who led the exodus from Egypt. On the survey's full 32 questions the national average was 16 correct; atheists and agnostics averaged 20.9, Jews 20.5, and Mormons 20.3 — the highest-scoring groups included people with no religious affiliation, while Protestants as a whole averaged 16 and Catholics 14.7.
place: United States (national poll)

title: Pew religious-knowledge quiz: the 2010 telephone wave vs the 2019 online wave — the inversion survived the mode change
claim: Between Pew Research Center's two U.S. religious-knowledge surveys, the survey mode changed completely. The 2010 wave ('U.S. Religious Knowledge Survey,' report Sept 28, 2010) was interviewer-administered by telephone — dual-frame landline + cell random-digit dial, n=3,412 U.S. adults, fielded May 19–June 6, 2010, in English and Spanish. The 2019 wave ('What Americans Know About Religion,' report July 23, 2019) was self-administered online — fielded Feb 4–19, 2019, n=10,971, mostly on Pew's American Trends Panel (10,429 panelists, probability-recruited online) plus 542 Ipsos KnowledgePanel oversample interviews (Jewish, Mormon, Hispanic Protestant subgroups), margin of sampling error ±1.5 points. The headline finding — the religiously unaffiliated outscoring the affiliated — survived the crossing: 2010 (telephone): atheists/agnostics 20.9 of 32, general public 16, Protestants 16, Catholics 14.7. 2019 (online): Jews 18.7, atheists 17.9, agnostics 17.0, general public 14.2. The group-ranking pattern held after demographic controls in both waves. The inversion is mode-robust: it was not an artifact of interviewer administration, and it did not vanish under self-administration.
place: United States (national polls)

title: Wind setdown as a physical crossing mechanism (Drews & Han 2010)
claim: Wind setdown — a sustained strong wind driving water back — can physically expose dry passage in shallow Delta waters: Drews & Han (2010, PLoS ONE) modeled a 28 m/s (63 mph) easterly wind for 12 hours opening a 3-4 km long, 5 km wide mudflat for about 4 hours at the reconstructed Lake of Tanis / Pelusiac branch, with the water standing as barriers on both sides of the exposed flats.
place: Lake of Tanis / Pelusiac branch reconstruction (eastern Nile Delta)

title: El Azizia's 136°F record decertified (2012)
claim: The 136.4°F (58°C) temperature recorded at El Azizia, Libya, on 13 September 1922 — the long-standing world heat record — was formally decertified by the World Meteorological Organization in 2012 after a committee investigation found it invalid.
place: El Azizia, Libya

title: The 2012 Mayan 'end of the world' — debunked
claim: The Mayan calendar predicted the end of the world on 21 December 2012.
place: Tortuguero, Tabasco, Mexico (site of Monument 6 — heavily quarried/damaged before its significance was recognized)

title: The Denisovan EPAS1 haplotype and Tibetan altitude adaptation
claim: Huerta-Sanchez et al. 2014 (Nature, doi 10.1038/nature13408): Tibetans carry a Denisovan-derived EPAS1 haplotype at ~80-87% frequency, conferring efficient blood-oxygen response to hypoxia without the heart-straining side effects of other high-altitude adaptations — the clearest case of adaptive archaic introgression.

title: Erebus (2014) and Terror (2016) - the wrecks, found where the testimony said
claim: Both Franklin expedition wrecks were found in the 2010s at Inuit-indicated locations. HMS Erebus was located in September 2014 in the Queen Maud Gulf, northeast of O'Reilly Island (Wilfrid Laurier area) - 'near to where Inukpujijuk told Hall it had sunk' (Parks Canada), after six years of sonar searching guided by Inuit oral history and Louie Kamookak's consultations; the find followed a Government of Nunavut team's recovery of cached Erebus artefacts from an island. HMS Terror was located in September 2016 in Terror Bay, about 60 miles north of Erebus, by the Arctic Research Foundation's vessel Martin Bergmann - after Inuk crewmember Sammy Kogvik reported having seen a mast-like object in the Terror Bay ice six years earlier; Parks Canada confirmed the wreck resting upright in about 24 metres of water in remarkably preserved condition. In both cases the technology found the ship; the testimony found the place.
place: Queen Maud Gulf (Erebus) and Terror Bay, King William Island coast (Terror), Nunavut

title: 'Found by technology alone' - the myth that erased the map-keepers
claim: The wrecks of HMS Erebus (found 2014) and HMS Terror (found 2016) were located purely by modern search technology - sonar, satellites, and systematic grid searching - with no meaningful help from Indigenous Inuit knowledge, and the Franklin expedition otherwise vanished without leaving any record of its fate.
place: Queen Maud Gulf / Terror Bay, Nunavut

title: The measured destruction of Syria's archaeological heritage, 2015–2025
claim: The destruction of archaeological heritage in Syria during and after the civil war is itself a measured, documented record: 59% of 199 surveyed sites suffered looting or destruction between 2015 and 2025 (vs 13% in 2011–2016), with mechanized bulldozer looting statistically associated with military activity — and the near-total leveling of Ain Dara by 2022. The pattern of what was destroyed, where, and by what means is evidence about the destroyers (actors, methods, motives), not merely loss.
place: Syria (199 surveyed sites incl. Palmyra, Mari, Apamea, Ain Dara)

title: YouGov 2015: the 41% who believe in coexistence
claim: In a 2015 YouGov survey of American adults, 41% said humans and dinosaurs either 'definitely' (14%) or 'probably' (27%) lived on Earth at the same time; 43% said they 'definitely' (25%) or 'probably' (18%) did not; 16% were unsure. Among self-described 'born-again' Christians, 56% believed in coexistence; among non-born-again Americans, 51% rejected it.
place: United States (national sample)

title: The 'Ein Gedi scroll proves the Hebrew Bible goes back 2000 years' 2026 telling — DEBUNKED
claim: The telling, recirculated September–October 2026 (a rehash of the 2016 virtual-unwrapping story), that the Ein Gedi Leviticus scroll constitutes 'the first physical evidence that the version of the Hebrew Bible used today goes back 2000 years.' The telling fails on both its load-bearing words. FIRST: older Masoretic-type Leviticus witnesses already exist among the Dead Sea Scrolls (2nd century BCE). 2000 YEARS: the Ein Gedi scroll itself dates to the 3rd–4th century CE — roughly 1,500–1,700 years old (Seales et al., Science Advances, September 2016; the scroll was excavated in 1970 from the synagogue ark at En-Gedi, carbonized in a fire). What the scroll genuinely proves — its consonantal text is identical to the medieval Masoretic text, bridging the Qumran-to-medieval gap — is real and important; the 'first' and '2000 years' claims are not.
place: En-Gedi synagogue, Dead Sea shore (scroll's findspot)

title: The Petra qibla theory (Gibson 2016–2017) — DEBUNKED
claim: Dan Gibson's claim (the 2016 film 'The Sacred City'; 'Qur'anic Geography' and 'Early Islamic Qiblas', 2017): the first mosques were built facing Petra, Jordan, not Mecca — the original qibla was Petra.
place: Petra, Jordan (the claimed qibla target)

title: The 2018 Moscow–Constantinople rupture (the Tomos schism)
claim: On 15 October 2018 the Russian Orthodox Church broke communion with the Ecumenical Patriarchate of Constantinople after Constantinople moved to grant autocephaly to a Ukrainian church; on 15 December 2018 the Kyiv Unification Council created the Orthodox Church of Ukraine (OCU) from the UOC-KP and UAOC, and on 5 January 2019 Patriarch Bartholomew issued the Tomos of Autocephaly to the OCU. As of October 2026 the rupture is unhealed: Moscow and Constantinople remain out of communion, the OCU is recognized by Constantinople and a small number of other churches, and the Ukrainian Orthodox Church under Moscow (UOC-MP) sits in a canonical limbo it did not choose.
place: Kyiv, Ukraine (Unification Council, St. Sophia)

title: Pew 2019: unbelievers again outscore believers on religious knowledge
claim: In Pew Research Center's 'What Americans Know About Religion' survey (report released July 23, 2019; nationally representative U.S. adults, 32 religious-knowledge questions), the highest-scoring groups were again the religiously unaffiliated critics of religion: Jews averaged 18.7 of 32 correct, self-described atheists 17.9, and agnostics 17.0 — above the general-public average of 14.2. Evangelical Protestants scored 15.5 (above average); mainline Protestants, Catholics, and Mormons scored 13.9-14.6, clustering near the public average. The group-score pattern held even after controlling for education and other demographics. Atheists were on a par with Catholics and Protestants on the Catholicism/Protestantism questions, more likely than any other group to answer the religion-in-public-life questions correctly, and averaged 8.6 of 14 on the Bible-and-Christianity items (vs 8.2 for agnostics and for Christians). The 2010 finding replicated: unbelievers outscore believers.
place: United States (national poll)

title: US creationism belief, Gallup June 2019
claim: In June 2019, 40% of US adults told Gallup that 'God created human beings pretty much in their present form at one time within the last 10,000 years or so' (33% said humans evolved with God's guidance, 22% without God's involvement).
place: United States (Gallup national sample, all 50 states + DC)

title: Ghost archaic introgression in West African populations (~600 ka divergence)
claim: Durvasula & Sankararaman 2020 (Science Advances, doi 10.1126/sciadv.aax5097) found that West African populations (Yoruba, Mende, Esan, Gambian groups) derive 2-19% of their ancestry from an unknown archaic lineage that diverged before the modern-human/Neanderthal split (~600 ka). No fossils or DNA of this 'ghost' source exist — its signature is statistical.

title: NBS 260108 — the 2026 FAST/K2-155 technosignature candidate
claim: A 2026 peer-reviewed pipeline re-analysis of 2021 Five-hundred-meter Aperture Spherical Telescope (FAST) observations of 33 exoplanet systems (Li, Z.-Q., et al., The Astronomical Journal 172, Article 180) found one narrow drifting radio signal toward K2-155 — NBS 260108, at 1148.4167 MHz with drift rate -0.038 Hz/s, seen in the on-target beam (Beam 1) and none of the other 18 beams. The authors classified it as a low-priority technosignature candidate, retained for internal follow-up only: the paper explicitly does not support an extraterrestrial explanation, and the suspected terrestrial or instrumental source has not been identified — the paper's own detail favors shared interference: the signal is strongly YY-polarized and absent in XX, and near-frequency YY-dominated features appeared toward K2-18, GJ 9066, and Ross 128 in the same 10 September 2021 session.
place: FAST, Dawodang, Guizhou, China (the observing instrument's site; K2-155 lies ~238 light-years distant in Eridanus)

title: Only 1.5-7% of our DNA is uniquely Homo sapiens (SARGE, 2021)
claim: Schaefer et al. 2021 (UC Santa Cruz, Richard Green lab; doi 10.1126/sciadv.abc0776) built the Speedy Ancestral Recombination Graph Estimator (SARGE) from one Denisovan, two Neanderthal, and 279 modern human genomes, finding that only ~7% of the autosomal genome is uniquely human ('archaic deserts'), narrowing to ~1.5% for high-frequency human-specific derived alleles. The human-unique regions cluster around genes for prenatal brain development.

title: Gallup 2022: biblical literalism at record low (20%)
claim: In Gallup's May 2022 Values and Beliefs poll (published June 2022), 20% of Americans said 'the Bible is the actual word of God and is to be taken literally, word for word' — the record low for biblical literalism in Gallup's four-decade trend (from 40% in 1980 to 20% in 2022), with 32% saying the Bible is inspired but not literal and 29% calling it ancient fables. The 2022 wave is the newest Gallup literalism measurement on the record.
place: United States (national poll)

title: Retraction of the 2022 Giza SAR Doppler tomography paper (August 2026)
claim: The journal Remote Sensing (MDPI) formally retracted the 2022 paper by Filippo Biondi and Corrado Malanga, 'Synthetic Aperture Radar Doppler Tomography Reveals Details of Undiscovered High-Resolution Internal Structure of the Great Pyramid of Giza,' on 10 August 2026, confirming serious methodological flaws and statistical errors that undermined the paper's conclusions. The authors disagreed with the retraction.
place: Great Pyramid of Giza (the paper's subject; the retraction is an editorial event)

title: LifeWay State of Theology 2022: 53% say the Bible is 'not literally true' (recirculated Oct 2026)
claim: In LifeWay Research's 2022 State of Theology survey (3,011 U.S. adults interviewed January 5-23, 2022; biennial study sponsored by Ligonier Ministries, measuring 'the current theological awareness of adult Americans'), about half of Americans said the Bible is 'completely accurate,' while 53% said it is 'not literally true' and 40% agreed that modern science disproves it. title: The Nazca tridactyl "alien mummies" (2023–2026 forensic verdict)
claim: The tridactyl "mummies" presented by Jaime Maussan at the Mexican Congress (2023–2024) and promoted as non-human entities or bodies of a non-human intelligence are modern composite fabrications assembled from human and animal remains; the claim that they are extraterrestrial or non-human is DEBUNKED on the physical evidence.

title: Pew RLS 2023-24: 65% of U.S. adults believe in 'other spirits or unseen spiritual forces'
claim: Pew Research Center's Religious Landscape Study 'spiritual beliefs' short report (published 2023-12-07, from the RLS 2023-24 wave) asked U.S. adults directly about unseen spirits: 65% said they believe 'other spirits or unseen spiritual forces exist,' 14% said they do not, and about one-fifth were unsure. Among all U.S. adults, 39% said spirits can be both helpful and harmful (10% generally helpful, 4% generally harmful, ~10% neither). 81% took the position that 'there is something spiritual beyond the natural world, even if we cannot see it' vs 17% 'the natural world is all there is.' Subgroups: Protestants 72% and Catholics 68% believe in spirits/unseen forces; religious 'nones' about half (nothing-in-particular 62%, agnostics 43%, atheists 17%). The record grades the ATTESTATION of the belief figures, never the existence of any entity — the widest direct U.S. measure of spirit belief on the belief ledger.
place: United States (national poll)

title: Pew Religious Landscape 2025: belief broad, certainty thinning
claim: Pew Research Center's third Religious Landscape Study (fielded 2023-2024; report released Feb 26, 2025) found 83% of U.S. adults believe in God or a universal spirit — 9 percentage points less than in 2007 — while the share who hold that belief with absolute certainty fell further, to 54% (17 points less than 2007). 86% of adults believe people have a soul or spirit in addition to their physical body; 79% believe there is something spiritual beyond the natural world even if it cannot be seen; 70% believe in an afterlife (heaven, hell, or both). The Christian share of adults has been roughly stable since 2019 after years of decline; evangelical Protestants edged from about 26% of adults in 2007 to roughly 23% in 2023-24, mainline Protestants from 18% to 11%. 35% of U.S. adults no longer identify with the religion in which they were raised (about 90 million people who changed religious identities).
place: United States (national poll)

title: AARO historical record report, Vol. I (8 March 2024): the Pentagon finds no evidence of extraterrestrial technology
claim: The All-Domain Anomaly Resolution Office (AARO), reviewing U.S. government UAP investigations back to 1945 with full access to sensitive programs, reported: 'AARO found no evidence that any USG investigation, academic-sponsored research, or official review panel has confirmed that any sighting of a UAP represented extraterrestrial technology.' It judged the alleged reverse-engineering programs 'inaccurate,' attributing them largely to circular reporting. Many cases remain unsolved, which AARO attributes to insufficient data quality.
place: The Pentagon, Arlington, Virginia (issuing office)

title: US creationism belief, Gallup May 2024
claim: In May 2024, 37% of US adults told Gallup that 'God created human beings pretty much in their present form at one time within the last 10,000 years or so' (34% said humans evolved with God's guidance, 24% said humans evolved over millions of years with no role for God). place: United States (Gallup national sample, all 50 states + DC)

title: Homo juluensis proposed (2024) — the Denisovan naming fight
claim: In November 2024, Christopher Bae and Xiujie Wu (Nature Communications) proposed uniting the taxonomically unhoused Middle Pleistocene fossils of Asia — Xuchang, Xujiayao, Xiahe, Penghu 1, Dali, and a Laos molar — under the species name Homo juluensis ('big head', ~1,700 cc braincases, robust anatomy), with the Denisovans folded into the same group. The proposal is contested: Denné Reed (2025) argues the informal name 'Denisovans' is the better system, that H. altaiensis is a nomen nudum, and that H. daliensis and H. mapaensis were conditionally proposed and are unavailable under ICZN Article 15.
place: Xuchang, Henan, China (and Xujiayao, Xiahe, Penghu, Dali, Laos)

title: 'The Wow! signal has been conclusively explained as natural'
claim: The 'Wow!' signal of 1977 has been conclusively explained as a natural phenomenon.
place: Arecibo Observatory, Puerto Rico (project site; Big Ear at 40.2492, -83.0456, demolished 1998)

title: American Christian belief, 2025 (Barna SALT Index, belief-ledger)
claim: Barna's 2025 State of Christianity in America (SALT Index, 6,037 U.S. adults, fielded November 2025) found: ~70% affirm Jesus died for our sins; 64% affirm the resurrection; 61% consider themselves followers of Jesus. Practice is narrower: ~60% pray or worship regularly, ~35% read the Bible weekly, ~31% have ever mentored/discipled another person.

title: Baylor 2025: the secular rationalists who kept religion believe in magic at double the rate
claim: A study published in the journal Social Forces (July 2026) analyzing the latest wave of the Baylor Religion Survey (a nationally representative survey of 1,812 American adults fielded by Gallup in early 2025) found that people who score high on 'secular rationalism' — the belief that science is the only way to understand the world and that morality should rest on reason — but who keep a tie to religion are about twice as likely to believe in 'magic' (ghosts, curses, talking to the dead): 40% vs 19% among Americans who believe in God, 28% vs 19% among service attenders. Among people who never attend services or do not believe in God, secular rationalism was no longer linked to belief in magic. Reported by the study's author via The Conversation (October 2026).
place: United States (national poll)

title: Baylor 2026: secular rationalism plus church ties predicts more magic belief
claim: Analysis of the latest Baylor Religion Survey wave (nationally representative, n=1,812 American adults, fielded by Gallup in early 2025) found that Americans who score high on 'secular rationalism' — the belief that science is the only way to understand the world, that morality should rest on reason, and that spiritual matters should be interpreted personally rather than trusted to religious authorities — but who keep some tie to religion are MORE likely to believe in magic (ghosts, curses, talking to the dead — six non-theistic supernatural items) than secular rationalists without church ties. Among Americans who believe in God, high secular rationalists were about twice as likely to lean toward magic as those who reject secular rationalism (40% vs 19%); among church attenders, 28% vs 19%; among non-attenders and non-believers, secular rationalism no longer predicted magic belief. The belief is graded here as belief: it attests the belief-state, never the entities.
place: United States (national sample)

title: Breakthrough Listen's technosignature search of interstellar object 3I/ATLAS (18 December 2025)
claim: On 18 December 2025, the Breakthrough Listen program used the 100-m Robert C. Byrd Green Bank Telescope to conduct a technosignature search toward the interstellar object 3I/ATLAS (one day before its 19 December 2025 closest approach to Earth), scanning 1–12 GHz — the most sensitive radio search for a technosignature from an interstellar object to date. The team reported a nondetection of candidate signals down to the 100 mW level.
place: Green Bank Observatory, West Virginia (observation) / 3I/ATLAS interstellar object (target)

title: Canadian paranormal belief, 2025 (belief-ledger)
claim: A nationally representative 2025 Canadian survey found that almost half of Canadians believe in at least one paranormal phenomenon, and about one-quarter report encounters with spirits — a new belief-ledger datum. The record grades the BELIEF-ATTESTATION (the poll), never the entities named in it.

title: Ancient southern-African genomes and the deep structured sapiens lineage (2026)
claim: Jakobsson, Schlebusch et al. (Nature 650(8100):156–163, online 3 Dec 2025, in print 2026, doi 10.1038/s41586-025-09811-4) sequenced 28 ancient southern-African genomes (10.2 ka to 150 years old), finding ≥200 kyr of long-term population isolation, a deepest population split vs other groups at ~310–240 ka, and 490 Homo sapiens-specific variants — the genomic anchor for a pan-African, structured-population emergence of our species, contradicting the old East-Africa-only-then-southward-spread model.
place: Southern Africa (the ancient genomes' origins)

title: The MUC19 'genetic sandwich': Denisovan DNA that arrived via Neanderthals (2025)
claim: Villanea, Peede et al. 2025 (Science, doi 10.1126/science.adl0882): a 72-kb Denisovan-specific region embedded in a 742-kb Neanderthal-derived haplotype at MUC19, at high frequency in Indigenous American populations (1 in 3 Mexicans vs ~1% of Central Europeans) under positive selection — the first clear case of Denisovan DNA entering modern humans indirectly, through Neanderthals.

title: The Iznik commemoration of Nicaea's 1700th anniversary, 28 November 2025
claim: On 28 November 2025, Pope Leo XIV and Ecumenical Patriarch Bartholomew led a joint ecumenical prayer service at Iznik, Turkey (ancient Nicaea) marking the 1700th anniversary of the First Council of Nicaea (325), jointly reciting the Nicene Creed — deliberately without the filioque clause — with the Greek Orthodox patriarchs of Antioch, Alexandria and Jerusalem (or their representatives) and Anglican and Protestant representatives present, on a platform overlooking the submerged Basilica of St. Neophytos in Lake Iznik.
place: Iznik (ancient Nicaea), Turkey — overlooking Lake Iznik

title: The Iznik commemoration of Nicaea's 1700th anniversary, 28 November 2025
claim: On 28 November 2025, Pope Leo XIV and Ecumenical Patriarch Bartholomew led a joint ecumenical prayer service at Iznik, Turkey (ancient Nicaea) marking the 1700th anniversary of the First Council of Nicaea (325), jointly reciting the Nicene Creed — deliberately without the filioque clause — with the Greek Orthodox patriarchs of Antioch, Alexandria and Jerusalem (or their representatives) and Anglican and Protestant representatives present, on a platform overlooking the submerged Basilica of St. Neophytos in Lake Iznik. place: Iznik (ancient Nicaea), Turkey — overlooking Lake Iznik

title: PHerc.172 identified as Philodemus's On Vices (still-rolled scroll, 2025)
claim: PHerc.172, a sealed Herculaneum scroll at Oxford's Bodleian Libraries (donated by Ferdinand IV of Naples in the early 19th century), was identified by virtual unwrapping as Philodemus's On Vices — an Epicurean ethical treatise whose full title reads On Vices and Their Opposite Virtues and In Whom They Are and About What. The end-title was deciphered from the inside of the still-rolled scroll: scanned July 2024 on Diamond Light Source's I12 beamline (unusually strong ink signal — denser contaminants, possibly lead), the title announced 5 February 2025 by the University of Oxford, independently achieved by Sean Johnson (Vesuvius Challenge) and by Marcel Roth & Micha Nowak (University of Würzburg), independently reviewed by Federica Nicolardi's papyrology team, awarded the Vesuvius Challenge First Title Prize ($60,000).
place: Bodleian Libraries, University of Oxford (current holding; excavated at Herculaneum, Villa of the Papyri, 40.8062, 14.3439)

title: Tomb of Thutmose II identified — first royal tomb since Tutankhamun (Feb 2025)
claim: On 18 February 2025, Egypt's Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities announced that Tomb C4 in the Western Wadis near Luxor — excavated by a joint Egyptian-British mission (Supreme Council of Antiquities + New Kingdom Research Foundation, field director Piers Litherland) — is the tomb of Thutmose II (18th Dynasty, ~1479 BCE): the first royal Egyptian tomb discovered since Tutankhamun's in 1922.
place: Wadi C, Theban Hills (~2.4 km west of the Valley of the Kings)

title: Wellcome Global Monitor 2026: Americans' trust in science, via Gallup World Poll
claim: The Wellcome Global Monitor 2026 — administered through the Gallup World Poll across 140+ nations, 140,000+ adults (2018, 2020, 2025 waves; Wellcome-funded) — found 52% of Americans report 'a lot' of trust in science vs a 26% global average, and 45% would accept recommended vaccines immediately vs 28% in Germany. Within the U.S., religious and non-religious Americans differed by 24 percentage points on whether science benefits most people (vs a 5-point average gap across other high-income countries); urban and rural Americans differed by 19 points (vs 3 elsewhere); and religious Americans' 'science benefits most people' rose 46% to 50% between 2018 and 2025. Attests trust-beliefs, never a scientific fact.
place: Global (140+ nations); U.S. national subsample

title: The 1831 mystery eruption identified: Zavaritskii caldera (Jan 2025)
claim: On 7 January 2025, Hutchison et al. published in PNAS the identification of the Zavaritskii caldera (Simushir Island, Kuril archipelago) as the source of the mystery 1831 eruption — via sulfur-isotope and cryptotephra analysis of Greenland ice cores: microscopic glass shards matching Zavaritskii's youngest Plinian chemistry, ~13 Tg of stratospheric sulfur, ~1°C Northern Hemisphere cooling, VEI 5–6, radiative forcing comparable to Pinatubo 1991 — closing a ~200-year cold case.
place: Zavaritskii caldera, Simushir Island, Kurils

title: SETI Institute's June 2026 technosignature scan of interstellar object 3I/ATLAS
claim: In June 2026, a SETI Institute team led by Sofia Sheikh used the Allen Telescope Array to listen to the interstellar object 3I/ATLAS for more than seven hours across ~1-9 GHz, finding no narrowband technosignature: ~74 million candidate narrowband signals were filtered to ~200 and all were identified as Earth-based radio-frequency interference or satellites; the null sets an upper limit of ~10-110 watts on any radio transmitter on or near the object.
place: Allen Telescope Array, Hat Creek Radio Observatory, Northern California

title: AARO FY2025 Consolidated Annual Report on UAP (July 2026)
claim: In July 2026, the Pentagon's All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office released its Fiscal Year 2025 Consolidated Annual Report on Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena (reporting period 2 June 2024–30 May 2025): 319 reports received; 114 resolved as balloons, birds, satellites, aircraft, unmanned aerial systems, one rocket launch, and one manned jet pack; 191 had insufficient data for a definitive explanation; 14 remained unexplained; cumulative holdings stood at 1,870 reports as of 30 May 2025. The report reiterated that none of the resolved cases indicate advanced foreign adversarial capabilities or breakthrough technologies, and disclosed one maritime-domain case — a Navy asset off the Virginia coast reporting ~100 airborne UAP and two likely uncrewed surface systems — under active investigation.
place: The Pentagon, Arlington, Virginia (report issued)

title: American biblical-miracle belief, 2026 (belief-ledger)
claim: The American Bible Society's State of the Bible 2026, Chapter 7: The Supernatural (released October 8, 2026; n=2,649 US adults, AmeriSpeak, fielded January 8–27) found: 53% of Americans say the resurrection of Jesus 'probably' or 'definitely' happened; 49% say the same of the virgin birth — the first time a major national survey recorded belief in the virgin birth below 50% (Pew 2017: 66%; Pew 2014: 73%, with different wording noted); 44% of the parting of the Red Sea. Among practicing Christians: 99% resurrection, 97% virgin birth, 92% Red Sea. The record grades the BELIEF-ATTESTATION (the poll), never the events' historicity.

title: ABS State of the Bible 2026: 44% of Americans believe the Red Sea parting

title: The 2026 molecular-clock revival of pre-Ediacaran animal origins (Durbin et al.)

title: Fire over ice: the first planetesimals were chondrule-rich from the onset (2026)

title: CORT intermission pattern, 2026 (UVA DOPS)

title: FAST's September 2026 candidate NBS 260108 near K2-155 — the one that didn't survive

title: The 2026 digital face of Jebel Irhoud (composite reconstruction)

The authors call it a 'morphologically plausible approximation', not a portrait — no soft tissue of any kind survives from Middle Pleistocene hominins, so the face on the poster is not one person's face and could not be.

title: The 2026 facial approximation of the Jebel Irhoud composite skull
claim: In September 2026, Moraes, Varotto, Habicht, Galassi, Moura & Abdullah published a digital facial approximation of a composite Jebel Irhoud skull (Heritage 9(9):369, doi 10.3390/heritage9090369, 13 Sept 2026) — built with open-source tools (Blender 2.91 + OrtogOnBlender), released in gray-anatomical and full-color versions, with a brain-volume estimate of ~1,230 cm³ (vs the prior CT endocranial estimate ~1,375 cm³). title: The 2026 Jiangchuan biota: complex animals in the waning Ediacaran, ~539 Ma (Dunn et al.)
claim: The April 2026 Science paper by Frankie Dunn (Oxford Museum of Natural History) and colleagues describes the Jiangchuan biota of Yunnan, China: 700+ fossils from ~539 million years ago — the waning Ediacaran, millions of years before the Cambrian boundary — including animals with mouths, anuses, the ability to hunt and burrow, and three-dimensional lives in the water column. Complex, recognizably animal traits, previously treated as Cambrian innovations, were already operational in the Ediacaran. The paper reframes the Cambrian explosion's 'integration cost': the transition was not from simple sponges to complex organisms, but from an already-complex transitional fauna.
place: Jiangchuan, Yunnan, China (near the Chengjiang World Heritage site)

title: The 2026 Hattusa Kadesh-treaty fragment (Articles 12-20: the fugitives provisions)
claim: On 21 September 2026 (International Day of Peace), Turkey's Ministry of Culture and Tourism announced the identification of a new cuneiform fragment of the Treaty of Kadesh, excavated at the Büyükkale (royal citadel) area of Hattusa near Building E, and authenticated after about a year of scientific and textual study. The Akkadian cuneiform fragment preserves portions of Articles 12-20 of the treaty — the provisions governing fugitives/refugees who crossed between Egypt and Hatti, including protections against destroying the refugees' homes — and joins the previously known Hattusa fragments (in Ankara, Berlin, Istanbul, and St. Petersburg) plus the Egyptian versions as a securely-located textual witness to the Hittite copy of the agreement. Excavation at Hattusa continues under the Istanbul branch of the German Archaeological Institute (Andreas Schachner); no full transcription of the new section was released with the announcement.
place: Hattusa, Büyükkale area near Building E (Boğazköy, Çorum Province, Türkiye)

title: Hittite royal archive of 184 tablets at Kayalıpınar (Oct 2026)

place: Kayalıpınar (Šamuḫa), Sivas Province, Türkiye

title: The "400–900-year manuscript gap" telling (Pfander Films, October 2026)
claim: In October 2026, confessional-polemic video coverage (Pfander Films, YouTube: "7th Century Rock Inscriptions Disprove Islam's History!", ~Oct 11, 2026) circulated the framing that the gap between Muhammad's death (632 CE) and the earliest surviving manuscripts of al-Bukhari's Sahih (14th–15th-century copies) and the sira literature (11th–16th-century manuscripts) — a "400–900-year" void — proves Islam's early history was fabricated centuries late.
place: Hijaz, Arabia (the region the telling is about)

title: The September 2026 'Hall of Records under Menkaure' press telling
claim: On or about 25 September 2026, the team of Filippo Biondi and Corrado Malanga announced that satellite synthetic-aperture-radar tomography had detected a vast underground complex beneath the Pyramid of Menkaure at Giza — vertical cylindrical voids, spiral ramp systems and possible cube-shaped cavities, claimed >90% similar to anomalies earlier announced beneath the Pyramid of Khafre — and framed it as a 'Hall of Records' in the Edgar Cayce lineage.
place: Pyramid of Menkaure, Giza plateau

title: The 'Mesen is fresh Exodus evidence' telling (Aug 2026)
claim: August 2026 press coverage of the Tell Abu Seifi lintel discovery framed the find as 'fresh evidence for the Bible's story of Moses and the Exodus' — i.e., that a Ramesses II-inscribed lintel at a candidate site for the lost city of Mesen constitutes evidence for the Exodus event itself.
place: Tell Abu Seifi, northeastern Sinai (the telling's claim-location)

title: TELLING (DEBUNKED): the Hebrew Bible horns Moses
claim: The telling under test: 'The Hebrew Bible describes Moses as physically horned' — i.e., the horns on Michelangelo's Moses reflect the original Hebrew of Exodus 34:29.
place: San Pietro in Vincoli, Rome (where the telling is met)

title: 2026 Nobel Prize in Chemistry — homochirality amplification (Kagan & Soai)
claim: On 7 October 2026 the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry to Henri B. Kagan (Universite Paris-Saclay) and Kenso Soai (Tokyo University of Science) 'for the discovery of non-linear effects and autocatalysis in asymmetric organic synthesis' — experimental chemistry showing how a tiny imbalance between mirror-image molecules can be amplified into near-total one-handedness: Kagan's 1986 non-linear effects in asymmetric catalysis, and Soai's 1995 asymmetric autocatalysis (a 2% enantiomeric excess amplified to 87%, the product catalyzing its own formation) and 2003 spontaneous symmetry breaking from achiral ingredients (~99.99% of one hand; re-running the reaction, the other hand can win — chance picks the hand). The prize recognizes the amplification chemistry; it does not establish how life's homochirality actually originated.
place: Stockholm, Sweden (Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences)

title: A lost planetary embryo: NWA 12774's 17.5-kbar crystals point to a destroyed Mars-sized world (2026)
claim: The angrite meteorite NWA 12774 (found 2019 at a Sahara site, Northwest Africa; one of fewer than 70 angrites among 80,000 cataloged meteorites) crystallized its aluminum-rich clinopyroxene at pressures of at least 17.5 kilobars — over 15 times the pressure at the bottom of the Pacific — implying a parent body at least 1,000 km in radius, modeled at ~3,300 km (Mars-sized), that formed within ~4 million years of the solar system's birth and was destroyed by a catastrophic impact that launched the fragment to Earth: Bell, Waters et al. 2026, using a new computational geobarometer, interpret the crystals as the first high-pressure record from an embryonic planet never previously identified.
place: Northwest Africa, Sahara (the 2019 find site of NWA 12774)

title: 'OUT OF AFRICA IS DEAD.' — the 2026 viral telling misreading the Reich preprint
claim: A ~19 October 2026 viral video claimed David Reich's preprint 'is challenging the out-of-africa theory' and that 'the traditional model of human migration is being tested' — i.e., that the African origin of Homo sapiens has been refuted.
place: Eurasia (the Neanderthal range the preprint models); the telling itself is internet-global

title: Patmos 2026: the global Bible-attitudes survey — 80% theism, 20% curious nones
claim: The Patmos World Bible Attitudes Survey (commissioned by the British and Foreign Bible Society, fielded by Gallup: 91,000+ respondents in 150 countries and 89 languages, grouped into six cultural 'clusters'; reported October 2026) found that eight out of ten people globally believe in God or a 'higher power.' Among respondents worldwide who do not consider themselves religious, one in five (20%) said they were 'interested in learning more about the Bible.' Christians aged 18-24 report the highest confidence in telling the Bible's story, finding relevant passages, and talking about its message. In western Europe / North America / Australasia ('cluster 5'), 40% say religion is important in daily life (half the global average) yet 63% say they definitely or probably believe in a higher being; 53% identify as Christian while 44% are closed/sceptical/indifferent. In central/eastern Europe ('cluster 2'): 39% say religion is important daily vs 80% believing in God or a higher power; 77% identify as Christian but only 40% say faith makes a difference daily.
place: Global (150 countries)

title: Pew May 2026: 37% say religion is gaining influence in American life (highest since 2002)
claim: Pew Research Center's May 14, 2026 report 'How Americans Feel About Religion's Influence in Government and Public Life' (survey of U.S. adults conducted April 6-12, 2026, ~3,592 adults, American Trends Panel) found: 37% of U.S. adults say religion is gaining influence in American life — the highest share since the series began in 2002, up 19 points in two years — while 61% say it is losing influence. 55% express a positive view of religion's role in American life. 17% say the federal government should declare Christianity the nation's official religion (up from 13% in 2024). Familiarity with the term 'Christian nationalism' is growing; support for ideas associated with it is mostly unchanged. Sharp partisan divides: 75% of Republicans view religion's influence positively vs 38% of Democrats. Margin of error ±1.9 points. The 61%-losing-influence figure was already chained on evt-mission-argument-001 (VIII.e, 2026-10-19); this record carries the wave's other toplines for the VI.34 belief side.
place: United States (national poll)

title: PHerc. 139 identified as Philodemus, 'On Gods' Book 8 (June 2026)
claim: In June 2026, the Vesuvius Challenge team identified the title and author of the still-rolled scroll PHerc. 139 as Philodemus, 'On Gods' (peri theon), Book 8 — extending the previously known run of that work (books 1 and possibly 3 were the only ones attested). The identification was reported in the same project preprint (Angelotti et al. 2026, 'Complete virtual unwrapping and reading of a rolled Herculaneum papyrus') that announced PHerc. 1667 as the first scroll ever virtually unwrapped and read end to end.
place: Herculaneum, Villa of the Papyri (findspot); scroll housed at the Biblioteca Nazionale di Napoli

title: The 'the fully-read scroll is Philodemus's On Vices' telling (June 2026)
claim: June 2026 press coverage of the first fully-read Herculaneum scroll (PHerc. 1667) reported it as '70 columns from On Vices, Book 1, a philosophical work attributed to the Epicurean thinker Philodemus' — i.e., that the scroll read end to end in June 2026 IS Philodemus's 'On Vices' Book 1.
place: Herculaneum, Villa of the Papyri (the scrolls' findspot)

title: First readable text from PHerc. 343 (Vesuvius Challenge $50K First Letters Prize, Oct 2026)
claim: PHerc. 343, a carbonized still-rolled Herculaneum scroll (Biblioteca Nazionale di Napoli, ~14 cm long), yielded its first-ever readable text since the 79 CE eruption: researcher Erwin Nieuwlaar identified ink on windings w047/w048 of a virtually unwrapped segment — four lines of text, the third line alone meeting the Vesuvius Challenge's strict criterion of 10 readable letters in 4 cm² — reading the sequence παντογινομ (papyrologists' reading: πᾶν τὸ γινόμε[νον, 'everything that happens/is generated'). Nieuwlaar traced the surface using the Challenge's open-source spiral-fitter on the 8.64 µm scan with his own scroll-axis estimate plus a new segment-snapping method. Awarded the Vesuvius Challenge $50,000 First Letters Prize (announced ~8 October 2026, project Substack). The scroll's authorship and work remain unidentified; only a fragment was read.
place: Biblioteca Nazionale di Napoli (current holding; excavated at Herculaneum, Villa of the Papyri, 40.8062, 14.3439)

title: The 'Ramesses II was the pharaoh of the Exodus' telling (Oct 2026)
claim: October 2026 press coverage of the Behbeit El-Hagar find described the uncovered statues as belonging to 'the biblical pharaoh who enslaved Israelites' / 'the pharaoh who allegedly challenged Moses' — i.e., that Ramesses II was the pharaoh of the Exodus, and that a statue identifying Ramesses II therefore bears on the Moses story.
place: Behbeit El-Hagar (the telling's claim-location)

title: The 2026 'chariot wheels found in the Red Sea' telling
claim: In 2026, viral press and content-farm articles claimed that divers had found Pharaoh's chariot wheels, weapons, skeletal remains, and gold artifacts inscribed with the name of Moses on the Red Sea floor — presented as new archaeological proof that the Exodus crossing happened word-for-word as written.
place: claimed Red Sea / Gulf of Aqaba seabed (no coordinates given by any version)

title: Research Co./NCSE July 2026 human-origins belief poll (US + Canada)
claim: In a July 2026 Research Co. two-country poll (reported by the National Center for Science Education, 2 July 2026), asked which statement comes closest to their view on the origin and development of human beings, 47% of Americans chose 'Human beings definitely (27%) or probably (20%) evolved from less advanced life forms over millions of years,' while 39% chose 'God probably (10%) or definitely (29%) created human beings in their present form within the last 10,000 years'; 14% were not sure. In Canada the split was 62% evolved (35% definitely, 27% probably), 20% created (6% probably, 14% definitely), 17% unsure.
place: United States (national sample); Canada (national sample)

title: Research Co. July 2026 two-country evolution/creationism poll (39% American creationist)
claim: Asked 'Which of these statements comes closest to your own point of view regarding the origin and development of human beings on earth?', 39% of Americans favored 'God created human beings in their present form within the last 10,000 years' (29% 'definitely', 10% 'probably'), 47% favored evolution from less advanced life forms over millions of years (27% 'definitely', 20% 'probably'), 14% were unsure; Canadians asked the same question: 62% favored evolution, 20% creationism, 17% unsure.
place: United States (with Canada as comparison sample) — a poll, not a place

title: RNA and amino acids help each other assemble (IISER Pune, 2026)
claim: In September 2026, researchers at the Indian Institute of Science Education and Research (IISER) Pune reported (Communications Chemistry) that nucleotide molecules and amino acids placed together under plausible prebiotic conditions promote each other's assembly - producing short RNA-like chains and peptides in a single reaction.
place: Pune, India (IISER Pune)

title: The RNA-only repair enzyme (DasGupta 2026)
claim: In July 2026, Saurja DasGupta's group at the University of Notre Dame reported an engineered RNA enzyme (ribozyme) that recognizes broken RNA by its distinguishing terminal phosphate group and pastes the pieces back together — a genome-maintenance function demonstrated with RNA alone, no proteins required.
place: Notre Dame, Indiana, USA (University of Notre Dame)

title: Romania 2026: the 7.6% who say humans lived with dinosaurs
claim: In a 2026-published peer-reviewed survey of post-pandemic Romania (Social Sciences 2026, 15, 551 — 'Correct, Incorrect, or Uncertain? Factual Science Knowledge, Conspiratorial Anti-Science Beliefs, and "Don't Know" Responses in Post-Pandemic Romania'; weighted clean analytic sample N=1007), on the core-fact item 'Humans lived with dinosaurs (False)', 68.1% answered correctly (False), 7.6% answered incorrectly, and 24.4% said they did not know.
place: Romania (national sample)

title: The March 2026 'second Sphinx discovered at Giza' telling
claim: A second Sphinx monument has been discovered buried beneath a sand mound on the Giza Plateau, mirroring the Great Sphinx — as claimed by the Khafre Research Project (Filippo Biondi et al.) from Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) Doppler tomography interpretations, announced March 2026 and elaborated at the June 2026 Bologna conference.
place: Giza Plateau, Egypt (the mound the claim points to — the pin marks the claimed location, not a confirmed monument)

title: The 1988 Shroud fragments re-examined (2026)
claim: Two surviving fragments from the University of Arizona's share of the 1988 Shroud radiocarbon sample, re-examined in 2026, are textilely consistent with the main Shroud cloth and show no evidence of invisible medieval repair or contamination that could explain away the 1988 date.
place: University of Arizona, Tucson (where the surviving fragments were kept)

title: The '2026 DNA study proves the Shroud came from India' telling
claim: In September–October 2026, headlines and viral posts claimed the July 2026 Scientific Reports DNA/metagenomics study (Barcaccia et al.) proves the Turin Shroud's genetic material comes from India — 'DNA links Shroud to India.'
place: Turin (the study concerns samples held in Turin)

title: Swabian Jura notation — structured marks 40,000 years before writing (Feb 2026)
claim: In February 2026, researchers (Christian Bentz, Saarland University; Ewa Dutkiewicz, Museum für Vor- und Frühgeschichte Berlin) published in PNAS a computational analysis of 3,000+ engraved signs on ~260 Aurignacian objects from the Swabian Jura (43,000–34,000 years old) — 22 recurring sign types (lines, dots, notches, crosses) in structured sequences with information density statistically comparable to early proto-cuneiform: a conventional notational system tens of millennia before writing.
place: Swabian Jura caves (Vogelherd, Geißenklösterle, Hohle Fels, Hohlenstein-Stadel)

title: Tell Abu Seifi: the August 2026 Mesen lintel find
claim: On 15 August 2026 the Egyptian Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities announced that excavations at Tell Abu Seifi (northeastern Sinai, ~145 km northeast of Cairo) uncovered a broken colossal sandstone lintel inscribed on three sides with the titles of Ramesses II, recording restoration work on a statue of Horus described as 'Lord of the City of Mesen' — the basis for the excavators' proposal that the site is the lost New Kingdom city of Mesen on the Horus Military Road. The identification is the excavators' stated hypothesis ('a strong archaeological and historical hypothesis'), explicitly not yet definitive; further excavation continues.
place: Tell Abu Seifi, northeastern Sinai, Egypt

title: The 2026 'Tell El-Kharouba fortress proves the Exodus' telling
claim: In October 2026 press coverage (e.g. Fox News Digital), the Egyptian Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities' October 11, 2026 announcement of a 3,000-year-old New Kingdom fortress at Tell El-Kharouba (Sheikh Zuweid, North Sinai, on the Horus Military Road; Thutmose I cartouche on a jar handle) was framed as fresh archaeological evidence supporting the Exodus narrative — with press explicitly invoking Exod 13:17's 'way of the land of the Philistines'.
place: Tell El-Kharouba, Sheikh Zuweid, North Sinai

title: The 2026 ERC 'Tracing Scribes and Scrolls' project — a materials database for the Dead Sea Scrolls
claim: In 2026 the European Research Council awarded a five-year grant of 2.5 million euros to Mladen Popović (University of Groningen), with the Israel Antiquities Authority and European laboratories, for the project 'Tracing Scribes and Scrolls': the first large-scale 'chemical signature' database of the Dead Sea Scrolls — parchment composition, collagen, processing residues, inks, organic substances — combined with palaeography, codicology and artificial intelligence, to reconstruct where the manuscripts were produced (their provenance), not just where they were hidden.
place: University of Groningen (project lead); Israel Antiquities Authority, Jerusalem (collaborator)

title: TELLING (DEBUNKED): Isaiah's Hebrew says 'virgin'
claim: The telling under test: 'Isaiah's Hebrew text prophesied that a virgin would conceive' — i.e., the original Hebrew of Isaiah 7:14 says 'virgin.'

title: American miracle-experience belief, 2026 (belief-ledger)
claim: A 2026 nationally representative American survey (Wheatley Institute at BYU, Survey of Lived Religion, n=2,005 adults via Qualtrics) found about half of Americans say they experience or witness what they consider a miracle at least a few times a year — 10% more than once a week, 9% weekly, 11% once or twice a month, 20% a few times a year; 26% seldom, 24% never. 68% report a spiritual experience, 46% within the previous month. The record grades the BELIEF/EXPERIENCE-ATTESTATION (the poll), never the supernatural character of any reported event.
place: United States (national survey)

title: Xujiayao proteome 2026 — the juluensis holotype is molecularly Denisovan
claim: Palaeoproteomics (LC-MS/MS) on two Xujiayao Middle Pleistocene specimens (parietal PA1490/XJY-6; mandible ramus PA1497/XJY-14, ~199–138 ka, Nihewan Basin, northern China) recovered 18 endogenous ancient proteins; the Denisovan-specific COL1A2-996K variant was identified in high-quality, deamidation-validated peptides, and a Bayesian phylogeny (2,074 amino-acid positions) places Xujiayao monophyletic with Denisova3 at >99% posterior support — the Xujiayao hominins are molecularly Denisovan.
place: Xujiayao, Nihewan Basin, Hebei Province, China

title: The 'London Zoo was the first zoo' myth
claim: London Zoo (founded 1828) was the world's first zoo.
place: London Zoo, Regent's Park, London (coordinates via map.geocode, FULL_ADDRESS match)

title: The Washington wooden-teeth myth
claim: George Washington's dentures were made of wood.
